s.t: Windows Event Logs are a critical component of the Windows operating system's logging and auditing framework, designed to provide comprehensive insights into system, security, and application activities. These logs capture detailed event data, including timestamps, process IDs, user account details, and system-level operations, enabling administrators and security professionals to monitor and analyze system behavior in real-time. The Windows Event Log service efficiently records application, security, and system events into centralized log files. This functionality supports proactive system health monitoring, rapid identification of security incidents, and effective troubleshooting of configuration or operational issues. Advanced security audit policies in Windows offer granular audit logging configurations, ensuring that critical activities such as logon attempts, privilege escalation, object access, and policy changes are captured with precision. By default, many of these policies are disabled, potentially creating blind spots in event monitoring. Enabling these policies enhances the ability to detect and investigate sophisticated attacks, such as privilege misuse, lateral movement, and unauthorized access. These audit logs are foundational for generating high-fidelity detections and facilitating forensic investigations.

Windows stores its event logs in several key locations depending on the log type: Log Type Path Description Application %SystemRoot%\System32\Winevt\Logs\Application.evtx Events logged by applications and programs Security %SystemRoot%\System32\Winevt\Logs\Security.evtx Security audit events, login attempts, resource access System %SystemRoot%\System32\Winevt\Logs\System.evtx System events from Windows components Setup %SystemRoot%\System32\Winevt\Logs\Setup.evtx Events related to application setup Forwarded Events %SystemRoot%\System32\Winevt\Logs\ForwardedEvents.evtx Events collected from remote computers Pro Tip: Use Event Viewer ( eventvwr.msc ) to browse these logs interactively, or PowerShell's Get-WinEvent cmdlet for scripted analysis.

Windows audit policy defines what types of events are written to the Security logs of your Windows servers. Establishing an effective audit policy helps you spot potential security problems, ensure user accountability and provide evidence in the event of a security breach. The recommended audit policy settings provided here are intended as a baseline for system administrators starting to define AD audit policies. You should be sure to consider the cybersecurity risks and compliance requirements of your organization. In addition, test and refine your policies before implementing them in your production environment. Common PowerShell commands for querying and managing Windows Event Logs. These examples demonstrate how to retrieve, filter, and export event logs for system monitoring and troubleshooting. Basic Event Log Query PS> Get-WinEvent -LogName 'System' -MaxEvents 10 Retrieves the 10 most recent events from the System event log. Copy Filter by Error Level PS> Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='Application'; Level=2} Retrieves all Error events (Level 2) from the Application log. Levels: 1=Critical, 2=Error, 3=Warning, 4=Information Copy Filter by Date Range PS> $startDate = (Get-Date).AddDays(-1) $endDate = Get-Date Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{ LogName='System' StartTime=$startDate EndTime=$endDate Level=1,2 } Retrieves all Critical and Error events from the System log in the last 24 hours. Copy Export to CSV PS> Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='System'; Level=1,2,3} -MaxEvents 100 | Select-Object TimeCreated, LevelDisplayName, ProviderName, Id, Message | Export-Csv -Path "C:\Logs\SystemErrors.csv" -NoTypeInformation Exports the 100 most recent Critical, Error, and Warning events from the System log to a CSV file. Copy List Audit Policies PS> auditpol /get /category:* Displays the current audit policy settings for all categories configured on the system. Copy Clear Event Log PS> Clear-EventLog -LogName "System" -Confirm:$false Clears all events from the System event log without prompting for confirmation. Use with caution! Copy Check Event Log Size PS> Get-WinEvent -ListLog * | Where-Object {$_.RecordCount -gt 0} | Select-Object LogName, RecordCount, FileSize, IsEnabled | Sort-Object RecordCount -Descending | Format-Table -AutoSize Lists all event logs with their record count and size, sorted by number of records. Copy Find Failed Logon Attempts PS> Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='Security'; ID=4625} | Select-Object TimeCreated, @{Name='Username';Expression={$_.Properties[5].Value}}, @{Name='Source';Expression={$_.Properties[19].Value}}, @{Name='Status';Expression={$_.Properties[7].Value}}, @{Name='SubStatus';Expression={$_.Properties[9].Value}} | Format-Table -AutoSize Retrieves failed logon attempts with username, source IP, and error codes. Copy Monitor Real-time Events PS> $query = New-Object System.Diagnostics.Eventing.Reader.EventLogQuery("Security", [System.Diagnostics.Eventing.Reader.PathType]::LogName) $watcher = New-Object System.Diagnostics.Eventing.Reader.EventLogWatc her($query) Register-ObjectEvent -InputObject $watcher -EventName EventRecordWritten -Action { $event = $Event.SourceEventArgs.EventRecord Write-Host "New event: $($event.Id) at $($event.TimeCreated)" } $watcher.Enabled = $true Sets up a real-time monitor for new events in the Security log. Copy Configure Audit Policy PS> auditpol /set /subcategory:"Logon" /success:enable /failure:enable Enables auditing of both successful and failed logon attempts. Copy Filter by Event ID PS> Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{ LogName='Security' ID=4624,4625,4634 } Retrieves login events (successful logins, failed logins, and logouts) from the Security log. Copy Filter by Provider PS> Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{ LogName='System' ProviderName='Microsoft-Windows-Disk' Level=2,3 } Retrieves all Error and Warning events related to disk operations. s.h: Best Practices for Windows Event Logging
s.t: Follow these guidelines to ensure effective event logging in Windows environments: 01 Increase Log Size Set larger default log sizes: Security (4GB), System (2GB), Application (2GB) to prevent log rotation during an incident. 02 Configure Retention Set "Retention method" to "As needed" or "Overwrite events by days" rather than "Overwrite events as needed". 03 Centralize Logs Forward critical events to a centralized SIEM solution for consolidated monitoring and analysis. 04 Advanced Audit Policies Implement granular Advanced Audit Policy Configuration through Group Policy settings. 05 Regular Backups Schedule regular backups of critical event logs to preserve evidence for forensic analysis. 06 Command Line Logging Enable process command line auditing (Event ID 4688) to capture command-line arguments. 07 Monitor Log Clearing Set alerts for log clearing activities (Event ID 1102) which may indicate tampering. 08 Critical Event Alerts Configure real-time alerting for high-priority security events that require immediate attention.

This is common behavior that can be used across different platforms and the network to evade defenses. Payloads may be compressed, archived, or encrypted in order to avoid detection. Windows Event IDs for Detection 4688 A new process has been created 4104 PowerShell script block logging 8 File creation (Sysmon) 1 Process creation (Sysmon) PowerShell Detection Query T1027 - PowerShell Obfuscation Detection Hunt PS> Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName="Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell/Operational"; Id=4104} | Where-Object {$_.Message -match "ToBase64String|FromBase64String|convert|encoding|encode|decode|compressed|gzipstream|io.compression|deflatestream"} | Select-Object TimeCreated, Id, @{Name="ScriptBlock";Expression={$_.Properties[2].Value}} Identifies PowerShell commands that may be attempting to encode, decode, or compress data, which are common techniques for obfuscating malicious code. Copy × SID-History Injection T1134.005 Adversaries may use SID-History injection to gain additional privileges. The Windows security identifier (SID) is a unique value that identifies a user or group account. SIDs are used by Windows security in both security descriptors and access tokens. An account can hold additional SIDs in the SID-History attribute, allowing users to maintain access to network resources after being moved to a different domain. Windows Event IDs for Detection 4765 SID History was added to an account 4766 An attempt to add SID History to an account failed 4738 A user account was changed 4624 An account was successfully logged on PowerShell Detection Query T1134.005 - SID-History Injection Detection Hunt PS> Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName="Security"; Id=4765} | Select-Object TimeCreated, @{Name="TargetUser";Expression={$_.Properties[0].Value}}, @{Name="TargetDomain";Expression={$_.Properties[1].Value}}, @{Name="TargetSid";Expression={$_.Properties[2].Value}}, @{Name="SubjectUser";Expression={$_.Properties[4].Value}}, @{Name="SubjectDomain";Expression={$_.Properties[5].Value}}, @{Name="SidHistory";Expression={$_.Properties[9].Value}} Identifies instances where SID History attributes have been added to user accounts, which may indicate privilege escalation attempts. Copy × Windows Service T1543.003 Adversaries may create or modify Windows services to execute malicious payloads as part of persistence. Windows services are programs that can be started automatically when the system boots, even before a user logs on. Services can be configured to run under the context of SYSTEM, LOCAL SERVICE, or NETWORK SERVICE accounts, or a specified user account that may have different permissions and access than the current user. Windows Event IDs for Detection 4697 A service was installed in the system 7045 A service was installed in the system 7040 The start type of a service was changed 4688 A new process has been created PowerShell Detection Query T1543.003 - Windows Service Detection Hunt PS> Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName="System"; Id=7045} | Select-Object TimeCreated, @{Name="ServiceName";Expression={$_.Properties[0].Value}}, @{Name="ImagePath";Expression={$_.Properties[1].Value}}, @{Name="ServiceType";Expression={$_.Properties[2].Value}}, @{Name="StartType";Expression={$_.Properties[3].Value}}, @{Name="Account";Expression={$_.Properties[4].Value}} | Where-Object {$_.ImagePath -match "powershell|cmd.exe|regsvr32|rundll32|wscript|cscript|\\\\|http"} Identifies suspicious newly installed services that contain potentially malicious command patterns in their execution paths. Copy × Valid Accounts T1078 Adversaries may obtain and abuse credentials of existing accounts as a means of gaining Initial Access, Persistence, Privilege Escalation, or Defense Evasion. Compromised credentials may be used to bypass access controls placed on various resources on systems within the network and may even be used for persistent access to remote systems and externally available services. Windows Event IDs for Detection 4624 An account was successfully logged on 4625 An account failed to log on 4648 A logon was attempted using explicit credentials 4776 The computer attempted to validate the credentials for an account PowerShell Detection Query T1078 - Valid Accounts Detection Hunt PS> Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName="Security"; Id=4624} | Where-Object {$_.Properties[8].Value -eq 3} | Select-Object TimeCreated, @{Name="UserName";Expression={$_.Properties[5].Value}}, @{Name="Domain";Expression={$_.Properties[6].Value}}, @{Name="SourceIP";Expression={$_.Properties[18].Value}} Identifies successful network logons (type 3), which may indicate use of stolen credentials or remote access using valid accounts. Copy × Brute Force T1110 Adversaries may use brute force techniques to gain access to accounts when passwords are unknown or when password hashes are obtained. Brute forcing can be used to attempt access to credentials valid for domain, local, cloud, and other types of accounts, as well as network services and web applications that require authentication. Windows Event IDs for Detection 4740 A user account was locked out 4625 An account failed to log on 4771 Kerberos pre-authentication failed 4776 The computer attempted to validate the credentials for an account PowerShell Detection Query T1110 - Brute Force Detection Hunt PS> Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName="Security"; Id=4625} | Group-Object -Property @{Expression={$_.Properties[5].Value}} | Where-Object {$_.Count -ge 5} | Select-Object Name, Count, @{Name="FailedLogonAttempts";Expression={$_.Group | Select-Object TimeCreated, @{Name="Username";Expression={$_.Properties[5].Value}}, @{Name="SourceIP";Expression={$_.Properties[19].Value}}}} Identifies multiple failed logon attempts (5+) for the same username, which may indicate brute force attempts. Copy × Command and Scripting Interpreter T1059 Adversaries may abuse command and script interpreters to execute commands, scripts, or binaries. These interfaces and languages provide ways of interacting with computer systems and are a common feature across many different platforms. Commands and scripts can be embedded in initial access payloads delivered to victims as lure documents or as secondary payloads downloaded from an existing C2. Windows Event IDs for Detection 4688 A new process has been created 4104 PowerShell script block logging PowerShell Detection Query T1059 - Command and Scripting Interpreter Detection Hunt PS> Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName="Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell/Operational"; Id=4104} | Where-Object {$_.Message -match "bypass|hidden|encodedcommand|IEX|Invoke-Expression|DownloadString|New-Object Net.WebClient|Start-BitsTransfer"} | Select-Object TimeCreated, Id, @{Name="ScriptBlock";Expression={$_.Properties[2].Value}} Identifies PowerShell script blocks containing suspicious patterns that may indicate malicious activity, such as execution bypass techniques, obfuscation, or download cradles. Copy × Boot or Logon Autostart Execution T1547.001 Adversaries may achieve persistence by adding a program to a startup folder or referencing it with a Registry run key. Adding an entry to the "run keys" in the Registry or startup folder will cause the program referenced to be executed when a user logs in. These programs will be executed under the context of the user and will have the account's associated permissions level. Data destruction is likely to render the data irrecoverable by forensic techniques through overwriting files or data on local and remote drives. Common tools, such as File Shredder and wipe, and built-in commands like Windows cipher can be used. When automated exfiltration is used, other exfiltration techniques likely apply as well to transfer the information out of the network, such as Exfiltration Over C2 Channel or Exfiltration Over Alternative Protocol. Logs play a critical role in Linux systems, serving as a central source of information about system operations, application performance, and security incidents. These logs are managed by tools like syslog daemons (e.g., rsyslog, syslog-ng) and systemd's journald, which provide robust logging functionalities tailored to the needs of administrators and security experts. The Linux logging architecture employs a structured hierarchy of facilities and priorities, enabling precise control over the type and destination of logged data. Most modern Linux distributions integrate systemd's journald with traditional syslog services, ensuring compatibility while offering advanced features like structured data storage and searchability. Administrators can fine-tune the Linux logging system through configuration files, allowing customization of log rotation, remote log management, and filtering options. This adaptability ensures that Linux logs remain invaluable for system monitoring, issue resolution, and auditing purposes. Linux systems dedicate a specific directory, /var/log, for storing logs. This directory houses a wide range of logs, including those generated by the operating system, services, and installed applications. It provides a centralized location for administrators to access critical information. Services such as PostgreSQL or Apache create their own log files in subdirectories within /var/log. For instance, if you're running an Apache server on a Debian-based Linux distribution, you can find its logs in the /var/log/apache2 directory. This directory typically contains separate files like access.log for tracking user requests and error.log for reporting issues.

Linux systems store logs in structured files across the filesystem. Here's a breakdown of common log files: Log File Description Location Important Fields Category syslog General system messages /var/log/syslog Timestamp, Hostname, Process, Message System auth.log Authentication and authorization events /var/log/auth.log Timestamp, User, Process, Message Security secure Security-related events /var/log/secure Timestamp, Host, Process, Message Security messages Global system messages /var/log/messages Timestamp, Host, Process, Message System dmesg Kernel ring buffer messages /var/log/dmesg Timestamp, Level, Message Kernel audit.log System call auditing /var/log/audit/audit.log Timestamp, Type, Message Security kern.log Kernel logs /var/log/kern.log Timestamp, Host, Message Kernel boot.log System boot messages /var/log/boot.log Timestamp, Service, Message System dpkg.log Package management logs /var/log/dpkg.log Timestamp, Action, Package, Status System utmp Active user session logs /var/run/utmp Username, Terminal, IP, Login Time System wtmp Login history logs /var/log/wtmp Username, Terminal, IP, Login/Logout Time System btmp Failed login attempts /var/log/btmp Username, IP, Time Security Pro Tip: Use commands like cat , less , grep , or journalctl to interactively search or monitor logs. Combine with awk or cut for parsing specific fields.

Linux provides a comprehensive and flexible logging ecosystem with multiple systems that work together to capture, store, and manage system events and application logs. Understanding these different logging mechanisms is essential for effective system monitoring, troubleshooting, and security analysis. Syslog Protocol Syslog is a standardized protocol that forms the foundation of Linux logging. It provides a consistent format for system and application messages. Standard RFC 5424 Port UDP 514, TCP 601 Format Timestamp, hostname, application name, PID, message Features Message categorization by facility and priority Rsyslog Rsyslog is a modern, high-performance implementation of the syslog protocol that extends the basic functionality with advanced features. Config /etc/rsyslog.conf Modules Input, parsing, database, output modules Templates Customizable message formats Features Filtering, TCP/TLS, database output Systemd Journal Journald is part of systemd and provides structured binary logging with powerful querying capabilities for modern Linux distributions. Config /etc/systemd/journald.conf Storage Binary format in /var/log/journal/ Access Via journalctl command Features Indexed fields, structured metadata Logrotate Logrotate manages log file rotation, compression, and removal to prevent logs from consuming excessive disk space. Config /etc/logrotate.conf, /etc/logrotate.d/ Rotation Daily, weekly, monthly, or size-based Actions Compression, truncation, mail delivery Features Post-rotation scripts, retention policies Detailed Linux Logging Information Syslog Facilities and Priorities Facilities Code Keyword Description 0 kern Kernel messages 1 user User-level messages 2 mail Mail system 3 daemon System daemons 4 auth Security/authorization messages 10 authpriv Authentication messages 16-23 local0-local7 Locally used facilities Priority Code Keyword Description 0 emergency System is unusable 1 alert Action must be taken immediately 2 critical Critical conditions 3 error Error conditions 4 warning Warning conditions 5 notice Normal but significant condition 6 info Informational messages 7 debug Debug-level messages

The rsyslog daemon is configured through /etc/rsyslog.conf and additional files in /etc/rsyslog.d/ . The configuration consists of modules, global directives, templates, and rules. Example rsyslog.conf # Load modules module(load="imuxsock") # provides support for local system logging module(load="imklog") # provides kernel logging support module(load="imudp") # UDP listener support input(type="imudp" port="514") # Global directives $WorkDirectory /var/spool/rsyslog $FileOwner root $FileGroup adm $FileCreateMode 0640 $DirCreateMode 0755 $IncludeConfig /etc/rsyslog.d/*.conf # Rules (facility.priority action) kern.* /var/log/kern.log mail.* /var/log/mail.log auth,authpriv.* /var/log/auth.log *.emerg :omusrmsg:* # Remote logging with TCP *.warning @@logserver.example.com:514

The systemd journal provides structured logging for systems using systemd. Unlike traditional syslog, journald stores logs in a binary format with indexed fields for efficient searching and filtering. Journald Configuration # /etc/systemd/journald.conf [Journal] Storage=persistent # persistent, volatile, auto, none Compress=yes # Compress with XZ SystemMaxUse=4G # Max disk space for journals SystemKeepFree=1G # Min free space to keep on disk MaxFileSec=1month # Max time to store entries ForwardToSyslog=yes # Send to syslog in parallel Common journalctl Commands # View all logs $ journalctl # View logs for a specific service $ journalctl -u httpd.service # Show logs from the last hour $ journalctl --since "1 hour ago" # Show only error and higher priority $ journalctl -p err # Follow new messages (like tail -f) $ journalctl -f

Feature Syslog (Basic) Rsyslog Systemd Journal Format Text Text, JSON Binary, structured Storage Flat files Files, databases Journal files Encryption No Yes (TLS) No (filesystem only) Remote logging Basic UDP UDP, TCP, RELP Via forwarding to syslog Filtering Basic Advanced Extensive querying Metadata Limited Configurable Extensive Database output No Yes (MySQL, PostgreSQL, etc.) No (but exportable) Performance Good High Very high

View Logs with Basic Tools # Display entire log file $ cat /var/log/syslog # View log with paging $ less /var/log/auth.log # Show last 10 lines $ tail /var/log/kern.log # Follow new entries $ tail -f /var/log/syslog Filter and Search Logs # Search for pattern in logs $ grep "error" /var/log/syslog # Case-insensitive search $ grep -i "failed password" /var/log/auth.log # Show context around matches $ grep -A 2 -B 1 "critical" /var/log/syslog # Find logs from a specific date $ grep "Jan 15" /var/log/syslog Advanced Log Processing # Extract specific columns $ awk '{print $1, $3, $5}' /var/log/syslog # Count occurrences by field $ awk '{print $5}' /var/log/syslog | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr # Complex filtering $ awk '/error/ && !/ignored/' /var/log/syslog Journalctl Examples # Filter by time range $ journalctl --since "2023-01-15 12:00:00" --until "2023-01-15 13:00:00" # Filter by unit and severity $ journalctl -u nginx.service -p err # Output formats $ journalctl -o json-pretty # Filter by field $ journalctl _SYSTEMD_UNIT=ssh.service _UID=0

Security Recommendations Enable logging for all authentication attempts (success and failure) Configure centralized logging to a secure log server Enable log integrity monitoring to detect tampering Protect log files with appropriate permissions (0640 or stricter) Implement encryption for logs transmitted over networks Performance Optimization Configure appropriate log rotation intervals based on system activity Use compression for archived logs to save disk space Implement rate limiting to prevent log flooding during attacks Consider using faster storage for active log files Monitor log storage space and set up alerts for low disk space Log Management Use consistent timestamps (preferably UTC) across all servers Establish a log retention policy compliant with regulations Categorize logs by type and importance for easier analysis Implement structured logging formats where possible Consider using log aggregation tools like Elasticsearch, Graylog, or Splunk Pro Tip: While multiple logging systems can coexist on a Linux system, it's best practice to forward all logs to a single destination. Configure rsyslog to receive journal logs via $ModLoad imjournal or set ForwardToSyslog=yes in journald.conf for a unified logging solution. Back

Logs play a critical role in macOS systems, serving as a primary source of information for understanding system behavior, diagnosing application issues, and investigating security events. macOS uses a sophisticated logging framework known as the Unified Logging System, which collects detailed log data from across the operating system and applications in a structured and centralized manner. The Unified Logging System replaces traditional text-based logs with a high-performance binary log format. It categorizes log messages by subsystem and category, making it easier to filter and analyze relevant data. Tools like the log command-line utility and the Console app allow users to search, stream, and explore logs in real-time or historically, providing flexibility for developers, system administrators, and security analysts. As shown in Apple's evolution from macOS X 10 Cheetah (2001) to macOS 13 Ventura (2022), logging capabilities have significantly improved. A major shift occurred with macOS Sierra (10.12) and High Sierra (10.13), which introduced the Apple File System (APFS) and enhanced logging infrastructure. With Big Sur (macOS 11), Apple dropped the "10." prefix from version numbers, though some components maintained 10.16 designations internally. For enterprise environments, it's worth noting that Mac users typically run macOS versions 2-3 years behind the latest release. When investigating logs across a fleet of machines, be mindful of the different logging systems that may be in place depending on the macOS version.

The two main areas where we encounter macOS in the enterprise are in desktop devices and laptops. Both categories share common features in the OS, with the most significant variation being in performance and user configurations. iOS devices (iPhone, iPad Mini, iPad Air, iPad Pro) share features with macOS in a scaled-down form, though specific iOS incident response is outside the scope of this documentation. Servers Although macOS devices are generally high performance, it is very uncommon to see macOS devices acting as servers in an enterprise. Finding a macOS system in a DMZ hosting a web server or application server would be unexpected. This function is heavily dominated by Linux and Windows devices. The macOS server range was discontinued in April 2022. Workstations One of the more common places to see macOS in the enterprise is as end-user computing workstations. Often, they are used by developers, graphical designers/AV teams, marketing, and R&D departments. Mobile Users Probably the most common deployment of enterprise Macs are with the mobile workforce. MacBooks (Pro or Air) can be found in every role in most large organizations. The drive toward "Bring Your Own Devices" (BYOD) in the early 2010s played a significant part in increasing the Mac presence in corporate environments. When analyzing logs in an enterprise context, understanding the device's role and usage pattern is crucial for effective incident response and threat hunting.

APFS is one of the more "modern" filesystems, having been developed around 2016. As a result, it includes lots of features found in other filesystems without some of the legacy challenges they have. The filesystem also brought in several improvements of HFS+ in areas such as timestamps/dates, snapshots, and links. Modern (2016) B-Tree Indexing Native Encryption Snapshots 64-bit Timestamps Atomic Safe Save Key Characteristics Filesystem Type: Modern filesystem using B-Tree indexing introduced in 2016 File Capacity: 64-bit inodes supporting 9 × 2⁶³ files on a volume (limited by blocks to ~2⁵⁶) File Size Limit: File names up to 255 UTF-8 characters, maximum single file size: 8 exabytes Timestamps: 64-bit with nanosecond accuracy (HFS+ had 1 second accuracy) Note: APFS timestamps record the number of nanoseconds since 1970-01-01. System times are recorded in UTC. Current version of APFS appears to be able to support dates between 1970-01-01 00:00:00 and 2554-07-21 23:34:33. Atomic Safe Save APFS is not a journaled filesystem in the way of HFS+ (or NTFS/EXT4, etc). Instead, Apple has implemented a technique called Atomic Safe Save (ASS) to avoid metadata corruption in the event of a crash. In this, rather than overwrite metadata and update journals, a write event creates an entirely new record, changes any pointers to the new record, and then releases the old record. This is sometimes referred to as redirect-on-write. Disk Encryption Support for full disk encryption is built into the filesystem! This allows for different options and for some devices will include hardware encryption (internal storage on devices that support it, such as iOS and macOS devices with T2 security chips). Software encryption uses a volume encryption key (VEK) which is secured by a key encryption key (KEK). The KEK is unlocked by a user's password, personal recovery key, institutional recovery key, or an iCloud recovery key. The disk encryption can be applied to the entire disk, specific volumes, or individual files. If a volume is encrypted, the filesystem tree and the file contents are encrypted. Important: Apple encryption is challenging to bypass without specialist tools and support. Your best option in enterprise IR is to capture data from a live system or rely on the institutional recovery key if it is a managed device.

macOS uses specific file extensions and formats that differ from other operating systems. These extensions are critical for system functionality, forensic analysis, and understanding how macOS organizes data. Extension Description Details .dmg Apple Disk Image Files These are Apple disk image files, often seen as part of software installers. They can be mounted and accessed as if they were physical disks, and can be formatted in different file systems (often FAT or HFS+). DMG files can be encrypted, compressed, and may contain multiple partitions. .kext Kernel Extension Bundles These act as the macOS version of a driver. The kext bundle isn't a single file but a directory containing files making up the driver. Kext files have been deprecated in macOS and third-party kernel extensions can no longer be loaded on demand since macOS 11 Big Sur. They now require user interaction and a restart to load. .plist Property List Files Configuration files that can be in plain text (XML) or binary format. These store settings and properties for applications, system services, and user preferences. They function similar to registry entries in Windows. Binary plists use bplist00 as a header signature, while XML plists begin with <?xml version= . .app Application Bundles Rather than being single files, these are formally structured directories containing all files and folders making up the application. This bundle structure contains the executable code, resources, metadata, and support files. Inside each .app is a standard structure including a Contents folder with Info.plist, MacOS (containing the binary), and Resources folders. .dylib Dynamic Libraries Dynamic library files containing code to be imported into applications. This is similar to DLLs (dynamic linked libraries) in Windows or SO (shared object) files in Linux. These can be loaded at runtime and shared between multiple applications to reduce memory usage and improve modularity. .pkg Installer Packages Installer package files for software distribution. This format evolved with macOS 10.5 Leopard to use the XAR archive format. PKG files are archive files that contain installation scripts, payload files, and metadata that guide the macOS Installer through the installation process. .xar Extensible Archive The extensible archive format files used for software installers and browser extensions. XAR provides better security features and hash verification compared to older formats. It allows for random access to archive contents and better compression options. Forensic Importance: Understanding macOS file extensions and bundle structures is critical for digital forensics. Many artifacts are stored within these structures, and the file extension often indicates the expected internal format and potential value to investigations.

The macOS filesystem organizes resources into four distinct "domains" - User, Local, Network, and System. This structure helps separate files based on their purpose, accessibility, and management requirements, improving both security and organization. Domain Description Path Location Access Level User Contains user-specific files, pictures, music, etc. /Users/<username>/ Full access for the specific user Local Applications and resources shared among all users /Applications , /Library Managed by admin users and System Network Resources on local network (Time Capsules, NAS, printers) /Network Managed by network administrator System Software installed by Apple, critical OS applications /System , /System/Library Managed by System User Domain Details The User Domain holds items related to a specific user account. Each account logs into the system with its own user domain that reflects the home directory of the current logged-in user. ~/Applications User-specific applications ~/Library Application configurations ~/Developer Developer tools ~/Public Files shared with others Security Note: The User Library ( ~/Library ) contains application sandboxes, preferences files (in .plist format), and cached data - all valuable for forensic investigations. Local Domain Details The Local Domain stores items that are local to the current computer and shared among all users. This domain is not a single physical directory but instead consists of multiple locations on the local boot volume. Primary Locations: /Applications , /Library Network Domain Details Stores network resources such as apps and documents shared among all users of a local area network. Can include Time Capsules, network printers, file shares, and other systems. System Domain Details This is where Apple-installed software resides. Contains critical OS applications and configuration items required by the operating system to function. User accounts cannot add, remove, or modify items in this domain. Important: Only Apple-developed applications should have any access to the System Domain. Pro Tip: In incident response, the User Domain often holds the main evidence of both malicious insider activity and initial signs of compromise. An attack which exploits a user process or runs in a user-sandboxed app will be largely constrained to this domain unless privilege escalation is possible.

macOS logging has evolved from traditional Unix text logs to sophisticated binary formats. Modern macOS versions leverage Apple Unified Logging (AUL) for comprehensive system and application event tracking with structured data and rich metadata. Unified Logging System The Apple Unified Log (AUL) captures events across all layers of macOS, including kernel, user-space applications, daemons, and services. Format Binary with structured metadata Location /var/db/diagnostics/ Since macOS Sierra (10.12) Access Console app or log command Legacy System Logs Older plain text logs (some still present in modern macOS) stored in the traditional Unix format. Format Plain text (Unix log format) Location /var/log/ directory Deprecated Mostly phased out since macOS Sierra Note Often compressed with gzip or bzip2 Crash Reports Generated when applications or system processes terminate abnormally. Useful for detecting exploitation attempts. Location ~/Library/Logs/DiagnosticReports/ Format Plain text with stack traces Use Case Malware crash detection Content Process ID, thread states, crash context Diagnostic Reports Generated when apps misbehave (hang, high resource usage). Useful for detecting stealthy malware. Location /Library/Logs/DiagnosticReports/ Format Text logs with app state data Use Case Identify resource abuse Features Performance metrics, thread details macOS Log Severity Levels Level Description Usage Default Standard system and application events Normal operations Info Informational logs, basic activity Successful operations Debug Verbose technical details Troubleshooting and development Error Recoverable failures Operation failed but process continues Fault Critical errors or crashes System integrity issues Important: Most logs have moved to the Apple Unified Logging format since macOS Sierra (10.12). Analysis on a macOS device is the best option for incident response.

macOS stores logs in various locations throughout the filesystem. Understanding these locations is crucial for effective incident response and threat hunting. Path Description Content Type IR Value /var/log Traditional system logs directory Text logs (system.log, install.log, etc.) Medium (legacy) /var/db/diagnostics System logs in Unified Log format Binary logs (.tracev3 files) High /var/db/uuidtext Unified logs message text storage Binary data for AUL High /Library/Logs System-wide application logs Mixed formats Medium ~/Library/Logs User-specific application logs Text & binary formats High ~/Library/Logs/DiagnosticReports Application crash reports Text files with crash details High /Library/Application Support/(App name) Application-specific logs Varies by application Medium Important Legacy Plaintext Logs /var/log/system.log System diagnostics and general messages /var/log/wifi.log Wi-Fi connections and known hotspots /var/log/install.log Software installation history /var/log/appfirewall.log Network firewall events /var/log/fsck_apfs.log Events related to the filesystem /var/log/DiagnosticMessages System diagnostic messages /var/log/asl/*.asl Apple System Log (deprecated) /var/log/DiskUtility.log Disk mounting and management

Property list (plist) files contain configuration information about the system, applications, and user preferences. They function similarly to the Registry in Microsoft Windows and are found throughout the macOS filesystem. XML Format This is an older format where the file is a human-readable XML document that can be viewed in any text editor. File Signature <?xml version=" Format Plain text XML Tools Any text editor Usage Still found on latest macOS versions Binary Format Newer plist files use a binary format that saves disk space and supports binary large object (BLOB) data. File Signature bplist00 Format Binary data structure Advantages Less disk space, BLOB support Challenges Requires specialized tools to read Plist Analysis Tools macOS Tools Native tools for viewing and editing plist files on macOS systems. Xcode: Shows plists in a GUI with property editor plutil: Command line utility for converting formats $ plutil -p file.plist $ plutil -convert xml1 file.plist Windows Tools Tools for analyzing plist files on Windows systems. iBackupBot Plist Editor: Commercial tool with plist parsing Notepad++: With the bplist plugin for binary plists Commercial forensic suites: Most include plist parsers Linux Tools Tools for analyzing plist files on Linux systems. libplist-utils: Command line tools for plist analysis $ sudo apt update && sudo apt install libplist-utils $ plistutil -i info.plist -o info.plist.xml -f xml Important: Starting with macOS Catalina (10.15), BLOB data in binary plists can be truncated when viewed in Xcode or plutil. With macOS Big Sur (11.0), Xcode became able to read the BLOB again, but they remain truncated in plutil. Forensically Significant Plist Locations /System/Library/CoreServices/SystemVersion.plist OS version and build information /Library/Preferences/SystemConfiguration/NetworkInterfaces.plist Network interface hardware data and MAC addresses /Library/Preferences/SystemConfiguration/preferences.plist Network configuration and hostname information /Library/Preferences/.GlobalPreferences.plist Device time zone and regional settings /Library/Preferences/com.apple.timezone.auto.plist Automatic time zone update settings /private/var/db/dhcpclient/leases/ DHCP lease information with router data and SSIDs /private/var/db/dslocal/nodes/Default/users User account information and configuration /Users/(username)/Library/Preferences/ User-specific application preferences Launch and Startup Plists System Startup These locations contain plists that execute during system boot. /Library/LaunchAgents Run as root when any user logs in /Library/LaunchDaemons System-wide daemons run as root /System/Library/LaunchAgents Apple-provided launch agents /System/Library/LaunchDaemons Apple-provided system daemons User Login These locations contain plists that execute when a specific user logs in. /Users/(username)/Library/LaunchAgents User-specific startup items Execution Run as the logged-in user Purpose User-specific background processes IR Value High (potential persistence mechanisms) Example Plist Structure (OneDrive Updater) <?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?> <!DOCTYPE plist PUBLIC "-//Apple//DTD PLIST 1.0//EN" "http://www.apple.com/DTDs/PropertyList-1.0.dtd"> <plist version="1.0"> <dict> <key>Label</key> <string>com.microsoft.OneDriveUpdaterDaemon</string> <key>Program</key> <string>/Applications/OneDrive.app/Contents/MacOS/OneDriveUpdaterDaemon</string> </dict> </plist> Key elements in launch plists: Label: The name of the task shown when launchctl list is used Program: Path to the executable that will be launched ProgramArguments: Alternative to Program, includes arguments for execution Incident Response and Forensic Value Property list files are highly valuable for forensic investigators and incident responders for several reasons: System Configuration: Provides insight into system settings, time zones, and network interfaces User Activity: Contains application preferences and user-specific settings Network History: DHCP leases reveal previously connected networks and router information Persistence Mechanisms: Launch plists are common locations for malware persistence Account Information: User details including IDs and potentially deleted accounts Forensic Analysis Approach Identify suspicious launch agents or daemons that don't appear to be from legitimate vendors Check executable paths referenced in plists to ensure they point to valid locations Compare creation/modification timestamps of plists against system installation and update times Examine network configuration plists for signs of network manipulation or redirection Search user preference plists for evidence of application usage and behavior

Due to the binary nature of modern macOS logs, specialized tools are required for effective analysis. Each approach offers different advantages for incident response and forensic investigation. Live Response Analysis Advantages Best alternative to SIEM Use system commands Can read binary formats Best data quality Limitations Requires access to the system Can change the system Logs can be modified by attackers Default logging rarely changed Native macOS Log Analysis Tools Console App GUI tool for reading and filtering Apple Unified Logs with a visual interface. Type: Graphical UI Strength: Visual filtering Limitation: No scripting log Command Command-line tool for querying the unified logging system with powerful filtering options. $ log show --last 1h $ log stream --predicate 'category == "network"' $ log show --info --debug syslog Command Tool for viewing legacy Apple System Logs (.asl files). Deprecated in newer macOS versions. $ syslog -f /var/log/asl/filename.asl Note: Deprecated in favor of 'log' command Live Analysis Examples Common commands for live system analysis during incident response. $ last Shows last logged in users $ syslog -f file.asl View ASL binary logs Third-Party Analysis Tools mac_apt - macOS Artifact Parsing Tool Cross-Platform Python-based tool for analyzing macOS and iOS artifacts including Unified Logs. Ideal for off-device forensic analysis. Key Features Cross-platform (Python 3.7+) Reads disk images & live systems Plugin-driven architecture Multiple output formats (CSV, XLSX) Limitations Work in progress Needs considerable disk space Running ALL plugins is very slow Some TSV/CSV parsing issues Example Usage # Extract user login data and shell history python /opt/mac_apt/mac_apt.py -o /analysis --csv -d E01 /diskimage.E01 UTMPX USERS TERMSESSIONS # Extract unified logs python /opt/mac_apt/mac_apt.py -o /analysis --xlsx -d MOUNTED /Volumes/MacintoshHD UNIFIEDLOGS # Run the FAST set of plugins (quicker analysis) python /opt/mac_apt/mac_apt.py -o /analysis --csv -d DD /disk.dd FAST GitHub Repository mac_apt macOS-UnifiedLogs by Mandiant Rust-based Open-source library for parsing Apple Unified Logs with the ability to extract detailed metadata from .tracev3 files. Extracted Elements Process & Thread IDs Activity IDs Log Messages Timestamps (Intel and ARM) Effective User ID (EUID) Subsystem & Category Limitations No error code lookups Limited custom object support No protocol buffer data support Work in progress GitHub Repository macos-UnifiedLogs Back

Internet Information Services (IIS) logs are essential for monitoring web server activity, capturing detailed records of client requests to the server. These logs include information such as client IP addresses, request methods, URLs accessed, user agents, status codes, and response times making them a critical tool for web administrators and security analysts. IIS logging is a built-in feature that stores activity data in text-based log files. These logs help detect performance issues, track user behavior, identify malicious access patterns, and support incident response by providing a timeline of HTTP interactions. Logs are typically stored in the W3C extended log file format and can be customized to capture specific fields depending on your operational needs. Effective use of IIS logs involves enabling comprehensive logging settings, regularly rotating and archiving logs, and integrating them with centralized logging platforms or SIEMs. Properly configured logs are invaluable for investigating web-based attacks such as SQL injection, cross-site scripting, unauthorized file access, and brute-force attempts. Analyzing IIS logs also contributes to optimizing web application performance and ensuring compliance with security policies.

IIS stores log files based on the site and configuration. Below are the default paths and common directories where you can find IIS logs: Log Scope Default Path Description Default Website %SystemDrive%\inetpub\logs\LogFiles\W3SVC1 Logs for the default IIS website (site ID 1) Additional Websites %SystemDrive%\inetpub\logs\LogFiles\W3SVC<SiteID> Each website has its own folder based on Site ID FTP Site Logs %SystemDrive%\inetpub\logs\LogFiles\FTPSVC1 FTP traffic logs (if FTP is enabled) Custom Log Path Defined in IIS Manager > Site > Logging settings Log path can be customized per site or application Pro Tip: Use the IIS Manager GUI or PowerShell ( Get-Website , Get-WebConfigurationProperty ) to identify log settings and paths for each hosted site.

Field Description Category Example Value date Date of the request Timestamp 2025-04-23 time Time of the request Timestamp 10:25:17 c-ip Client IP address Source 192.168.1.55 cs-method HTTP method used Request Type GET cs-uri-stem Requested resource path Request /admin/login.aspx cs-uri-query Query string from the URL Request user=admin'-- sc-status HTTP response code Response 403 sc-substatus Detailed status code Response 1 sc-win32-status Windows system-level status Response 2147942405 cs(User-Agent) Client software or tool Source sqlmap/1.5.2 cs(Referer) Previous page the user came from Source https://example.com/home time-taken Processing time (ms) Performance 382

This table lists common HTTP response codes as seen in IIS logs (fields like sc-status ). sc-status Meaning 200 OK: Request succeeded 301 / 302 Redirect: Resource moved 400 Bad Request: Malformed request 401 Unauthorized: Authentication required 403 Forbidden: Access denied 404 Not Found: Resource unavailable 405 Method Not Allowed: Disallowed HTTP verb 500 Internal Server Error: Server-side failure 502 / 503 Bad Gateway / Service Unavailable

Use these Log Parser commands to uncover hidden threats, misuse of HTTP methods, abnormal behavior patterns, and attacker-controlled user agents in IIS logs. List All User Agents CMD> logparser "SELECT cs(User-Agent), COUNT(*) AS Hits FROM u_ex*.log GROUP BY cs(User-Agent) ORDER BY Hits DESC" -i:IISW3C Detect bots or suspicious scripts by listing and counting user agents. Top Destination IPs CMD> logparser "SELECT s-ip, COUNT(*) AS Hits FROM u_ex*.log GROUP BY s-ip ORDER BY Hits DESC" -i:IISW3C Shows which server IPs are receiving the most traffic, useful in load-balanced or cloud-hosted environments. POST with 200 CMD> logparser "SELECT c-ip, cs-uri-stem, COUNT(*) AS Total FROM u_ex*.log WHERE cs-method='POST' AND sc-status=200 GROUP BY c-ip, cs-uri-stem ORDER BY Total DESC" -i:IISW3C Finds IPs that performed successful POST requests, useful for finding form submission abuse or C2 callbacks. Automated POST Requests CMD> logparser "SELECT date, time, c-ip, cs(User-Agent), cs-uri-stem FROM u_ex*.log WHERE cs-method='POST' AND (cs(User-Agent) NOT LIKE '%%Mozilla%%' AND cs(User-Agent) NOT LIKE '%%Chrome%%' AND cs(User-Agent) NOT LIKE '%%Safari%%')" -i:IISW3C Detects POST requests made by suspicious or non-browser clients such as scripts, bots, or exploit tools, useful to identify automation abuse or early attack stages. Copy Requests for EXE Files CMD> logparser "SELECT date, time, c-ip, cs-uri-stem FROM u_ex*.log WHERE cs-uri-stem LIKE '%%.exe'" -i:IISW3C Flags potential malware downloads or attempts to access executables hosted on the server. IPs with Multiple Failed Requests CMD> logparser "SELECT c-ip, COUNT(*) AS Failures FROM u_ex*.log WHERE sc-status = 403 OR sc-status = 401 GROUP BY c-ip HAVING Failures > 5 ORDER BY Failures DESC" -i:IISW3C Identifies brute force attempts or enumeration from clients repeatedly denied access. Most Accessed Endpoints CMD> logparser "SELECT TOP 5 cs-uri-stem, COUNT(*) AS Hits FROM u_ex*.log GROUP BY cs-uri-stem ORDER BY Hits DESC" -i:IISW3C Lists the top 5 most frequently accessed resources, a quick view into what attackers or users target. User Agent Diversity per IP CMD> logparser "SELECT c-ip, COUNT(DISTINCT cs(User-Agent)) AS UniqueAgents FROM u_ex*.log GROUP BY c-ip ORDER BY UniqueAgents DESC" -i:IISW3C Highlights IPs rotating User Agents, often a sign of obfuscation or botnets.

s.h: Best Practices for IIS Log Management
s.t: Follow these practices to maximize the forensic value, performance insights, and detection capabilities of your IIS log data: 01 Enable All Critical Fields Ensure fields like cs-uri-stem , cs-uri-query , c-ip , cs(User-Agent) , and time-taken are enabled to capture essential request context. 02 Use W3C Extended Log Format The W3C format is flexible, widely supported, and optimal for correlation in SIEMs and Log Parser tools. 03 Rotate Logs Daily Configure daily log file rotation to improve searchability and reduce the risk of log corruption or size overflows. 04 Centralize & Archive Logs Forward IIS logs to a SIEM or central log server and retain them for at least 90 days to ensure full incident coverage. 05 Monitor Anomalies Look for patterns like repeated 404s, spikes in POST requests, or new User-Agents to detect potential attacks or scanning activity. 06 Correlate with Other Logs Correlate IIS data with Windows Event Logs, firewall logs, and endpoint telemetry to uncover multi-stage intrusions. 07 Secure the Logs Restrict access to log files and monitor for changes or deletions, which may indicate tampering or evasion attempts. 08 Automate Analysis Use tools like LogParser , PowerShell, or Python to automate detection of suspicious patterns and reduce manual effort.

s.h: OWASP Top 10 Web Application Security Risks
s.t: The OWASP Top 10 is a standard awareness document for developers and web application security practitioners. It represents a broad consensus about the most critical security risks to web applications based on frequency of discovery, severity, and potential impact. A01:2021 - Broken Access Control Restrictions on authenticated users aren't properly enforced. Attackers can exploit flaws to access unauthorized functionality or data. Detection Critical Risk A02:2021 - Cryptographic Failures Failures related to cryptography that often lead to sensitive data exposure. Includes weak encryption, improper certificate validation, or using deprecated functions. Detection High Risk A03:2021 - Injection User-supplied data is not validated, filtered, or sanitized. SQL, NoSQL, OS, and LDAP injection flaws can result in data exfiltration or system compromise. Detection High Risk A04:2021 - Insecure Design Flaws related to design and architectural security failures. Represents a shift from remediation to designing with security in mind from the start. Detection High Risk A05:2021 - Security Misconfiguration Missing security hardening, improper permissions, unnecessary features enabled, default accounts/passwords, and overly informative error messages. Detection Medium Risk A06:2021 - Vulnerable Components Using outdated libraries, frameworks, or components with known vulnerabilities. Includes failure to track vulnerable dependencies and patch management. Detection Medium Risk A07:2021 - Auth Failures Incorrect implementation of authentication and session management. Includes weak passwords, improper session handling, and credential exposure. Detection Medium Risk A08:2021 - Software Integrity Failures Failures to verify integrity of software updates, critical data, CI/CD pipelines, or unsigned libraries. Includes auto-update functionality without integrity checks. Detection Medium Risk A09:2021 - Logging Failures Insufficient logging, monitoring, and alerting. Inadequate detection, escalation, and response to active breaches. Logs missing critical details or improperly stored. Detection Medium Risk A10:2021 - Server-Side Request Forgery Web application fetches remote resources without validating user-supplied URLs. Attackers can force the server to connect to internal services or read unauthorized data. Detection Medium Risk Security Note: The OWASP Top 10 should be viewed as a starting point, not a comprehensive security program. Organizations should develop additional security measures based on their specific threat landscape and risk profile. Back

Apache HTTP Server logs are vital for tracking web server activity and analyzing client interactions. These logs provide detailed information such as IP addresses, request methods, requested resources, HTTP status codes, referrers, and user agents, enabling administrators and security teams to monitor traffic and investigate potential threats. Apache uses two primary log types: the access.log and the error.log . The access log records each request processed by the server, while the error log captures diagnostic information, such as startup/shutdown events, configuration errors, and runtime exceptions. Logs are typically stored in a customizable text format defined by the LogFormat directive. To get the most value from Apache logs, it’s important to configure detailed log formats, implement log rotation, and forward logs to centralized analysis platforms like ELK or SIEM systems. Apache logs play a crucial role in detecting and investigating common web threats such as directory traversal, SQL injection, unauthorized access, and brute-force login attempts. They also support performance tuning and help ensure compliance with audit and security standards.

Apache stores logs based on the server configuration. Below are common default paths and locations for Apache access and error logs: Log Type Default Path Description Access Log /var/log/apache2/access.log Records all incoming HTTP requests to the server Error Log /var/log/apache2/error.log Contains server errors, diagnostic messages, and crash information Virtual Host Logs Defined in <VirtualHost> config block Each virtual host can define its own access and error log files Custom Log Paths Defined in apache2.conf or httpd.conf via CustomLog and ErrorLog Paths can be changed depending on environment or OS Pro Tip: Use apachectl -V or httpd -S to check configuration paths and log directives for Apache on your system.

Field Description Category Example Value ip Client IP address Source 192.168.1.55 ident RFC 1413 identity of the client (usually "-") Source - authuser Username for authenticated requests Source john.doe date Date and time of the request Timestamp [23/Apr/2025:10:25:17 +0300] request Full request line from the client Request GET /admin/login.php?user=admin HTTP/1.1 status HTTP response code Response 403 bytes Size of the response in bytes Response 728 referer Previous page (Referer header) Source https://example.com/home user-agent Client software or tool (User-Agent header) Source sqlmap/1.5.2 response-time Time taken to serve the request (if enabled) Performance 382

This table lists common HTTP status codes as seen in Apache access logs. Status Code Meaning 200 OK: Request succeeded 301 / 302 Redirect: Resource moved 400 Bad Request: Malformed syntax 401 Unauthorized: Authentication required 403 Forbidden: Access denied 404 Not Found: Resource not found 405 Method Not Allowed: HTTP method not permitted 429 Too Many Requests: Rate limited 500 Internal Server Error: Server issue 503 Service Unavailable: Server overloaded or down

Use these Linux CLI commands to analyze Apache access logs, detect abuse, and uncover suspicious patterns in web traffic. List All User Agents BASH> awk -F'"' '{print $6}' access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr Detect bots or scripts by listing and counting unique User-Agent headers. Top Destination IPs BASH> awk '{print $1}' access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr Shows which client IPs are making the most requests, helpful for detecting scanning or spikes. POST with 200 BASH> awk '$6 ~ /POST/ && $9 == 200 {print $1, $7}' access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr Finds successful POST request patterns, useful for detecting suspicious uploads or interactions. Automated POST Requests BASH> awk '$6 ~ /POST/ && $0 !~ /Mozilla|Chrome|Safari/' access.log Detects automated tools and non-browser clients sending POST requests, potentially exploit attempts. Requests for EXE Files BASH> grep ".exe" access.log Highlights access to `.exe` files, which could signal malware delivery or reconnaissance. IPs with Multiple Failed Requests BASH> awk '$9 ~ /403|401/ {print $1}' access.log | sort | uniq -c | awk '$1 > 5' | sort -nr Identifies clients repeatedly denied access, possible brute-force or path probing behavior. Most Accessed Endpoints BASH> awk '{print $7}' access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr | head -n 5 Lists the most requested URIs, great for identifying popular or targeted content. User Agent Diversity per IP BASH> awk '{print $1 "|" $12}' access.log | sort | uniq | cut -d'|' -f1 | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr Detects IPs switching User-Agents, common in bots or evasive crawlers.

s.h: Best Practices for Apache Log Management
s.t: Follow these practices to enhance visibility, improve security detection, and support forensic investigations using Apache access and error logs: 01 Enable Combined Log Format Use the combined log format to capture critical fields like client IP, request method, referrer, and User-Agent for each HTTP request. 02 Rotate Logs Daily Use logrotate or built-in Apache rotation tools to rotate logs daily, improving manageability and preventing file bloating. 03 Archive Logs Securely Compress and store archived logs in a secure, centralized location with retention policies of at least 90 days for compliance and investigations. 04 Monitor Access and Error Logs Regularly review both access.log and error.log to detect abnormal request patterns, server errors, or exploitation attempts. 05 Filter Malicious Indicators Use grep or custom scripts to flag suspicious URIs, high frequency 404s, non-browser User-Agents, and known attack signatures. 06 Integrate with SIEM Forward logs to your SIEM (e.g., Splunk, ELK) using syslog or filebeat to enable real-time alerting and cross-log correlation. 07 Restrict Log Access Limit file access using Linux permissions ( chmod , chown ) and monitor for unauthorized changes or deletions. 08 Automate Threat Hunting Automate log analysis using tools like awk , grep , goaccess , or Python to reduce time-to-detection and improve scalability.
