Microsoft SQL Server produces several independent streams of log data, and no single one of them tells the whole story. The SQL Server Error Log records engine health, startup parameters, and by default every failed login. SQL Server Audit , built on Extended Events, is the purpose-built security auditing framework that writes structured records of logons, permission changes, schema modifications, and data access. The Default Trace quietly captures a small set of high-value configuration and DDL events even when nothing else is enabled, and the Windows Application and Security event logs receive a mirrored copy of login auditing. The distinction matters operationally. A default SQL Server installation logs failed logins only, which means an attacker who successfully authenticates with stolen credentials, escalates privileges, and exfiltrates a customer table produces almost no evidence. Turning on SQL Server Audit with the correct action groups is what converts the database from a blind spot into a monitored asset. Both NIST SP 800-92 and the Saudi NCA Essential Cybersecurity Controls require auditing of privileged account activity and access to sensitive data, and for a database tier that requirement is satisfied by a server audit specification, not by the error log alone. SQL Server Audit writes to one of three targets: a binary .sqlaudit file, the Windows Application log, or the Windows Security log. The file target is the most reliable and the highest performing, and it can be read back into T-SQL through sys.fn_get_audit_file or shipped to a SIEM. The Security log target offers the strongest tamper resistance because a database administrator cannot clear it without Windows-level privileges, which is precisely why it is preferred in high-assurance environments where the DBA is inside the threat model.

SQL Server generates several distinct log types that serve different monitoring and forensic purposes. Understanding which stream holds which evidence is essential when reconstructing an incident: Log Type Description SQL Server Error Log The primary operational log, written as a plain text file (ERRORLOG) and cycled on every service restart. Records service startup and shutdown, database recovery, backup and restore operations, memory and I/O warnings, and login auditing messages such as error 18456. This is the first log to check when the instance behaves abnormally. SQL Server Audit The dedicated security audit framework introduced in SQL Server 2008 and available in all editions since 2016 SP1. Writes structured, tamper-evident records for server-level and database-level actions defined by audit specifications. This is the authoritative source for privileged activity, permission changes, and sensitive data access. Default Trace A lightweight server-side trace enabled by default that retains a rolling set of five 20 MB trace files. Captures object creation and deletion, database changes, security-relevant configuration modifications, log file growth, and audit changes. Extremely valuable in incident response because it is often the only evidence present on an unmonitored server. Extended Events (XEvents) The modern, low-overhead event tracing engine that replaced SQL Trace and Profiler. Highly flexible sessions can capture statement execution, errors, deadlocks, and login activity with fine-grained filtering. The system_health session runs by default and retains recent errors, deadlocks, and severity 20+ events. Windows Application / Security Log SQL Server mirrors login auditing and severe engine errors into the Windows Application log under the source MSSQLSERVER or MSSQL$<InstanceName>. SQL Server Audit can additionally target the Windows Security log, which cannot be cleared by a DBA and is therefore the tamper-resistant option. SQL Server Agent Log Records job execution history, job step failures, alert firing, and Agent service events. Frequently overlooked, yet SQL Agent jobs are a common persistence mechanism because they run under privileged service accounts and can execute operating system commands or PowerShell. Transaction Log (LDF) The write-ahead log that guarantees durability and supports point-in-time recovery. Not a security log and not human readable, but forensically valuable: with the right tooling it can reveal DELETE and UPDATE operations that were never captured by any audit, provided the log has not yet been truncated. Pro Tip: The Default Trace is the single highest-value artifact on an otherwise unmonitored SQL Server. Before an attacker has a chance to overwrite it, query sys.fn_trace_gettable for event class 164 (Object:Altered) and 46 (Object:Created) to see what changed and when.

Default paths vary by SQL Server version because the instance directory encodes the internal version number. The table below uses SQL Server 2022 (MSSQL16) as the reference; substitute the correct number for your version. Log Default Location Error Log C:\Program Files\Microsoft SQL Server\MSSQL16.MSSQLSERVER\MSSQL\Log\ERRORLOG Audit Files Defined by the FILEPATH argument of CREATE SERVER AUDIT, commonly a dedicated volume such as D:\SQLAudit\ containing .sqlaudit files Default Trace C:\Program Files\Microsoft SQL Server\MSSQL16.MSSQLSERVER\MSSQL\Log\log_<n>.trc system_health XEvent C:\Program Files\Microsoft SQL Server\MSSQL16.MSSQLSERVER\MSSQL\Log\system_health_*.xel SQL Agent Log C:\Program Files\Microsoft SQL Server\MSSQL16.MSSQLSERVER\MSSQL\Log\SQLAGENT.OUT Windows Application Log %SystemRoot%\System32\Winevt\Logs\Application.evtx (source: MSSQLSERVER) Setup / Patch Logs C:\Program Files\Microsoft SQL Server\160\Setup Bootstrap\Log\Summary.txt Pro Tip: Do not guess the path. Run SELECT SERVERPROPERTY('ErrorLogFileName') to get the exact error log location for the running instance, and query sys.server_file_audits for the configured audit file path.

SQL Server Audit is created in three steps: define the audit object and its destination, attach a server audit specification listing the action groups to capture, then enable both. All statements below require CONTROL SERVER permission. Step 1: Create the Server Audit Object USE master; GO CREATE SERVER AUDIT [HTL_Security_Audit] TO FILE ( FILEPATH = 'D:\SQLAudit\' , MAXSIZE = 256 MB , MAX_ROLLOVER_FILES = 50 , RESERVE_DISK_SPACE = OFF ) WITH ( QUEUE_DELAY = 1000 , ON_FAILURE = CONTINUE , AUDIT_GUID = NEWID() ); GO Creates a file-based audit retaining up to 50 rollover files of 256 MB each. QUEUE_DELAY of 1000 ms buffers writes for performance; set it to 0 for synchronous, guaranteed-write auditing at the cost of throughput. Step 2: Create the Server Audit Specification CREATE SERVER AUDIT SPECIFICATION [HTL_Server_Spec] FOR SERVER AUDIT [HTL_Security_Audit] ADD (FAILED_LOGIN_GROUP), ADD (SUCCESSFUL_LOGIN_GROUP), ADD (LOGOUT_GROUP), ADD (SERVER_ROLE_MEMBER_CHANGE_GROUP), ADD (DATABASE_ROLE_MEMBER_CHANGE_GROUP), ADD (SERVER_PERMISSION_CHANGE_GROUP), ADD (DATABASE_PERMISSION_CHANGE_GROUP), ADD (SERVER_PRINCIPAL_CHANGE_GROUP), ADD (DATABASE_PRINCIPAL_CHANGE_GROUP), ADD (SCHEMA_OBJECT_CHANGE_GROUP), ADD (DATABASE_CHANGE_GROUP), ADD (SERVER_OBJECT_CHANGE_GROUP), ADD (AUDIT_CHANGE_GROUP), ADD (BACKUP_RESTORE_GROUP), ADD (DBCC_GROUP) WITH (STATE = ON); GO Captures authentication, privilege and role changes, schema modifications, backup activity, and any attempt to tamper with the audit configuration itself. AUDIT_CHANGE_GROUP is mandatory: it is what tells you the attacker disabled your auditing. Step 3: Enable the Audit ALTER SERVER AUDIT [HTL_Security_Audit] WITH (STATE = ON); GO -- Verify the audit is running SELECT a.name, a.is_state_enabled, a.on_failure_desc, f.log_file_path FROM sys.server_audits a LEFT JOIN sys.server_file_audits f ON a.audit_id = f.audit_id; The audit object must be enabled separately from the specification. Confirm is_state_enabled returns 1 for both the audit and the specification, otherwise records are silently discarded. Step 4: Audit Sensitive Data Access at the Database Level USE [CustomerDB]; GO CREATE DATABASE AUDIT SPECIFICATION [HTL_PII_Access] FOR SERVER AUDIT [HTL_Security_Audit] ADD (SELECT, UPDATE, DELETE ON dbo.Customers BY public), ADD (SELECT ON dbo.PaymentCards BY public), ADD (EXECUTE ON SCHEMA::dbo BY public) WITH (STATE = ON); GO Server-level auditing does not record row access. To satisfy sensitive-data monitoring requirements you must add a database audit specification naming the specific tables that hold regulated data. Step 5: Set Login Auditing to Capture Both Success and Failure EXEC xp_instance_regwrite N'HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE', N'Software\Microsoft\MSSQLServer\MSSQLServer', N'AuditLevel', REG_DWORD, 3; GO -- 0 = None, 1 = Successful logins, 2 = Failed logins (default), 3 = Both -- Requires a service restart to take effect Sets the legacy login auditing level that writes to the error log and Windows Application log. This is independent of SQL Server Audit and provides a useful secondary source, but it requires a service restart. Security Note: ON_FAILURE = CONTINUE keeps the instance available if the audit target becomes unwritable, but it means auditing can silently stop. In regulated environments consider ON_FAILURE = SHUTDOWN or FAIL_OPERATION so that loss of audit capability is treated as a failure condition rather than an inconvenience.

SQL Server exposes more than eighty audit action groups. Enabling all of them generates unusable volume. The groups below represent a balanced baseline that satisfies common regulatory requirements while keeping event rates manageable. FAILED_LOGIN_GROUP Records every unsuccessful authentication attempt against the instance. The foundation for brute force and password spraying detection. Enable Critical SUCCESSFUL_LOGIN_GROUP Records successful authentications. High volume on busy instances, but without it a compromised credential is invisible. Filter rather than disable. Enable Critical SERVER_ROLE_MEMBER_CHANGE_GROUP Fires when a login is added to or removed from a fixed server role. Adding an account to sysadmin is the single most important privilege escalation event on the instance. Enable Critical AUDIT_CHANGE_GROUP Captures creation, modification, and deletion of audit objects and specifications. This is the anti-tampering control that reveals an attacker turning your logging off. Enable Critical SERVER_PERMISSION_CHANGE_GROUP Records GRANT, REVOKE, and DENY of server-scoped permissions such as CONTROL SERVER, IMPERSONATE, and ALTER ANY LOGIN. Enable High Risk SCHEMA_OBJECT_CHANGE_GROUP Captures CREATE, ALTER, and DROP against schema objects. Detects malicious stored procedures, trigger-based persistence, and destructive DDL. Enable High Risk SERVER_PRINCIPAL_CHANGE_GROUP Fires on creation, alteration, and deletion of logins, including password changes and account enabling. Detects attacker-created backdoor accounts. Enable High Risk BACKUP_RESTORE_GROUP Records BACKUP and RESTORE operations. An unscheduled backup written to a network share or local temp folder is a classic bulk exfiltration technique. Enable High Risk DBCC_GROUP Captures DBCC command execution. Undocumented DBCC commands are used to read memory, dump page contents, and manipulate the engine in ways that bypass normal access control. Enable Medium Risk Security Note: Action groups are all-or-nothing at the server level and cannot be filtered by login inside the specification. If SUCCESSFUL_LOGIN_GROUP volume is unmanageable, apply a WHERE predicate on the audit object using ALTER SERVER AUDIT ... WHERE server_principal_name <> 'app_service_account' rather than dropping the group entirely.

Audit records read through sys.fn_get_audit_file expose a consistent set of columns regardless of the action being audited. These are the fields that matter for detection engineering and SIEM field mapping. Field Description Category Example Value event_time UTC timestamp of the audited action Timestamp 2025-07-14 09:41:22.813 action_id Four-character code identifying the action Detection LGIF succeeded Whether the action completed successfully Result 0 server_principal_name Login that performed the action Identity svc_reporting database_principal_name Database user context of the action Identity dbo client_ip Source IP address of the session Source 10.20.4.87 application_name Client application string supplied by the driver Source sqlcmd host_name Client workstation name Source WKS-FIN-014 database_name Database in which the action occurred Target CustomerDB object_name Securable that was acted upon Target PaymentCards statement The T-SQL statement executed Action SELECT * FROM dbo.PaymentCards session_id SPID of the session Session 73 permission_bitmask Permissions granted, denied, or revoked Authorization 0x00000000000001

These error numbers appear in the SQL Server Error Log and the Windows Application log. Error 18456 in particular carries a state code that reveals exactly why authentication failed, which is what separates a mistyped password from a targeted attack. Event / Error Meaning Why It Matters 18456 State 5 Login attempted with a user name that does not exist Username enumeration or password spraying against guessed account names 18456 State 8 Password mismatch for a valid login Classic brute force indicator when repeated against the same account 18456 State 11 / 12 Valid Windows login but server access denied A domain account probing the instance without an explicit grant, common in lateral movement 18456 State 18 Password must be changed Indicates use of a stale or newly provisioned account, often a forgotten default 18456 State 38 Login valid but the requested database is inaccessible Reconnaissance enumerating which databases a compromised account can reach 18453 / 18454 Successful login using Windows or SQL authentication Baseline for detecting logons from unexpected hosts, applications, or hours 17806 SSPI handshake failed Kerberos or NTLM failure, frequently seen during relay attacks and misconfigured SPNs 15457 Configuration option changed Fires when sp_configure alters a setting such as xp_cmdshell or CLR enabled 3041 Backup failed to complete May indicate ransomware interfering with backups or an attacker probing backup paths 825 Read-retry required on a page Early warning of storage corruption that can also result from destructive tampering Pro Tip: SQL Server deliberately reports state 1 to the client for almost every 18456 failure to avoid leaking information to an attacker. The real state code is only written to the error log, so client-side application logs are useless for this analysis.

Use these T-SQL and SIEM queries to hunt for authentication attacks, privilege escalation, configuration tampering, and bulk data access on SQL Server. Read the Audit File SQL> SELECT event_time, action_id, succeeded, server_principal_name, client_ip, statement FROM sys.fn_get_audit_file('D:\SQLAudit\*.sqlaudit', DEFAULT, DEFAULT) ORDER BY event_time DESC; Reads the binary audit files back into a queryable result set. Wildcards let you span all rollover files at once. Brute Force Detection SQL> SELECT client_ip, server_principal_name, COUNT(*) AS Failures FROM sys.fn_get_audit_file('D:\SQLAudit\*.sqlaudit', DEFAULT, DEFAULT) WHERE action_id = 'LGIF' AND event_time > DATEADD(HOUR, -1, GETUTCDATE()) GROUP BY client_ip, server_principal_name HAVING COUNT(*) > 10; Surfaces source IPs generating more than ten failed logins in an hour, the signature of credential guessing. Sysadmin Role Additions SQL> SELECT event_time, server_principal_name, target_server_principal_name, statement FROM sys.fn_get_audit_file('D:\SQLAudit\*.sqlaudit', DEFAULT, DEFAULT) WHERE action_id IN ('APRL','ADSP') AND statement LIKE '%sysadmin%'; Detects any login being granted membership in the sysadmin fixed server role, the top privilege escalation event. xp_cmdshell Enabled SQL> SELECT name, value_in_use FROM sys.configurations WHERE name IN ('xp_cmdshell','Ole Automation Procedures','clr enabled','Ad Hoc Distributed Queries') AND value_in_use = 1; Any of these returning 1 means the instance can execute code outside the database engine. Alert on the change event, not just the state. Default Trace: Object Changes SQL> SELECT StartTime, LoginName, HostName, ApplicationName, DatabaseName, ObjectName, EventClass FROM sys.fn_trace_gettable(CONVERT(VARCHAR(500), (SELECT TOP 1 [path] FROM sys.traces WHERE is_default = 1)), DEFAULT) WHERE EventClass IN (46, 47, 164) ORDER BY StartTime DESC; Pulls object created (46), deleted (47), and altered (164) events from the Default Trace. Often the only DDL evidence on an unaudited server. Error Log Failed Logins SQL> EXEC xp_readerrorlog 0, 1, N'Login failed', NULL, NULL, NULL, N'desc'; Searches the current error log for failed logins including the true state code. Change the first parameter to read archived logs. Unexpected Backup Activity SQL> SELECT bs.database_name, bs.backup_start_date, bs.user_name, bmf.physical_device_name FROM msdb.dbo.backupset bs JOIN msdb.dbo.backupmediafamily bmf ON bs.media_set_id = bmf.media_set_id WHERE bmf.physical_device_name LIKE '\\\\%' OR bmf.physical_device_name LIKE 'C:\Users\%' ORDER BY bs.backup_start_date DESC; Finds backups written to UNC paths or user profile folders instead of the approved backup target, a strong exfiltration indicator. Linked Server Inventory SQL> SELECT s.name, s.data_source, s.is_rpc_out_enabled, l.remote_name FROM sys.servers s LEFT JOIN sys.linked_logins l ON s.server_id = l.server_id WHERE s.is_linked = 1; Linked servers with RPC out enabled allow command execution to pivot between instances. Any unexpected entry warrants investigation. Off-Hours Sensitive Table Access SIEM> source="mssql:audit" object_name IN ("PaymentCards","Customers") | eval hr=strftime(_time,"%H") | where hr<6 OR hr>20 | stats count by server_principal_name, client_ip, object_name Correlates access to regulated tables outside business hours, one of the highest fidelity insider threat signals. Audit Tampering SIEM> source="mssql:audit" action_id IN ("AUSC","AUAC","ASSC") | table _time, server_principal_name, client_ip, statement Any change to an audit object or specification should be alerted on immediately. Legitimate changes are rare and scheduled.

s.h: Best Practices for SQL Server Logging
s.t: Apply these practices to make SQL Server logging complete, durable, and actually usable during an investigation: 01 Forward Audit Logs Off the Host An attacker with sysadmin can delete .sqlaudit files. Ship audit records to a SIEM continuously, or target the Windows Security log, so that evidence survives compromise of the database itself. 02 Increase Error Log Retention SQL Server keeps only six archived error logs by default and cycles on every restart. Raise the count to at least 30 and schedule sp_cycle_errorlog nightly so a restart cannot destroy weeks of history. 03 Always Audit the Auditors Include AUDIT_CHANGE_GROUP in every server audit specification and alert on it in real time. Disabling auditing is a standard step in the attacker playbook and should never happen silently. 04 Audit Sensitive Tables Explicitly Server-level audit specifications never record row access. Identify tables holding personal, financial, or health data and create database audit specifications naming those objects directly. 05 Separate the Audit Volume Write audit files to a dedicated disk with its own capacity monitoring. If the audit target fills up under ON_FAILURE = CONTINUE, auditing stops while the database happily keeps serving queries. 06 Baseline Application Identities Record which application names, host names, and source IPs each service account normally uses. A service account logging in from sqlcmd or SSMS instead of its application is an immediate red flag. 07 Synchronize Time to a Trusted Source SQL Server Audit stamps events in UTC while the error log uses local server time. Ensure NTP synchronization and normalize both to UTC at ingest so correlation across sources holds up. 08 Preserve the Default Trace Do not disable the Default Trace for performance reasons. Its overhead is negligible and it regularly provides the only surviving record of schema and configuration changes on unmonitored instances.

Recognising how attacks appear in real SQL Server log output is what turns configuration into detection. Below are representative entries from the error log and SQL Server Audit. Failed Login: Password Mismatch (Brute Force) 2025-07-14 09:41:22.81 Logon Error: 18456, Severity: 14, State: 8. 2025-07-14 09:41:22.81 Logon Login failed for user 'sa'. Reason: Password did not match that for the login provided. [CLIENT: 203.0.113.77] State 8 confirms the login exists and the password was wrong. Repeated entries for 'sa' from a single external IP is textbook brute force against the built-in administrator account. Failed Login: Unknown User (Account Enumeration) 2025-07-14 09:43:07.12 Logon Error: 18456, Severity: 14, State: 5. 2025-07-14 09:43:07.12 Logon Login failed for user 'admin'. Reason: Could not find a login matching the name provided. [CLIENT: 203.0.113.77] State 5 means the account name itself does not exist. A rapid series of state 5 events with different usernames from one source is enumeration, not a user error. Privilege Escalation: Sysadmin Role Granted event_time action_id succeeded server_principal_name target_server_principal_name statement 2025-07-14 10:02:55.447 APRL 1 svc_reporting bkp_admin ALTER SERVER ROLE [sysadmin] ADD MEMBER [bkp_admin]; client_ip = 10.20.4.87 application_name = Microsoft SQL Server Management Studio host_name = WKS-FIN-014 A service account (svc_reporting) adding another login to sysadmin from an interactive SSMS session on a finance workstation. Service accounts should never perform role changes interactively. Command Execution: xp_cmdshell Enabled 2025-07-14 10:05:31.09 spid73 Configuration option 'show advanced options' changed from 0 to 1. Run the RECONFIGURE statement to install. 2025-07-14 10:05:31.44 spid73 Configuration option 'xp_cmdshell' changed from 0 to 1. Run the RECONFIGURE statement to install. The two-step pattern of enabling advanced options followed immediately by xp_cmdshell is the standard route from SQL injection or a compromised sysadmin account to operating system command execution. Data Exfiltration: Bulk Read of a Sensitive Table event_time action_id succeeded server_principal_name database_name object_name statement 2025-07-14 02:17:44.902 SL 1 svc_reporting CustomerDB PaymentCards SELECT * FROM dbo.PaymentCards client_ip = 10.20.4.87 application_name = sqlcmd host_name = WKS-FIN-014 session_id = 73 An unfiltered SELECT against a payment card table at 02:17 using sqlcmd rather than the reporting application. Time of day, tool, and lack of a WHERE clause together make this high confidence. Anti-Forensics: Audit Specification Disabled event_time action_id succeeded server_principal_name statement 2025-07-14 10:11:03.276 ASSC 1 bkp_admin ALTER SERVER AUDIT SPECIFICATION [HTL_Server_Spec] WITH (STATE = OFF); client_ip = 10.20.4.87 application_name = Microsoft SQL Server Management Studio The newly escalated account immediately turns off auditing. Because AUDIT_CHANGE_GROUP was enabled, this final action was itself recorded before logging stopped. Persistence: SQL Agent Job Running OS Commands 2025-07-14 10:24:18 - ! [298] SQLServer Error: 22022, Job 'IndexMaintenance_Nightly' step 2 subsystem 'CmdExec' command: powershell.exe -enc SQBFAFgAIAAoAE4AZQB3AC0ATwBiAGoAZQBjAHQA... 2025-07-14 10:24:19 - + [396] An idle CPU condition has not been defined - OnIdle job schedules will have no effect A maintenance job modified to run base64-encoded PowerShell through the CmdExec subsystem. SQL Agent jobs execute under the Agent service account and are a durable persistence mechanism that survives reboots. Back

Oracle Database separates diagnostic logging from security auditing, and the two live in completely different places. Diagnostic output (instance startup, ORA- errors, structural changes, and background process messages) is written to the alert log and trace files inside the Automatic Diagnostic Repository (ADR). Security auditing is written to the database itself, either to the modern UNIFIED_AUDIT_TRAIL introduced in Oracle 12c or to the legacy AUD$ table used by earlier releases. A third stream, the listener log , sits outside the database entirely and records every connection request that reaches the instance, including those that never authenticate successfully. Unified Auditing consolidated what used to be at least six separate audit trails into a single read-only view. It is enabled in mixed mode by default from 12c onward, which means a small set of predefined policies is active but most security-relevant activity is not captured until an administrator explicitly enables the right policies. Oracle ships several ready-made policies ( ORA_SECURECONFIG , ORA_LOGON_FAILURES , ORA_ACCOUNT_MGMT , and ORA_DATABASE_PARAMETER ), and enabling them takes a single statement each, yet they remain switched off on a large proportion of production estates. For sensitive data, Unified Auditing alone can be too coarse. Fine-Grained Auditing (FGA) allows a policy to fire only when a specific column is selected or when a boolean condition is met, so you can audit access to a salary column without generating a record for every query against the employee table. Combined with the alert log for structural events and the listener log for connection-level reconnaissance, these sources give a complete picture that satisfies the privileged-activity and sensitive-data monitoring requirements in NIST SP 800-92 and the Saudi NCA controls.

Oracle produces several log streams with very different retention, format, and access models. Knowing which one answers which question saves critical time during an investigation: Log Type Description Alert Log The chronological diagnostic log for the instance, available as plain text (alert_<SID>.log) and as structured XML (log.xml). Records startup and shutdown, ORA- errors, tablespace and datafile changes, redo log switches, and ALTER SYSTEM operations. Always the first artifact to review. Unified Audit Trail The consolidated security audit trail exposed through the UNIFIED_AUDIT_TRAIL view. Captures logon and logoff, privilege use, DDL, DML, Data Pump and RMAN activity, and Database Vault events in a single read-only stream. Cannot be modified with DML, even by SYS. Listener Log Written by the TNS listener process outside the database. Records every connection request with source host, program name, and service name, including attempts that fail before authentication. The primary source for detecting service enumeration and TNS-level attacks. Fine-Grained Audit Trail Policy-driven auditing at column and row granularity, queried through DBA_FGA_AUDIT_TRAIL or the unified trail. Fires only when a defined condition matches, which makes it the practical way to audit access to sensitive columns without overwhelming volume. Traditional Audit Trail (AUD$) The pre-12c audit trail stored in SYS.AUD$ and surfaced through DBA_AUDIT_TRAIL, plus optional OS-file and XML destinations. Still present in mixed-mode deployments. Unlike the unified trail it lives in a normal table, so a privileged attacker can delete rows from it. Trace Files and Incident Dumps Per-process trace files and ADR incident packages generated on serious errors. Contain SQL text, bind variables, and call stacks. Highly sensitive because bind data can include cleartext credentials and personal data. Redo and Archive Logs The change stream used for recovery and replication. Not a security log, but with LogMiner it can reconstruct DML that no audit policy captured, provided the relevant archive logs are still retained. Pro Tip: The unified audit trail is protected against DML, but records are still purgeable through DBMS_AUDIT_MGMT.CLEAN_AUDIT_TRAIL . Audit that package explicitly, otherwise a privileged attacker can erase the trail through a supported interface without ever issuing a DELETE.

Oracle 11g and later organise diagnostic output under the ADR base, whose root is normally $ORACLE_BASE . Resolve the exact paths for a running instance rather than assuming defaults. Log Default Location Alert Log (text) $ORACLE_BASE/diag/rdbms/<db_name>/<instance>/trace/alert_<SID>.log Alert Log (XML) $ORACLE_BASE/diag/rdbms/<db_name>/<instance>/alert/log.xml Listener Log $ORACLE_BASE/diag/tnslsnr/<hostname>/listener/trace/listener.log Unified Audit Trail AUDSYS schema in the database; spillover files in $ORACLE_BASE/audit/<instance>/ when the database is unavailable Mandatory SYSDBA Audit $ORACLE_BASE/admin/<db_name>/adump/ (controlled by AUDIT_FILE_DEST) User and Background Traces $ORACLE_BASE/diag/rdbms/<db_name>/<instance>/trace/ Incident Dumps $ORACLE_BASE/diag/rdbms/<db_name>/<instance>/incident/ Pro Tip: Run SELECT value FROM v$diag_info WHERE name = 'Diag Trace'; to get the exact trace directory, or use adrci with show alert -tail -f to follow the alert log live without hunting for the path.

Unified Auditing works through named policies. You create a policy describing what to capture, then enable it, optionally scoped to specific users or excluding noisy service accounts. All statements require the AUDIT_ADMIN role. Step 1: Confirm the Auditing Mode SELECT value FROM v$option WHERE parameter = 'Unified Auditing'; -- TRUE = pure unified auditing -- FALSE = mixed mode (traditional AUD$ still active alongside unified) SELECT policy_name, enabled_option, entity_name, success, failure FROM audit_unified_enabled_policies ORDER BY policy_name; Establishes which mode the database runs in and which policies are already enabled. On a default 19c installation expect only ORA_SECURECONFIG and ORA_LOGON_FAILURES. Step 2: Enable the Oracle-Supplied Baseline Policies AUDIT POLICY ORA_SECURECONFIG; AUDIT POLICY ORA_LOGON_FAILURES; AUDIT POLICY ORA_ACCOUNT_MGMT; AUDIT POLICY ORA_DATABASE_PARAMETER; AUDIT POLICY ORA_DV_AUDPOL; -- only if Database Vault is licensed AUDIT POLICY ORA_RAS_POLICY_MGMT; -- Real Application Security policy changes Covers privilege and role grants, security configuration changes, account creation and modification, and failed logons with almost no tuning effort. This is the minimum viable audit baseline. Step 3: Create a Custom Policy for Privileged Activity CREATE AUDIT POLICY htl_privileged_activity PRIVILEGES CREATE ANY TABLE, DROP ANY TABLE, SELECT ANY TABLE, ALTER ANY TABLE, CREATE ANY PROCEDURE, EXECUTE ANY PROCEDURE, GRANT ANY PRIVILEGE, GRANT ANY ROLE, BECOME USER ACTIONS LOGON, LOGOFF, CREATE USER, ALTER USER, DROP USER, CREATE ROLE, GRANT, REVOKE, ALTER SYSTEM, ALTER DATABASE ACTIONS COMPONENT = DATAPUMP EXPORT, IMPORT CONTAINER = CURRENT; AUDIT POLICY htl_privileged_activity; Combines system privilege use, security-relevant actions, and Data Pump component auditing in one policy. Data Pump coverage matters because expdp is the most convenient bulk exfiltration tool on any Oracle host. Step 4: Audit Sensitive Objects Only CREATE AUDIT POLICY htl_pii_access ACTIONS SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE ON hr.employees, SELECT ON finance.payment_cards, SELECT ON hr.salaries; AUDIT POLICY htl_pii_access EXCEPT app_service_user; Object-level auditing scoped to regulated tables. The EXCEPT clause suppresses the high-volume application account while still recording every human and every other identity that touches the data. Step 5: Add Fine-Grained Auditing for Column-Level Sensitivity BEGIN DBMS_FGA.ADD_POLICY( object_schema => 'HR', object_name => 'EMPLOYEES', policy_name => 'FGA_SALARY_ACCESS', audit_column => 'SALARY, NATIONAL_ID', audit_condition => NULL, statement_types => 'SELECT,UPDATE', audit_trail => DBMS_FGA.DB + DBMS_FGA.EXTENDED); END; / Fires only when the SALARY or NATIONAL_ID column is referenced. The EXTENDED trail additionally records the full SQL text and bind variables, which is what makes the record actionable. Step 6: Configure Audit Trail Retention and Purging BEGIN DBMS_AUDIT_MGMT.INIT_CLEANUP( audit_trail_type => DBMS_AUDIT_MGMT.AUDIT_TRAIL_UNIFIED, default_cleanup_interval => 24); DBMS_AUDIT_MGMT.SET_LAST_ARCHIVE_TIMESTAMP( audit_trail_type => DBMS_AUDIT_MGMT.AUDIT_TRAIL_UNIFIED, last_archive_time => SYSTIMESTAMP - 180); DBMS_AUDIT_MGMT.CREATE_PURGE_JOB( audit_trail_type => DBMS_AUDIT_MGMT.AUDIT_TRAIL_UNIFIED, audit_trail_purge_interval => 24, audit_trail_purge_name => 'HTL_UNIFIED_PURGE', use_last_arch_timestamp => TRUE); END; / Purges only records older than the archive timestamp, guaranteeing that 180 days remain queryable. Without a purge job the AUDSYS tablespace grows until the database stops accepting connections. Security Note: Auditing of SYSDBA and SYSOPER connections is mandatory and cannot be disabled, but those records are written as operating system files in AUDIT_FILE_DEST , not into the database. Anyone with OS-level access to the Oracle account can delete them, so forward that directory to a remote collector.

Oracle ships a set of predefined unified audit policies that cover the majority of regulatory requirements. Enabling them costs nothing and requires no tuning, yet they are frequently left disabled. ORA_SECURECONFIG Audits security-critical configuration: ALTER SYSTEM, privilege and role grants, user creation, audit policy changes, and Data Pump activity. The single most valuable policy on the instance. Enable Critical ORA_LOGON_FAILURES Records every unsuccessful logon with the originating host and program. The basis for brute force, password spraying, and default-credential detection. Enable Critical ORA_ACCOUNT_MGMT Captures CREATE USER, ALTER USER, DROP USER, CREATE ROLE, and profile changes. Detects backdoor accounts and password resets on dormant identities. Enable Critical ORA_DATABASE_PARAMETER Audits changes to initialization parameters through ALTER SYSTEM and ALTER DATABASE. Catches attempts to weaken security settings such as O7_DICTIONARY_ACCESSIBILITY or REMOTE_OS_AUTHENT. Enable High Risk Data Pump Component Auditing ACTIONS COMPONENT = DATAPUMP records export and import operations. An unscheduled expdp of a full schema is one of the clearest bulk exfiltration signals Oracle produces. Enable High Risk Fine-Grained Audit Policies Column and condition scoped auditing through DBMS_FGA. The only practical way to monitor access to a sensitive column on a high-traffic table without unusable volume. Enable Medium Risk Security Note: Enabling a policy with AUDIT POLICY p BY user restricts it to that user, while EXCEPT user excludes them. Using BY on a policy intended for whole-instance coverage is a common misconfiguration that silently leaves everyone else unaudited.

The UNIFIED_AUDIT_TRAIL view exposes more than ninety columns. These are the fields that carry investigative value and should be mapped into your SIEM schema. Field Description Category Example Value EVENT_TIMESTAMP_UTC UTC time the audited event occurred Timestamp 2025-07-14 06:41:22.481 DBUSERNAME Database user who performed the action Identity APP_REPORT CLIENT_PROGRAM_NAME Client executable that opened the session Source sqlplus.exe USERHOST Hostname of the connecting client Source WKS-DBA-03 OS_USERNAME Operating system account of the client Identity a.alharbi ACTION_NAME The audited action performed Action SELECT OBJECT_SCHEMA Schema owning the target object Target HR OBJECT_NAME Name of the object acted upon Target EMPLOYEES SQL_TEXT Full statement text (requires EXTENDED trail) Action SELECT salary FROM hr.employees SQL_BINDS Bind variable values supplied with the statement Action #1(3):101 RETURN_CODE ORA error number, 0 on success Result 1017 SYSTEM_PRIVILEGE_USED System privilege exercised to permit the action Authorization SELECT ANY TABLE AUDIT_TYPE Source of the record Metadata Standard / FineGrainedAudit / Datapump SESSIONID Audit session identifier Session 4294967295

These ORA codes appear in the alert log, the listener log, and the RETURN_CODE column of the unified audit trail. They are the highest-signal values to alert on. Code Meaning Why It Matters ORA-01017 Invalid username or password The core failed-authentication code. Repetition against one account is brute force; across many accounts it is password spraying ORA-28000 The account is locked Confirms a brute force attempt reached the FAILED_LOGIN_ATTEMPTS profile limit, or that an attacker locked out a legitimate account ORA-28001 The password has expired Frequently reveals dormant or forgotten service accounts being probed with old credentials ORA-01031 Insufficient privileges A valid session attempting actions beyond its grants, a strong indicator of post-compromise privilege probing ORA-00942 Table or view does not exist In bursts this is object enumeration or blind SQL injection rather than an application defect ORA-12514 Listener does not know of the requested service Service name enumeration against the listener, a standard first step in Oracle reconnaissance ORA-12541 No listener Port scanning or an attempt to reach a listener that has been stopped, possibly by an attacker ORA-01578 Data block corrupted Storage failure or deliberate tampering with datafiles at the operating system level ORA-00600 / ORA-07445 Internal error / core dump Engine-level faults that can result from exploitation attempts against the database process itself Pro Tip: ORA-01017 events reach the unified audit trail only if ORA_LOGON_FAILURES or an equivalent policy is enabled. If your instance shows zero failed logons over a long period, assume the policy is missing rather than concluding nobody is attacking you.

Run these against the unified audit trail and the listener log to detect authentication attacks, privilege abuse, bulk exports, and audit tampering. Failed Logon Bursts SQL> SELECT dbusername, userhost, client_program_name, COUNT(*) AS fails FROM unified_audit_trail WHERE action_name = 'LOGON' AND return_code = 1017 AND event_timestamp > SYSTIMESTAMP - INTERVAL '1' HOUR GROUP BY dbusername, userhost, client_program_name HAVING COUNT(*) > 5 ORDER BY fails DESC; Groups ORA-01017 failures by account and source host to separate a mistyped password from a sustained attack. Privilege and Role Grants SQL> SELECT event_timestamp, dbusername, action_name, object_name, sql_text FROM unified_audit_trail WHERE action_name IN ('GRANT','REVOKE','CREATE USER','ALTER USER') ORDER BY event_timestamp DESC FETCH FIRST 100 ROWS ONLY; Every grant of DBA, SYSDBA, or ANY privileges should be reconciled against a change ticket. Data Pump Export Activity SQL> SELECT event_timestamp, dbusername, userhost, dp_text_parameters1, dp_boolean_parameters1 FROM unified_audit_trail WHERE audit_type = 'Datapump' ORDER BY event_timestamp DESC; Reveals expdp jobs including the schemas and dump file paths requested. Unscheduled full-schema exports are prime exfiltration candidates. SYSDBA Connections SQL> SELECT event_timestamp, dbusername, os_username, userhost, client_program_name FROM unified_audit_trail WHERE dbusername = 'SYS' OR system_privilege_used LIKE '%SYSDBA%' ORDER BY event_timestamp DESC; SYSDBA sessions bypass most access control. Every one should map to a named human and an approved maintenance window. Audit Trail Purging SQL> SELECT event_timestamp, dbusername, action_name, object_name, sql_text FROM unified_audit_trail WHERE object_name = 'DBMS_AUDIT_MGMT' OR sql_text LIKE '%CLEAN_AUDIT_TRAIL%' OR action_name = 'NOAUDIT' ORDER BY event_timestamp DESC; Detects both supported purging of the audit trail and NOAUDIT statements disabling policies. Alert on these in real time. Listener Service Enumeration bash> grep "TNS-12514" $ORACLE_BASE/diag/tnslsnr/$(hostname)/listener/trace/listener.log | awk -F'HOST=' '{print $2}' | cut -d')' -f1 | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head Counts unknown-service errors per source host in the listener log, exposing hosts brute forcing SID and service names. Fine-Grained Audit Hits SQL> SELECT event_timestamp, dbusername, object_schema, object_name, fga_policy_name, sql_text FROM unified_audit_trail WHERE audit_type = 'FineGrainedAudit' ORDER BY event_timestamp DESC; Returns only the queries that actually touched an audited sensitive column, with full SQL text when the EXTENDED trail is used. Alert Log Errors bash> adrci exec="set home diag/rdbms/orcl/orcl; show alert -p \"message_text like '%ORA-%'\" -term" | tail -50 Extracts recent ORA- errors from the alert log through adrci without needing to locate the file manually. Verify Enabled Policies SQL> SELECT policy_name, enabled_option, entity_name, entity_type, success, failure FROM audit_unified_enabled_policies ORDER BY policy_name; Run this as a scheduled control check. A policy silently disappearing from this list means someone issued NOAUDIT. Off-Hours Sensitive Access SIEM> source="oracle:unified_audit" object_schema="HR" action_name="SELECT" | eval hr=strftime(_time,"%H") | where hr<6 OR hr>20 | stats count values(sql_text) by dbusername, userhost Correlates access to HR data outside working hours with the originating workstation, a high fidelity insider threat signal.

Follow these practices to keep Oracle audit data complete, performant, and trustworthy: 01 Move AUDSYS to Its Own Tablespace By default the unified audit trail lives in SYSAUX. A busy audit policy can fill SYSAUX and take the database down. Relocate AUDSYS with DBMS_AUDIT_MGMT.SET_AUDIT_TRAIL_LOCATION and monitor its growth separately. 02 Enable the Predefined Policies First ORA_SECURECONFIG, ORA_LOGON_FAILURES, and ORA_ACCOUNT_MGMT deliver the majority of required coverage with no tuning and negligible overhead. Turn them on before designing anything custom. 03 Forward the Trail Off the Database An attacker with AUDIT_ADMIN can purge records through supported interfaces. Continuously export the unified audit trail to a SIEM so the evidence exists somewhere the database administrator cannot reach. 04 Collect the Listener Log The listener log records connection attempts that never become sessions and therefore never appear in any audit trail. It is the only place service enumeration and pre-authentication attacks are visible. 05 Use FGA Instead of Blanket Object Auditing Auditing every SELECT on a high-traffic table produces volume nobody reads. A fine-grained policy on the sensitive columns delivers the same compliance outcome at a fraction of the cost. 06 Protect Trace Files and Incident Dumps Trace files can contain bind variable values including credentials and personal data. Restrict directory permissions, include them in data classification, and purge them on a defined schedule. 07 Schedule Purging, Never Manual Deletion Create a DBMS_AUDIT_MGMT purge job tied to an archive timestamp. Ad hoc purging is indistinguishable from anti-forensics and destroys the retention guarantee auditors rely on. 08 Alert on NOAUDIT Immediately Legitimate policy changes are rare and planned. Treat any NOAUDIT statement or audit policy drop as a potential incident and page on it rather than reviewing it in the next audit cycle.

These entries show how the same attack chain surfaces across the listener log, the alert log, and the unified audit trail. Listener Log: Service Name Enumeration 14-JUL-2025 06:12:44 * (CONNECT_DATA=(SID=ORCL)(CID=(PROGRAM=)(HOST=__jdbc__)(USER=))) * (ADDRESS=(PROTOCOL=tcp)(HOST=203.0.113.44)(PORT=51884)) * establish * ORCL * 12514 TNS-12514: TNS:listener does not currently know of service requested in connect descriptor An empty PROGRAM field and a generic __jdbc__ host, repeated with different SID values from one address, is automated service name brute forcing rather than a misconfigured client. Unified Audit Trail: Failed Logon (ORA-01017) EVENT_TIMESTAMP_UTC : 2025-07-14 06:41:22.481 DBUSERNAME : SYSTEM ACTION_NAME : LOGON RETURN_CODE : 1017 USERHOST : kali OS_USERNAME : root CLIENT_PROGRAM_NAME : sqlplus@kali (TNS V1-V3) AUTHENTICATION_TYPE : (TYPE=(DATABASE));(CLIENT ADDRESS=((PROTOCOL=tcp)(HOST=203.0.113.44)(PORT=51902))) Return code 1017 against the SYSTEM account, from an OS user named root on a host called kali. The client metadata alone is enough to justify immediate containment. Account Lockout After Brute Force (ORA-28000) EVENT_TIMESTAMP_UTC : 2025-07-14 06:44:10.229 DBUSERNAME : SYSTEM ACTION_NAME : LOGON RETURN_CODE : 28000 USERHOST : kali UNIFIED_AUDIT_POLICIES : ORA_LOGON_FAILURES The profile's FAILED_LOGIN_ATTEMPTS limit has been reached and the account is now locked. This also means a denial of service against a real account is trivially achievable. Privilege Escalation: DBA Role Granted EVENT_TIMESTAMP_UTC : 2025-07-14 07:02:18.774 DBUSERNAME : APP_ADMIN ACTION_NAME : GRANT OBJECT_NAME : DBA SQL_TEXT : GRANT DBA TO batch_svc SYSTEM_PRIVILEGE_USED : GRANT ANY ROLE USERHOST : appsrv01 CLIENT_PROGRAM_NAME : sqlplus.exe UNIFIED_AUDIT_POLICIES : ORA_SECURECONFIG An application account granting the DBA role to a batch service account. Application identities should never hold GRANT ANY ROLE, and this grant reaches full database control in one statement. Bulk Exfiltration: Unscheduled Data Pump Export EVENT_TIMESTAMP_UTC : 2025-07-14 07:19:53.006 AUDIT_TYPE : Datapump DBUSERNAME : BATCH_SVC DP_TEXT_PARAMETERS1 : MASTER TABLE: "BATCH_SVC"."SYS_EXPORT_SCHEMA_01" JOB_TYPE: EXPORT SCHEMAS: HR,FINANCE DUMPFILE: /tmp/.cache/exp01.dmp USERHOST : appsrv01 A full export of the HR and FINANCE schemas written to a hidden directory under /tmp. The dump file path is the strongest indicator here: legitimate exports go to a registered directory object. Fine-Grained Audit: Salary Column Access EVENT_TIMESTAMP_UTC : 2025-07-14 02:31:09.118 AUDIT_TYPE : FineGrainedAudit FGA_POLICY_NAME : FGA_SALARY_ACCESS DBUSERNAME : R_ALMUTAIRI OBJECT_SCHEMA : HR OBJECT_NAME : EMPLOYEES SQL_TEXT : SELECT employee_id, national_id, salary FROM hr.employees CLIENT_PROGRAM_NAME : Toad.exe USERHOST : WKS-HR-22 A full extract of national ID and salary columns at 02:31 using an ad hoc query tool. The FGA policy fired precisely because the protected columns were referenced. Alert Log: Security Parameter Weakened 2025-07-14T07:26:41.882110+03:00 ALTER SYSTEM SET remote_os_authent=TRUE SCOPE=SPFILE; 2025-07-14T07:27:03.441207+03:00 Shutting down instance (immediate) (OS id: 44219) Stopping background process SMON Setting REMOTE_OS_AUTHENT to TRUE allows a client to assert its own operating system identity for authentication. Followed immediately by a restart to apply it, this is a deliberate backdoor. Back

MySQL and MariaDB provide five distinct logs, and only one of them is enabled by default. The error log records server startup and shutdown, plugin loading, replication problems, and, depending on verbosity, aborted connections. The general query log captures every statement the server receives, the slow query log captures statements exceeding a duration threshold, and the binary log records every data-modifying statement for replication and point-in-time recovery. Security auditing proper comes from a plugin: MySQL Enterprise Audit on Oracle's commercial edition, or the freely available server_audit plugin bundled with MariaDB and packaged by Percona for MySQL. This split creates a well-known blind spot. The general query log is the only built-in source that shows what an attacker actually ran, but it logs everything from every client with no filtering, writes credentials in cleartext when a user runs SET PASSWORD , and imposes real overhead. As a result it is almost never enabled in production, and most MySQL estates have no record of executed statements at all. The audit plugin exists precisely to close that gap: it can be scoped to connections, queries, and table access, filtered by user, and written in a structured format suitable for a SIEM. MySQL is also unusual in how directly the database maps to operating system compromise. SELECT ... INTO OUTFILE writes attacker-controlled content anywhere the mysql user can write, which is the classic route from SQL injection to a web shell. LOAD DATA LOCAL INFILE can be turned against the client to read files from the connecting host. User-defined functions loaded from a shared library grant direct command execution. Every one of these leaves a trace, but only if the general query log or the audit plugin is capturing statements. Enabling one of them is the single highest-value logging change you can make to a MySQL server.

Each MySQL log answers a different question. Understanding the trade-off between coverage and overhead determines which combination is realistic for your environment: Log Type Description Error Log The only log enabled by default. Records server startup and shutdown, plugin initialisation, InnoDB recovery, replication errors, and aborted connections. At verbosity level 3 it also logs access denied messages, making it a usable authentication failure source without the cost of the general log. Audit Plugin Log Produced by MariaDB server_audit, Percona Audit Log, or MySQL Enterprise Audit. Records connections, disconnections, executed queries, and table access as structured JSON, XML, or CSV. The only production-appropriate way to get full statement visibility with filtering. General Query Log Logs every client connection and every statement received, in the order received, regardless of whether it succeeds. Complete but unfiltered and expensive. Useful for short, targeted investigation windows rather than continuous operation. Slow Query Log Records statements exceeding long_query_time and, optionally, those not using indexes. Primarily a performance tool, but valuable in security because bulk extraction queries and time-based blind SQL injection are both inherently slow. Binary Log The replication and recovery stream containing every data-modifying statement or row change. Readable with mysqlbinlog. Frequently the only surviving evidence of an UPDATE or DELETE when no audit plugin was installed. Relay Log On replicas, the local copy of events received from the source server. Relevant when investigating whether malicious changes originated locally or were replicated in from a compromised primary. Pro Tip: If you cannot deploy an audit plugin, set log_error_verbosity = 3 and log_slow_extra = ON . The combination gives you authentication failures and slow bulk queries at almost no cost, which covers two of the three most common database attack signals.

Paths differ between distributions. Debian and Ubuntu packages use /var/log/mysql/ , while Red Hat family packages default to /var/log/ and the data directory. Log Default Location Error Log /var/log/mysql/error.log (Debian) or /var/log/mysqld.log (RHEL) General Query Log /var/log/mysql/mysql.log or <datadir>/<hostname>.log Slow Query Log /var/log/mysql/mysql-slow.log or <datadir>/<hostname>-slow.log Binary Logs /var/lib/mysql/binlog.000001 (MySQL 8) or /var/log/mysql/mysql-bin.000001 (Debian) Audit Plugin Log <datadir>/server_audit.log (MariaDB) or <datadir>/audit.log (Percona / Enterprise) Configuration File /etc/mysql/my.cnf, /etc/my.cnf, or /etc/mysql/mysql.conf.d/mysqld.cnf Windows Data Directory C:\ProgramData\MySQL\MySQL Server 8.0\Data\ Pro Tip: Never trust the packaged default. Run SHOW VARIABLES WHERE Variable_name IN ('log_error','general_log_file','slow_query_log_file','log_bin_basename','datadir'); to get the live paths from the running server.

Most logging can be switched on at runtime with SET GLOBAL, but the settings must also be written to the configuration file to survive a restart. The audit plugin must be installed before it can be configured. Step 1: Configure the Error Log for Full Verbosity [mysqld] log_error = /var/log/mysql/error.log log_error_verbosity = 3 # 1=errors, 2=+warnings, 3=+notes (includes access denied) log_timestamps = UTC # normalise timestamps for SIEM correlation log_error_services = 'log_filter_internal; log_sink_internal' Verbosity 3 is what makes failed connection attempts appear in the error log. UTC timestamps prevent correlation errors when the server is in a non-UTC timezone. Step 2: Install and Configure the MariaDB Audit Plugin -- Install the plugin (MariaDB, or Percona build of MySQL) INSTALL PLUGIN server_audit SONAME 'server_audit.so'; -- Verify it loaded SELECT plugin_name, plugin_status FROM information_schema.plugins WHERE plugin_name = 'SERVER_AUDIT'; The plugin must be present in the plugin_dir. Confirm with SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'plugin_dir' if the INSTALL statement fails to find the shared object. Step 3: Set the Audit Plugin Parameters [mysqld] plugin_load_add = server_audit server_audit_logging = ON server_audit_events = CONNECT,QUERY_DDL,QUERY_DML,QUERY_DCL,TABLE server_audit_output_type = FILE server_audit_file_path = /var/log/mysql/server_audit.log server_audit_file_rotate_size = 1000000000 server_audit_file_rotations = 30 server_audit_excl_users = app_readonly # suppress high-volume app noise server_audit_query_log_limit = 1024 Capturing CONNECT, DDL, DML, DCL, and TABLE events gives authentication, schema change, data change, and privilege change coverage. Excluding a single read-only application account removes most of the volume without losing security signal. Step 4: Enable the Slow Query Log [mysqld] slow_query_log = ON slow_query_log_file = /var/log/mysql/mysql-slow.log long_query_time = 2 log_queries_not_using_indexes = ON log_slow_extra = ON # MySQL 8.0.14+: adds rows_examined, errors, bytes sent log_slow_extra adds the rows examined and bytes sent counters, which turn the slow log into a practical bulk-extraction detector rather than a pure performance tool. Step 5: Enable the General Query Log Temporarily -- Runtime only, no restart, no persistence across restart SET GLOBAL general_log_file = '/var/log/mysql/investigation.log'; SET GLOBAL general_log = 'ON'; -- ... capture the window you need, then ... SET GLOBAL general_log = 'OFF'; The correct pattern for incident response: turn it on for a bounded window, collect, turn it off. Leaving it on in production degrades throughput and writes sensitive values in cleartext. Step 6: Harden File Access Privileges [mysqld] secure_file_priv = /var/lib/mysql-files # restrict OUTFILE/INFILE to one directory local_infile = OFF # block LOAD DATA LOCAL INFILE log_bin = /var/lib/mysql/binlog binlog_expire_logs_seconds = 2592000 # 30 days of binary log retention secure_file_priv is the control that prevents SELECT INTO OUTFILE from dropping a web shell into the document root. Setting it to an empty value disables the restriction entirely and should be treated as a finding. Security Note: The general query log records statements before they are parsed, which means SET PASSWORD , CREATE USER ... IDENTIFIED BY , and application connection strings appear in cleartext. Treat the file as a credential store: restrict it to mode 0600, exclude it from general log shipping, and purge it after the investigation.

The server_audit plugin groups events into classes controlled by the server_audit_events variable. This baseline balances coverage against volume on a typical production server. CONNECT Logs successful connections, failed connections, and disconnections with source host and username. The foundation for brute force detection and session reconstruction. Enable Critical QUERY_DCL Captures GRANT, REVOKE, CREATE USER, DROP USER, and SET PASSWORD. Every privilege escalation and backdoor account creation passes through this class. Enable Critical QUERY_DDL Records CREATE, ALTER, and DROP of databases, tables, functions, and triggers. Detects malicious UDF creation and destructive schema changes. Enable High Risk TABLE Emits a record naming each table touched by a statement, without the full query text. A compact way to monitor access to sensitive tables at manageable volume. Enable High Risk QUERY_DML Logs INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, and optionally SELECT. High volume on transactional systems, so consider QUERY_DML_NO_SELECT to keep writes without the read flood. Tune Medium Risk server_audit_excl_users Excludes named accounts from auditing. Use it for a single high-volume read-only application user, never for administrative or write-capable accounts. Tune Medium Risk Security Note: An attacker with SUPER privilege can disable auditing at runtime with SET GLOBAL server_audit_logging = OFF . The plugin records this change as its final entry, so alert on any audit configuration event rather than assuming a quiet log means a quiet server.

The server_audit plugin writes comma-separated records with a fixed field order. Mapping these positions correctly is the first step in any MySQL SIEM integration. Field Description Category Example Value timestamp Event time in server timezone Timestamp 20250714 09:41:22 serverhost Hostname of the database server Metadata db-prod-01 username Account used for the connection Identity app_rw host Client hostname or IP address Source 10.30.2.61 connectionid Server-assigned connection identifier Session 84213 queryid Sequential query identifier within the session Session 91744 operation Event class of the record Action QUERY / CONNECT / TABLE database Default schema for the statement Target shopdb object Statement text, or table name for TABLE events Action SELECT * FROM customers retcode MySQL error code, 0 on success Result 1045 Pro Tip: Return code 1045 is access denied, 1044 is access denied for a database, and 1142 is a missing table-level privilege. Alerting on 1142 catches an authenticated attacker probing tables their account cannot reach.

These are the statements and errors most worth building detections around. Each maps to a specific stage of a MySQL compromise. Pattern Technique Why It Matters SELECT ... INTO OUTFILE File write Writes arbitrary content to any path the mysql user can reach. The standard route from SQL injection to a web shell in the document root LOAD DATA LOCAL INFILE File read A malicious server can request arbitrary files from the connecting client, turning a database connection into client-side file theft CREATE FUNCTION ... SONAME Command execution Loads a user-defined function from a shared library, giving direct operating system command execution as the mysql user GRANT ALL ... WITH GRANT OPTION Privilege escalation Full privilege grant, frequently to a newly created account with an innocuous name such as backup or monitor SELECT ... FROM mysql.user Credential access Reads password hashes directly from the system schema for offline cracking Error 1045 bursts Brute force Access denied for user, repeated from one source. The core authentication attack signal UNION SELECT / information_schema SQL injection Schema enumeration through injected queries, usually visible in the general or audit log even when the application logs nothing SLEEP() / BENCHMARK() Blind SQL injection Time-based inference. Appears in the slow query log by definition because the attack works by making queries slow DROP DATABASE / TRUNCATE Destruction Ransom and wiper activity. Also seen as the cleanup stage after exfiltration completes

Use these shell and SQL commands to extract authentication attacks, file operations, privilege changes, and bulk extraction from MySQL logs. Failed Logins by Source bash> grep "Access denied for user" /var/log/mysql/error.log | grep -oP "@'\K[^']+" | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -20 Counts access-denied events per source host. Requires log_error_verbosity set to 3. Web Shell Drop Attempts bash> grep -iE "into (outfile|dumpfile)" /var/log/mysql/server_audit.log Any hit deserves immediate investigation. Legitimate applications almost never write files through the database engine. UDF Command Execution bash> grep -iE "create function.*soname|sys_exec|sys_eval" /var/log/mysql/server_audit.log Detects loading of a user-defined function library, the standard MySQL-to-shell escalation. sys_exec and sys_eval are the canonical function names. Privilege and Account Changes bash> grep -iE "grant |create user|drop user|set password|alter user" /var/log/mysql/server_audit.log | grep -v "app_deploy" Filters out the known deployment account so only unexpected privilege changes remain. Password Hash Theft bash> grep -iE "from mysql\.(user|global_priv)" /var/log/mysql/server_audit.log Direct reads of the system credential tables. Only monitoring tools and DBAs should ever appear here. SQL Injection Indicators bash> grep -iE "union.+select|information_schema\.(tables|columns)|sleep\([0-9]|benchmark\(" /var/log/mysql/server_audit.log Catches schema enumeration and time-based blind injection reaching the database even when the web tier logs nothing useful. Bulk Extraction via Slow Log bash> mysqldumpslow -s c -t 20 /var/log/mysql/mysql-slow.log Aggregates the slow log by normalised query. With log_slow_extra enabled, look for high Rows_sent values against customer tables. Reconstruct Changes from Binlog bash> mysqlbinlog --base64-output=DECODE-ROWS --verbose --start-datetime="2025-07-14 09:00:00" /var/lib/mysql/binlog.000042 | grep -iE "^### (DELETE|UPDATE)" -A 5 Recovers row-level changes when no audit plugin was running. Often the only way to prove what an attacker modified. Audit Account Privileges SQL> SELECT user, host, plugin, account_locked, password_expired FROM mysql.user WHERE Super_priv='Y' OR File_priv='Y' OR Create_user_priv='Y'; Lists every account holding SUPER, FILE, or CREATE USER. FILE privilege is what makes INTO OUTFILE possible and should be held by nobody. Audit Plugin Disabled SIEM> source="mysql:audit" object IN ("SET GLOBAL server_audit_logging=OFF","UNINSTALL PLUGIN server_audit") OR object="*server_audit_events*" | table _time, username, host, object The plugin logs its own shutdown as the last record written. Treat any gap in audit records as an incident until proven otherwise.

Apply these practices to get real security visibility from MySQL without crippling performance: 01 Deploy an Audit Plugin The built-in logs were designed for troubleshooting, not security. server_audit or an equivalent plugin is the only way to get filtered, structured statement visibility that a production server can sustain. 02 Set Error Log Verbosity to 3 At the default verbosity, failed authentication is not recorded at all. This one-line change gives you brute force detection at effectively zero cost. 03 Restrict secure_file_priv Point it at a single dedicated directory and never leave it empty. This is the control that stops SELECT INTO OUTFILE from writing a web shell into a web-accessible path. 04 Keep the General Log for Investigations Only Enable it at runtime for a bounded window, collect what you need, then disable it. It writes credentials in cleartext and measurably reduces throughput when left running. 05 Retain Binary Logs for at Least 30 Days The binary log is frequently the only record of what data an attacker changed. Set binlog_expire_logs_seconds deliberately rather than accepting whatever the distribution shipped. 06 Ship Logs Off the Host Immediately MySQL log files are owned by the mysql user and are trivially deleted by anyone who compromises the service. Forward with rsyslog or a log agent so a local wipe does not destroy the evidence. 07 Normalise Timestamps to UTC Set log_timestamps to UTC. MySQL defaults vary between versions and distributions, and mixed timezones across a replica set make timeline reconstruction unreliable. 08 Exclude Only Read-Only Accounts When tuning audit volume, exclude a single read-only application user at most. Excluding an account that can write, grant, or administer defeats the purpose of auditing entirely.

Real output from the error log, the audit plugin, and the slow query log, showing how a MySQL compromise unfolds across sources. Error Log: Brute Force Against root 2025-07-14T09:41:22.481203Z 84210 [Note] [MY-010926] [Server] Access denied for user 'root'@'203.0.113.44' (using password: YES) 2025-07-14T09:41:22.902118Z 84211 [Note] [MY-010926] [Server] Access denied for user 'root'@'203.0.113.44' (using password: YES) 2025-07-14T09:41:23.334902Z 84212 [Note] [MY-010926] [Server] Access denied for user 'root'@'203.0.113.44' (using password: YES) Three failures in under two seconds from one external address. "using password: YES" confirms a password was supplied, distinguishing an attack from a misconfigured client connecting with no credentials. Audit Log: Successful Connection After Brute Force 20250714 09:44:07,db-prod-01,root,203.0.113.44,84219,0,CONNECT,,,0 20250714 09:44:11,db-prod-01,root,203.0.113.44,84219,91740,QUERY,,'SELECT @@version, @@datadir, @@secure_file_priv',0 20250714 09:44:15,db-prod-01,root,203.0.113.44,84219,91741,QUERY,mysql,'SELECT user,host,authentication_string FROM mysql.user',0 Return code 0 on CONNECT means the brute force succeeded. The immediate follow-up queries fingerprint the server and dump password hashes: textbook post-authentication reconnaissance. Audit Log: Web Shell Written via INTO OUTFILE 20250714 09:47:33,db-prod-01,root,203.0.113.44,84219,91746,QUERY,shopdb,'SELECT 0x3C3F70687020737973... INTO OUTFILE \'/var/www/html/uploads/config.php\'',0 20250714 09:47:33,db-prod-01,root,203.0.113.44,84219,91746,TABLE,shopdb,,0 Hex-encoded PHP written directly into the web root. This succeeds only when secure_file_priv is empty and the account holds FILE privilege: two configuration failures combining into remote code execution.
