Outbound blocking caught it, and that block is the clearest possible account compromise alert. Back

An Intrusion Detection System observes traffic and reports what it recognises. An Intrusion Prevention System sits inline and can drop the traffic instead. The distinction is a deployment decision rather than a product one, and it matters enormously when reading the logs: an IDS alert means something was seen, while an IPS alert with a drop action means something was stopped. Confusing the two leads analysts to chase attacks that never landed, or worse, to assume an attack was blocked when the sensor was only watching. Detection engines fall into two broad families. Signature based engines match traffic against rules describing known attack patterns, a model shared by open source engines such as Suricata and Snort and by commercial platforms from Palo Alto Networks, Cisco, Fortinet, Check Point, and Trellix. Anomaly and behaviour based engines instead build a baseline of normal traffic and alert on deviation from it. Whatever the vendor, a detection event carries the same core elements: a rule or threat identifier, a classification, a severity, the five-tuple of the connection, the action taken, and often the payload that triggered it. The field names differ between platforms, the meaning does not, and the mapping table further down this page lines the common ones up. Most sensors emit far more than alerts. Protocol transaction records document every observed HTTP request, DNS query, TLS handshake, and file transfer regardless of whether a rule matched. Suricata calls this EVE JSON , Zeek writes one log per protocol, and commercial platforms expose the same data as traffic, URL, application, or connection events. That protocol metadata is frequently more valuable than the alerts themselves, because it provides context for events no signature covers. The persistent operational problem with these systems is signal to noise. A default ruleset on a busy link will generate tens of thousands of alerts a day, the overwhelming majority of them informational or irrelevant to the environment. Tuning is not optional maintenance, it is the difference between a functioning detection capability and an ignored console. Equally important is placement: a sensor that cannot see traffic cannot alert on it, and in networks where most traffic is encrypted, an IDS without TLS inspection or JA3 fingerprinting is blind to the payloads it was bought to inspect.

s.h: Key IDS and IPS Log Types
s.t: Modern sensors produce far more than alerts. Understanding each output stream determines how much value you extract from the deployment: Log Type Description Alert Log The core output. One record per rule match, containing the signature identifier, revision, message, classification, priority, and the connection five-tuple. In IPS mode it also carries the action taken, which is what tells you whether the traffic was blocked or merely observed. Unified Event Stream A single structured stream carrying alerts plus protocol transaction records under one schema. Suricata calls this EVE JSON, commercial platforms deliver the equivalent over syslog in CEF, LEEF, or JSON. Always the preferred output for SIEM integration because every event type shares a common set of fields. Protocol Transaction Logs Records of every observed HTTP request, TLS handshake, DNS query, and SMB session, regardless of whether any rule matched. Invaluable for hunting and for reconstructing an intrusion whose technique had no signature at the time. File Transaction and Extraction Log Metadata for files observed crossing the sensor, including name, size, MIME type, and hash. With file store enabled the file itself is written to disk, allowing retrospective analysis against threat intelligence. Flow and NetFlow Records Connection summaries with byte and packet counts in each direction plus duration. The basis for detecting beaconing, long-lived sessions, and asymmetric transfers that indicate exfiltration. Packet Capture (PCAP) The raw packets that triggered an alert, either the single triggering packet or a full session capture. The definitive evidence for confirming a detection but expensive to retain at scale. Engine and Statistics Log Sensor health output including packet drop counters, rule load errors, and memory usage. Critical and routinely ignored: a sensor dropping 40 percent of packets is missing 40 percent of attacks silently. Pro Tip: Collect the statistics log and alert on the drop counter, whatever your platform calls it: capture.kernel_drops on Suricata, dataplane packet descriptors on Palo Alto, snort instance drops on Firepower, IPS engine bypass on FortiGate. A sensor under-provisioned for its link produces fewer alerts, which looks exactly like a quiet network. Packet loss is the most common cause of an IDS missing an intrusion it had a valid signature for.

Software sensors write to the local filesystem, while appliances and managed services expose logs through a console, an API, or syslog forwarding rather than a path you can read directly. Know which model you are dealing with before planning collection. Platform Log Location or Access Method Suricata Unified JSON, text alerts, engine, statistics /var/log/suricata/eve.json, fast.log, suricata.log, stats.log. Config at /etc/suricata/suricata.yaml, rules under /var/lib/suricata/rules/ Snort Alert log and configuration /var/log/snort/alert or alert_fast.txt. Config at /etc/snort/snort.conf (Snort 2) or snort.lua (Snort 3) Zeek Per protocol transaction logs /opt/zeek/logs/current/ with notice.log, conn.log, http.log, dns.log, ssl.log, files.log Palo Alto Networks Threat, traffic, and WildFire logs Monitor tab in the web interface, show log threat in the CLI, or syslog forwarding via a Log Forwarding Profile. Panorama for aggregated retention Cisco Secure Firewall (Firepower, FTD) Intrusion events FMC under Analysis then Intrusions then Events. Export by eStreamer or syslog. Local troubleshooting via /var/log/messages and /ngfw/var/log/ Fortinet FortiGate IPS attack log Log and Report then Intrusion Prevention, execute log filter category ips in the CLI, or forwarding to FortiAnalyzer and syslog Check Point Threat Prevention logs SmartConsole under Logs and Monitor. On the management server $FWDIR/log/*.log, readable with fw log or exported by LEA and syslog Cloud and managed services Managed detection findings AWS GuardDuty and Network Firewall to CloudWatch Logs, S3, or EventBridge. Azure Firewall Premium IDPS to Azure Monitor. Retrieved by API rather than file Extracted files and packet capture Evidence artefacts /var/log/suricata/filestore/ on Suricata, packet capture attached to the event record on commercial platforms and downloaded from the console Pro Tip: For any software sensor, give the log directory its own volume. Full protocol logging on a busy link produces tens of gigabytes per day, and filling the root filesystem takes the sensor down along with everything else on the host. For appliances the same risk appears as silent log rollover, where the console shows only a few hours of history and older events are gone before anyone investigates.

Every platform exposes the same six decisions through different interfaces. The principle in each step below applies regardless of engine, and the snippet shows one concrete implementation alongside the equivalent on other platforms. Step 1: Emit Structured Output Rather Than Text # Suricata: structured JSON covering alerts and protocol records outputs: - eve-log: enabled: yes filename: eve.json community-id: true # portable flow hash for correlation types: - alert: payload: yes metadata: yes - http: extended: yes - dns: version: 2 - tls: extended: yes - files: force-hash: [md5, sha256] - flow # Palo Alto: Device > Log Settings, or a Log Forwarding Profile per rule # forward Threat and Traffic logs to syslog, format set to JSON or CEF # Cisco FTD: Policies > Intrusion > Logging, or stream events by eStreamer # FortiGate: config log syslogd setting, then set format cef # Check Point: SmartConsole log exporter, target format syslog or CEF Text alert formats drop most of the context the engine already has. Always choose the structured option, and where the platform supports a portable flow identifier such as community ID, enable it so sensor events join cleanly to firewall and proxy records. Step 2: Define What Counts as Internal # Suricata and Snort: named address and port variables vars: address-groups: HOME_NET: "[10.0.0.0/8,192.168.0.0/16,172.16.0.0/12]" EXTERNAL_NET: "!$HOME_NET" HTTP_SERVERS: "[10.20.5.0/24]" DNS_SERVERS: "[10.10.0.10,10.10.0.11]" port-groups: HTTP_PORTS: "[80,81,8000,8080,8443]" # Palo Alto, FortiGate, Check Point: the same concept is expressed as # security zones and address objects applied to each policy rule # Cisco FTD: Objects > Variable Set, per intrusion policy Rules are written in terms of internal versus external. Whether your platform calls it HOME_NET, a trusted zone, or a variable set, defining it incorrectly is the single most common serious misconfiguration and silently breaks directionality across the whole ruleset. Step 3: Keep the Ruleset Current # Suricata: manage sources and reload without dropping traffic suricata-update list-sources suricata-update enable-source et/open suricata-update suricatasc -c reload-rules # Snort: PulledPork or the Talos subscription feed # Palo Alto: Device > Dynamic Updates, schedule Applications and Threats # Cisco FTD: System > Updates > Rule Updates, then redeploy the policy # FortiGate: FortiGuard IPS definitions, verify with # diagnose autoupdate versions | grep -A2 IPS Apply updates to a running sensor without a restart wherever the platform allows it, because restarting an inline sensor means a network outage. On commercial platforms a downloaded update does nothing until the policy is redeployed, which is a routinely missed step. Step 4: Tune Noisy Signatures Rather Than Deleting Them # Suricata: rate limit rather than remove # /etc/suricata/threshold.config threshold gen_id 1, sig_id 2001219, type limit, track by_src, count 1, seconds 60 suppress gen_id 1, sig_id 2001219, track by_src, ip 10.50.9.14 # /etc/suricata/disable.conf (last resort) 2013028 # expected User-Agent from internal monitoring # Palo Alto: Objects > Security Profiles > Anti-Spyware or Vulnerability, # add a Threat Exception scoped to a specific source or destination # Cisco FTD: set the rule state to Disabled, or add an event threshold # and a suppression entry scoped by source # FortiGate: IPS sensor filters with an exempt-ip entry Prefer thresholding and scoped exceptions over disabling. Thresholding keeps the detection alive at reduced volume, whereas disabling removes coverage permanently and silently. Record every tuning decision with the reason so a future analyst knows why a signature is quiet. Step 5: Move from Detection to Prevention Deliberately # Suricata: place the sensor inline, then convert selected rules iptables -I FORWARD -j NFQUEUE --queue-num 0 suricata -c /etc/suricata/suricata.yaml -q 0 # /etc/suricata/modify.conf 2010935 "alert" "drop" # Palo Alto: profile action set to reset-both, drop, or block-ip # Cisco FTD: intrusion policy in Drop when Inline mode, rule state # set to Drop and Generate Events # FortiGate: IPS sensor action set to block or reset # Then audit what is actually being enforced jq -r 'select(.event_type=="alert") | .alert.action' /var/log/suricata/eve.json | sort | uniq -c Inline deployment does not by itself mean prevention. Most rules ship in an alerting state on every platform, so traffic is only stopped once a rule is explicitly set to drop or block. Teams regularly discover during an incident that a sensor they believed was preventing had been watching all along. Step 6: Monitor Sensor Health # Suricata: periodic statistics with drop counters outputs: - stats: enabled: yes interval: 30 suricatasc -c "dump-counters" | jq '.message.capture' # Palo Alto: show running resource-monitor ingress-backlogs # Cisco FTD: show snort statistics, plus FMC Health Monitor # FortiGate: diagnose ips status, watch for fail-open events # Check Point: fw ctl multik stat and cpview Any sustained drop rate above roughly one percent means the sensor is losing visibility. Treat it as an availability incident rather than a performance tuning task, because the resulting gap is invisible in the alert stream. Security Note: Enabling payload: yes writes the triggering packet contents into your logs. For rules that match on authentication traffic or personal data this means credentials and regulated data land in the SIEM. Scope payload logging to the rule categories that genuinely need it.

Reading the detection logic is what lets an analyst decide whether an alert is a true positive. Signature based engines are built from the same components whether the rule is written in open syntax you can edit, shipped as a vendor threat signature, or exposed read only in a management console. Action What the engine did: alert, drop, reject, or pass in open syntax, and allow, block, reset, or sinkhole on commercial platforms. In passive deployment every action behaves as alert. Only an inline sensor makes blocking meaningful, which is the first thing to check when triaging. Read First Critical Header Protocol, source, source port, direction, destination, destination port. Expressed in terms of internal and external address groups or security zones, so direction tells you whether this is inbound attack or outbound compromise. Read First Critical Signature ID and Revision The stable identifier for the detection and its revision number. Called sid and rev in open rule syntax, Threat ID on Palo Alto, and GID:SID on Snort based engines including Firepower. This is the key for tuning, suppression, and tracking a detection over time, so always record it in your case notes. Read First High Risk Classification and Severity Categorises the alert and ranks it. Open rule syntax uses classtype with priority 1 (highest) to 4, while commercial platforms use named tiers such as critical, high, medium, low, and informational. Malware and privilege gain categories warrant immediate attention, policy and informational categories usually do not. Triage High Risk Match Conditions The actual detection logic: byte sequences and regular expressions applied to the payload or to protocol fields such as the HTTP URI. Open engines expose this as content and pcre options. Commercial platforms usually hide it, in which case the vendor threat encyclopedia entry is the substitute. Verify Medium Risk metadata and reference Links the signature to CVE identifiers, MITRE ATT&CK techniques, malware families, and creation dates. The fastest route from an alert to understanding what it actually detects. Enrich Medium Risk Security Note: Direction matters more than severity. A high severity alert for an exploit aimed at a service you do not run is noise, while a low severity outbound alert from a workstation to an unknown host can be the first sign of an active compromise.

Every detection event carries the same conceptual fields. The table below uses open engine naming as the reference, and the mapping table underneath translates each concept to the major commercial platforms so a single set of detection rules can be written against any of them. Field Description Category Example Value timestamp Time the event was generated Timestamp 2025-07-14T09:41:22.481203+0000 event_type Record type within the unified stream, distinguishing alerts from protocol and flow records Metadata alert src_ip / src_port Source of the triggering traffic Source 203.0.113.44:52144 dest_ip / dest_port Destination of the triggering traffic Target 10.20.5.40:445 proto Transport protocol Protocol TCP alert.signature_id Rule identifier that fired Detection 2024897 alert.rev Revision of the signature Detection 3 alert.signature Human readable rule message Detection ET EXPLOIT SMB Remote Code Execution Attempt alert.category Classification assigned by the rule Detection Attempted Administrator Privilege Gain alert.severity Priority from 1 (highest) to 4 Severity 1 alert.action allowed or blocked Response blocked flow_id Identifier linking all events for one flow Session 1874203911402318 community_id Portable flow hash for cross-tool correlation Session 1:LQU9qZlK+B5F3KDmev6m5PMibrg= payload_printable Human readable triggering payload Evidence GET /../../etc/passwd HTTP/1.1 Field Name Mapping Across Platforms Normalise to these concepts when building correlation rules or dashboards that must work across more than one sensor type. Concept Suricata and Snort Palo Alto Cisco Firepower Fortinet Rule identifier alert.signature_id, gid:sid threatid GID:SID, Snort ID attackid Rule name alert.signature threat_name Message attackname Classification alert.category, classtype subtype, category Classification eventtype Severity alert.severity (1 to 4) severity (critical to informational) Impact and Priority severity, crlevel Action taken alert.action action Inline Result action Source and destination src_ip, dest_ip, src_port, dest_port src, dst, sport, dport Initiator IP, Responder IP srcip, dstip, srcport, dstport Session identifier flow_id, community_id sessionid Connection ID sessionid Application or protocol app_proto, proto app, proto Application Protocol service, proto Direction Derived from internal address groups from_zone, to_zone, direction Ingress and Egress Interface srcintf, dstintf, direction Pro Tip: Severity scales run in opposite directions between platforms. Open engines treat 1 as the most urgent, while several commercial products use ascending numeric severity where higher is worse. Normalise severity explicitly at ingestion, because a dashboard sorting the raw value across mixed sensors will put the least important events at the top.

Classification drives triage on every platform. The names below are the open engine classtypes, which are the most widely documented set. Commercial products use their own vocabulary for the same tiers: Palo Alto splits detections into vulnerability, spyware, and virus subtypes, Cisco uses impact flags from 0 to 4, and Fortinet groups by attack category. Map yours onto this hierarchy once and the triage logic transfers unchanged. Classification Priority Triage Guidance trojan-activity 1 Known malware traffic, usually outbound command and control. Treat as active compromise and investigate the source host immediately attempted-admin 1 Attempted administrator privilege gain. If the target runs the affected service, escalate at once successful-admin 1 Successful privilege gain observed. Among the highest confidence alerts any sensor produces shellcode-detect 1 Executable code detected in a payload. High value but prone to false positives on binary file transfers web-application-attack 1 Injection, traversal, or deserialisation against a web application. Correlate with the WAF and web server logs to confirm the response code attempted-recon 2 Scanning and enumeration. Low individual value, high value in aggregate as an early indicator of targeting policy-violation 2 Acceptable use rather than security, such as cleartext credentials or unapproved tooling. Route to IT rather than the SOC protocol-command-decode 3 Unusual but not inherently malicious protocol usage. Almost always noise on its own misc-activity 3 Catch-all informational category. Suppress aggressively unless a specific signature has proven value in your environment not-suspicious 3 Explicitly benign traffic recorded for context. Should never generate a ticket Pro Tip: Alert on the combination rather than the classification alone. A single attempted-recon event is noise, but attempted-recon followed by web-application-attack followed by trojan-activity from the same source within an hour is an intrusion narrated in three lines.

s.h: IDS and IPS Log Analysis Queries
s.t: These queries are written against the normalised field names from the mapping table above, so substitute your platform's equivalents. Where a query can only run on the sensor itself the prompt shows bash and the example uses open engine tooling. Top Firing Signatures SIEM> event_type="alert" | stats count, dc(src_ip) as sources, dc(dest_ip) as targets by signature_id, signature | sort - count | head 25 The starting point for every tuning exercise on any platform. The top ten signatures usually account for most of the volume and almost none of the value. A signature with high count but only one or two distinct sources is a tuning candidate rather than a campaign. Highest Severity Alerts Only SIEM> event_type="alert" severity IN ("1","critical","high") | table _time, src_ip, dest_ip, category, signature, action | sort - _time Strips the stream down to what the ruleset authors considered critical, the correct default view for a triage queue. Match the severity values to your platform, remembering that open engines count down from 1 while most commercial products count up. Outbound Malware and C2 by Internal Host SIEM> event_type="alert" category IN ("*Trojan*","*Malware*","*Command and Control*","spyware") src_ip IN (10.0.0.0/8,192.168.0.0/16) | stats count, values(signature), dc(dest_ip) by src_ip | sort - count Filtering to internal sources turns a noisy category into a list of probably compromised hosts. Outbound direction is what makes this high confidence, and the wildcards absorb the naming differences between vendors. Blocked Versus Allowed SIEM> event_type="alert" | stats count by action, signature | eventstats sum(count) as total by signature | eval enforced=round(count/total*100,1) | where action IN ("blocked","drop","reset","deny") Confirms which rules are actually preventing traffic rather than observing it. Run this on any inline deployment, because most rules ship in alerting state on every platform and are only enforced once explicitly changed. Sensor Packet Loss bash> jq -r 'select(.event_type=="stats") | [.timestamp, .stats.capture.kernel_packets, .stats.capture.kernel_drops] | @tsv' eve.json | tail -10 # PAN: show running resource-monitor | FTD: show snort statistics | FortiGate: diagnose ips status Drops divided by packets is your blind spot percentage. Anything sustained above one percent means the sensor is missing attacks it has signatures for. Every platform exposes this counter somewhere, and on all of them it is the single most under-monitored metric. Rare TLS Fingerprints and Destinations SIEM> event_type="tls" OR event_type="ssl" | stats count, dc(src_ip) as hosts, values(sni) by ja3_hash, dest_ip | where hosts <= 2 AND count > 50 | sort - count Client TLS fingerprints identify malware families inside encrypted traffic without decryption. Where your platform does not expose JA3, substitute the certificate subject and SNI, which are available on every product that inspects TLS metadata. Executable Downloads SIEM> event_type IN ("fileinfo","file","wildfire") file_type IN ("*executable*","PE32","ELF","*msdownload*") | table _time, src_ip, dest_ip, filename, sha256, verdict | sort - _time Every executable observed crossing the sensor with its hash, ready to check against threat intelligence. Platforms with a sandbox attach a verdict to the same record, which turns this from a hunting query into a detection. Full Session Context for an Alert SIEM> session_id="1874203911402318" OR community_id="1:LQU9qZlK+B5F3KDmev6m5PMibrg=" | table _time, event_type, signature, url, sni, filename, action | sort _time Pivoting on the session identifier reconstructs every record for one connection: the alert, the HTTP request, the TLS handshake, and the file transfer. Community ID is the better key when the connection crosses several products, because it is computed identically by each of them. Attack Chain by Source SIEM> event_type="alert" | stats dc(category) as stages, values(category), min(_time) as first, max(_time) as last by src_ip | where stages >= 3 | sort - stages Sources triggering three or more distinct alert categories are progressing through an attack rather than generating incidental noise. Verify the Ruleset Actually Loaded bash> suricatasc -c "ruleset-stats" # PAN: show system info | match threat-version | FTD: show snort counters | FortiGate: diagnose autoupdate versions Rules that fail to load are reported once at startup and never mentioned again. Check the loaded count and the installed content version after every update, and on managed platforms confirm the policy was redeployed, since a downloaded update that was never pushed changes nothing.

s.h: Best Practices for IDS and IPS Logging
s.t: Apply these practices to keep a sensor deployment useful rather than ignored: 01 Define Your Internal Boundary Correctly Nearly every rule is written in terms of internal versus external. Whether the platform calls it HOME_NET, a trusted zone, or a variable set, a wrong or default value silently breaks directionality across the entire ruleset. This is the most common serious misconfiguration in the field. 02 Monitor Packet Drop as an Outage A saturated sensor produces fewer alerts, which resembles a quiet network. Alert on whichever drop counter your platform exposes and treat sustained loss with the same urgency as a sensor being offline. 03 Threshold Before You Disable Thresholding keeps a detection alive at lower volume while disabling removes coverage permanently. Record every tuning decision so future analysts know why a signature is quiet. 04 Keep the Protocol Logs, Not Just Alerts HTTP, DNS, TLS, and file records let you investigate techniques no signature covers. Most successful hunts use this metadata rather than the alerts. 05 Normalise Fields at Ingestion Map every sensor onto one schema for rule identifier, severity, action, and direction, and enable a portable flow identifier such as community ID where the platform supports it. Detection content written once then works across every sensor you own, including the one you replace this vendor with. 06 Verify That Blocking Is Actually Blocking Inline deployment does not mean prevention. Rules ship with the alert action, so audit the ratio of drop to alert actions regularly and confirm it matches your intent. 07 Place Sensors Where They Can See A sensor on the perimeter misses all lateral movement. Internal segments, the data centre core, and the VPN concentrator are where post-compromise activity is visible. 08 Plan for Encryption Most traffic is TLS, so payload signatures see nothing. Compensate with JA3 fingerprinting, SNI logging, certificate metadata, and flow analysis rather than assuming content inspection still works.

s.h: Common IDS and IPS Log Examples
s.t: Sensor output from reconnaissance through to command and control. The same detection is shown first in the three formats you will meet in practice, plain text alert, structured JSON, and syslog CEF from a commercial appliance, so you can recognise it whichever product produced it. Text Alert Format: Exploit Attempt Against SMB 07/14/2025-09:41:22.481203 [**] [1:2024897:3] ET EXPLOIT SMB Remote Code Execution Attempt (EternalBlue) [**] [Classification: Attempted Administrator Privilege Gain] [Priority: 1] {TCP} 203.0.113.44:52144 -> 10.20.5.40:445 The compact format: sid 2024897 revision 3, priority 1, external source to an internal host on SMB. Priority 1 plus attempted-admin means this goes to the top of the queue. Structured JSON: The Same Alert with Full Context {"timestamp":"2025-07-14T09:41:22.481203+0000","flow_id":1874203911402318,"event_type":"alert", "src_ip":"203.0.113.44","src_port":52144,"dest_ip":"10.20.5.40","dest_port":445,"proto":"TCP", "community_id":"1:LQU9qZlK+B5F3KDmev6m5PMibrg=", "alert":{"action":"blocked","gid":1,"signature_id":2024897,"rev":3, "signature":"ET EXPLOIT SMB Remote Code Execution Attempt (EternalBlue)", "category":"Attempted Administrator Privilege Gain","severity":1, "metadata":{"attack_target":["Server"],"mitre_technique_id":["T1210"],"cve":["CVE-2017-0144"]}}, "flow":{"pkts_toserver":14,"pkts_toclient":9,"bytes_toserver":4218,"bytes_toclient":1902}} The action field confirms the traffic was blocked, and the metadata maps directly to CVE-2017-0144 and MITRE technique T1210. This is why the structured format is always preferred over the text one. Syslog CEF: The Same Detection From a Commercial Appliance CEF:0|Palo Alto Networks|PAN-OS|10.2|vulnerability|Microsoft SMB Remote Code Execution|9| rt=Jul 14 2025 09:41:22 src=203.0.113.44 spt=52144 dst=10.20.5.40 dpt=445 proto=tcp act=reset-both cs1Label=Rule cs1=Inbound-DC-Access cn1Label=ThreatID cn1=51234 cat=vulnerability cs2Label=Severity cs2=critical cs3Label=Direction cs3=client-to-server externalId=7714029183 cs4Label=CVE cs4=CVE-2017-0144 The same event, different vocabulary. threatid replaces signature_id, act replaces action, and severity is a word rather than a number. Everything an analyst needs is present, which is why normalising these three fields at ingestion lets one detection rule cover every sensor in the estate. Reconnaissance: Port Scan Detected 07/14/2025-09:38:02.117441 [**] [1:2010935:3] ET SCAN Suspicious inbound to MSSQL port 1433 [**] [Classification: Potentially Bad Traffic] [Priority: 2] {TCP} 198.51.100.203:44120 -> 10.40.1.15:1433 07/14/2025-09:38:02.119882 [**] [1:2010936:3] ET SCAN Suspicious inbound to mySQL port 3306 [**] [Classification: Potentially Bad Traffic] [Priority: 2] {TCP} 198.51.100.203:44121 -> 10.40.1.15:3306 07/14/2025-09:38:02.124019 [**] [1:2002910:5] ET SCAN Potential VNC Scan 5900-5920 [**] [Classification: Attempted Information Leak] [Priority: 2] {TCP} 198.51.100.203:44122 -> 10.40.1.15:5900 Three database and remote access ports probed within seven milliseconds from one source. Individually priority 2 noise, together an unmistakable service sweep. Web Application Attack: Path Traversal {"timestamp":"2025-07-14T09:47:33.221004+0000","event_type":"alert", "src_ip":"203.0.113.44","dest_ip":"10.20.5.40","dest_port":443, "alert":{"action":"allowed","signature_id":2006445,"signature":"ET WEB_SERVER Possible Directory Traversal Attempt", "category":"Web Application Attack","severity":1}, "http":{"hostname":"portal.example.com","url":"/download?file=../../../../etc/passwd", "http_user_agent":"python-requests/2.31.0","http_method":"GET","status":200,"length":2841}, "payload_printable":"GET /download?file=../../../../etc/passwd HTTP/1.1"} Status 200 with 2841 bytes returned means the traversal succeeded. The action field says allowed, so the sensor watched this happen without stopping it. Command and Control: Outbound Beacon {"timestamp":"2025-07-14T10:02:44.881229+0000","event_type":"alert", "src_ip":"10.30.2.61","src_port":52190,"dest_ip":"203.0.113.44","dest_port":443, "alert":{"action":"allowed","signature_id":2033102, "signature":"ET MALWARE Cobalt Strike Beacon Observed","category":"A Network Trojan was detected","severity":1, "metadata":{"mitre_technique_id":["T1071.001"],"malware_family":["CobaltStrike"]}}, "tls":{"sni":"cdn-assets.badinfra.top","ja3":{"hash":"a0e9f5d64349fb13191bc781f81f42e1"}, "subject":"CN=cdn-assets.badinfra.top","issuerdn":"CN=R3, O=Let's Encrypt"}} The direction is what matters: an internal workstation initiating this. The JA3 hash identified Cobalt Strike inside TLS without any decryption, and the certificate is a free one issued days ago. Sensor Health: Packet Loss {"timestamp":"2025-07-14T10:05:00.000000+0000","event_type":"stats", "stats":{"uptime":86402, "capture":{"kernel_packets":1842119004,"kernel_drops":412887221}, "decoder":{"pkts":1429231783,"bytes":1102847119228}, "detect":{"alert":18442}}} 412 million drops against 1.84 billion packets is a 22 percent loss rate. Roughly one in five packets was never inspected, so any conclusion drawn from these alerts is unreliable. Data Exfiltration: Asymmetric Flow {"timestamp":"2025-07-14T10:18:12.774119+0000","event_type":"flow", "src_ip":"10.30.2.61","src_port":52240,"dest_ip":"203.0.113.91","dest_port":443,"proto":"TCP", "flow":{"pkts_toserver":1284119,"pkts_toclient":42881, "bytes_toserver":1884221904,"bytes_toclient":3218844, "start":"2025-07-14T02:11:04.221000+0000","end":"2025-07-14T10:18:12.774000+0000","age":29228, "state":"established","reason":"timeout"}} 1.88 GB uploaded against 3.2 MB downloaded over an eight hour session. No rule fired at all, yet the flow record alone describes bulk exfiltration. This is why flow logging matters. Back

A web proxy sits between users and the internet, and because every outbound request passes through it, the access log becomes the most detailed record of user and malware behaviour available on the network. Where a firewall log records that a host contacted an address on port 443, the proxy log records the full URL, the authenticated username, the site category, the user agent, the referrer, the exact byte counts in each direction, and whether the request was allowed or blocked. That difference in richness is why proxy logs are usually the first place an analyst looks when investigating a suspected compromise. The dominant deployments are Squid in open source environments, Zscaler and Netskope as cloud-delivered secure web gateways, and Symantec Blue Coat ProxySG in traditional enterprises. They differ in format but log the same fundamental transaction. Squid writes a compact native format by default that omits the user agent and referrer entirely, which is a significant gap: the combined log format must be configured explicitly to capture them, and without them a large fraction of proxy-based detection simply does not work. The critical architectural question is whether the proxy performs TLS inspection. Without it, an HTTPS request appears only as a CONNECT to a hostname and port, with byte counts but no URL path, no response content, and no file visibility. With inspection enabled the proxy sees the full request as if it were cleartext. Most organisations run a hybrid, inspecting general browsing while bypassing banking, healthcare, and government categories for privacy and legal reasons. Knowing which categories are bypassed is essential context, because those are precisely the categories attackers prefer to hide behind.

Proxies produce several streams. Only the first carries most of the security value, but the others matter during troubleshooting and incident response: Log Type Description Access Log One record per client request. Contains the timestamp, client address, authenticated user, request method, full URL, HTTP status, bytes transferred, result code, content type, and the policy decision. This is the primary security log and the one that should always be forwarded to a SIEM. Policy and Block Log Records requests denied by category filtering, threat intelligence, or acceptable use policy, with the rule that caused the denial. On Squid these appear in the access log as TCP_DENIED, while commercial gateways often separate them into their own stream. TLS Inspection Log Details of intercepted HTTPS sessions including the server certificate subject and issuer, negotiated cipher, SNI value, and any validation failures. Certificate errors logged here frequently reveal command and control infrastructure using self-signed certificates. Cache Log The proxy's own operational log covering startup, configuration reload, upstream failures, and errors. Squid writes this to cache.log. Not a security source, but it explains gaps in the access log. Malware Scanning Log Verdicts from inline antivirus or sandbox detonation performed on downloaded content, typically including the file hash, name, and detection name. The link between a web request and a delivered payload. Authentication Log Records how each session was attributed to a user, whether by Kerberos, NTLM, or captive portal. Authentication failures here can indicate credential problems or attempts to evade user attribution. Store Log Squid-specific record of objects entering and leaving the cache. Rarely enabled and of limited security value, but occasionally useful for proving what content was served from cache rather than fetched fresh. Pro Tip: Squid's default squid log format contains no user agent and no referrer. Switch to the combined format or define a custom logformat before you need those fields, because they cannot be recovered retrospectively.

Cloud proxies deliver logs through a streaming connector rather than a file, which changes how collection is architected. Log Default Location Squid Access Log /var/log/squid/access.log Squid Cache Log /var/log/squid/cache.log Squid Configuration /etc/squid/squid.conf Blue Coat ProxySG Uploaded by FTP or HTTP to a configured server, commonly in the bcreportermain_v1 or W3C ELFF format Zscaler Streamed through Nanolog Streaming Service (NSS) to a syslog collector, or pulled from the Log Streaming Service API Netskope Delivered through the Cloud Log Shipper or the REST API v2 events endpoint Forcepoint Web Security /opt/Websense/bin/ on the log server, or via the SIEM integration connector Squid on Windows C:\Squid\var\log\squid\access.log Pro Tip: Cloud proxy feeds are delivered from the vendor's infrastructure, not from your network. If the streaming connector stops, log flow ends silently while browsing continues to work normally. Monitor event volume per hour and alert when it drops.

These Squid directives produce an access log with the fields security analysis actually requires, rather than the sparse default. Step 1: Define a Security-Focused Log Format # /etc/squid/squid.conf logformat htlsec %ts.%03tu %6tr %>a %Ss/%03>Hs %<st %rm %ru %[un %Sh/%<a %mt "%{Referer}>h" "%{User-Agent}>h" %>st %<st access_log /var/log/squid/access.log htlsec # Field reference: # %ts.%03tu epoch seconds and milliseconds %rm request method # %6tr response time in milliseconds %ru full request URL # %>a client address %[un authenticated username # %Ss/%03>Hs squid result code / HTTP status %Sh hierarchy code # %<st bytes delivered to client %mt MIME content type # %>st bytes received from client Logging both %>st and %<st is what makes upload detection possible. The default format records only the response size, so large outbound POSTs are invisible. Step 2: Log Human Readable Timestamps # Squid logs epoch time by default, which is unreadable during triage logformat htlsec_iso %{%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S%z}tl %6tr %>a %Ss/%03>Hs %<st %rm %ru %[un %Sh/%<a %mt # Or convert an existing log on the fly perl -pe 's/^(\d+)\.\d+/localtime($1)/e' /var/log/squid/access.log | head If your SIEM handles epoch parsing correctly, keep the native format for precision. If analysts read raw files, ISO timestamps save time on every investigation. Step 3: Require Authentication for User Attribution auth_param negotiate program /usr/lib/squid/negotiate_kerberos_auth -k /etc/squid/HTTP.keytab -s GSS_C_NO_NAME auth_param negotiate children 20 startup=5 idle=2 auth_param negotiate keep_alive on acl authenticated proxy_auth REQUIRED http_access deny !authenticated http_access allow authenticated Without authentication the log attributes activity to an IP address only. On shared or DHCP-assigned addresses that makes user attribution guesswork rather than evidence. Step 4: Enable TLS Inspection Selectively http_port 3128 ssl-bump generate-host-certificates=on \ dynamic_cert_mem_cache_size=8MB tls-cert=/etc/squid/proxyCA.pem acl step1 at_step SslBump1 acl no_inspect ssl::server_name_regex "/etc/squid/bypass_domains.txt" ssl_bump peek step1 ssl_bump splice no_inspect # bypass banking, health, government ssl_bump bump all # inspect everything else Spliced connections are logged as CONNECT with a hostname and byte counts only. Keep the bypass list short and reviewed, because every entry is a blind spot an attacker can use. Step 5: Configure Rotation and Retention logfile_rotate 30 debug_options ALL,1 # /etc/logrotate.d/squid /var/log/squid/*.log { daily rotate 90 compress delaycompress missingok postrotate /usr/sbin/squid -k rotate endscript } The postrotate hook signalling Squid is essential. Rotating the file without it leaves Squid writing to a deleted inode, and logging stops silently until the service restarts. Step 6: Forward to a SIEM in Real Time # Squid can write directly to syslog access_log syslog:local4.info htlsec # /etc/rsyslog.d/49-squid.conf local4.* @@siem-collector.corp.local:6514 Streaming over TCP with TLS avoids the loss inherent in reading rotated files and ensures logs survive compromise of the proxy host itself. Security Note: Full URL logging captures query strings, which routinely contain session tokens, password reset links, and personal data. Proxy logs inherit the sensitivity of everything your users browse. Restrict access to them accordingly and define a retention period that reflects that, not just storage cost.

Proxy logs expose a distinctive set of attacker behaviours. These are the patterns worth building detections around. Command and Control Beaconing Regular polling of a controller over HTTP or HTTPS. Signature: highly consistent intervals, small consistent response sizes, few distinct URLs, and a single internal client. Detect Critical Data Exfiltration Large outbound transfers to file sharing services or unknown hosts. Signature: request bytes vastly exceeding response bytes, sustained POST or PUT activity, uncategorised destination. Detect Critical Non-Browser User Agents Requests from curl, wget, python-requests, PowerShell, or empty user agent strings. On a user workstation these almost always indicate scripted activity rather than browsing. Detect Critical Uncategorised Destinations Sites the categorisation engine does not recognise, which correlates strongly with newly registered attacker infrastructure. Low volume in most environments and therefore highly reviewable. Detect High Risk Direct IP Requests URLs containing an address instead of a hostname. Legitimate browsing almost never does this, while malware frequently hardcodes addresses to avoid DNS-based blocking. Detect High Risk Suspicious Downloads Executables, scripts, and archives fetched from uncategorised sites, or content whose MIME type contradicts its file extension. The delivery stage of most intrusions. Detect Medium Risk Security Note: Attackers increasingly host command and control on legitimate, well-categorised platforms such as cloud storage, code repositories, and collaboration tools. Category-based detection alone will not catch this. Behaviour, specifically timing regularity and byte ratios, remains effective where reputation fails.

These fields appear across Squid, Blue Coat, and cloud gateways under different names. Normalise them once and every detection works against all of them. Field Description Category Example Value timestamp Time the request completed Timestamp 1752486082.481 duration Time taken to service the request in milliseconds Performance 884 client_ip Address of the requesting host Source 10.30.2.61 username Authenticated user, or a dash when unauthenticated Identity CORP\r.almutairi result_code Proxy cache and policy result Result TCP_DENIED http_status HTTP status code returned to the client Result 403 method HTTP request method Request Type POST url Full requested URL including query string Target https://cdn-assets.badinfra.top/upload bytes_sent Bytes uploaded by the client Volume 188422190 bytes_received Bytes delivered to the client Volume 412 content_type MIME type of the response Content application/octet-stream user_agent Client application string Source python-requests/2.31.0 referer Page that originated the request Context https://portal.corp.local/ category Content classification assigned by the proxy Policy Uncategorised action Policy decision applied Response blocked

Squid encodes both the cache outcome and the policy decision into a single result code. Reading it correctly is essential to interpreting the log. Code Meaning Security Relevance TCP_DENIED Request refused by an access control rule The policy block record. Repeated denials to one destination from one host indicate malware retrying against a blocked controller TCP_MISS Object not cached, fetched from the origin The normal case for dynamic content and the majority of security-relevant traffic TCP_HIT Served from cache without contacting the origin Confirms the client received content but the origin was never contacted for this request TCP_TUNNEL CONNECT tunnel established, contents not inspected An uninspected HTTPS session. Byte counts are still recorded, which is often enough to spot exfiltration TCP_REFRESH_MODIFIED Cached object revalidated and found changed Rapid repeated revalidation of one object can indicate polling behaviour TCP_MISS_ABORTED Client disconnected before the transfer completed Common in interrupted downloads, but bursts can indicate scripted activity or a failing tunnel HIER_DIRECT Fetched directly from the origin server The standard hierarchy code, showing no upstream parent proxy was involved HIER_NONE No upstream connection was made Accompanies denials and cache hits. Confirms the request never left the network NONE/503 Upstream unreachable or DNS failure Bursts of these to random hostnames can reveal domain generation algorithm activity reaching the proxy Pro Tip: TCP_DENIED entries are a detection opportunity, not just a compliance record. Malware does not know a domain is blocked, so it retries. A host generating dozens of denials to the same uncategorised domain is infected regardless of the fact that the traffic was stopped.

These commands surface beaconing, exfiltration, scripted clients, and blocked malware retries from proxy logs. Large Outbound Transfers SIEM> source="proxy" method IN ("POST","PUT") | stats sum(bytes_sent) as uploaded, sum(bytes_received) as downloaded, dc(url) by client_ip, dest_host | where uploaded > 100000000 AND uploaded > downloaded*10 Finds hosts uploading far more than they download. The ratio matters more than the absolute volume for distinguishing exfiltration from normal use. Scripted User Agents bash> awk '{print $12}' /var/log/squid/access.log | grep -iE "curl|wget|python|powershell|go-http|libwww|^\"-\"$" | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn Non-browser agents on a workstation are scripted activity. Baseline the legitimate ones from monitoring tools, then alert on everything else. Beacon Detection SIEM> source="proxy" | sort client_ip, dest_host, _time | streamstats current=f last(_time) as prev by client_ip, dest_host | eval gap=_time-prev | stats count, stdev(gap) as jitter, avg(gap) as interval, avg(bytes_received) as avg_size by client_ip, dest_host | where count > 30 AND jitter < 10 Consistent intervals with consistent small response sizes is machine behaviour. This finds command and control that no reputation feed has flagged. Repeated Blocks (Infected Host) bash> grep TCP_DENIED /var/log/squid/access.log | awk '{print $3, $7}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -25 A host repeatedly hitting the same blocked destination is not a user browsing, it is malware retrying. The block worked, the infection remains. Direct IP Requests bash> grep -oP 'https?://\K(\d{1,3}\.){3}\d{1,3}[^ ]*' /var/log/squid/access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -20 Browsers use hostnames. URLs containing a raw address are typically hardcoded malware destinations designed to survive DNS blocking. Uncategorised Destinations SIEM> source="proxy" category IN ("Uncategorized","Unknown","Newly Registered Domain") | stats count, sum(bytes_sent) as up, dc(client_ip) as hosts by dest_host | where hosts <= 2 | sort - up Uncategorised domains visited by only one or two hosts are the highest yield review queue on the proxy. Executable and Script Downloads bash> grep -iE "\.(exe|dll|ps1|hta|scr|jar|vbs|bat|iso|img)(\?|$| )" /var/log/squid/access.log | awk '$4 ~ /200/ {print $3, $7, $11}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn Successful executable downloads, filtered to status 200. Cross-reference the destination against category and domain age. Off-Hours Browsing SIEM> source="proxy" | eval hr=strftime(_time,"%H") | where hr<6 OR hr>21 | stats count, dc(dest_host) as sites by username, client_ip | sort - count Automated malware browses at 3am. Compare each user's off-hours volume against their own baseline rather than a global threshold. Certificate Anomalies SIEM> source="proxy" event="tls_inspection" (cert_validation="failed" OR cert_self_signed="true") | stats count, values(cert_subject) by dest_host, client_ip | sort - count Self-signed and invalid certificates on outbound connections frequently mark command and control servers set up in a hurry. Log Flow Health SIEM> source="proxy" | timechart span=1h count | where count < 1000 Cloud proxy feeds fail silently while browsing continues. An unexplained volume drop means you have lost visibility, not that the network went quiet.

Follow these practices to get investigation-grade evidence out of a web proxy: 01 Log the User Agent and Referrer Squid's default format omits both. They are among the most useful fields for detecting scripted clients and reconstructing how a user reached a malicious page, and they cannot be recovered later. 02 Record Bytes in Both Directions Response size alone hides exfiltration completely. Logging request bytes as well is what turns the proxy into a data loss detection source. 03 Authenticate Every Session An IP address is not an identity. Kerberos or NTLM attribution converts every proxy record into evidence tied to a named person. 04 Keep the TLS Bypass List Short Every bypassed category is a blind spot. Review the list regularly and document the legal or privacy justification for each entry. 05 Retain Blocked Requests Denied requests are frequently more valuable than allowed ones, because they identify infected hosts that policy successfully contained. Never filter TCP_DENIED out to save storage. 06 Signal Squid on Rotation Rotating the access log without running squid -k rotate leaves the daemon writing to a deleted file. Logging stops silently and nothing alerts you. 07 Monitor Feed Continuity Cloud gateway connectors fail without affecting user browsing. Alert on hourly event volume so a broken feed is detected in an hour rather than during an investigation. 08 Treat Proxy Logs as Sensitive Data Full URLs contain session tokens, reset links, and personal browsing history. Apply access controls and a defined retention period that reflect that sensitivity.

A single compromise viewed through the proxy, from initial download to exfiltration. Normal Browsing Baseline 1752486082.481 284 10.30.2.61 TCP_MISS/200 48221 GET https://www.example.com/index.html CORP\r.almutairi HIER_DIRECT/93.184.216.34 text/html "https://portal.corp.local/" "Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64) AppleWebKit/537.36" 842 48221 A healthy record: authenticated user, real browser agent, internal referrer, HTML content, and far more bytes down than up. Everything an attacker's traffic will fail to look like. Malware Delivery: Executable from an Uncategorised Site 1752486721.883 1482 10.30.2.61 TCP_MISS/200 2841776 GET http://cdn-assets.badinfra.top/update/setup.exe CORP\r.almutairi HIER_DIRECT/203.0.113.44 application/octet-stream "-" "Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64)" 412 2841776 A 2.8 MB executable over plain HTTP from a domain with no referrer and no category. The empty referrer means the user did not click a link to get here. Command and Control Beacon 1752487082.114 88 10.30.2.61 TCP_MISS/200 412 GET https://cdn-assets.badinfra.top/api/v1/status CORP\r.almutairi HIER_DIRECT/203.0.113.44 application/json "-" "python-requests/2.31.0" 284 412 1752487142.229 91 10.30.2.61 TCP_MISS/200 412 GET https://cdn-assets.badinfra.top/api/v1/status CORP\r.almutairi HIER_DIRECT/203.0.113.44 application/json "-" "python-requests/2.31.0" 284 412 1752487202.338 87 10.30.2.61 TCP_MISS/200 408 GET https://cdn-assets.badinfra.top/api/v1/status CORP\r.almutairi HIER_DIRECT/203.0.113.44 application/json "-" "python-requests/2.31.0" 284 408 Exactly sixty seconds apart, nearly identical response sizes, and a python-requests user agent on a user workstation. Three independent indicators of automation in one pattern. Blocked Retry Loop: Contained but Infected 1752487262.441 2 10.30.2.61 TCP_DENIED/403 3821 GET https://c2-fallback.badinfra.top/api/v1/status CORP\r.almutairi HIER_NONE/- text/html "-" "python-requests/2.31.0" 284 3821 1752487322.552 2 10.30.2.61 TCP_DENIED/403 3821 GET https://c2-fallback.badinfra.top/api/v1/status CORP\r.almutairi HIER_NONE/- text/html "-" "python-requests/2.31.0" 284 3821 TCP_DENIED with HIER_NONE means the request never left the network. The block is working, but the host is still infected and still beaconing on schedule. Data Exfiltration: Large Upload 1752488292.774 38812 10.30.2.61 TCP_MISS/200 118 POST https://cdn-assets.badinfra.top/upload CORP\r.almutairi HIER_DIRECT/203.0.113.44 application/json "-" "python-requests/2.31.0" 188422190 118 188 MB uploaded, 118 bytes returned, over 38 seconds. The byte ratio alone identifies this, which is exactly why logging request bytes is not optional. Uninspected HTTPS Tunnel 1752488421.008 29228 10.30.2.61 TCP_TUNNEL/200 3218844 CONNECT secure-files.example.net:443 CORP\r.almutairi HIER_DIRECT/198.51.100.7 - "-" "-" 1884221904 3218844 A spliced connection, so no URL or content is visible. The byte counts survive though: 1.88 GB uploaded over eight hours. Even without inspection this is detectable. Domain Generation Algorithm Reaching the Proxy 1752488502.117 8 10.30.2.61 NONE/503 4218 GET http://kjhsdfuiwer.biz/gate.php CORP\r.almutairi HIER_NONE/- text/html "-" "-" 284 4218 1752488502.229 7 10.30.2.61 NONE/503 4218 GET http://pqwoeirutyx.info/gate.php CORP\r.almutairi HIER_NONE/- text/html "-" "-" 284 4218 1752488502.341 9 10.30.2.61 NONE/503 4218 GET http://zmxncbvlkjh.top/gate.php CORP\r.almutairi HIER_NONE/- text/html "-" "-" 284 4218 Random hostnames, identical URL path, resolution failures returning 503, milliseconds apart. The shared /gate.php path across random domains is the malware family's fingerprint. Back

The VPN concentrator is the front door to the internal network, and it is exposed to the internet by design. That combination makes it one of the most consistently targeted assets in any environment: credential stuffing against the portal, exploitation of the appliance itself, and abuse of valid stolen credentials all converge here. VPN logs are where those attempts become visible, and they are frequently the earliest evidence available in an intrusion timeline, because remote access is where so many intrusions begin. A VPN log records two distinct things that are easy to conflate. The first is authentication : who attempted to log in, from which public address, using which method, and whether it succeeded. The second is the session : the tunnel that was established, the internal address assigned to the client, how long it lasted, and how much data crossed it. Detection depends on both. Authentication events reveal brute force, password spraying, and multi-factor fatigue, while session events provide the crucial mapping from an assigned internal address to a named user, without which every subsequent internal log entry for that address is unattributable. Because attackers increasingly use valid credentials rather than exploits, the highest value VPN detections are behavioural rather than signature based. Impossible travel between two logins, a successful authentication from a country where the organisation has no presence, an unusual client version, a session at an hour the user has never worked, or a burst of MFA prompts followed by one acceptance are all patterns that only emerge when VPN logs are enriched with geolocation and compared against a per-user baseline. A successful login is not evidence of legitimacy, and treating it as such is why credential-based intrusions persist undetected for so long.

Remote access logging spans the concentrator, the identity provider, and the endpoint posture system. A complete picture requires all three: Log Type Description Authentication Log Records every login attempt with the username, source public address, authentication method, tunnel group, and result. The primary source for brute force, password spraying, and credential stuffing detection, and the first log to review in any suspected account compromise. Session Establishment Log Written when a tunnel is created. Contains the assigned internal address, the client software version, the negotiated encryption, and the group policy applied. The assigned address is what links this user to every subsequent internal log entry. Session Teardown Log Written when a tunnel closes, carrying the session duration, total bytes sent and received, and the reason for disconnection. Byte counts here are the simplest available signal for exfiltration over remote access. Posture and Compliance Log Results of endpoint health checks performed before access is granted, covering antivirus status, patch level, disk encryption, and certificate presence. Records both which devices failed and which were admitted anyway under a remediation policy. Multi-Factor Authentication Log Usually produced by the identity provider or RADIUS server rather than the concentrator. Records each factor challenge and its outcome, which is the only way to distinguish a user approving a legitimate prompt from a user approving one under fatigue. Administrative Access Log Logins to the appliance management interface and configuration changes made there. An attacker who compromises the concentrator itself can create tunnel groups and disable logging, so this stream needs independent monitoring. Tunnel Traffic Log Connection records for traffic inside the tunnel, subject to the split tunnelling policy. Shows what internal resources the remote user actually reached once connected. Pro Tip: The mapping between assigned tunnel address and username exists only in the session logs, and pools are reused constantly. Without retaining session establishment and teardown records, an internal alert on a VPN pool address cannot be attributed to a person after the fact.

Appliances rarely store logs locally in any useful quantity. Syslog forwarding is not an enhancement here, it is the only viable collection method. Platform Default Location Cisco ASA / Firepower Internal buffer only, viewed with show logging. Forward via syslog to a collector Fortinet FortiGate Local disk if fitted, otherwise FortiAnalyzer or syslog. View with execute log display Palo Alto GlobalProtect System and GlobalProtect log types in the firewall, forwarded via Log Forwarding Profile OpenVPN /var/log/openvpn.log or /var/log/openvpn/openvpn-status.log OpenVPN Configuration /etc/openvpn/server.conf WireGuard Kernel log via journalctl -u wg-quick@wg0, plus wg show for peer handshake times strongSwan IPsec /var/log/charon.log or the system journal Windows Always On VPN RAS logs in %SystemRoot%\tracing and NPS accounting in %SystemRoot%\System32\LogFiles\IN*.log Pro Tip: WireGuard is deliberately minimal and logs almost nothing by design. It records handshake times per peer but no session or authentication events, so deployments need external accounting through wg show polling or a management layer on top.

Default logging levels on most concentrators are too low to capture authentication detail. These configurations raise them to a useful level without flooding the collector. Step 1: Configure Cisco ASA Syslog logging enable logging timestamp rfc5424 logging host INSIDE 10.50.9.20 6/1514 logging trap informational logging device-id hostname no logging message 302013 ! suppress high volume connection build no logging message 302014 ! Ensure the VPN specific classes are retained logging list VPNLOG message 113004-113020 logging list VPNLOG message 722022-722051 logging list VPNLOG message 716038-716059 Informational level is required: authentication messages such as 113004 and 113005 are severity 6 and are lost entirely at the default warning level. Step 2: Configure FortiGate SSL VPN Logging config log syslogd setting set status enable set server "10.50.9.20" set port 514 set facility local7 set format rfc5424 end config vpn ssl settings set log-session-info enable end config log setting set fwpolicy-implicit-log enable set resolve-ip enable end log-session-info adds the tunnel address assignment and byte counters to session records, which is what makes user attribution and exfiltration detection possible. Step 3: Configure OpenVPN Verbosely Enough # /etc/openvpn/server.conf log-append /var/log/openvpn.log status /var/log/openvpn/openvpn-status.log 30 status-version 3 verb 4 # 3 is default, 4 adds authentication detail mute 0 # never suppress repeated messages # Record the real client address and assigned tunnel address push "route 10.0.0.0 255.0.0.0" client-connect /etc/openvpn/scripts/log-connect.sh client-disconnect /etc/openvpn/scripts/log-disconnect.sh Verbosity 4 exposes certificate common names and authentication outcomes. Setting mute to 0 matters because the default suppresses repeated messages, which hides brute force bursts. Step 4: Capture the Identity Provider Side # The concentrator sees "authentication succeeded" but not which factors were used. # Collect the RADIUS or IdP log alongside it: # Microsoft NPS : %SystemRoot%\System32\LogFiles\IN*.log (event IDs 6272/6273) # FreeRADIUS : /var/log/freeradius/radius.log # Entra ID : SignInLogs table, authenticationDetails field # Okta : System Log API, eventType user.authentication.auth_via_mfa # Correlate on username plus timestamp plus source address MFA fatigue attacks are invisible in concentrator logs, which record only the final successful authentication. The repeated denied prompts that preceded it exist only in the identity provider log. Step 5: Enrich with Geolocation at Ingest # Example enrichment pipeline (Logstash) filter { if [event_type] == "vpn_auth" { geoip { source => "src_ip" target => "geo" } if [geo][country_code2] not in ["SA","AE","GB"] { mutate { add_tag => ["vpn_unexpected_country"] } } } } Geolocation must be applied at ingest, not at query time. Impossible travel detection requires the country and coordinates to already be on the event when correlation runs. Step 6: Retain Address Assignment Mappings # Build a lookup of tunnel address to user for the retention period source="vpn" (event="session_established" OR event="session_terminated") | eval end_time=if(event=="session_terminated", _time, now()) | table username, assigned_ip, src_ip, _time, end_time, bytes_sent, bytes_received | outputlookup vpn_session_history.csv This lookup is what lets an analyst resolve a VPN pool address in an internal alert back to a person weeks later. Pools recycle within hours, so the mapping must be historical. Security Note: VPN appliances have been among the most heavily exploited enterprise products in recent years, with pre-authentication vulnerabilities affecting every major vendor. Monitor the administrative access log and the appliance's own system log as closely as the user authentication log, because a compromised concentrator can issue itself valid sessions.

Remote access attacks follow recognisable shapes. These are the highest value detections to build from VPN telemetry. Impossible Travel Two successful authentications for one account from locations too far apart for the elapsed time. Among the highest confidence indicators of credential compromise available. Detect Critical MFA Fatigue Repeated push notifications until the user approves one out of irritation. Signature: many denied or timed out factor challenges followed by a single acceptance, all within minutes. Detect Critical Password Spraying One or two password attempts against many accounts, staying below lockout thresholds. Signature: a single source address failing against dozens of distinct usernames. Detect Critical Anomalous Session Timing Connections at hours a user has never worked, or sessions lasting far longer than their norm. Effective precisely because attackers operate in their own timezone, not the victim's. Detect High Risk Exfiltration Over Tunnel Session teardown records showing bytes received by the client far exceeding the user's baseline. A remote session pulling gigabytes from file shares is bulk data theft. Detect High Risk Concurrent Sessions One account with simultaneous tunnels from different addresses or countries. Either credential sharing or an attacker connected alongside the legitimate user. Detect Medium Risk Security Note: Commercial VPN and residential proxy services are widely used to defeat geolocation detections, placing an attacker's apparent source inside the expected country. Maintain a list of known hosting and anonymiser ranges and treat authentications from them as anomalous regardless of the country they resolve to.

These fields appear across all major concentrators under different names. Normalising them is what allows one detection to run against Cisco, Fortinet, and Palo Alto data together. Cisco ASA and FortiGate identify events by numeric identifiers that remain stable across software versions, making them reliable detection anchors. Message ID Meaning Why It Matters ASA-6-113005 AAA user authentication rejected The core VPN authentication failure. Bursts against one account are brute force, across many accounts is spraying ASA-6-113004 AAA user authentication successful The baseline for behavioural detection. Every impossible travel and off-hours alert starts here ASA-6-113015 AAA user authentication rejected, user not found Distinguishes username enumeration from password guessing against real accounts ASA-6-722022 TCP or SSL connection established Tunnel establishment carrying the assigned internal address, the key to user attribution ASA-4-113019 Group and user disconnected Session teardown with duration and byte counts, the simplest exfiltration signal available ASA-6-716039 WebVPN authentication rejected Clientless portal login failure, frequently the target of automated credential stuffing ASA-6-605005 Login permitted to the management interface Administrative access to the appliance itself. Should be rare, scheduled, and from known addresses only ASA-3-713061 IKE peer rejected, no matching policy IPsec negotiation failures, often scanning of the VPN endpoint by unauthorised peers Fortinet 0101039426 SSL VPN login failed FortiGate authentication failure. The action field ssl-login-fail is the equivalent detection anchor Fortinet 0101039424 SSL VPN tunnel up Tunnel establishment with the assigned address and the user group applied Pro Tip: Suppressing ASA messages 302013 and 302014 is standard practice for volume control, but be careful not to suppress the 7xxxx range along with them. Those are the VPN session messages, and losing them removes address-to-user attribution entirely.

These queries surface credential attacks, geographic anomalies, and data theft over remote access. Impossible Travel SIEM> source="vpn" result="success" | sort username, _time | streamstats current=f last(src_country) as prev_country, last(_time) as prev_time by username | eval gap_hr=(_time-prev_time)/3600 | where prev_country!=src_country AND gap_hr < 4 Two successful logins from different countries within four hours. Whitelist adjacent-country commuting patterns before deploying this. Password Spraying SIEM> source="vpn" result="failed" | bucket _time span=30m | stats dc(username) as targets, count as attempts by src_ip, _time | where targets > 15 AND attempts/targets < 3 Many usernames with few attempts each is the defining spray signature, deliberately staying under account lockout thresholds. MFA Fatigue SIEM> source="idp" eventType="*mfa*" | bucket _time span=15m | stats count(eval(result=="denied")) as denied, count(eval(result=="success")) as approved by username, _time | where denied >= 5 AND approved >= 1 Five or more rejected prompts followed by an approval in the same window is a user giving in, not a user authenticating. Brute Force Then Success SIEM> source="vpn" | bucket _time span=1h | stats count(eval(result=="failed")) as fails, count(eval(result=="success")) as wins, values(src_ip) by username, _time | where fails > 20 AND wins > 0 The highest priority VPN alert there is: sustained failures against one account followed by a success in the same hour. Logins from Unexpected Countries SIEM> source="vpn" result="success" NOT src_country IN ("SA","AE","GB") | stats count, values(src_ip), values(src_country) by username | sort - count Define the allowed country list from where your workforce actually is, not from where you have offices. Travel exceptions should be temporary and documented. Exfiltration Over Tunnel SIEM> source="vpn" event="session_terminated" | stats sum(bytes_sent) as downloaded, avg(duration) as avg_dur by username, session_id | eventstats avg(downloaded) as user_avg by username | where downloaded > user_avg*10 AND downloaded > 1000000000 Compares each session against the user's own baseline rather than a global threshold, which is what makes it usable in practice. Concurrent Sessions SIEM> source="vpn" event="session_established" | bucket _time span=1h | stats dc(src_ip) as sources, dc(src_country) as countries, values(src_ip) by username, _time | where sources > 1 One account tunnelled from two addresses at once is either shared credentials or an attacker connected alongside the real user. Unusual Client Versions SIEM> source="vpn" event="session_established" | stats count, dc(username) as users by client_version | where users < 3 | sort count Rare client versions can indicate an attacker using an unmanaged device or an open source client against your corporate concentrator. Resolve a Tunnel Address to a User SIEM> source="vpn" assigned_ip="10.99.4.117" | table _time, event, username, src_ip, src_country, session_id | sort _time The standard pivot when an internal alert names a VPN pool address. Bound the search by the alert time because pools recycle within hours. Appliance Administrative Access SIEM> source="vpn" (message_id="605005" OR message_id="111008" OR action="config_change") | table _time, username, src_ip, message | sort - _time Configuration changes on the concentrator itself. An attacker here can create tunnel groups, disable MFA, and turn logging off.

Apply these practices to make remote access logging capable of catching credential-based intrusion: 01 Log at Informational Severity Authentication messages are severity 6 on Cisco platforms. At the default warning level they are never emitted, so the most important VPN events simply do not exist. 02 Retain Address Assignment History Keep session establishment and teardown records for the full retention period. Without them a VPN pool address in an internal alert can never be traced to a person. 03 Collect the Identity Provider Logs Too The concentrator records only the final authentication result. MFA fatigue, factor type, and denied prompts exist solely in the RADIUS or identity provider log. 04 Geolocate at Ingest Impossible travel detection needs country and coordinates already attached to the event. Enriching at query time is too slow and breaks correlation across time windows. 05 Baseline Per User, Not Globally Working hours, session length, and data volume vary enormously between roles. A per-user baseline finds anomalies that any global threshold either misses or drowns in false positives. 06 Alert on Successful Logins, Not Only Failures Attackers using stolen credentials generate a clean success. Failure-only monitoring is blind to exactly the attack type that matters most today. 07 Monitor the Appliance Itself VPN concentrators are among the most exploited enterprise products. Watch administrative logins, configuration changes, and firmware version alongside user authentication. 08 Forward Off the Appliance Immediately Concentrators hold only a small local buffer that wraps in minutes under load. Syslog forwarding is the only collection method that survives both volume and compromise.
