Almost every action on a network begins with a DNS lookup. Before malware reaches its command and control server, before a user lands on a phishing page, and before data leaves through a tunnel, something has to resolve a name. That property makes DNS the broadest single source of visibility available to a SOC: one log stream that observes nearly every host, every application, and every outbound connection attempt, including the ones that fail. DNS produces two very different kinds of log. Query logging records the questions clients ask and the answers they receive, which is the security-relevant stream. Debug or diagnostic logging records protocol level detail intended for troubleshooting and is far too verbose to keep running. On Windows, the modern approach is the DNS Server Analytical log delivered through Event Tracing for Windows, which replaced the old text-based debug log and can sustain production query rates. On BIND, query logging is a channel configured in named.conf . On endpoints, Sysmon event ID 22 captures the resolving process, which is the one thing server-side DNS logs can never tell you. The gap that matters most in modern environments is encrypted DNS. DNS over HTTPS and DNS over TLS move resolution off port 53 and out of the view of your internal resolver entirely, and every major browser now supports it. A host configured to use a public DoH resolver produces no useful DNS log at all. Blocking outbound port 53 to anything other than approved resolvers, disabling browser DoH through policy, and monitoring for connections to known DoH endpoints are prerequisites for DNS logging to remain meaningful.

DNS visibility can be collected at the server, at the endpoint, or on the wire. Each vantage point answers a different question, and a mature deployment uses more than one: Log Type Description Windows DNS Analytical Log An ETW-based channel introduced in Windows Server 2012 R2 that records every query, response, recursion, and dynamic update handled by the server. Designed for production use with roughly 5 percent overhead at 100,000 queries per second, and the correct replacement for the legacy debug log. Windows DNS Audit Log Enabled by default on Windows Server 2012 R2 and later. Records administrative changes such as zone creation and deletion, record additions and removals, and configuration changes. This is the tamper-detection stream, distinct from query activity. BIND Query Log Configured as a logging channel with the queries category in named.conf. Records the client address, query name, class, type, and flags for every request. The response is logged separately through the querylog and resolver categories. Sysmon Event ID 22 DNSEvent, generated on the endpoint rather than the server. Uniquely records the process image that performed the lookup, which is the difference between knowing a host resolved a malicious domain and knowing which binary did it. Passive DNS Resolution data captured from network traffic and stored historically, either by a sensor such as Zeek or by a commercial feed. Enables retrospective questions such as which internal hosts ever resolved a domain that has only now been identified as malicious. Zeek dns.log Protocol-aware network monitoring output containing the query, response, record types, response code, and round-trip time for every DNS transaction observed on the wire. Independent of server configuration, so it captures lookups sent to unauthorised resolvers. Windows DNS Debug Log The legacy text-based packet log configured through the DNS Manager console. Extremely verbose and a significant performance cost. Superseded by the analytical log and generally only appropriate for short troubleshooting windows. Pro Tip: Server-side DNS logs attribute a query to an IP address, not to a process or a user. Pair them with Sysmon event 22 for process attribution and with DHCP leases for device attribution, otherwise an alert on a malicious domain leaves you with an address and no owner.

DNS log destinations differ substantially between platforms, and on Windows the analytical channel is written as an ETL file rather than a normal event log. Log Default Location Windows Analytical Log %SystemRoot%\System32\Winevt\Logs\Microsoft-Windows-DNSServer%4Analytical.etl Windows Audit Log %SystemRoot%\System32\Winevt\Logs\Microsoft-Windows-DNSServer%4Audit.evtx Windows Debug Log %SystemRoot%\System32\dns\dns.log (path configurable in DNS Manager) BIND Query Log /var/log/named/query.log or /var/named/data/named.run, set by the channel definition BIND Configuration /etc/named.conf (RHEL) or /etc/bind/named.conf.options (Debian) Zeek DNS Log /opt/zeek/logs/current/dns.log Sysmon Event 22 Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational channel on each endpoint dnsmasq /var/log/dnsmasq.log or the system journal when no log-facility is set Pro Tip: The Windows analytical log is an ETL trace, not an EVTX file, so it cannot be opened directly in Event Viewer while the trace is running. Stop the channel first, or read it with Get-WinEvent -Path ... -Oldest , which handles ETL correctly.

Query logging is disabled by default on every major DNS platform because of its volume. These are the correct commands to turn it on in a way production can sustain. Step 1: Enable the Windows DNS Analytical Log # Confirm the channel exists and check its current state Get-WinEvent -ListLog "Microsoft-Windows-DNSServer/Analytical" | Format-List * # Enable it with a bounded file size $log = New-Object System.Diagnostics.Eventing.Reader.EventLogConfiguration ` "Microsoft-Windows-DNSServer/Analytical" $log.LogFilePath = "C:\DNSLogs\Analytical.etl" $log.MaximumSizeInBytes = 2GB $log.IsEnabled = $true $log.SaveChanges() The analytical channel must be disabled before its properties can be changed. Setting IsEnabled last is what actually starts the trace. Step 2: Verify Windows DNS Audit Logging # Audit logging is on by default, but confirm it Get-WinEvent -ListLog "Microsoft-Windows-DNSServer/Audit" | Select-Object LogName, IsEnabled, MaximumSizeInBytes, LogMode # Raise retention so a busy server does not overwrite weeks of changes wevtutil sl "Microsoft-Windows-DNSServer/Audit" /ms:1073741824 /rt:false The audit channel records zone and record modifications. Because it is low volume and high value, it should be sized generously and forwarded without filtering. Step 3: Configure BIND Query Logging // /etc/named.conf logging { channel query_channel { file "/var/log/named/query.log" versions 30 size 500m; severity info; print-time yes; print-category yes; print-severity yes; }; category queries { query_channel; }; category query-errors { query_channel; }; category security { query_channel; }; category client { query_channel; }; }; The versions and size arguments give BIND its own rotation, retaining 30 files of 500 MB. Without them the log grows until the filesystem fills. Step 4: Toggle BIND Query Logging at Runtime # Turn query logging on or off without restarting named rndc querylog on rndc querylog off # Check the current state rndc status | grep -i querylog rndc querylog is a runtime toggle, useful for enabling full query capture during an investigation without a service restart or configuration change. Step 5: Enable Sysmon DNS Logging on Endpoints <Sysmon schemaversion="4.90"> <EventFiltering> <RuleGroup name="DNS" groupRelation="or"> <DnsQuery onmatch="exclude"> <!-- Exclude high volume, low value internal noise --> <QueryName condition="end with">.corp.local</QueryName> <QueryName condition="end with">.in-addr.arpa</QueryName> <Image condition="is">C:\Windows\System32\svchost.exe</Image> </DnsQuery> </RuleGroup> </EventFiltering> </Sysmon> Sysmon event 22 is the only DNS source that names the resolving process. Use exclude rules rather than include rules so that unexpected lookups are captured by default. Step 6: Close the Encrypted DNS Bypass # Block outbound DNS to anything except approved resolvers (firewall policy) deny udp any any eq 53 unless dst in {10.10.0.10, 10.10.0.11} deny tcp any any eq 853 # DNS over TLS # Disable DoH in Microsoft Edge and Chrome via Group Policy HKLM\Software\Policies\Microsoft\Edge\DnsOverHttpsMode = "off" HKLM\Software\Policies\Google\Chrome\DnsOverHttpsMode = "off" Without these controls a single browser setting removes a host from DNS monitoring entirely, and the absence of logs looks identical to a quiet endpoint. Security Note: Never enable the legacy Windows DNS debug log on a busy domain controller as a monitoring solution. It writes synchronously to a text file and has been documented to cause noticeable query latency. The analytical channel exists specifically to solve this problem.

DNS abuse follows a small number of recognisable shapes. Each has a distinct statistical signature, which is what makes DNS such a productive detection surface. DNS Tunnelling Data encoded into subdomain labels and carried out through TXT or NULL records. Signature: very long query names, high entropy, huge query volume to one parent domain, and TXT records dominating. Detect Critical Domain Generation Algorithms Malware algorithmically generates candidate domains until one resolves. Signature: a burst of NXDOMAIN responses for random-looking names from a single host, followed by one successful resolution. Detect Critical Command and Control Beaconing Regular check-in intervals to a controller. Signature: highly consistent timing between lookups of the same domain, often with very low TTL values and few distinct clients. Detect Critical Newly Registered Domains Phishing and malware infrastructure is typically used within days of registration. Any lookup of a domain registered in the last 30 days is disproportionately likely to be malicious. Detect High Risk Fast Flux A single domain rotating rapidly through many IP addresses to resist takedown. Signature: very low TTL combined with a high count of distinct answers over a short window. Detect High Risk Resolver Bypass Hosts querying external resolvers directly, or using DoH and DoT. Signature: outbound port 53 or 853 to non-approved addresses, or TLS connections to known DoH providers. Detect High Risk Security Note: A sudden drop in DNS log volume from a host is itself a detection. It usually means the host has switched to an external or encrypted resolver, which is exactly what an attacker wants before starting command and control traffic.

These are the fields available across the major DNS log sources. Normalising to a common schema is what allows one detection to run against Windows, BIND, and Zeek data at the same time. Field Description Category Example Value timestamp Time the query was received Timestamp 2025-07-14 09:41:22.481 client_ip Address of the host that issued the query Source 10.30.2.61 query_name The fully qualified name requested Target a7f3c19e.tunnel.example.com query_type Record type requested Request Type TXT query_class Protocol class, almost always IN Request Type IN response_code Result status of the query Result NXDOMAIN answers Records returned in the response Response 203.0.113.44 ttl Time to live of the returned record Response 60 recursion_desired Whether the client requested recursion Flags true transport UDP or TCP Protocol UDP process_image Resolving process, Sysmon event 22 only Identity C:\Users\public\svc.exe query_length Character length of the query name Detection 214

Certain record types and response codes carry far more security weight than their share of traffic would suggest. Type / Code Meaning Why It Matters TXT Arbitrary text record The preferred carrier for DNS tunnelling and for staged payload delivery, because it holds arbitrary data. Normal TXT volume is low, so spikes stand out NULL Undefined record type Almost never used legitimately. Its presence is a strong tunnelling indicator, notably used by Iodine CNAME Canonical name alias Long CNAME chains are used for tunnelling and for cloaking the true destination of phishing infrastructure ANY Request for all records Deprecated for normal use. Appears in reconnaissance and in DNS amplification reflection attacks AXFR Full zone transfer An unauthorised AXFR hands an attacker a complete map of internal hostnames and addresses in one request NXDOMAIN Name does not exist Bursts of NXDOMAIN from one host is the defining signature of domain generation algorithm malware searching for its controller SERVFAIL Server failure Can indicate DNSSEC validation failure, which may mean tampering, or a poorly configured attacker-controlled zone REFUSED Server refused to answer Frequently the response to an attempted zone transfer or to recursion requested by an unauthorised client SRV Service location record Queries for _ldap._tcp and _kerberos._tcp are how an attacker locates domain controllers immediately after landing on a network Pro Tip: Baseline your normal NXDOMAIN rate per host before alerting on it. Misconfigured applications and search-domain suffixes generate steady background NXDOMAIN traffic, so a static threshold produces constant false positives while a per-host deviation does not.

These queries surface tunnelling, algorithmic domains, beaconing, and resolver bypass from DNS logs in a SIEM or directly on disk. Long Query Names (Tunnelling) SIEM> source="dns" | eval qlen=len(query_name) | where qlen > 100 | stats count, avg(qlen) as avg_len, dc(query_name) as unique by client_ip, parent_domain | sort - count Normal DNS names are short. Sustained queries over 100 characters to one parent domain is tunnelling until proven otherwise. NXDOMAIN Burst (DGA) SIEM> source="dns" response_code="NXDOMAIN" | bucket _time span=5m | stats dc(query_name) as failed_domains by client_ip, _time | where failed_domains > 50 Fifty or more distinct failed lookups in five minutes from one host is the classic domain generation algorithm pattern. Excessive TXT Queries SIEM> source="dns" query_type IN ("TXT","NULL") | stats count by client_ip, parent_domain | where count > 100 | sort - count TXT is normally a trickle used for SPF and domain verification. High volume to a single domain is data transfer, not lookups. Beacon Interval Detection SIEM> source="dns" | sort client_ip, query_name, _time | streamstats current=f last(_time) as prev by client_ip, query_name | eval gap=_time-prev | stats count, stdev(gap) as jitter, avg(gap) as interval by client_ip, query_name | where count > 20 AND jitter < 5 Very low jitter across many lookups means a machine, not a human. This is the single most reliable beacon detection available from DNS. Fast Flux and Low TTL SIEM> source="dns" ttl<120 | stats dc(answers) as distinct_ips, values(answers) by query_name | where distinct_ips > 10 A domain resolving to more than ten addresses with a TTL under two minutes is either a large CDN or fast flux infrastructure. Whitelist the former. Zone Transfer Attempts bash> grep -iE "AXFR|IXFR" /var/log/named/query.log | grep -v "10.10.0.1[01]" | awk '{print $6, $8}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn Any zone transfer request from an address other than your authorised secondaries is reconnaissance against your internal namespace. Resolver Bypass SIEM> source="firewall" dest_port IN (53,853) NOT dest_ip IN ("10.10.0.10","10.10.0.11") action="allowed" | stats count by src_ip, dest_ip, dest_port Detects hosts talking DNS directly to the internet, bypassing your logging and filtering entirely. Read the Windows Analytical Log PS> Get-WinEvent -Path "C:\DNSLogs\Analytical.etl" -Oldest | Where-Object { $_.Id -eq 257 } | Select-Object TimeCreated, @{n='Query';e={$_.Properties[6].Value}}, @{n='Client';e={$_.Properties[1].Value}} | Select-Object -First 50 Event ID 257 is RESPONSE_SUCCESS in the analytical channel. The -Oldest switch is mandatory when reading ETL files. Process Attribution via Sysmon SIEM> source="WinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational" EventCode=22 | stats dc(QueryName) as domains by Image, Computer | where NOT Image IN ("*\chrome.exe","*\msedge.exe","*\svchost.exe") | sort - domains Reveals which binaries resolve names. A process in a user profile or temp directory performing many lookups is malware. Domain Controller Discovery SIEM> source="dns" query_type="SRV" query_name IN ("_ldap._tcp*","_kerberos._tcp*","_gc._tcp*") | stats count by client_ip | sort - count Domain-joined machines do this at boot. A non-domain host or a server that never normally does it is performing Active Directory reconnaissance.

Apply these practices to turn DNS from a high volume nuisance into the most productive detection source you have: 01 Log at the Internal Resolver Collect on the server your clients actually query, not at the forwarder. Once queries leave your recursive resolver they are aggregated and the originating client address is lost forever. 02 Force All DNS Through Approved Resolvers Block outbound port 53 and 853 at the perimeter except from your resolvers, and disable browser DoH by policy. Logging is worthless if a host can simply opt out of it. 03 Use the Analytical Channel on Windows The legacy debug log writes synchronously to text and measurably slows a domain controller. The ETW analytical channel was built for production query rates and is the supported approach. 04 Add Process Attribution Deploy Sysmon event 22 alongside server logging. Knowing that a host resolved a malicious domain is useful, knowing which executable did it turns an alert into an investigation. 05 Enrich with Domain Age and Reputation Join lookups against newly registered domain feeds and threat intelligence at ingest. Domain age alone is one of the strongest single predictors of maliciousness available. 06 Filter at Collection, Not at Detection Exclude reverse lookups, internal zones, and known-good telemetry domains before they reach the SIEM. DNS volume is the main reason teams abandon DNS logging, and most of it carries no signal. 07 Retain Long Enough to Look Backwards Threat intelligence arrives after the fact. Ninety days of DNS history lets you answer which hosts contacted a domain that was only identified as malicious last week. 08 Alert on Missing Logs Monitor query volume per host. A machine that stops producing DNS logs has usually switched resolvers or been taken off the corporate path, and both warrant investigation.

DHCP logs answer a question that almost every other log implicitly assumes has already been answered: which physical device was using this IP address at this moment. Firewall logs, proxy logs, IDS alerts, and DNS queries all identify actors by address, and on any network using dynamic addressing those addresses move between devices constantly. Without DHCP records, an alert saying that 10.30.2.61 contacted a command and control server identifies a lease, not a laptop, and the investigation stops there. The protocol itself is a four-message exchange: the client broadcasts a DHCPDISCOVER , servers respond with a DHCPOFFER , the client requests a specific offer with DHCPREQUEST , and the server confirms with DHCPACK . Each message carries the client hardware address, and most clients also supply a hostname and a vendor class identifier. That combination of MAC address, hostname, and vendor string is what makes DHCP logs valuable beyond simple attribution: it is effectively a passive asset inventory, recording every device that joins the network including the ones nobody registered. DHCP is also an attack surface in its own right. Because the protocol has no authentication, any host on a segment can answer a discover broadcast. A rogue DHCP server that wins the race supplies its own address as the default gateway and DNS server, placing the attacker in the middle of the victim's traffic. Related techniques include starvation attacks that exhaust the address pool to force clients onto a rogue server, and DHCP-based DNS redirection. Windows Server mitigates the rogue server problem within a domain through authorisation in Active Directory, and switches can enforce DHCP snooping, but both controls need their logs collected to be useful.

DHCP visibility comes from the server, from the switch infrastructure, and from the lease database itself: Log Type Description Server Audit Log The primary record, written by Windows DHCP Server or ISC dhcpd. Contains one entry per protocol message with the event code, address, MAC, and hostname. Windows rotates these into seven daily files named by weekday, which is a critical retention limitation. Lease Database The current state of all allocations rather than a chronological log. Windows stores this in a JET database, ISC dhcpd in a plain text leases file. Shows what is assigned right now, including lease start and expiry times. DHCP Snooping Log Produced by switches enforcing trusted and untrusted ports. Records offers seen on untrusted ports, which is the definitive rogue DHCP server detection, plus binding table entries mapping MAC to address to physical port. Server Authorisation Events Windows-specific records showing whether the DHCP service is authorised in Active Directory. An unauthorised server refusing to start is a strong signal that someone attempted to stand up a rogue server inside the domain. Dynamic DNS Update Log Records the server registering or removing DNS records on behalf of clients. Failures here explain stale DNS entries, and unexpected updates can indicate name-based redirection attempts. Relay Agent Log Router or switch records of DHCP requests forwarded between subnets, including Option 82 circuit and remote identifiers. Option 82 adds the physical port to the record, which is the strongest form of device attribution available. Pro Tip: Windows DHCP audit logs rotate on a seven day cycle by weekday name, so Monday's file is overwritten the following Monday. An investigation into activity from ten days ago will find the evidence already gone unless the logs are forwarded off the server.

Windows and ISC dhcpd take completely different approaches to storage, and the Windows weekday rotation scheme catches many teams out. Log Default Location Windows Audit Log %SystemRoot%\System32\dhcp\DhcpSrvLog-Mon.log through DhcpSrvLog-Sun.log Windows IPv6 Audit Log %SystemRoot%\System32\dhcp\DhcpV6SrvLog-Mon.log through Sun Windows Lease Database %SystemRoot%\System32\dhcp\dhcp.mdb Windows Event Channel Microsoft-Windows-DHCP-Server/Operational and /Admin ISC dhcpd Log /var/log/dhcpd.log, or syslog facility local7 by default ISC Lease File /var/lib/dhcp/dhcpd.leases (Debian) or /var/lib/dhcpd/dhcpd.leases (RHEL) ISC Configuration /etc/dhcp/dhcpd.conf Kea DHCP /var/log/kea-dhcp4.log with leases in /var/lib/kea/kea-leases4.csv Cisco DHCP Snooping Device syslog, plus the binding table via show ip dhcp snooping binding Pro Tip: The Windows audit log file is written with a header block repeated at the top of each file listing every event ID and its meaning. When parsing, skip the first 30 or so lines or your ingestion pipeline will create events out of the documentation.

Audit logging is on by default on Windows but with restrictive size limits, and ISC dhcpd needs an explicit syslog facility to separate its output from everything else. Step 1: Verify and Tune Windows DHCP Audit Logging # Check current state Get-DhcpServerAuditLog # Raise the size cap and relocate to a dedicated volume Set-DhcpServerAuditLog -Enable $true ` -Path "D:\DHCPLogs" ` -MaxMBFileSize 500 ` -DiskCheckInterval 50 ` -MinMBDiskSpace 100 Restart-Service DHCPServer The default cap is 70 MB shared across all seven files. On a large network that fills within hours, and the server silently stops logging when MinMBDiskSpace is reached. Step 2: Enable the Windows Operational Channel wevtutil sl "Microsoft-Windows-Dhcp-Server/Operational" /e:true /ms:268435456 wevtutil sl "Microsoft-Windows-Dhcp-Server/FilterNotifications" /e:true # Confirm Get-WinEvent -ListLog "Microsoft-Windows-Dhcp-Server/*" | Select-Object LogName, IsEnabled, MaximumSizeInBytes The operational channel carries service state, scope changes, and authorisation events in proper event log format, which forwards far more cleanly than the text audit file. Step 3: Configure ISC dhcpd Logging # /etc/dhcp/dhcpd.conf log-facility local7; # Record the vendor class and hostname for asset identification option space vendor; set vendor-string = option vendor-class-identifier; on commit { log(info, concat("COMMIT lease=", binary-to-ascii(10,8,".",leased-address), " mac=", binary-to-ascii(16,8,":",substring(hardware,1,6)), " host=", pick-first-value(option host-name, "unknown"), " vendor=", pick-first-value(vendor-string, "unknown"))); } The on commit block produces a single enriched line per lease containing everything needed for attribution and asset inventory in one record. Step 4: Separate DHCP from General Syslog # /etc/rsyslog.d/40-dhcpd.conf local7.* /var/log/dhcpd.log local7.* @@siem-collector.corp.local:6514 & stop # /etc/logrotate.d/dhcpd /var/log/dhcpd.log { daily rotate 90 compress missingok postrotate systemctl reload rsyslog > /dev/null 2>&1 || true endscript } Ninety days of retention is the practical minimum. Attribution questions routinely arrive weeks after the activity they concern. Step 5: Enable DHCP Snooping on Switches ! Cisco IOS ip dhcp snooping ip dhcp snooping vlan 10,20,30 no ip dhcp snooping information option ! unless the relay expects Option 82 interface GigabitEthernet1/0/1 description Uplink to distribution ip dhcp snooping trust ! interface range GigabitEthernet1/0/2 - 48 ip dhcp snooping limit rate 15 ! mitigate starvation attacks ! ip dhcp snooping database flash:snooping.db Only uplinks toward the legitimate DHCP server should be trusted. Any offer arriving on an untrusted access port is dropped and logged, which is the definitive rogue server detection. Step 6: Add Option 82 for Port-Level Attribution ! On the relay agent ip dhcp relay information option ip dhcp relay information policy replace ! ISC dhcpd side, log the circuit ID on commit { log(info, concat("PORT circuit=", binary-to-ascii(16,8,":",option agent.circuit-id), " remote=", binary-to-ascii(16,8,":",option agent.remote-id))); } Option 82 records the switch and physical port a request arrived on. This upgrades attribution from an address to a wall socket, which is decisive when tracking an unregistered device. Security Note: Windows DHCP audit logging stops entirely when free disk space drops below the MinMBDiskSpace threshold, and the service keeps issuing leases while silently logging nothing. Monitor both the free space on that volume and the age of the newest log entry.

DHCP abuse is limited in variety but high in impact, because success places the attacker in the path of all victim traffic. Rogue DHCP Server An unauthorised server answering discover broadcasts, supplying itself as gateway and DNS. Achieves a machine in the middle position for every client that accepts its offer. Detect Critical Pool Starvation Flooding requests with spoofed MAC addresses to exhaust the scope. Denies service to legitimate clients and is usually the setup phase for a rogue server attack. Detect Critical MAC Spoofing Cloning an authorised device's hardware address to inherit its network access and reservations. Signature: the same MAC appearing on two switch ports, or an abrupt hostname change for one MAC. Detect High Risk Unauthorised Devices Personal laptops, unmanaged IoT, and attacker hardware requesting leases. The vendor class identifier and hostname frequently identify these immediately. Detect High Risk Address Conflicts Event 13 on Windows means the server found an address already in use before offering it. Sustained conflicts can indicate a rogue server issuing overlapping addresses or manual static assignment inside the pool. Investigate Medium Risk MAC Randomisation Noise Modern phones and laptops randomise their hardware address per network by default. Not an attack, but it inflates apparent device counts and breaks MAC-based tracking if not accounted for. Baseline Medium Risk Security Note: Locally administered MAC addresses have the second least significant bit of the first octet set, which shows as a second character of 2, 6, A, or E. This distinguishes randomised or spoofed addresses from real vendor-assigned ones and is a useful first filter when triaging unknown devices.

The Windows audit log is comma separated with a fixed column order. These are the fields and their ISC dhcpd equivalents. Field Description Category Example Value ID Numeric event code for the DHCP message type Detection 10 Date / Time Local date and time of the event Timestamp 07/14/25 09:41:22 Description Text description of the event code Action Assign IP Address Address leased or referenced Target 10.30.2.61 Host Name Client-supplied hostname Identity WKS-FIN-014 MAC Address Client hardware address Identity 00155D8A4C12 User Name Authenticated user where NAP or 802.1X applies Identity CORP\r.almutairi TransactionID Identifier linking the four-message exchange Session 1874203911 QResult NAP quarantine result Policy 0 VendorClass Client vendor class identifier, hex or ASCII Asset MSFT 5.0 UserClass Client-supplied user class Asset Default Routing Class RelayAgentInformation Option 82 circuit and remote identifiers Source 0108000600040101

Windows DHCP audit event codes are stable and well documented, which makes them precise detection anchors. Event ID Meaning Why It Matters 10 A new IP address was leased to a client The core attribution record. Every new device joining the network appears here first 11 A lease was renewed by a client Confirms continued presence. Useful for building device dwell time on the network 12 A lease was released by a client Marks the end of an address to device binding, closing the attribution window 13 An IP address was found in use on the network Address conflict. Sustained occurrences suggest a rogue server or unauthorised static addressing 14 A lease request could not be satisfied, scope exhausted Pool exhaustion, which may be organic growth or an active starvation attack 15 A lease was denied (NAK) Frequently seen when a client presents a lease from a different, possibly rogue, server 20 A BOOTP address was leased to a client Legacy protocol usage. Unexpected BOOTP can indicate network boot attacks or old embedded devices 31 DNS dynamic update failed Leaves stale DNS entries that cause misattribution in every DNS-derived investigation 51 The server was authorised to start Normal service start within the domain, and the baseline for spotting the failure case below 54 Authorisation failed, server not authorised in Active Directory Someone stood up a DHCP server inside the domain without approval. Investigate the host immediately Pro Tip: Active Directory authorisation only restrains Windows DHCP servers that are domain members. A Linux host, a consumer router plugged into a wall port, or an attacker's laptop will happily serve DHCP with no authorisation check at all. Switch-level snooping is the control that actually stops those.

Use these to resolve addresses to devices, find rogue servers, and spot unmanaged hardware on the network. Resolve an Address to a Device SIEM> source="dhcp" ip_address="10.30.2.61" earliest=-7d | table _time, event_id, description, mac_address, host_name, vendor_class | sort _time The fundamental DHCP query. Always bound it by time, because the same address may have served a dozen devices in a week. Rogue DHCP Server bash> grep -iE "DHCP_SNOOPING_DENY|DHCP_SNOOPING_UNTRUSTED_PORT|dhcp server.*not authorized" /var/log/network/switches.log | awk '{print $1, $2, $NF}' | sort | uniq -c DHCP snooping denials name the exact switch port the rogue offer came from, which is enough to physically locate the device. Pool Starvation Attack SIEM> source="dhcp" event_id=10 | bucket _time span=5m | stats dc(mac_address) as new_devices by _time, scope | where new_devices > 50 Fifty new hardware addresses in five minutes on one scope is not organic. Compare against event 14 to confirm the pool was exhausted. MAC Address Conflict SIEM> source="dhcp" event_id IN (10,11) | stats dc(host_name) as names, values(host_name), dc(ip_address) as addrs by mac_address | where names > 1 One hardware address presenting two different hostnames is either MAC spoofing or a rebuilt machine. Both warrant a look. Unmanaged Devices SIEM> source="dhcp" event_id=10 | lookup asset_inventory mac_address OUTPUT owner, asset_tag | where isnull(asset_tag) | stats count, values(host_name), values(vendor_class) by mac_address Joining leases against the asset inventory turns DHCP into continuous rogue device detection. Randomised or Spoofed MACs bash> grep -oP '^10,.*?,\K[0-9A-F]{12}' /var/log/dhcp/DhcpSrvLog-Mon.log | grep -iE '^.[26AE]' | sort -u | wc -l Filters for locally administered addresses, the marker of randomised or manually set MACs. A rising count usually reflects modern device defaults rather than attack. Address Conflicts and Denials SIEM> source="dhcp" event_id IN (13,14,15) | timechart span=1h count by event_id A sudden rise in conflicts and NAKs is the fingerprint of a second DHCP server operating on the segment. Snooping Binding Table IOS> show ip dhcp snooping binding | include 10.30.2.61 Returns the MAC, address, lease time, VLAN, and physical interface in one line. The most direct route from an address to a wall port. Current Windows Leases PS> Get-DhcpServerv4Scope | Get-DhcpServerv4Lease | Where-Object { $_.AddressState -ne 'Active' } | Select-Object IPAddress, ClientId, HostName, AddressState, LeaseExpiryTime Non-active lease states such as ActiveReservation or Declined often mark conflicts and devices behaving unexpectedly. Logging Continuity SIEM> source="dhcp" | timechart span=1h count | where count < 10 Windows silently stops audit logging when disk space runs low while continuing to issue leases. Volume monitoring is the only way to notice.

Apply these practices so that every other log on the network remains attributable: 01 Forward Logs Off the Server Immediately Windows overwrites each audit file on a seven day weekday cycle. Any investigation reaching back further than a week finds nothing unless the logs were shipped elsewhere. 02 Retain for at Least Ninety Days Attribution requests arrive long after the event. Retention shorter than the rest of your log estate makes every other network log unattributable for the same period. 03 Enable DHCP Snooping Everywhere Active Directory authorisation only restrains domain-joined Windows servers. Snooping is what stops a Linux host or consumer router from serving addresses on an access port. 04 Capture Vendor Class and Hostname These fields turn the lease log into a passive asset inventory, identifying device type and operating system without any agent or scan. 05 Add Option 82 Where Possible Circuit and remote identifiers record the switch and port a request arrived on, upgrading attribution from an address to a physical location. 06 Join Leases to the Asset Inventory Enriching each lease with the registered owner at ingest means unknown devices surface automatically instead of requiring someone to go looking. 07 Monitor Free Disk Space on the Server Windows DHCP stops logging when free space falls below the configured minimum, yet continues issuing leases normally. Nothing alerts you that visibility has been lost. 08 Account for MAC Randomisation Phones and modern laptops randomise hardware addresses by default. Track devices by certificate or 802.1X identity where accuracy matters, and expect inflated device counts otherwise.

Normal allocation, attribution, and the two attacks DHCP logs are best at revealing. The MSFT 5.0 vendor class confirms Windows, and Option 82 records the originating port. ISC dhcpd: The Full Four-Message Exchange Jul 14 09:41:21 dhcp01 dhcpd[1284]: DHCPDISCOVER from 00:15:5d:8a:4c:12 via eth0 Jul 14 09:41:21 dhcp01 dhcpd[1284]: DHCPOFFER on 10.30.2.61 to 00:15:5d:8a:4c:12 (WKS-FIN-014) via eth0 Jul 14 09:41:22 dhcp01 dhcpd[1284]: DHCPREQUEST for 10.30.2.61 (10.10.0.5) from 00:15:5d:8a:4c:12 (WKS-FIN-014) via eth0 Jul 14 09:41:22 dhcp01 dhcpd[1284]: DHCPACK on 10.30.2.61 to 00:15:5d:8a:4c:12 (WKS-FIN-014) via eth0 The complete handshake. Note that this control does nothing against non-Windows rogue servers. Pool Starvation Attack Jul 14 10:02:44 dhcp01 dhcpd[1284]: DHCPDISCOVER from 3a:1f:7c:04:9e:22 via eth0 Jul 14 10:02:44 dhcp01 dhcpd[1284]: DHCPDISCOVER from 6e:88:2b:f1:04:c7 via eth0 Jul 14 10:02:44 dhcp01 dhcpd[1284]: DHCPDISCOVER from a2:41:9d:3e:77:10 via eth0 Jul 14 10:02:45 dhcp01 dhcpd[1284]: DHCPDISCOVER from ee:03:b4:2a:81:5f via eth0 Jul 14 10:03:19 dhcp01 dhcpd[1284]: no free leases on subnet 10.30.2.0/24 Randomised hardware addresses arriving in the same second, all locally administered (second character 2, 6, A, or E). The pool exhausts in 35 seconds, clearing the way for a rogue server. MAC Spoofing: One Address, Two Identities 10,07/14/25,08:14:02,Assign,10.30.2.61,WKS-FIN-014,00155D8A4C12,,1874203911,0 12,07/14/25,09:38:41,Release,10.30.2.61,WKS-FIN-014,00155D8A4C12,,1874203911,0 10,07/14/25,09:39:02,Assign,10.30.2.61,kali,00155D8A4C12,,1874204882,0 The same hardware address releases a lease as WKS-FIN-014 and reclaims it 21 seconds later as kali. The MAC was cloned to inherit the legitimate workstation's network access. Unmanaged Device Joining the Network Jul 14 10:18:12 dhcp01 dhcpd[1284]: DHCPACK on 10.30.2.184 to 8a:3f:2c:91:0e:44 (raspberrypi) via eth0 vendor-class-identifier = "dhcpcd-9.4.1:Linux-6.1.21-v8+:aarch64:BCM2835" Jul 14 10:18:12 dhcp01 dhcpd[1284]: COMMIT lease=10.30.2.184 mac=8a:3f:2c:91:0e:44 host=raspberrypi vendor=dhcpcd-9.4.1:Linux-6.1.21-v8+ The vendor class identifies a Raspberry Pi running Linux on ARM. No asset record exists for this device, and single-board computers are a common drop-box for persistent network access. Back

Routers and switches are the infrastructure every other system depends on, and they are consistently the least monitored assets in the estate. An attacker who compromises a core switch can mirror traffic to a collector, alter routing to intercept sessions, disable access control lists, and modify the very logging that would reveal any of it. Network devices are also increasingly targeted directly, with state-aligned actors known to persist on routers for years because nobody was watching the configuration. These devices log through syslog , and the critical architectural fact is that they retain almost nothing locally. A Cisco switch keeps a small in-memory buffer that wraps within minutes on a busy device and is cleared entirely by a reboot. There is no local disk log to recover after an incident. If syslog forwarding is not configured, the evidence does not exist. That single property makes network device logging an all-or-nothing proposition in a way that server logging is not. The most valuable records fall into three groups. Configuration and authentication events reveal who logged into the management plane and what they changed, which is the core of detecting device compromise. Access control list denials provide segmentation enforcement evidence and reveal lateral movement attempts between zones. Port security and 802.1X events expose unauthorised devices connecting to physical ports. Command accounting through TACACS+ goes further still, recording every individual command an administrator typed rather than merely that a configuration change occurred.

Network devices emit several categories of message. Only some carry security value, and separating them is the key to a manageable event rate: Log Type Description Configuration Change Log Records entry into configuration mode and, with the archive feature, the exact commands applied. The single most important stream on any network device: every attacker modification to routing, access control, or logging appears here. Authentication and Authorisation Log Management plane logins over SSH, console, and the web interface, plus privilege escalation to enable mode. Failed authentication bursts against infrastructure are a strong precursor to device compromise. ACL Denial Log Packets dropped by access control lists, subject to the log keyword being present on the entry. The primary evidence that network segmentation is being enforced and the primary detection for lateral movement between zones. Port Security and 802.1X Log Violations where an unexpected MAC address appeared on a port, and results of port-based authentication. Detects unauthorised devices plugged into physical infrastructure, including rogue access points and drop boxes. Interface State Log Link up and down transitions and line protocol changes. Mostly operational, but an interface coming up on a previously unused port, or repeated flapping, can indicate physical tampering. Routing Protocol Log Neighbour adjacency changes for OSPF, BGP, and EIGRP. An unexpected new neighbour is a serious event, since a rogue peer can inject routes that redirect traffic through attacker infrastructure. Command Accounting Delivered through TACACS+ rather than syslog. Records every command executed by every administrator with full attribution. The gold standard for management plane auditing and worth deploying for this alone. Spanning Tree and Layer 2 Log Root bridge changes, BPDU guard actions, and loop detection. A spanning tree topology change caused by an unauthorised device can redirect entire VLANs through an attacker-controlled path. Pro Tip: ACL denials are only logged when the log or log-input keyword is present on the individual access list entry. A device with a hundred ACL lines and no log keywords produces perfect enforcement and zero visibility. Add log-input to deny entries specifically, since it also records the ingress interface and source MAC.

Unlike servers, network devices have no meaningful local log storage. These are the destinations available and their retention characteristics. Destination Characteristics Memory Buffer Cisco: viewed with show logging. Typically 4 to 16 KB by default, wraps within minutes, and is lost completely on reload. Useful for live troubleshooting only Remote Syslog The only viable collection method. Configured with logging host on Cisco or set system syslog host on Junos. Should use TCP with TLS where the platform supports it Console and Terminal Lines Real time display to an attached session. Console logging at high verbosity can hang the device under load and should be disabled in production Configuration Archive Cisco archive feature storing configuration snapshots to flash or a remote server, with the log config subcommand capturing individual commands TACACS+ Accounting Command level accounting sent to an authentication server such as Cisco ISE. Retained centrally with full attribution, independent of syslog SNMP Traps Event notifications to a network management platform. Useful for availability monitoring but a poor security log, as trap coverage is inconsistent Junos Local Files /var/log/messages, /var/log/interactive-commands, and /var/log/authorization. Junos retains more locally than IOS but still requires forwarding Flash Storage Some platforms support logging to onboard flash. Survives reload but has limited capacity and is erasable by anyone with device access Pro Tip: Run show logging before you do anything else when responding to a suspected device compromise. The buffer holds the most recent events and will be destroyed by the reload that is often the first instinct during troubleshooting.

These configurations produce attributable, timestamped, centrally stored records from Cisco IOS and Juniper Junos devices. Step 1: Configure Cisco IOS Syslog service timestamps log datetime msec localtime show-timezone year service sequence-numbers logging buffered 65536 informational no logging console logging host 10.50.9.20 transport tcp port 1514 logging trap informational logging source-interface Loopback0 logging origin-id hostname logging facility local6 The timestamp directive is critical. IOS defaults to uptime rather than wall clock time, producing entries like "3d04h" that are useless for correlation. Sequence numbers reveal messages lost in transit. Step 2: Enable Configuration Change Logging archive log config logging enable logging size 1000 notify syslog contenttype plaintext hidekeys path tftp://10.50.9.30/$h-config write-memory time-period 10080 Without this, a configuration change produces only a generic CONFIG_I message saying something changed. With it, every individual command is logged and attributed. hidekeys prevents passwords appearing in the log. Step 3: Log Authentication Events login on-failure log every 1 login on-success log every 1 login block-for 300 attempts 5 within 60 aaa new-model aaa authentication login default group tacacs+ local aaa authorization commands 15 default group tacacs+ local aaa accounting commands 15 default start-stop group tacacs+ aaa accounting exec default start-stop group tacacs+ Success and failure logging are both off by default. Command accounting at privilege 15 is what records every individual command an administrator runs, with full attribution. Step 4: Add Logging to Access Control Lists ip access-list extended SEGMENT-USERS-TO-SERVERS permit tcp 10.30.0.0 0.0.255.255 10.40.1.0 0.0.0.255 eq 443 deny ip 10.30.0.0 0.0.255.255 10.40.1.0 0.0.0.255 log-input deny ip any any log-input ! ip access-list logging interval 250 logging rate-limit 100 except critical log-input records the ingress interface and source MAC alongside the packet, which is what turns a denial into an investigable event. Rate limiting protects the control plane from a logging-induced denial of service. Step 5: Enable Port Security and Layer 2 Protection interface range GigabitEthernet1/0/2 - 48 switchport mode access switchport port-security switchport port-security maximum 2 switchport port-security violation restrict switchport port-security aging time 120 spanning-tree bpduguard enable spanning-tree portfast ! errdisable recovery cause psecure-violation errdisable recovery interval 300 The restrict violation mode drops offending traffic and logs it, whereas shutdown disables the port entirely and protect drops silently with no log at all. Only restrict gives both enforcement and visibility. Step 6: Configure Juniper Junos Logging set system syslog host 10.50.9.20 any notice set system syslog host 10.50.9.20 authorization info set system syslog host 10.50.9.20 interactive-commands any set system syslog host 10.50.9.20 change-log any set system syslog host 10.50.9.20 structured-data set system syslog host 10.50.9.20 source-address 10.50.1.5 set system syslog file interactive-commands interactive-commands any set system syslog time-format year millisecond The interactive-commands and change-log facilities are Junos equivalents of Cisco command accounting. structured-data emits RFC 5424 format, which parses far more reliably than the legacy format. Security Note: Traditional syslog over UDP is unauthenticated and unencrypted, so anyone on the path can forge or read device logs. Use TCP with TLS where supported, restrict the syslog destination with an access control list, and treat the syslog collector as a tier zero asset.

Syslog severity runs from 0 to 7 with lower numbers being more severe. Setting the trap level too low is the most common cause of missing security events, because most authentication and configuration messages sit at level 5 and 6. 0 to 2: Emergency, Alert, Critical System unusable, immediate action required, or critical condition. Includes port security violations at level 2 and hardware failures. Always page on these. Alert Critical 3: Error Error conditions including interface link failures and IKE negotiation problems. Operationally important and occasionally security relevant. Collect High Risk 4: Warning Warning conditions including failed login attempts on many platforms. The default trap level on Cisco, which is precisely why level 5 and 6 events go missing. Collect High Risk 5: Notification Normal but significant conditions. Configuration changes (CONFIG_I), successful logins, and line protocol changes all sit here. Security critical despite the modest name. Collect Critical 6: Informational Informational messages including ACL denials (IPACCESSLOGP) and login successes. The correct trap level for security monitoring, and the reason to move off the default. Collect Critical 7: Debug Debug level messages. Enormous volume and capable of destabilising the device under load. Enable only during active troubleshooting and never as a standing configuration. Avoid Medium Risk Security Note: Set logging trap informational rather than accepting the default. Configuration changes are severity 5 and ACL denials are severity 6, so a device left at the warning default silently discards the two most valuable security streams it produces.

Cisco IOS messages follow a rigid structure. Parsing the mnemonic correctly is what makes detection rules portable across a fleet. Field Description Category Example Value sequence Message counter, gaps reveal dropped messages Metadata 001284 timestamp Date and time with milliseconds and timezone Timestamp Jul 14 2025 09:41:22.481 AST facility Subsystem that generated the message Metadata SEC_LOGIN severity Numeric level from 0 to 7 Severity 4 mnemonic Unique message identifier within the facility Detection LOGIN_FAILED description Message text with embedded variables Action Login failed [user: admin] [Source: 203.0.113.44] device_id Hostname or configured origin identifier Source sw-core-01 user Account associated with the event Identity netadmin src_ip Source address for management or ACL events Source 203.0.113.44 interface Physical or logical interface involved Target GigabitEthernet1/0/24 acl_name Access list that matched Policy SEGMENT-USERS-TO-SERVERS action Permitted or denied Response denied

These Cisco IOS mnemonics carry the highest security value. Junos equivalents are noted where they differ substantially. Message Meaning Why It Matters %SYS-5-CONFIG_I Configuration changed from a source Every device modification passes through this. Correlate against your change window and ticket system, and alert on anything unmatched %PARSER-5-CFGLOG_LOGGEDCMD Individual configuration command executed Produced by the archive log config feature. Shows the exact command rather than merely that a change occurred %SEC_LOGIN-4-LOGIN_FAILED Management login failed Failed authentication against infrastructure. Bursts from one source are brute force against the management plane %SEC_LOGIN-5-LOGIN_SUCCESS Management login succeeded The baseline for detecting logins outside change windows or from unexpected addresses %SEC_LOGIN-1-QUIET_MODE_ON Login blocking activated after repeated failures Confirms a brute force attempt reached the configured threshold. Severity 1 makes it hard to miss %SEC-6-IPACCESSLOGP Packet permitted or denied by an ACL Segmentation enforcement evidence. Denials between security zones frequently reveal lateral movement attempts %PORT_SECURITY-2-PSECURE_VIOLATION Unauthorised MAC address on a secured port An unexpected device connected to physical infrastructure. Severity 2 and always worth investigating %SPANTREE-2-BLOCK_BPDUGUARD BPDU received on a port with BPDU guard Someone connected a switch to an access port. Either shadow IT or an attempt to manipulate the layer 2 topology %DOT1X-5-FAIL 802.1X authentication failed on a port A device failed port-based authentication. Repeated failures on one port indicate an unauthorised connection attempt %BGP-5-ADJCHANGE BGP neighbour state changed An unexpected new peer can inject routes that redirect traffic through attacker-controlled infrastructure %SYS-5-RELOAD Device reload requested Clears the memory buffer entirely. An unscheduled reload may be an attempt to destroy volatile evidence %SYS-6-LOGGINGHOST_STARTSTOP Syslog host configuration changed Removal of a logging destination is a hallmark anti-forensic step and should page immediately Pro Tip: Alert on the absence of logs as well as their content. A device that normally emits a steady trickle of messages and then goes silent has either failed, been reloaded, or had its logging destination removed. All three matter.

These queries surface unauthorised configuration changes, management plane attacks, and rogue devices on physical ports. Configuration Changes Outside the Window SIEM> source="network_device" mnemonic="CONFIG_I" | eval hr=strftime(_time,"%H"), dow=strftime(_time,"%a") | where NOT (dow=="Sat" AND hr>=22) AND NOT (hr>=1 AND hr<=4) | table _time, device_id, user, src_ip, message Every change outside the approved maintenance window, ready to reconcile against tickets. Unmatched entries are the investigation queue. Management Plane Brute Force SIEM> source="network_device" mnemonic IN ("LOGIN_FAILED","AUTHFAIL") | bucket _time span=10m | stats count, dc(device_id) as devices, values(user) by src_ip, _time | where count > 10 A source failing against multiple devices is sweeping your infrastructure with a credential list, not mistyping a password. Logging Destination Removed SIEM> source="network_device" (message="*no logging host*" OR message="*no logging trap*" OR mnemonic="LOGGINGHOST_STARTSTOP" OR message="*no aaa accounting*") | table _time, device_id, user, src_ip, message Page on this immediately. It is almost never a legitimate change and it is usually the last message that device will ever send you. Port Security Violations SIEM> source="network_device" mnemonic="PSECURE_VIOLATION" | stats count, values(mac_address), values(interface) by device_id | sort - count Names the switch, the port, and the offending hardware address, which is enough to physically locate the unauthorised device. Cross-Zone ACL Denials SIEM> source="network_device" mnemonic="IPACCESSLOGP" action="denied" | stats count, dc(dest_ip) as targets, dc(dest_port) as ports by src_ip | where targets > 10 OR ports > 10 | sort - targets One internal source denied against many destinations or ports is scanning across a segmentation boundary, which is textbook lateral movement. Unexpected Routing Neighbours SIEM> source="network_device" mnemonic IN ("ADJCHANGE","NBRCHANGE","NEIGHBOR") | stats values(neighbor_ip), count by device_id | search NOT neighbor_ip IN ("10.50.1.1","10.50.1.2","10.50.1.3") Compare observed adjacencies against the approved topology. A rogue peer can inject routes and redirect entire subnets. Layer 2 Topology Attacks SIEM> source="network_device" mnemonic IN ("BLOCK_BPDUGUARD","ROOTGUARD_BLOCK","TOPOTRAP","LOOPGUARD_BLOCK") | table _time, device_id, interface, message BPDU guard firing means a switch was connected to an access port. Root guard firing means something tried to become the spanning tree root. Command Accounting Review SIEM> source="tacacs" service="shell" | search cmd IN ("no logging*","no aaa*","monitor session*","username*","snmp-server*","ip nat*") | table _time, user, device_id, cmd A watchlist of commands that create backdoors, mirror traffic, or disable auditing. Command accounting is what makes this level of detail possible. Traffic Mirroring Configured SIEM> source="network_device" (message="*monitor session*" OR message="*port-mirror*" OR message="*analyzer*") | table _time, device_id, user, src_ip, message A SPAN session created outside a documented troubleshooting exercise means someone is copying traffic to a destination of their choosing. Silent Devices SIEM> source="network_device" earliest=-24h | stats latest(_time) as last_seen by device_id | eval age_hr=(now()-last_seen)/3600 | where age_hr > 6 | sort - age_hr Devices that have stopped logging. Given that these devices retain nothing locally, silence means total loss of visibility rather than a quiet period.

s.h: Best Practices for Network Device Logging
s.t: Follow these practices to make infrastructure logging complete and trustworthy: 01 Fix Timestamps Before Anything Else IOS defaults to uptime rather than wall clock time. Configure service timestamps with datetime, msec, timezone, and year, and synchronise every device to NTP or correlation is impossible. 02 Set Trap Level to Informational Configuration changes are severity 5 and ACL denials are severity 6. The default warning level discards both, which removes the two most useful security streams the device produces. 03 Enable Archive Log Config Without it a change produces only a generic notification. With it you get the exact command, the user, and the source, which is the difference between knowing something changed and knowing what. 04 Deploy TACACS+ Command Accounting Per-command attribution is the strongest management plane audit available, and it is stored on the authentication server independently of syslog, so it survives device compromise. 05 Add log-input to Deny Entries ACLs enforce silently unless the log keyword is present. log-input additionally records the ingress interface and source MAC, turning a denial into something investigable. 06 Use restrict for Port Security The protect mode drops violating traffic with no log at all, and shutdown creates an outage. Only restrict gives you both enforcement and a record of what happened. 07 Rate Limit Logging ACL denial logging is punted to the control plane processor. Without logging rate-limit, a deliberate flood of denied packets can degrade or crash the device. 08 Monitor for Silence These devices hold nothing locally. A device that stops sending logs has lost all visibility, so absence of events must be alerted on as loudly as their content.

A compromise of network infrastructure, from management plane brute force through to traffic interception. QUIET_MODE_ON confirms login blocking engaged, which means the threshold configured in step 3 was reached. Cross-referencing the VPN session log identifies which user held that lease, and whether their account was already compromised. Individual Commands via Archive Logging 001404: Jul 14 2025 09:41:14.882 AST: %PARSER-5-CFGLOG_LOGGEDCMD: User:netadmin logged command:monitor session 1 source vlan 40 001405: Jul 14 2025 09:41:22.104 AST: %PARSER-5-CFGLOG_LOGGEDCMD: User:netadmin logged command:monitor session 1 destination interface Gi1/0/24 001406: Jul 14 2025 09:41:38.771 AST: %PARSER-5-CFGLOG_LOGGEDCMD: User:netadmin logged command:username svc_backup privilege 15 secret ***** 001407: Jul 14 2025 09:41:55.229 AST: %PARSER-5-CFGLOG_LOGGEDCMD: User:netadmin logged command:no logging host 10.50.9.20 The full attack in four commands: mirror the server VLAN to a port, create a privileged backdoor account, then remove the syslog destination. Without archive log config, all of this would appear as a single CONFIG_I message. Unauthorised Device on a Physical Port 001450: Jul 14 2025 09:52:10.774 AST: %PORT_SECURITY-2-PSECURE_VIOLATION: Security violation occurred, caused by MAC address 000c.298f.2a41 on port GigabitEthernet1/0/24. 001451: Jul 14 2025 09:52:10.881 AST: %PM-4-ERR_DISABLE: psecure-violation error detected on Gi1/0/24, putting Gi1/0/24 in err-disable state 001452: Jul 14 2025 09:52:11.004 AST: %SPANTREE-2-BLOCK_BPDUGUARD: Received BPDU on port GigabitEthernet1/0/24 with BPDU Guard enabled. Disabling port. The same port used as the SPAN destination now shows an unknown MAC and is sending BPDUs, meaning a switch or virtual machine was plugged in there. The 000c.29 prefix is VMware. Lateral Movement Blocked by an ACL 001478: Jul 14 2025 10:02:44.229 AST: %SEC-6-IPACCESSLOGP: list SEGMENT-USERS-TO-SERVERS denied tcp 10.30.2.61(52190) (GigabitEthernet1/0/12 0015.5d8a.4c12) -> 10.40.1.15(445), 1 packet 001479: Jul 14 2025 10:02:44.334 AST: %SEC-6-IPACCESSLOGP: list SEGMENT-USERS-TO-SERVERS denied tcp 10.30.2.61(52191) (GigabitEthernet1/0/12 0015.5d8a.4c12) -> 10.40.1.16(445), 1 packet 001480: Jul 14 2025 10:02:44.441 AST: %SEC-6-IPACCESSLOGP: list SEGMENT-USERS-TO-SERVERS denied tcp 10.30.2.61(52192) (GigabitEthernet1/0/12 0015.5d8a.4c12) -> 10.40.1.17(445), 1 packet A workstation sweeping SMB across the server segment. The log-input keyword supplied the ingress interface and source MAC, so the offending machine is identified without any further lookup. Rogue Routing Neighbour 001502: Jul 14 2025 10:11:03.118 AST: %OSPF-5-ADJCHG: Process 1, Nbr 10.30.2.61 on GigabitEthernet1/0/12 from LOADING to FULL, Loading Done 001503: Jul 14 2025 10:11:04.229 AST: %OSPF-4-ERRRCV: Received invalid packet: mismatched area ID, from backbone area must be virtual-link but not found from 10.30.2.61, GigabitEthernet1/0/12 An OSPF adjacency formed with a host on a user access port. No workstation should ever be an OSPF neighbour. This peer can now inject routes and pull traffic through itself.
