Evidence Destruction: Unscheduled Reload 001540: Jul 14 2025 10:24:18.229 AST: %SYS-5-CONFIG_I: Configured from console by netadmin on vty0 (10.99.4.117) 001541: Jul 14 2025 10:24:31.774 AST: %SYS-5-RELOAD: Reload requested by netadmin on vty0 (10.99.4.117). Reload Reason: Reload Command. A reload clears the in-memory buffer completely. Because syslog forwarding had already been removed in an earlier command, these two lines are the last records the collector ever received from this device. Back

A vSphere environment concentrates enormous risk into a small number of hosts. Compromise a single ESXi server and every virtual machine on it becomes accessible at the disk level, bypassing every guest operating system control, endpoint agent, and disk encryption scheme that depends on the guest being running. Compromise vCenter and the same applies across the entire estate. This is why ransomware groups shifted to targeting hypervisors directly: encrypting a datastore takes out hundreds of servers at once, and the guest agents that would have detected it are inside the machines being encrypted. Logging spans two layers. Each ESXi host writes a set of plain text logs under /var/log , with hostd.log recording host agent operations and authentication, vmkernel.log recording kernel and storage events, auth.log recording SSH and shell authentication, and shell.log recording every command typed in the ESXi shell. Above that, vCenter Server maintains vpxd.log plus a structured events and tasks database that records every administrative action performed through the management interface, attributed to a named user. The critical operational weakness is retention. ESXi logs live on a small local scratch partition and rotate aggressively, and on hosts booting from SD card or USB the logs may be held in a RAM disk that is lost entirely on reboot. An attacker who reboots a host after acting on it destroys the evidence without needing any anti-forensic tooling. Configuring a remote syslog target is therefore not a refinement but the precondition for any hypervisor investigation being possible at all.

ESXi and vCenter produce complementary streams. Host logs show what happened on the hypervisor, vCenter events show who requested it: Log Type Description hostd.log The ESXi host agent log, recording virtual machine power operations, configuration changes, datastore activity, and local authentication. The primary host-level security log and the first place to look after a host compromise. auth.log Authentication to the host itself over SSH, the Direct Console interface, and the shell. Where brute force against ESXi and successful attacker logins appear. shell.log Every command executed in the ESXi shell, with timestamps and the invoking user. The single most valuable forensic artifact on a compromised host, since ransomware operators work almost entirely through the shell. vpxd.log The vCenter Server daemon log, covering all management operations, host connectivity, and API sessions. Correlates administrative intent with the host-level actions that resulted. vCenter Events and Tasks Structured records in the vCenter database exposed through the UI and API. Every virtual machine creation, clone, deletion, permission change, and login is recorded here with the responsible user. The most queryable vSphere source. vmkernel.log VMkernel messages covering storage paths, device events, and resource conditions. Mostly operational, but datastore access errors during mass encryption surface here first. vpxa.log The vCenter agent running on each ESXi host, showing tasks pushed down from vCenter. Useful for distinguishing actions taken through vCenter from actions taken directly on the host. SSO and Identity Logs vmware-sts-idmd.log and related files recording Single Sign-On authentication against vCenter, including failures. Where credential attacks against the management plane appear. Virtual Machine Logs A vmware.log file alongside each virtual machine on the datastore, recording power events, snapshot operations, and device changes for that specific machine. Pro Tip: Actions taken directly on an ESXi host through SSH do not appear in vCenter events at all. An attacker who bypasses vCenter and works on the host leaves traces only in shell.log and auth.log , which is precisely why those two files must be forwarded off the host.

ESXi paths are consistent across versions. vCenter Server Appliance paths differ from the older Windows-based installations. Log Location ESXi Host Agent /var/log/hostd.log ESXi Authentication /var/log/auth.log ESXi Shell Commands /var/log/shell.log ESXi VMkernel /var/log/vmkernel.log and /var/log/vmkwarning.log ESXi vCenter Agent /var/log/vpxa.log vCenter Daemon /var/log/vmware/vpxd/vpxd.log on the appliance vCenter SSO /var/log/vmware/sso/vmware-sts-idmd.log vCenter Events Database Embedded PostgreSQL, queried through the UI, PowerCLI, or the vSphere API Per Virtual Machine /vmfs/volumes/<datastore>/<vm-name>/vmware.log Support Bundle Generated with vm-support on a host or the vCenter UI, collecting all of the above Pro Tip: Check whether the host has persistent scratch storage with vim-cmd hostsvc/advopt/view ScratchConfig.CurrentScratchLocation . If it points at /tmp or a RAM disk, all host logs are lost on every reboot and remote syslog is your only source of history.

These commands establish remote syslog from every host and raise the retention of the vCenter events database beyond its defaults. Step 1: Configure ESXi Remote Syslog esxcli system syslog config set --loghost='tcp://10.50.9.20:1514' \ --logdir-unique=true \ --default-rotate=20 \ --default-size=10240 esxcli system syslog reload # Verify esxcli system syslog config get Use TCP rather than UDP so that log loss under load is detectable. The logdir-unique flag gives each host its own directory, which matters when several hosts share a scratch datastore. Step 2: Open the Firewall for Syslog esxcli network firewall ruleset set --ruleset-id=syslog --enabled=true esxcli network firewall refresh esxcli network firewall ruleset list --ruleset-id=syslog The ESXi firewall blocks outbound syslog by default. Configuring a loghost without opening this ruleset produces a configuration that looks correct and delivers nothing. Step 3: Apply Syslog Settings Across the Cluster # PowerCLI, applied to every host at once Get-VMHost | Foreach-Object { Set-VMHostAdvancedConfiguration -VMHost $_ -Name Syslog.global.logHost ` -Value "tcp://10.50.9.20:1514" Get-VMHostFirewallException -VMHost $_ -Name "syslog" | Set-VMHostFirewallException -Enabled $true } # Confirm none were missed Get-VMHost | Select Name, @{N="LogHost";E={ ($_ | Get-AdvancedSetting -Name Syslog.global.logHost).Value }} Host profiles or PowerCLI loops are essential. A single host added to the cluster without syslog configured becomes a blind spot an attacker can operate from freely. Step 4: Increase vCenter Event Retention # vCenter UI: Configure, Settings, General, Database # Event retention : 365 days (default 30) # Task retention : 365 days (default 30) # Equivalent via PowerCLI advanced settings Get-AdvancedSetting -Entity $vcenter -Name event.maxAge | Set-AdvancedSetting -Value 365 Get-AdvancedSetting -Entity $vcenter -Name event.maxAgeEnabled | Set-AdvancedSetting -Value $true Thirty days of event retention is the default and is shorter than typical time to detection. Raising it costs only database storage. Step 5: Enforce Lockdown Mode and Restrict Shell Access # Strict lockdown blocks all direct host access including DCUI vim-cmd hostsvc/advopt/update UserVars.SuppressShellWarning long 0 esxcli system settings advanced set -o /UserVars/ESXiShellTimeOut -i 600 esxcli system settings advanced set -o /UserVars/ESXiShellInteractiveTimeOut -i 600 # PowerCLI: enable lockdown across the cluster Get-VMHost | ForEach-Object { ($_ | Get-View).EnterLockdownMode() } Get-VMHost | Get-VMHostService | Where-Object {$_.Key -eq "TSM-SSH"} | Stop-VMHostService Lockdown mode forces all administration through vCenter, which means all administration is logged and attributed. SSH left enabled is the most common finding on compromised ESXi hosts. Step 6: Forward vCenter Appliance Logs # vCenter UI: Administration, System Configuration, Syslog Configuration # Add up to three remote syslog targets # Or via the appliance shell /opt/vmware/share/vami/vami_set_syslog 10.50.9.20 1514 tcp systemctl restart rsyslog # Confirm vpxd and SSO logs are included grep -E "vpxd|sso" /etc/vmware-syslog/syslog.conf vCenter is a Photon OS appliance running rsyslog. Forwarding its own logs is separate from forwarding ESXi host logs and is frequently overlooked. Security Note: On hosts booting from SD card or USB, ESXi places logs on a RAM disk unless persistent scratch is configured. Every log is lost on reboot, and a reboot is trivially disguised as maintenance. Verify persistent scratch on every host, then forward remotely regardless.

Hypervisor attacks bypass every guest control at once. These are the patterns that define real vSphere incidents. Datastore Ransomware Encrypting VMDK files directly on the datastore after powering off every virtual machine. Signature: mass power-off events, SSH enabled, and shell commands iterating over /vmfs/volumes. Detect Critical SSH and Shell Enablement Starting the TSM-SSH service or disabling lockdown mode to gain direct host access. Almost always the first step, because actions taken on the host bypass vCenter logging entirely. Detect Critical Virtual Machine Cloning and Export Cloning a domain controller or database server and exporting it as OVF. Copies an entire system including its disk contents without any guest-side agent noticing. Detect Critical Datastore Browsing and Download Downloading VMDK files through the datastore browser or HTTPS file API. Extracts a full disk image that can be mounted offline, defeating guest access controls entirely. Detect High Risk Malicious VIB Installation Installing an unsigned installation bundle to persist on the hypervisor across reboots and updates. Requires the acceptance level to be lowered, which is itself logged. Detect High Risk vCenter Permission Escalation Granting the Administrator role at the root folder, or adding an account to the SSO administrators group. Yields control of every host and virtual machine in the inventory. Detect Critical Security Note: Encrypting a datastore defeats guest disk encryption because BitLocker and LUKS protect data at rest inside a powered-off machine, not the VMDK container itself. Hypervisor-level backup and immutable snapshots are the only controls that meaningfully address this.

ESXi logs follow a consistent structure. vCenter events are structured objects with a richer field set. Field Description Category Example Value timestamp UTC time with milliseconds Timestamp 2025-07-14T09:41:22.481Z severity Message level Severity info / warning / error process Emitting component and thread Metadata Hostd[2098412] opID Operation identifier linking related entries Session opID=8f2a1c04 user Account performing the operation Identity VSPHERE.LOCAL\administrator eventType vCenter structured event class Action VmClonedEvent vm.name Virtual machine involved Target DC01-PROD host.name ESXi host involved Target esxi-prod-04.corp.local datastore Datastore path referenced Target [SAN-VOL-02] DC01-PROD/DC01-PROD.vmdk ipAddress Source of the management session Source 10.99.4.117 userAgent Client that issued the API call Source pyvmomi Python/3.11 result Task outcome Result success

vCenter event types are stable identifiers, making them precise detection anchors in a SIEM. Event Type Meaning Why It Matters UserLoginSessionEvent A user authenticated to vCenter Baseline for detecting logins from unexpected addresses, at unusual hours, or with scripted user agents BadUsernameSessionEvent Failed authentication to vCenter Bursts against the SSO administrator account are brute force against the entire virtual estate PermissionAddedEvent A role was granted on an inventory object Administrator role at the root folder is total control. Every occurrence needs a matching change ticket VmClonedEvent A virtual machine was cloned Cloning a domain controller copies the entire directory database including every credential hash DatastoreFileDownloadEvent A file was downloaded from a datastore VMDK download is full disk exfiltration that no guest agent will observe VmPoweredOffEvent A virtual machine was powered off Individually routine. Dozens within minutes is the opening move of datastore ransomware VmRemovedEvent A virtual machine was deleted from inventory Destructive action, and also used to hide a cloned machine after its disks have been copied HostServiceStartedEvent A host service such as SSH was started TSM-SSH starting is the precursor to direct host access that bypasses vCenter logging LockdownModeDisabledEvent Lockdown mode was turned off on a host Re-opens direct host administration. Effectively never legitimate outside a documented break-glass procedure VmAcquiredTicketEvent A console or MKS ticket was acquired Someone opened the virtual console of a machine, which provides keyboard access with no guest authentication logging HostEsxAdminsGrantedEvent A group was granted host admin rights Adding a group named ESX Admins in Active Directory historically granted automatic host administrator access Pro Tip: VmAcquiredTicketEvent is heavily underused. Console access means an attacker can interact with a machine at the keyboard level, and nothing inside the guest records how that session arrived. Alert on console access to tier zero systems.

These PowerCLI, shell, and SIEM queries cover hypervisor compromise from host access through to mass encryption. SSH Enabled on a Host PowerCLI> Get-VMHost | Get-VMHostService | Where-Object {$_.Key -eq "TSM-SSH" -and $_.Running -eq $true} | Select-Object VMHost, Label, Running, Policy SSH running on a production host is either a forgotten troubleshooting session or an attacker. Both need closing. Mass Power-Off (Ransomware Precursor) SIEM> source="vcenter" eventType="VmPoweredOffEvent" | bucket _time span=10m | stats dc(vm_name) as vms, values(user) by _time, host_name | where vms > 10 More than ten machines powered off in ten minutes is either a major outage or the opening move of datastore encryption. Both warrant an immediate page. Shell Commands on the Host bash> grep -iE "esxcli|vim-cmd|vmkfstools|find /vmfs|chmod \+x|wget|curl|python" /var/log/shell.log shell.log records every command typed on the host. Ransomware operators work almost entirely here, so this file is the highest value forensic artifact on a compromised ESXi server. Host Authentication Failures bash> grep -iE "authentication failed|Failed password|Cannot login" /var/log/auth.log | awk '{print $NF}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn Brute force against the root account of an ESXi host. Since ESXi root has no lockout by default, this can continue indefinitely. Virtual Machine Cloning and Export PowerCLI> Get-VIEvent -MaxSamples 100000 -Start (Get-Date).AddDays(-30) | Where-Object {$_ -is [VMware.Vim.VmClonedEvent] -or $_ -is [VMware.Vim.VmBeingDeployedEvent]} | Select-Object CreatedTime, UserName, @{N="Source";E={$_.SourceVm.Name}}, @{N="Clone";E={$_.Vm.Name}} Cloning a domain controller copies the entire Active Directory database. Reconcile every clone against a change request. Datastore File Downloads SIEM> source="vcenter" eventType="DatastoreFileDownloadEvent" | search datastore="*.vmdk" OR datastore="*.vmx" | table _time, user, ipAddress, datastore Downloading a VMDK extracts a complete disk image that can be mounted offline, bypassing every access control inside the guest. Permission Grants PowerCLI> Get-VIEvent -MaxSamples 100000 -Start (Get-Date).AddDays(-30) | Where-Object {$_ -is [VMware.Vim.PermissionAddedEvent]} | Select-Object CreatedTime, UserName, @{N="Grantee";E={$_.Principal}}, @{N="Role";E={$_.Role.Name}}, @{N="On";E={$_.Entity.Name}} Administrator role granted at the root folder is control of the entire virtual estate in a single action. Lockdown Mode Changes PowerCLI> Get-VMHost | Select-Object Name, @{N="Lockdown";E={(Get-View $_).Config.LockdownMode}}, ConnectionState | Where-Object {$_.Lockdown -eq "lockdownDisabled"} Any host with lockdown disabled permits direct administration that never reaches vCenter events. Track this as a configuration drift metric. Unsigned VIB Installation bash> esxcli software acceptance get ; esxcli software vib list | grep -viE "VMware|VMwareCertified|VMwareAccepted" An acceptance level of CommunitySupported combined with an unrecognised VIB is hypervisor-level persistence surviving reboots and patches. Syslog Configuration Drift PowerCLI> Get-VMHost | Select Name, @{N="LogHost";E={($_ | Get-AdvancedSetting -Name Syslog.global.logHost).Value}} | Where-Object {[string]::IsNullOrEmpty($_.LogHost)} Any host returned here keeps its logs only locally, where a reboot destroys them. Run this as a scheduled control check.

Apply these practices so hypervisor evidence survives the incident it is meant to document: 01 Configure Remote Syslog on Every Host ESXi logs rotate quickly and may live on a RAM disk. Without remote syslog, a reboot erases the entire history and an attacker needs no anti-forensic tooling at all. 02 Open the Syslog Firewall Ruleset ESXi blocks outbound syslog by default. Setting a loghost without enabling the ruleset produces a configuration that appears correct and delivers nothing. 03 Collect shell.log and auth.log Specifically Direct host activity never appears in vCenter events. These two files are the only record of an attacker who bypassed the management plane. 04 Enable Lockdown Mode and Disable SSH Forcing administration through vCenter means every action is attributed to a named user. SSH left running is the single most common finding on compromised hosts. 05 Raise vCenter Event Retention Thirty days is the default and is shorter than typical dwell time. Increasing it to a year costs only database storage and preserves the attribution layer. 06 Alert on Mass Power-Off Bulk power-off precedes datastore encryption. It is one of the few detections that can catch hypervisor ransomware in the window before damage becomes irreversible. 07 Treat vCenter as a Tier Zero Asset It controls every virtual machine including domain controllers. Separate administrative accounts, require MFA, and never join it to the domain it manages. 08 Verify Persistent Scratch Storage Hosts booting from SD or USB may keep logs in memory only. Check ScratchConfig on every host, because the failure is silent and total.

A hypervisor ransomware incident traced from stolen vCenter credentials to encrypted datastores. vCenter Brute Force 2025-07-14T09:12:04.117Z info vpxd[07412] [Originator@6876 sub=Vimsvc.ha-eventmgr] Event 84210 : Cannot login administrator@vsphere.local@10.99.4.117 2025-07-14T09:12:09.882Z info vpxd[07412] [Originator@6876 sub=Vimsvc.ha-eventmgr] Event 84211 : Cannot login administrator@vsphere.local@10.99.4.117 2025-07-14T09:12:15.229Z info vpxd[07412] [Originator@6876 sub=Vimsvc.ha-eventmgr] Event 84212 : Cannot login root@10.99.4.117 Repeated failures against the SSO administrator from a VPN pool address. Cross-referencing the VPN session log identifies whose credentials were used to reach this point. Successful Login from a Scripted Client 2025-07-14T09:40:53.221Z info vpxd[07412] [Originator@6876 sub=Vimsvc.ha-eventmgr] Event 84290 : User administrator@VSPHERE.LOCAL@10.99.4.117 logged in as pyvmomi Python/3.11.6 (Linux; x86_64) 2025-07-14T09:40:54.118Z info vpxd[07412] [Originator@6876 sub=Vimsvc] [Auth]: User VSPHERE.LOCAL\administrator The user agent is the tell. Administrators use the HTML5 client or PowerCLI, so a raw pyvmomi session against the SSO administrator account is scripted tooling. From here only shell.log tells the story. Host Login and Reconnaissance in shell.log 2025-07-14T09:47:33Z auth.log: SSH login for 'root' from 10.99.4.117 2025-07-14T09:47:41Z shell[2104881]: [root]: esxcli vm process list 2025-07-14T09:47:52Z shell[2104881]: [root]: df -h 2025-07-14T09:48:04Z shell[2104881]: [root]: ls -lah /vmfs/volumes/ 2025-07-14T09:48:19Z shell[2104881]: [root]: find /vmfs/volumes/ -name "*.vmdk" | wc -l Enumerating running machines, storage capacity, and counting VMDK files. That file contains NTDS.dit and every credential hash in the domain. No agent inside DC01-PROD observed any of this. Machines must be powered off before their VMDK files can be encrypted, which is what makes bulk power-off the last useful warning. Datastore Encryption 2025-07-14T10:04:55Z shell[2104881]: [root]: chmod +x /tmp/.x/encrypt 2025-07-14T10:04:58Z shell[2104881]: [root]: /tmp/.x/encrypt -p /vmfs/volumes/SAN-VOL-02 -t 40 2025-07-14T10:05:31.882Z warning vmkernel: WARNING: FS3J: Failed to lock file /vmfs/volumes/SAN-VOL-02/DC01-PROD/DC01-PROD-flat.vmdk 2025-07-14T10:06:14.229Z info shell[2104881]: [root]: echo 'READ_ME.txt' > /vmfs/volumes/SAN-VOL-02/READ_ME.txt An unsigned binary staged in a hidden temp directory encrypting the datastore with 40 parallel threads. Guest disk encryption offers no protection here, because the VMDK container itself is what gets encrypted. Evidence Destruction: Log Clearing and Reboot 2025-07-14T10:11:03Z shell[2104881]: [root]: esxcli system syslog config set --loghost='' 2025-07-14T10:11:09Z shell[2104881]: [root]: > /var/log/shell.log 2025-07-14T10:11:12Z shell[2104881]: [root]: > /var/log/auth.log 2025-07-14T10:11:18Z shell[2104881]: [root]: reboot The loghost is cleared, local logs truncated, and the host rebooted. Everything above survived only because it had already been forwarded to the syslog collector before line one of this block executed. Back

Hyper-V logging differs fundamentally from vSphere in one respect that shapes everything else: the hypervisor runs on Windows Server, so the host produces the full set of Windows Security, System, and Application events alongside its virtualisation-specific channels. A compromised Hyper-V host generates event 4624 for the logon, 4672 for the privileges assigned, and 4688 for the process created, exactly as any Windows server would. Hyper-V events sit on top of that foundation rather than replacing it, which means an organisation with mature Windows logging already has most of what it needs. The virtualisation channels themselves are numerous and narrowly scoped. Hyper-V-VMMS records the Virtual Machine Management Service: creation, deletion, import, export, and migration of virtual machines. Hyper-V-Worker records the per-machine worker process handling power state and runtime events. Hyper-V-VMSwitch covers virtual networking including port and mirroring configuration, and Hyper-V-Compute covers the newer host compute service used by containers and modern management tooling. Most are enabled by default but sized small, and several useful channels are analytic or debug channels that are disabled entirely. The distinctive Hyper-V blind spot is PowerShell Direct . An administrator on the host can open a session inside any running virtual machine using Enter-PSSession -VMName , which travels over the VMBus rather than the network. It bypasses the guest firewall, produces no network connection, and appears in no network log. The guest records a logon, but nothing indicates it arrived through the hypervisor. Detecting this requires correlating host-side PowerShell operational logs with guest logons, and it is the technique most likely to be missed entirely.

Hyper-V spreads its events across many narrow channels. These are the ones that carry security value: Channel Description Hyper-V-VMMS The Virtual Machine Management Service, covering creation, deletion, import, export, checkpoint, and migration of virtual machines. The primary lifecycle channel and the one that records bulk exfiltration through export operations. Hyper-V-Worker Per-machine worker process events including power state transitions, saved state operations, and runtime errors. Where mass power-off preceding an attack becomes visible. Hyper-V-VMSwitch Virtual switch operations covering port creation, VLAN assignment, and port mirroring configuration. Enabling mirroring on a virtual port copies another machine's traffic to an attacker-controlled guest. Hyper-V-Compute The Host Compute Service used by containers, WSL, and modern management APIs. Increasingly the channel through which programmatic virtual machine manipulation appears. Hyper-V-Config Configuration file access and modification for virtual machines, including errors reading VMCX files. Useful for spotting direct tampering with machine definitions on disk. Windows Security Log The host is a Windows server, so 4624 logons, 4672 special privileges, 4688 process creation, and 5140 share access all apply. Frequently more informative than the Hyper-V channels themselves. PowerShell Operational Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell/Operational with script block logging enabled. The only host-side record of PowerShell Direct sessions into guest machines. Hyper-V-High-Availability Failover clustering events for clustered Hyper-V, covering machine movement between nodes. Unexpected migrations can indicate an attacker relocating a target to a host they control. SCVMM Job History System Center Virtual Machine Manager records administrative jobs with the initiating user. Where a management layer is deployed, this is the attribution source. Pro Tip: Because the Hyper-V host is a domain-joined Windows server, an attacker with Hyper-V Administrators group membership gains full control of every guest without ever holding Domain Admin. Audit that group as closely as you audit Domain Admins, because it is functionally equivalent in a virtualised estate.

Event channels live in the standard Windows event log directory. Virtual machine files and configuration have their own defaults worth knowing during an investigation. Item Location VMMS Channel %SystemRoot%\System32\Winevt\Logs\Microsoft-Windows-Hyper-V-VMMS-Admin.evtx Worker Channel %SystemRoot%\System32\Winevt\Logs\Microsoft-Windows-Hyper-V-Worker-Admin.evtx VMSwitch Channel %SystemRoot%\System32\Winevt\Logs\Microsoft-Windows-Hyper-V-VmSwitch-Operational.evtx Compute Channel %SystemRoot%\System32\Winevt\Logs\Microsoft-Windows-Hyper-V-Compute-Admin.evtx Virtual Machine Configuration C:\ProgramData\Microsoft\Windows\Hyper-V\Virtual Machines\ (VMCX and VMRS files) Virtual Hard Disks C:\Users\Public\Documents\Hyper-V\Virtual hard disks\ or a cluster shared volume Cluster Shared Volumes C:\ClusterStorage\Volume1\ on clustered deployments Windows Security Log %SystemRoot%\System32\Winevt\Logs\Security.evtx SCVMM Logs C:\ProgramData\VMMLogs\ on the VMM management server Pro Tip: A VHDX file copied off the host is a complete disk image of the guest. Monitor file share access (event 5145) and process creation for copy operations against the virtual hard disk directory, because that is exfiltration no guest agent will ever see.

Default channel sizes are small and several valuable channels are disabled. These commands establish adequate coverage on a Hyper-V host. Step 1: Enlarge the Hyper-V Channels $channels = @( "Microsoft-Windows-Hyper-V-VMMS-Admin", "Microsoft-Windows-Hyper-V-VMMS-Operational", "Microsoft-Windows-Hyper-V-Worker-Admin", "Microsoft-Windows-Hyper-V-VmSwitch-Operational", "Microsoft-Windows-Hyper-V-Compute-Admin", "Microsoft-Windows-Hyper-V-Config-Admin", "Microsoft-Windows-Hyper-V-High-Availability-Admin" ) foreach ($c in $channels) { wevtutil sl $c /ms:268435456 /rt:false } wevtutil gl Microsoft-Windows-Hyper-V-VMMS-Admin Default channel sizes are around 1 MB, which wraps within hours on an active host. Retention set to false means overwrite as needed rather than stopping when full. Step 2: Enable Windows Auditing on the Host auditpol /set /subcategory:"Logon" /success:enable /failure:enable auditpol /set /subcategory:"Special Logon" /success:enable auditpol /set /subcategory:"Process Creation" /success:enable auditpol /set /subcategory:"File Share" /success:enable /failure:enable auditpol /set /subcategory:"Detailed File Share" /success:enable auditpol /set /subcategory:"Security Group Management" /success:enable # Include the command line in process creation events reg add "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System\Audit" /v ProcessCreationIncludeCmdLine_Enabled /t REG_DWORD /d 1 /f Detailed File Share auditing produces event 5145, which is what records a VHDX file being read across the network. Without the command line in 4688, process events lose most of their value. Step 3: Enable PowerShell Script Block Logging # Group Policy path: # Computer Configuration, Administrative Templates, Windows Components, # Windows PowerShell, Turn on PowerShell Script Block Logging reg add "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\ScriptBlockLogging" /v EnableScriptBlockLogging /t REG_DWORD /d 1 /f reg add "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\ModuleLogging" /v EnableModuleLogging /t REG_DWORD /d 1 /f reg add "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\ModuleLogging\ModuleNames" /v Hyper-V /t REG_SZ /d Hyper-V /f This is the only way to see PowerShell Direct sessions into guests. Event 4104 in the PowerShell Operational channel records the script block, including Enter-PSSession with a VMName parameter. Step 4: Audit the Hyper-V Administrators Group Get-LocalGroupMember -Group "Hyper-V Administrators" # Alert on membership change (event 4732 for local, 4728 for domain groups) Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName="Security"; ID=4732,4728,4756} -MaxEvents 100 | Where-Object { $_.Message -match "Hyper-V Administrators" } | Select-Object TimeCreated, @{N="Detail";E={$_.Message -split "`n" | Select-String "Account Name|Group Name"}} Membership in this group grants full control of every guest without Domain Admin. Treat additions with the same urgency as a Domain Admin grant. Step 5: Forward Channels to a Collector # Windows Event Forwarding subscription (XPath filter on the collector) <QueryList> <Query Id="0"> <Select Path="Microsoft-Windows-Hyper-V-VMMS-Admin">*</Select> <Select Path="Microsoft-Windows-Hyper-V-Worker-Admin">*</Select> <Select Path="Microsoft-Windows-Hyper-V-VmSwitch-Operational">*</Select> <Select Path="Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell/Operational">*[System[(EventID=4104)]]</Select> <Select Path="Security">*[System[(EventID=4624 or EventID=4672 or EventID=4688 or EventID=5145)]]</Select> </Query> </QueryList> Combining the Hyper-V channels with the relevant Security and PowerShell events in one subscription gives a complete picture of host activity in a single stream. Step 6: Enable Shielded VM Attestation Logging # On the Host Guardian Service Get-HgsTrace -RunDiagnostics -Detailed wevtutil sl "Microsoft-Windows-HostGuardianService-Attestation/Admin" /ms:104857600 # On the guarded host, confirm attestation status Get-HgsClientConfiguration | Select-Object IsHostGuarded, AttestationStatus, AttestationOperationMode A host that fails attestation cannot start shielded machines. Attestation failures are worth alerting on because they can indicate boot configuration tampering on the host itself. Security Note: Hyper-V analytic and debug channels contain far more detail but are disabled by default and can generate enormous volume. Enable them only for a specific investigation, and remember that enabling an analytic channel clears whatever it previously contained.

Hyper-V attacks exploit the host's privileged position over its guests. These are the techniques worth building detections around. PowerShell Direct Enter-PSSession with a VMName parameter opens a session inside a guest over the VMBus. Bypasses the guest firewall entirely, creates no network connection, and appears in no network log. Detect Critical Virtual Machine Export Export-VM writes a complete copy of a machine including its disks to any path. Exporting a domain controller copies the entire directory database with every credential hash. Detect Critical VHDX Theft Copying a virtual hard disk directly from the filesystem or a cluster shared volume. Mountable offline, defeating every access control inside the guest operating system. Detect Critical Virtual Switch Port Mirroring Setting a virtual network adapter to mirror mode copies another guest's traffic to an attacker-controlled machine. Entirely invisible from inside the victim guest. Detect High Risk Checkpoint Manipulation Creating a checkpoint captures memory contents including credentials, and reverting one can roll a machine back to before a patch was applied or an account was disabled. Detect High Risk Hyper-V Administrators Abuse Membership grants complete control of every guest without Domain Admin, which makes it an attractive and frequently under-monitored escalation target. Detect Critical Security Note: A checkpoint of a running machine includes a memory image. Anyone who can read the resulting AVHDX and VMRS files can extract credentials, encryption keys, and in-memory secrets without ever authenticating to the guest.

Hyper-V events use the standard Windows event schema. These are the fields that matter for correlation and attribution. Field Description Category Example Value TimeCreated Event timestamp Timestamp 2025-07-14T09:41:22.481Z EventID Numeric identifier within the channel Detection 13002 Channel Log channel that produced the event Metadata Hyper-V-VMMS-Admin Computer Hyper-V host that generated the event Source HV-PROD-04.corp.local VmName Virtual machine referenced Target DC01-PROD VmId Stable GUID of the virtual machine Target a1b2c3d4-1122-6874-0000-0010f4e21b00 SubjectUserName Account performing the action, from the Security log Identity CORP\hv-admin IpAddress Source of the management session Source 10.99.4.117 ProcessName Executable involved, from event 4688 Action C:\Windows\System32\WindowsPowerShell\v1.0\powershell.exe CommandLine Full command line when auditing is configured Action Export-VM -Name DC01-PROD -Path E:\tmp ScriptBlockText PowerShell script content from event 4104 Action Enter-PSSession -VMName DC01-PROD ShareName / RelativeTargetName Share and file path from event 5145 Target \\*\C$ ClusterStorage\Volume1\DC01.vhdx

These identifiers span the Hyper-V channels and the Windows Security log. Both are needed for a complete picture. Event ID Channel and Meaning Why It Matters 13002 VMMS: Virtual machine created New machines outside the provisioning process are attacker infrastructure, often used as a foothold inside the trusted network 13003 VMMS: Virtual machine deleted Destructive, and also used to remove a temporary clone after its disks have been copied 13004 / 13005 VMMS: Virtual machine imported or exported Export writes a full copy of a machine including disks. The clearest bulk exfiltration event Hyper-V produces 18500 / 18502 Worker: Virtual machine started or stopped Individually routine, but many stops within minutes precedes disk-level encryption or theft 18304 / 18306 VMMS: Live migration started and completed Unexpected migration can indicate a machine being relocated to a host the attacker controls 20415 VMMS: Checkpoint created A checkpoint of a running machine captures memory, exposing credentials and keys to anyone who can read the files 4104 PowerShell: Script block executed The only host-side record of PowerShell Direct. Search the script block text for VMName parameters 4688 Security: Process created With command line auditing enabled, captures Export-VM, Copy-Item against VHDX paths, and vmconnect usage 5145 Security: Network share object access checked Records VHDX files read over the network, which is disk-level exfiltration no guest agent will observe 4732 / 4728 Security: Member added to a group Additions to Hyper-V Administrators grant total control over every guest without Domain Admin 26010 VMSwitch: Port setting changed Mirroring configuration on a virtual port copies another guest's traffic to an attacker-controlled machine Pro Tip: Correlate host event 4104 containing a VMName parameter against guest event 4624 with logon type 3 and no corresponding network connection. That combination is the signature of PowerShell Direct, and it is essentially invisible from the guest alone.

These PowerShell and SIEM queries cover guest access, machine theft, and network interception on a Hyper-V host. PowerShell Direct Sessions PS> Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName="Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell/Operational"; ID=4104} | Where-Object { $_.Message -match "-VMName|-VMId|VMConnect" } | Select-Object TimeCreated, UserId, @{N="Script";E={$_.Message.Substring(0,200)}} The only reliable detection for PowerShell Direct. Without script block logging enabled, these sessions leave no host-side trace at all. Virtual Machine Export PS> Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName="Microsoft-Windows-Hyper-V-VMMS-Admin"; ID=13005,13004} | Select-Object TimeCreated, Id, Message Export copies an entire machine including its disks. Reconcile every occurrence against a documented backup or migration task. VHDX File Access SIEM> source="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=5145 RelativeTargetName="*.vhdx" OR RelativeTargetName="*.avhdx" | stats count, values(RelativeTargetName) by SubjectUserName, IpAddress | sort - count A VHDX read across the network is a full disk image leaving the host. Only backup service accounts should ever appear here. Mass Guest Shutdown SIEM> source="WinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-Hyper-V-Worker-Admin" EventCode=18502 | bucket _time span=10m | stats dc(VmName) as vms by _time, Computer | where vms > 10 Bulk shutdown precedes disk-level encryption, since VHDX files cannot be encrypted while the machine holds them open. Hyper-V Administrators Changes SIEM> source="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode IN (4728,4732,4756) TargetUserName="Hyper-V Administrators" | table _time, SubjectUserName, MemberName, Computer Equivalent in impact to a Domain Admin grant in a virtualised estate, and far less frequently monitored. Port Mirroring Enabled PS> Get-VM | Get-VMNetworkAdapter | Where-Object { $_.PortMirroringMode -ne "None" } | Select-Object VMName, Name, PortMirroringMode, SwitchName A guest adapter in Destination mode receives copies of other machines' traffic. Outside a documented troubleshooting exercise this is interception. Checkpoint Activity PS> Get-VM | Get-VMSnapshot | Select-Object VMName, Name, SnapshotType, CreationTime | Where-Object { $_.CreationTime -gt (Get-Date).AddDays(-7) } Recent checkpoints on production machines, especially domain controllers, capture memory contents including credentials. Unexpected Virtual Machines PS> Get-VM | Select-Object Name, State, CreationTime, @{N="Notes";E={$_.Notes}} | Where-Object { $_.CreationTime -gt (Get-Date).AddDays(-30) } | Sort-Object CreationTime -Descending Machines created outside the provisioning pipeline. An attacker-created guest sits inside the trusted network with no endpoint agent on it. Console Connections SIEM> source="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=4688 (New_Process_Name="*vmconnect.exe" OR CommandLine="*vmconnect*") | table _time, SubjectUserName, CommandLine, Computer vmconnect opens the virtual console, giving keyboard access to a guest with nothing inside the guest recording how the session arrived. Channel Health Check PS> Get-WinEvent -ListLog "Microsoft-Windows-Hyper-V-*" | Select-Object LogName, IsEnabled, MaximumSizeInBytes, RecordCount | Where-Object { $_.MaximumSizeInBytes -lt 100MB } Channels still at their small defaults wrap within hours. Run this as a scheduled configuration check across the cluster.

Apply these practices so the hypervisor layer is as well monitored as the guests running on it: 01 Enable PowerShell Script Block Logging PowerShell Direct travels over the VMBus and produces no network evidence. Event 4104 on the host is the only record that a session was opened into a guest. 02 Enlarge the Hyper-V Channels Defaults around 1 MB wrap within hours on a busy host. Raising them to 256 MB costs almost nothing and preserves days rather than hours of history. 03 Treat the Host as a Windows Server Events 4624, 4672, 4688, and 5145 apply here exactly as anywhere else, and are frequently more informative than the Hyper-V specific channels. 04 Audit Hyper-V Administrators Like Domain Admins Membership grants complete control of every guest without any domain privilege. In a virtualised estate the two groups are functionally equivalent. 05 Monitor VHDX File Access Enable Detailed File Share auditing so event 5145 records disk images being read. A copied VHDX is a full disk exfiltration that no guest agent will ever see. 06 Alert on Export and Checkpoint Operations Both produce a complete copy of a machine, and checkpoints of running guests additionally capture memory containing credentials and keys. 07 Never Run Domain Controllers on a Domain-Joined Host If the host is a member of the domain it hosts, compromising the domain compromises the hypervisor and vice versa. Break that circular dependency. 08 Forward Everything to a Collector Windows Event Forwarding with a subscription covering the Hyper-V channels plus the relevant Security and PowerShell events puts the full picture in one place off the host.

An attack against a Hyper-V host, from privileged group abuse to guest disk theft. Escalation via Hyper-V Administrators Log Name: Security Event ID: 4732 Task Category: Security Group Management Description: A member was added to a security-enabled local group. Subject: Account Name: CORP\helpdesk-svc Logon ID: 0x4E2A1C Member: Account Name: CORP\r.almutairi Group: Group Name: Hyper-V Administrators Group Domain: HV-PROD-04 A helpdesk service account adding a user to Hyper-V Administrators. That single membership grants full control over every guest on the host, including domain controllers, with no Domain Admin required. Host Logon and Privilege Assignment Log Name: Security Event ID: 4624 Logon Type: 10 (RemoteInteractive) Account Name: r.almutairi Account Domain: CORP Source Network Address: 10.99.4.117 Logon Process: User32 Event ID: 4672 Privileges: SeSecurityPrivilege, SeBackupPrivilege, SeRestorePrivilege, SeTakeOwnershipPrivilege, SeDebugPrivilege An RDP logon from a VPN pool address followed by special privilege assignment. SeBackupPrivilege alone allows reading any file on the host, including every VHDX. PowerShell Direct into a Domain Controller Log Name: Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell/Operational Event ID: 4104 Level: Warning Description: Creating Scriptblock text (1 of 1): $c = Get-Credential; Enter-PSSession -VMName "DC01-PROD" -Credential $c ScriptBlock ID: 8f2a1c04-1122-4e91-b7d2-0010f4e21b00 Path: A session opened directly into the domain controller over the VMBus. The guest will log a 4624 with no matching network connection, and the guest firewall never saw a thing. Domain Controller Exported Log Name: Security Event ID: 4688 New Process Name: C:\Windows\System32\WindowsPowerShell\v1.0\powershell.exe Process Command Line: powershell.exe -c "Export-VM -Name DC01-PROD -Path E:\temp\.stage" Creator Subject: CORP\r.almutairi Log Name: Microsoft-Windows-Hyper-V-VMMS-Admin Event ID: 13005 Description: Virtual machine 'DC01-PROD' was exported successfully. (Virtual machine ID a1b2c3d4-1122-6874-0000-0010f4e21b00) The command line from event 4688 and the VMMS confirmation together prove what was exported, by whom, and to where. Without command line auditing, event 13005 alone would not name the destination. VHDX Copied Off the Host Log Name: Security Event ID: 5145 Description: A network share object was checked to see whether client can be granted desired access. Subject: Account Name: r.almutairi Logon ID: 0x4E2A1C Network Information: Source Address: 10.99.4.117 Share Name: \\*\E$ Relative Target Name: temp\.stage\DC01-PROD\Virtual Hard Disks\DC01-PROD.vhdx Access Request Information: Accesses: ReadData (or ListDirectory) The exported disk being read across the administrative share. That file contains NTDS.dit and every credential hash in the domain, extractable offline with no authentication to the guest. Traffic Interception via Port Mirroring Log Name: Microsoft-Windows-Hyper-V-VmSwitch-Operational Event ID: 26010 Description: Port setting changed on switch 'Prod-vSwitch'. Port: 8f2a1c04-... VM: TEST-UTIL-09 Adapter: Network Adapter Setting: PortMirroringMode Old Value: None New Value: Destination An unremarkable test machine set as a mirroring destination now receives copies of every other guest's traffic on that switch. Nothing inside the victim guests indicates this is happening. Checkpoint Capturing Live Memory Log Name: Microsoft-Windows-Hyper-V-VMMS-Admin Event ID: 20415 Description: Checkpoint operation for 'DC01-PROD' completed successfully. Checkpoint type: Standard (includes memory state) Files: C:\ClusterStorage\Volume1\DC01-PROD\Snapshots\ a1b2c3d4-1122-6874-0000-0010f4e21b00.VMRS (memory) DC01-PROD_8f2a1c04.avhdx (disk delta) A standard checkpoint of a running domain controller writes a full memory image to the VMRS file. Anyone who can read that file can extract credentials and keys directly from memory. Mass Shutdown Preceding Encryption Log Name: Microsoft-Windows-Hyper-V-Worker-Admin Event ID: 18502 'SQL-PROD-01' was turned off (09:58:02) Event ID: 18502 'APP-PROD-03' was turned off (09:58:03) Event ID: 18502 'FILE-PROD-02' was turned off (09:58:03) Event ID: 18502 'WEB-PROD-01' was turned off (09:58:04) Event ID: 18502 'DC01-PROD' was turned off (09:58:05) Five machines stopped in four seconds. VHDX files cannot be encrypted while a running machine holds them open, which makes bulk shutdown the last practical warning before the damage becomes irreversible. Back

In AWS every action is an API call, and CloudTrail records them. Launching an instance, reading a secret, attaching a policy, or deleting a bucket are all the same kind of event from the platform's perspective: an identity called an API, from an address, at a time, with parameters, and either succeeded or was denied. That uniformity is what makes CloudTrail the single most important log in any AWS environment. There is no equivalent of an unmonitored server here, because there is no way to act on AWS resources without generating an event. CloudTrail splits into two categories that behave very differently. Management events cover control plane operations and are logged free of charge for the first copy, with 90 days of history available in the console even with no trail configured. Data events cover operations on the contents of resources, such as reading an S3 object or invoking a Lambda function, and they are disabled by default and billed by volume. This distinction produces the most common gap in AWS monitoring: an organisation records that a bucket policy was changed but has no record of the objects subsequently downloaded, because data events were never enabled. Around CloudTrail sit several complementary sources. VPC Flow Logs capture network metadata that CloudTrail never sees, since traffic between instances involves no API call. GuardDuty applies managed detections to CloudTrail, DNS, and flow data, producing findings that are usually the fastest route to noticing credential abuse. S3 server access logs and CloudFront logs record content requests, and Config tracks resource state over time. A mature deployment uses an organisation trail delivering to a dedicated logging account that even administrators in member accounts cannot modify, which is the control that prevents an attacker from erasing their own tracks.

AWS produces many log types with very different coverage, cost, and default state. Knowing which are off by default is the practical starting point: Log Type Description CloudTrail Management Events Every control plane API call across the account: identity changes, resource creation and deletion, policy modifications, and console logins. The authoritative audit trail. Free for the first copy but only retained 90 days unless a trail delivers it to S3. CloudTrail Data Events Operations on resource contents such as S3 GetObject and PutObject, Lambda Invoke, and DynamoDB item access. Disabled by default and billed per event. Without these you cannot prove what data an attacker actually read. CloudTrail Insights Managed anomaly detection over management event volume, flagging unusual rates of API activity. Useful for spotting enumeration bursts and mass deletion without writing detections yourself. VPC Flow Logs Network metadata for traffic in and out of network interfaces, including source, destination, ports, bytes, and accept or reject decisions. Captures lateral movement between instances that generates no API call and is therefore invisible to CloudTrail. GuardDuty Findings Managed threat detection analysing CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs, DNS query logs, EKS audit logs, and S3 data events. Produces enriched findings such as credential exfiltration and cryptomining with severity scores. S3 Server Access Logs Detailed request records for a bucket, independent of CloudTrail data events. Higher latency and best-effort delivery, but includes fields such as the referrer and turnaround time that data events omit. AWS Config Point-in-time snapshots of resource configuration and a timeline of changes. Answers what a security group looked like last Tuesday, which CloudTrail can only reconstruct by replaying events. CloudWatch Logs Application and system logs shipped from EC2, Lambda, and containers. Also the destination for VPC Flow Logs and Route 53 resolver query logs when real-time analysis is needed. Pro Tip: CloudTrail records the API call, not its effect on data. GetObject appears only if S3 data events are enabled for that bucket. An organisation that skipped data events on cost grounds cannot answer the one question that matters after a breach: which files were taken.

AWS logs are delivered to services rather than filesystem paths. Where each stream lands determines how you query it and how long it survives. Log Destination CloudTrail Event History Console only, last 90 days of management events, not configurable and not exportable in bulk CloudTrail Trail s3://bucket/AWSLogs/<account>/CloudTrail/<region>/YYYY/MM/DD/ as gzipped JSON CloudTrail Lake Managed event data store queryable with SQL, retention up to 10 years VPC Flow Logs CloudWatch Logs group, S3 bucket, or Kinesis Data Firehose GuardDuty GuardDuty console, EventBridge events, and optional S3 export S3 Server Access Logs A separate target bucket, delivered best-effort with delay of minutes to hours AWS Config S3 delivery channel plus the Config console timeline Organisation Trail A single bucket in a dedicated logging account, covering every member account centrally Pro Tip: Console Event History is not a substitute for a trail. It covers management events only, holds 90 days, cannot be queried programmatically at scale, and disappears entirely if the account is closed. Always configure a trail delivering to S3 in a separate account.

These commands establish a tamper-resistant organisation trail and the supporting log sources that CloudTrail alone does not cover. Step 1: Create a Multi-Region Organisation Trail aws cloudtrail create-trail \ --name htl-org-trail \ --s3-bucket-name htl-security-logs-central \ --is-organization-trail \ --is-multi-region-trail \ --enable-log-file-validation \ --kms-key-id arn:aws:kms:me-south-1:111122223333:key/abcd-1234 aws cloudtrail start-logging --name htl-org-trail Multi-region is essential: attackers deliberately operate in regions you do not use. Log file validation produces signed digest files that prove the log has not been altered. Step 2: Enable Data Events for Sensitive Resources aws cloudtrail put-event-selectors \ --trail-name htl-org-trail \ --advanced-event-selectors '[ {"Name":"Management events", "FieldSelectors":[{"Field":"eventCategory","Equals":["Management"]}]}, {"Name":"S3 data events on sensitive buckets", "FieldSelectors":[ {"Field":"eventCategory","Equals":["Data"]}, {"Field":"resources.type","Equals":["AWS::S3::Object"]}, {"Field":"resources.ARN","StartsWith":["arn:aws:s3:::htl-customer-data/"]}]}]' Scoping data events to specific buckets controls cost while preserving the ability to prove what was read. Enabling them account-wide is usually financially impractical. Step 3: Protect the Log Bucket from Tampering # Object Lock in compliance mode makes objects immutable, even to root aws s3api put-object-lock-configuration \ --bucket htl-security-logs-central \ --object-lock-configuration '{"ObjectLockEnabled":"Enabled", "Rule":{"DefaultRetention":{"Mode":"COMPLIANCE","Days":400}}}' # Deny deletion and policy changes from outside the security account aws s3api put-bucket-policy --bucket htl-security-logs-central \ --policy file://deny-delete-except-security-role.json aws s3api put-public-access-block --bucket htl-security-logs-central \ --public-access-block-configuration \ BlockPublicAcls=true,IgnorePublicAcls=true,BlockPublicPolicy=true,RestrictPublicBuckets=true Compliance mode Object Lock cannot be removed by anyone including the account root user. This is what guarantees an attacker with full administrative access still cannot erase the evidence. Step 4: Enable VPC Flow Logs aws ec2 create-flow-logs \ --resource-type VPC \ --resource-ids vpc-0a1b2c3d4e5f67890 \ --traffic-type ALL \ --log-destination-type s3 \ --log-destination arn:aws:s3:::htl-security-logs-central/vpcflow/ \ --max-aggregation-interval 60 \ --log-format '${version} ${account-id} ${interface-id} ${srcaddr} ${dstaddr} ${srcport} ${dstport} ${protocol} ${packets} ${bytes} ${start} ${end} ${action} ${log-status} ${vpc-id} ${subnet-id} ${instance-id} ${tcp-flags} ${type} ${pkt-srcaddr} ${pkt-dstaddr} ${flow-direction} ${traffic-path}' The custom format adds fields absent from the default, notably pkt-srcaddr which reveals the original source behind a NAT gateway, and flow-direction which removes ambiguity about who initiated. Step 5: Enable GuardDuty Across the Organisation aws guardduty create-detector --enable \ --finding-publishing-frequency FIFTEEN_MINUTES \ --data-sources '{"S3Logs":{"Enable":true}, "Kubernetes":{"AuditLogs":{"Enable":true}}, "MalwareProtection":{"ScanEc2InstanceWithFindings":{"EbsVolumes":true}}}' aws guardduty create-members --detector-id <id> \ --account-details file://member-accounts.json aws guardduty update-organization-configuration --detector-id <id> --auto-enable Auto-enable ensures new accounts are covered from creation. A new unmonitored account is a favourite place for an attacker to operate. Step 6: Alert on Logging Being Disabled { "source": ["aws.cloudtrail"], "detail": { "eventName": ["StopLogging","DeleteTrail","UpdateTrail", "PutEventSelectors","DeleteFlowLogs", "DisassociateMembers","DeleteDetector"] } } # Attach this EventBridge rule to an SNS topic that pages, not one that emails a shared inbox Disabling logging is among the first actions an attacker takes after gaining administrative access. This rule must reach a human within minutes. Security Note: CloudTrail delivers to S3 with a typical latency of about five minutes and an upper bound of fifteen. An attacker who moves quickly can complete an entire operation before the first log file lands. For time-critical detection, use EventBridge rules on management events, which fire in near real time.

Cloud intrusions follow a consistent arc: obtain credentials, enumerate permissions, escalate, persist, then exfiltrate. Each stage has a distinct CloudTrail signature. Credential Compromise Access keys leaked in code repositories or stolen from instance metadata. Signature: an existing key suddenly used from a new address, new region, or unfamiliar user agent such as an SDK version never seen before. Detect Critical Permission Enumeration Rapid discovery of what the stolen identity can do. Signature: a burst of List, Describe, and Get calls across many services, often with a high proportion of AccessDenied results. Detect Critical Privilege Escalation Using existing IAM permissions to acquire more. AttachUserPolicy with AdministratorAccess, CreatePolicyVersion, PassRole into a service, or UpdateAssumeRolePolicy are the classic paths. Detect Critical Persistence Establishing durable access independent of the original credential. CreateAccessKey for another user, CreateUser, CreateLoginProfile, or adding an external principal to a role trust policy. Detect Critical Data Exfiltration Snapshot sharing to an external account, bucket policy changes granting public access, or mass GetObject. Sharing a snapshot copies an entire database without ever reading a row through the database itself. Detect Critical Defence Evasion StopLogging, DeleteTrail, DeleteFlowLogs, DeleteDetector, or operating in an unused region where monitoring was never configured. Frequently the first action after escalation. Detect Critical Security Note: The userAgent field is one of the most underused detection surfaces in CloudTrail. Automation uses consistent SDK strings, so an identity that normally appears as a Terraform or Boto3 user agent suddenly calling from aws-cli/2.x on a different platform is a strong indicator of stolen credentials.

Every CloudTrail record shares the same JSON structure regardless of which service it came from. These are the fields that carry detection value. Field Description Category Example Value eventTime UTC time the API call was made Timestamp 2025-07-14T09:41:22Z eventName The API action invoked Action AttachUserPolicy eventSource Service that handled the call Target iam.amazonaws.com userIdentity.type Identity class making the call Identity AssumedRole userIdentity.arn Full ARN of the calling principal Identity arn:aws:sts::1111:assumed-role/Deploy/i-0abc userIdentity.accessKeyId Access key used, ASIA prefix means temporary Identity AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE sourceIPAddress Caller address, or an AWS service principal Source 203.0.113.44 userAgent SDK or tool that issued the request Source aws-cli/2.15.4 Python/3.11 Linux awsRegion Region the call was made in Target ap-southeast-2 errorCode Present only when the call failed Result AccessDenied requestParameters Arguments supplied to the API Action policyArn: AdministratorAccess responseElements Values returned, including created secrets Response accessKeyId: AKIAI44QH8DHBEXAMPLE mfaAuthenticated Whether MFA was used for this session Authorization false readOnly Whether the call modified state Metadata false Pro Tip: When a service makes a call on your behalf, sourceIPAddress contains a service name such as ec2.amazonaws.com rather than an address. Detections that assume this field is always an IP will silently skip every service-initiated event.

A small number of API calls account for most of the damage in AWS intrusions. These belong on a watchlist with real-time alerting. API Call Stage Why It Matters StopLogging / DeleteTrail Evasion Disables the audit trail itself. Effectively never legitimate outside a documented decommissioning, and should page immediately CreateAccessKey Persistence Creating a key for another user is a durable backdoor surviving password resets. Creating one for yourself is routine AttachUserPolicy / AttachRolePolicy Escalation Especially with AdministratorAccess or PowerUserAccess. The single most direct route to full account control UpdateAssumeRolePolicy Persistence Adding an external account to a role trust policy grants a permanent foothold that survives credential rotation entirely ModifySnapshotAttribute Exfiltration Sharing an EBS or RDS snapshot with an external account copies entire volumes without touching the running system PutBucketPolicy / PutBucketAcl Exfiltration Bucket policy changes granting public or cross-account access are the mechanism behind most large S3 data exposures GetSecretValue / Decrypt Credential Access Bulk retrieval from Secrets Manager or KMS decryption at abnormal volume indicates credential harvesting CreateUser / CreateLoginProfile Persistence New identities with console access created outside the provisioning pipeline are attacker backdoors AssumeRole with external ID Lateral Movement Role chaining across accounts. Legitimate in many architectures, so baseline the normal chains and alert on new ones DeactivateMFADevice Evasion Removing MFA from a privileged identity weakens the control specifically protecting it RunInstances in unused regions Impact Cryptomining almost always starts in regions the organisation never uses, precisely because monitoring is thinner there

These Athena and CLI queries cover the full intrusion arc from credential abuse through to exfiltration. Logging Disabled Athena> SELECT eventtime, useridentity.arn, sourceipaddress, eventname FROM cloudtrail_logs WHERE eventname IN ('StopLogging','DeleteTrail','UpdateTrail','PutEventSelectors','DeleteFlowLogs','DeleteDetector') ORDER BY eventtime DESC; The highest priority query in AWS. Any result outside a documented change is an active incident. Privilege Escalation Athena> SELECT eventtime, useridentity.arn, eventname, requestparameters FROM cloudtrail_logs WHERE eventname IN ('AttachUserPolicy','AttachRolePolicy','PutUserPolicy','CreatePolicyVersion','UpdateAssumeRolePolicy') AND requestparameters LIKE '%Administrator%'; Catches administrative policy attachment in one query. Reconcile every hit against a change ticket. Permission Enumeration Athena> SELECT useridentity.arn, sourceipaddress, count(*) AS denied, count(DISTINCT eventsource) AS services FROM cloudtrail_logs WHERE errorcode = 'AccessDenied' AND from_iso8601_timestamp(eventtime) > current_timestamp - interval '1' hour GROUP BY 1,2 HAVING count(*) > 25; Many AccessDenied results across many services is an attacker mapping what a stolen credential can reach. Snapshot Shared Externally Athena> SELECT eventtime, useridentity.arn, requestparameters FROM cloudtrail_logs WHERE eventname IN ('ModifySnapshotAttribute','ModifyDBSnapshotAttribute','ModifyImageAttribute') AND requestparameters LIKE '%all%' OR requestparameters LIKE '%restore%'; Sharing a snapshot with another account or making it public exfiltrates an entire volume in one API call. Access Key Created for Another User Athena> SELECT eventtime, useridentity.arn AS creator, json_extract_scalar(requestparameters,'$.userName') AS target, sourceipaddress FROM cloudtrail_logs WHERE eventname = 'CreateAccessKey' AND json_extract_scalar(requestparameters,'$.userName') IS NOT NULL; When userName is present the key was created for a different identity, which is the backdoor pattern rather than routine self-service. Activity in Unused Regions Athena> SELECT awsregion, eventname, useridentity.arn, count(*) AS calls FROM cloudtrail_logs WHERE awsregion NOT IN ('me-south-1','eu-west-1') AND readonly = false GROUP BY 1,2,3 ORDER BY calls DESC; Attackers favour regions you do not use because monitoring and guardrails are weaker there. Any write activity is worth review. Root Account Usage Athena> SELECT eventtime, eventname, sourceipaddress, useragent, useridentity.sessioncontext.attributes.mfaauthenticated AS mfa FROM cloudtrail_logs WHERE useridentity.type = 'Root' ORDER BY eventtime DESC; Root should be used essentially never. Any usage, especially without MFA, warrants immediate confirmation with the account owner. User Agent Anomaly Athena> SELECT useridentity.arn, useragent, count(*) AS calls, min(eventtime) AS first_seen FROM cloudtrail_logs GROUP BY 1,2 HAVING min(from_iso8601_timestamp(eventtime)) > current_timestamp - interval '24' hour ORDER BY calls DESC; A new user agent for an established identity often means the credential is now being used by someone else's tooling. Bulk S3 Object Reads Athena> SELECT useridentity.arn, sourceipaddress, count(*) AS objects FROM cloudtrail_logs WHERE eventname = 'GetObject' AND eventcategory = 'Data' GROUP BY 1,2 HAVING count(*) > 1000 ORDER BY objects DESC; Requires data events to be enabled. Without them this query returns nothing regardless of how much data was taken. Outbound Volume from Flow Logs Athena> SELECT srcaddr, dstaddr, sum(bytes)/1073741824.0 AS gb FROM vpc_flow_logs WHERE action='ACCEPT' AND flow_direction='egress' GROUP BY 1,2 HAVING sum(bytes) > 10737418240 ORDER BY gb DESC; Finds instances sending more than 10 GB outbound. Catches exfiltration that never involves an S3 API call.

Apply these practices so that AWS logs remain complete, immutable, and actually queryable during an incident: 01 Use an Organisation Trail to a Separate Account Logs must live where the compromised account cannot reach them. A dedicated logging account with restrictive bucket policies is the single most important control in AWS logging architecture. 02 Always Enable Multi-Region Attackers deliberately operate in regions you never use. A single-region trail leaves every other region completely unmonitored while appearing configured. 03 Enable Data Events on Sensitive Buckets Management events prove a policy changed. Only data events prove which objects were read. Scope them to the buckets holding regulated data to keep the cost defensible. 04 Apply Object Lock in Compliance Mode Compliance mode retention cannot be shortened or removed by anyone, including the root user. It is what makes the audit trail genuinely tamper-proof rather than merely protected. 05 Turn On Log File Validation CloudTrail produces signed digest files that let you prove logs were not altered or deleted. Essential for any investigation whose findings might be disputed. 06 Use EventBridge for Time-Critical Alerts S3 delivery lags by five to fifteen minutes, long enough for an attacker to finish. EventBridge rules on management events fire in near real time. 07 Baseline Identity Behaviour Record the normal region, source address, and user agent for every role and key. Deviation from that baseline is the most reliable signal of credential theft available. 08 Do Not Rely on Console Event History It holds 90 days of management events only, cannot be exported in bulk, and vanishes with the account. It is a convenience feature, not an audit trail.

A complete AWS intrusion in CloudTrail records, from leaked key to exfiltrated database. Stolen Access Key Used from a New Location {"eventTime":"2025-07-14T09:41:22Z","eventName":"GetCallerIdentity","eventSource":"sts.amazonaws.com", "awsRegion":"us-east-1","sourceIPAddress":"203.0.113.44", "userAgent":"aws-cli/2.15.4 Python/3.11.6 Linux/6.1.0 exe/x86_64.kali", "userIdentity":{"type":"IAMUser","arn":"arn:aws:iam::111122223333:user/svc-backup", "accessKeyId":"AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE"},"readOnly":true} GetCallerIdentity is the first call almost every attacker makes: it answers "whose key is this". The user agent contains "kali" and the region is one this service account never uses. Permission Enumeration with Access Denied {"eventTime":"2025-07-14T09:42:04Z","eventName":"ListBuckets","eventSource":"s3.amazonaws.com","errorCode":"AccessDenied","sourceIPAddress":"203.0.113.44"} {"eventTime":"2025-07-14T09:42:06Z","eventName":"ListUsers","eventSource":"iam.amazonaws.com","errorCode":"AccessDenied","sourceIPAddress":"203.0.113.44"} {"eventTime":"2025-07-14T09:42:08Z","eventName":"DescribeInstances","eventSource":"ec2.amazonaws.com","sourceIPAddress":"203.0.113.44","readOnly":true} {"eventTime":"2025-07-14T09:42:11Z","eventName":"ListAttachedUserPolicies","eventSource":"iam.amazonaws.com","sourceIPAddress":"203.0.113.44","readOnly":true} {"eventTime":"2025-07-14T09:42:14Z","eventName":"DescribeDBSnapshots","eventSource":"rds.amazonaws.com","sourceIPAddress":"203.0.113.44","readOnly":true} Five services probed in ten seconds with a mix of denials and successes. No human clicks this fast, and the mixed results are the attacker mapping the boundary of what the key permits. Privilege Escalation via Policy Attachment {"eventTime":"2025-07-14T09:47:33Z","eventName":"AttachUserPolicy","eventSource":"iam.amazonaws.com", "sourceIPAddress":"203.0.113.44","userIdentity":{"type":"IAMUser","arn":"arn:aws:iam::111122223333:user/svc-backup"}, "requestParameters":{"userName":"svc-backup","policyArn":"arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/AdministratorAccess"}, "responseElements":null,"readOnly":false} The compromised service account attaching AdministratorAccess to itself. This single call converts a limited backup credential into full control of the account. Persistence: Backdoor Key for Another User {"eventTime":"2025-07-14T09:52:10Z","eventName":"CreateAccessKey","eventSource":"iam.amazonaws.com", "sourceIPAddress":"203.0.113.44","userIdentity":{"arn":"arn:aws:iam::111122223333:user/svc-backup"}, "requestParameters":{"userName":"cloudops-admin"}, "responseElements":{"accessKey":{"accessKeyId":"AKIAI44QH8DHBEXAMPLE","userName":"cloudops-admin","status":"Active"}}} A key created for a different, more privileged user. This survives rotation of the original stolen credential entirely, which is exactly the point. Cross-Account Persistence via Trust Policy {"eventTime":"2025-07-14T09:55:41Z","eventName":"UpdateAssumeRolePolicy","eventSource":"iam.amazonaws.com", "sourceIPAddress":"203.0.113.44","requestParameters":{"roleName":"OrganizationAccountAccessRole", "policyDocument":"{\"Version\":\"2012-10-17\",\"Statement\":[{\"Effect\":\"Allow\", \"Principal\":{\"AWS\":\"arn:aws:iam::999988887777:root\"},\"Action\":\"sts:AssumeRole\"}]}"}} An external account (999988887777) added to the trust policy of a privileged role. The attacker can now assume this role from their own account indefinitely, with no credential to rotate. Data Exfiltration via Snapshot Sharing {"eventTime":"2025-07-14T10:02:44Z","eventName":"CreateDBSnapshot","eventSource":"rds.amazonaws.com", "requestParameters":{"dBInstanceIdentifier":"prod-customers","dBSnapshotIdentifier":"tmp-snap-01"}} {"eventTime":"2025-07-14T10:11:03Z","eventName":"ModifyDBSnapshotAttribute","eventSource":"rds.amazonaws.com", "sourceIPAddress":"203.0.113.44", "requestParameters":{"dBSnapshotIdentifier":"tmp-snap-01","attributeName":"restore", "valuesToAdd":["999988887777"]}} The entire customer database snapshotted then shared with an external account. Note that no database query was ever run, so database audit logs show nothing at all. S3 Bucket Exposed Publicly {"eventTime":"2025-07-14T10:14:22Z","eventName":"PutBucketPolicy","eventSource":"s3.amazonaws.com", "sourceIPAddress":"203.0.113.44","requestParameters":{"bucketName":"htl-customer-data", "bucketPolicy":{"Statement":[{"Effect":"Allow","Principal":"*","Action":"s3:GetObject", "Resource":"arn:aws:s3:::htl-customer-data/*"}]}}} {"eventTime":"2025-07-14T10:14:31Z","eventName":"DeletePublicAccessBlock","eventSource":"s3.amazonaws.com", "requestParameters":{"bucketName":"htl-customer-data"}} A wildcard principal granted read access, then the public access block removed so the policy takes effect. Both calls are needed, and either one alone should alert. Defence Evasion: Trail Stopped {"eventTime":"2025-07-14T10:18:12Z","eventName":"StopLogging","eventSource":"cloudtrail.amazonaws.com", "sourceIPAddress":"203.0.113.44","userIdentity":{"arn":"arn:aws:iam::111122223333:user/svc-backup"}, "requestParameters":{"name":"arn:aws:cloudtrail:me-south-1:111122223333:trail/htl-org-trail"}} {"eventTime":"2025-07-14T10:18:19Z","eventName":"DeleteFlowLogs","eventSource":"ec2.amazonaws.com", "requestParameters":{"flowLogIdSet":["fl-0a1b2c3d4e5f67890"]}} The trail is stopped and flow logs deleted. Because the log bucket used Object Lock in compliance mode, everything already written survives, which is why these two records exist at all. Cryptomining in an Unused Region {"eventTime":"2025-07-14T10:24:18Z","eventName":"RunInstances","eventSource":"ec2.amazonaws.com", "awsRegion":"ap-southeast-2","sourceIPAddress":"203.0.113.44", "requestParameters":{"instanceType":"p4d.24xlarge","maxCount":8,"minCount":8, "imageId":"ami-0abcdef1234567890"},"readOnly":false} Eight GPU instances launched in a region the organisation does not operate in. At roughly 32 USD per hour each, this becomes expensive within hours and is usually noticed by billing before security. Back

Azure logging divides along a line that does not exist in other clouds: the control plane for Azure resources and the identity plane managed by Microsoft Entra ID, formerly Azure Active Directory. The Activity Log records operations against subscriptions and resources, while Entra ID sign-in and audit logs record authentication and directory changes. Because Entra ID also underpins Microsoft 365, an attacker who compromises an identity gains access to mail, files, and Teams alongside Azure infrastructure. That coupling is why identity logs, not resource logs, are where most Azure investigations begin and end. The default retention is the trap that catches most organisations. Activity Log entries are kept for 90 days, Entra ID sign-in and audit logs for 30 days on paid tiers and only 7 days on the free tier, and resource logs are not collected at all until a diagnostic setting is created. Every one of those defaults is shorter than the average time to detect an intrusion. Exporting to a Log Analytics workspace or a storage account is not an optimisation, it is the difference between having evidence and not. Modern attacks against Azure rarely involve exploiting infrastructure. They target tokens and consent. Device code phishing tricks a user into authorising an attacker's session, illicit consent grants give a malicious application standing access to mailboxes without any password, and primary refresh token theft lets an attacker replay authentication from their own machine while satisfying multi-factor requirements. None of these produce a failed login. They produce clean, successful sign-ins with unusual properties, which means detection depends on scrutinising successes rather than counting failures.

Azure separates its telemetry into several distinct streams, each enabled and retained independently: Log Type Description Entra ID Sign-in Logs Every authentication attempt with the user, application, source address, device, conditional access outcome, and risk assessment. Split into interactive, non-interactive, service principal, and managed identity sign-ins, each collected separately. The most important log in the tenant. Entra ID Audit Logs Directory changes including role assignments, group membership, application registration, consent grants, and conditional access policy modification. Where privilege escalation and persistence become visible. Azure Activity Log Control plane operations against subscriptions and resources: creation, deletion, configuration change, and role assignment at the Azure RBAC level. Equivalent in role to AWS CloudTrail management events. Resource Logs Data plane operations inside individual services such as Key Vault secret retrieval, storage account access, and SQL auditing. Not collected at all until a diagnostic setting is configured per resource. Microsoft 365 Unified Audit Log Activity across Exchange, SharePoint, OneDrive, and Teams. Shares the Entra ID identity plane, so a compromised account appears here and in Azure logs simultaneously. Searched through Purview or the Office 365 Management API. Identity Protection Risk Events Managed risk detections such as anonymous IP address use, impossible travel, leaked credentials, and anomalous token issuance. Requires Entra ID P2 licensing for full detail. NSG Flow Logs Network metadata for traffic through network security groups, comparable to VPC Flow Logs. Being superseded by virtual network flow logs, which offer better coverage. Defender for Cloud Alerts Threat detections across Azure workloads, containers, databases, and storage, correlated into incidents. The fastest path to noticing well-known attack patterns without writing detections. Pro Tip: Non-interactive sign-ins are a separate log category and are excluded from the default sign-in view. Token refreshes, service principal authentication, and most automated access appear only there, which is precisely where token replay attacks hide.

Default retention is short across the board. These are the built-in limits and where each stream can be exported. Log Default Retention and Destination Entra ID Sign-in Logs 30 days with P1 or P2, only 7 days on the free tier. Export to Log Analytics, storage, or Event Hub Entra ID Audit Logs 30 days with P1 or P2, 7 days on free. Same export options Azure Activity Log 90 days in the platform, not configurable. Export required for anything longer Resource Logs Not collected at all by default. Requires a diagnostic setting on each resource Microsoft 365 Unified Audit Log 180 days on E3, one year on E5 or with an audit add-on. Searchable via Purview Log Analytics Workspace Configurable from 30 days to 2 years interactive, with archive up to 12 years Microsoft Sentinel Built on Log Analytics with the same retention model plus security analytics Storage Account Export Indefinite retention at the lowest cost, but not directly queryable Pro Tip: Diagnostic settings are configured per resource, not per subscription. A new storage account or Key Vault created next week collects nothing unless Azure Policy applies a setting automatically. Deploy that policy before you need the logs.

These commands export the critical streams to a Log Analytics workspace and ensure new resources are covered automatically. Step 1: Export Entra ID Logs to Log Analytics az monitor diagnostic-settings create \ --name htl-entra-export \ --resource /providers/Microsoft.AadIam/diagnosticSettings \ --workspace /subscriptions/<sub>/resourceGroups/rg-sec/providers/Microsoft.OperationalInsights/workspaces/htl-sec-law \ --logs '[{"category":"SignInLogs","enabled":true}, {"category":"AuditLogs","enabled":true}, {"category":"NonInteractiveUserSignInLogs","enabled":true}, {"category":"ServicePrincipalSignInLogs","enabled":true}, {"category":"ManagedIdentitySignInLogs","enabled":true}, {"category":"RiskyUsers","enabled":true}, {"category":"UserRiskEvents","enabled":true}]' All five sign-in categories must be listed individually. Enabling only SignInLogs captures interactive logons and misses service principal abuse and token refresh entirely. Step 2: Export the Activity Log az monitor diagnostic-settings subscription create \ --name htl-activity-export \ --location me-central-1 \ --workspace <workspace-resource-id> \ --logs '[{"category":"Administrative","enabled":true}, {"category":"Security","enabled":true}, {"category":"ServiceHealth","enabled":true}, {"category":"Alert","enabled":true}, {"category":"Policy","enabled":true}, {"category":"Autoscale","enabled":false}, {"category":"ResourceHealth","enabled":true}]' The Administrative and Policy categories carry role assignments and policy changes, which is where Azure privilege escalation appears. Step 3: Enforce Diagnostic Settings with Azure Policy az policy assignment create \ --name htl-require-diagnostics \ --policy-set-definition "Enable allLogs category group resource logging for supported resources to Log Analytics" \ --scope /subscriptions/<sub> \ --location me-central-1 \ --mi-system-assigned \ --role Contributor \ --identity-scope /subscriptions/<sub> \ --params '{"logAnalytics":{"value":"<workspace-resource-id>"}}' az policy remediation create --name fix-existing \ --policy-assignment htl-require-diagnostics DeployIfNotExists policy applies diagnostic settings to resources as they are created. Without it, coverage decays continuously as the estate grows.
