Step 4: Enable Key Vault and Storage Data Plane Logging # Key Vault: record every secret and key retrieval az monitor diagnostic-settings create --name kv-audit \ --resource <keyvault-resource-id> \ --workspace <workspace-resource-id> \ --logs '[{"category":"AuditEvent","enabled":true}, {"category":"AzurePolicyEvaluationDetails","enabled":true}]' # Storage: record blob read and write operations az monitor diagnostic-settings create --name storage-audit \ --resource <storage-id>/blobServices/default \ --workspace <workspace-resource-id> \ --logs '[{"category":"StorageRead","enabled":true}, {"category":"StorageWrite","enabled":true}, {"category":"StorageDelete","enabled":true}]' Key Vault AuditEvent is the Azure equivalent of AWS S3 data events: without it you can prove a vault was accessed but not which secrets were read. Step 5: Enable the Microsoft 365 Unified Audit Log Connect-ExchangeOnline Set-AdminAuditLogConfig -UnifiedAuditLogIngestionEnabled $true Get-AdminAuditLogConfig | Select-Object UnifiedAuditLogIngestionEnabled # Enable mailbox auditing for all mailboxes including owner actions Set-OrganizationConfig -AuditDisabled $false Get-Mailbox -ResultSize Unlimited | Set-Mailbox -AuditEnabled $true -AuditOwner @{Add="MailItemsAccessed","Send","SoftDelete","HardDelete"} MailItemsAccessed is the only record proving an attacker actually read mail rather than merely having access. It requires E5 or an equivalent add-on licence. Step 6: Extend Retention Beyond the Defaults az monitor log-analytics workspace update \ --resource-group rg-sec --workspace-name htl-sec-law \ --retention-time 365 # Per-table retention with cheaper long term archive az monitor log-analytics workspace table update \ --resource-group rg-sec --workspace-name htl-sec-law \ --name SigninLogs --retention-time 365 --total-retention-time 2555 Interactive retention is queryable immediately, archive retention is cheaper but requires a restore job. Keeping sign-in logs for a year is the practical minimum for identity investigations. Security Note: Entra ID free tier keeps sign-in logs for seven days. Given that the median dwell time for identity compromise is measured in weeks, a tenant on the free tier will have destroyed the evidence of the initial compromise long before anyone notices it happened.

Azure attacks target identity rather than infrastructure. These patterns dominate real incidents and most of them produce successful sign-ins, not failures. Password Spraying One password tried against many accounts to avoid lockout. Signature: result code 50126 across dozens of distinct users from one address, often targeting legacy authentication endpoints. Detect Critical Illicit Consent Grant A user is tricked into consenting to a malicious application, granting it standing access to mail and files. Requires no password and survives password reset entirely. Detect Critical Device Code Phishing The attacker initiates a device code flow and persuades the victim to enter the code. The resulting token belongs to the attacker and satisfies MFA. Signature: device code authentication from an unexpected client. Detect Critical Token and PRT Theft Stolen refresh tokens replayed from attacker infrastructure. Produces successful non-interactive sign-ins with a mismatch between the device identity and the source address. Detect Critical Privileged Role Assignment Adding an account to Global Administrator, Privileged Role Administrator, or Application Administrator. The last two allow escalation to full tenant control indirectly. Detect Critical Conditional Access Tampering Disabling a policy, adding an exclusion for a compromised account, or switching to report-only mode. Silently removes MFA enforcement while the policy still appears to exist. Detect Critical Security Note: Adding a credential to an existing service principal, through Update application: Certificates and secrets management , is one of the stealthiest persistence techniques in Entra ID. The application continues to work normally, no user is involved, and the attacker holds a credential that no password reset affects.

These fields appear in the Entra ID SigninLogs table. The device and conditional access fields are what distinguish legitimate access from token replay. Field Description Category Example Value TimeGenerated UTC time of the sign-in attempt Timestamp 2025-07-14T09:41:22Z UserPrincipalName Account attempting to authenticate Identity r.almutairi@corp.com AppDisplayName Application being accessed Target Microsoft Office 365 Portal IPAddress Source address of the request Source 203.0.113.44 LocationDetails Geolocated city and country Source Amsterdam, NL ResultType Numeric outcome, 0 means success Result 50126 ResultDescription Text explanation of the outcome Result Invalid username or password ClientAppUsed Protocol or client type used Source Other clients (legacy auth) ConditionalAccessStatus Whether policies applied, failed, or were not applied Policy notApplied AuthenticationRequirement Single or multi factor Authorization singleFactorAuthentication RiskLevelDuringSignIn Identity Protection risk assessment Detection high DeviceDetail.deviceId Registered device identifier, empty if unmanaged Identity (empty) UserAgent Client software string Source python-requests/2.31.0 AuthenticationProtocol Flow used to obtain the token Authorization deviceCode

Entra ID result codes are stable and precise, which makes them excellent detection anchors. These are the ones that matter most. Code Meaning Why It Matters 0 Sign-in succeeded Token theft, consent abuse, and device code phishing all produce this. Successes need scrutiny, not just failures 50126 Invalid username or password The core failure code. Many distinct users from one address is password spraying 50053 Account locked by smart lockout Confirms sustained guessing reached the threshold, or an attacker locking a user out deliberately 50055 / 50057 Password expired or account disabled Attempts against dormant accounts, a common sign that a stale credential list is being tested 50074 / 50076 Strong authentication required MFA was demanded. A burst followed by a success is the shape of an MFA fatigue attack 50140 Keep me signed in interrupt Normal in interactive flows, but useful for distinguishing genuine browser sessions from scripted ones 53003 Blocked by conditional access policy Policy enforcement working. Repeated blocks for one account from an unusual location is an attacker being stopped 530032 Blocked by security defaults or policy Similar enforcement signal, frequently seen when legacy authentication is attempted 50158 External security challenge not satisfied A third party MFA or risk challenge failed, often during token replay from an unexpected location 65001 User or administrator has not consented Precedes consent grant activity. A burst can indicate an application probing for what it can obtain Pro Tip: ConditionalAccessStatus of notApplied on a successful sign-in means no policy evaluated that request at all. On a privileged account that is a policy gap worth fixing immediately, because MFA was never actually required.

These KQL queries run in Log Analytics or Microsoft Sentinel and cover the dominant Azure attack paths. Password Spraying KQL> SigninLogs | where ResultType == 50126 | summarize Targets=dcount(UserPrincipalName), Attempts=count() by IPAddress, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h) | where Targets > 20 and Attempts/Targets < 3 Many users with few attempts each is the spray signature, deliberately staying below smart lockout thresholds. Illicit Consent Grant KQL> AuditLogs | where OperationName has_any ("Consent to application","Add delegated permission grant","Add app role assignment to service principal") | extend perms=tostring(TargetResources[0].modifiedProperties) | where perms has_any ("Mail.Read","Mail.ReadWrite","Files.ReadWrite.All","Directory.ReadWrite.All") Consent granting mailbox or directory-wide permissions. Survives password reset entirely, so it must be revoked explicitly. Device Code Phishing KQL> SigninLogs | where AuthenticationProtocol == "deviceCode" | summarize Apps=make_set(AppDisplayName), IPs=make_set(IPAddress), count() by UserPrincipalName, Location Device code flow is legitimate only for input-constrained devices. On a normal workstation account it almost always means phishing. Privileged Role Assignment KQL> AuditLogs | where OperationName == "Add member to role" | extend Role=tostring(TargetResources[0].modifiedProperties[1].newValue) | where Role has_any ("Global Administrator","Privileged Role Administrator","Application Administrator","Cloud Application Administrator") | project TimeGenerated, InitiatedBy, Role, TargetResources Assignment to any of these four roles is effectively full tenant compromise. Application Administrator escalates indirectly by adding credentials to privileged service principals. Service Principal Credential Added KQL> AuditLogs | where OperationName in ("Update application - Certificates and secrets management","Add service principal credentials") | project TimeGenerated, InitiatedBy, TargetResources, Result One of the stealthiest persistence techniques in Entra ID. The application keeps working, no user is involved, and no password reset affects it. Conditional Access Tampering KQL> AuditLogs | where Category == "Policy" and OperationName has_any ("Update conditional access policy","Delete conditional access policy","Add conditional access policy") | project TimeGenerated, InitiatedBy, OperationName, TargetResources Adding an exclusion or switching a policy to report-only silently removes MFA enforcement while the policy still appears to exist. Impossible Travel KQL> SigninLogs | where ResultType == 0 | sort by UserPrincipalName asc, TimeGenerated asc | extend prevCountry=prev(Location), prevTime=prev(TimeGenerated), prevUser=prev(UserPrincipalName) | where prevUser == UserPrincipalName and prevCountry != Location and datetime_diff("minute", TimeGenerated, prevTime) < 240 Two successful sign-ins from different countries within four hours. Whitelist VPN egress points and adjacent-country commuting before deploying. Legacy Authentication KQL> SigninLogs | where ClientAppUsed in ("Other clients","IMAP4","POP3","SMTP","Exchange ActiveSync","Authenticated SMTP") | summarize count(), Users=dcount(UserPrincipalName) by ClientAppUsed, IPAddress | order by count_ desc Legacy protocols cannot enforce MFA, which is exactly why attackers target them. Any remaining usage is both a finding and an attack surface. Token Replay Indicators KQL> AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs | where ResultType == 0 | where isempty(tostring(DeviceDetail.deviceId)) | summarize IPs=dcount(IPAddress), Countries=dcount(tostring(LocationDetails.countryOrRegion)) by UserPrincipalName | where Countries > 1 Non-interactive successes from an unregistered device across multiple countries is the shape of a stolen refresh token being replayed. Key Vault Secret Harvesting KQL> AzureDiagnostics | where ResourceType == "VAULTS" and OperationName in ("SecretGet","KeyGet","CertificateGet") | summarize Secrets=dcount(id_s), count() by identity_claim_upn_s, CallerIPAddress | where Secrets > 10 One identity pulling many distinct secrets in a short window is credential harvesting, not normal application behaviour. Azure RBAC Role Assignments KQL> AzureActivity | where OperationNameValue == "MICROSOFT.AUTHORIZATION/ROLEASSIGNMENTS/WRITE" and ActivityStatusValue == "Success" | project TimeGenerated, Caller, CallerIpAddress, Properties Azure RBAC is separate from Entra ID directory roles. Owner or Contributor at subscription scope grants control of every resource beneath it. Mailbox Access and Forwarding KQL> OfficeActivity | where Operation in ("New-InboxRule","Set-InboxRule","Set-Mailbox","Add-MailboxPermission") | where Parameters has_any ("ForwardTo","RedirectTo","DeleteMessage") | project TimeGenerated, UserId, Operation, Parameters Inbox rules that forward externally or delete messages are the classic business email compromise persistence and concealment technique.

Apply these practices so identity evidence still exists when you finally go looking for it: 01 Export Entra ID Logs Immediately Seven days on the free tier and thirty on paid tiers are both shorter than typical dwell time. Exporting to Log Analytics is the single highest value logging change in any Azure tenant. 02 Enable All Five Sign-in Categories Interactive sign-ins are only one category. Non-interactive, service principal, and managed identity sign-ins are where token replay and automation abuse appear, and they are excluded by default. 03 Enforce Diagnostic Settings with Policy Settings are per resource. Without a DeployIfNotExists policy, every new Key Vault and storage account arrives with no logging, and coverage silently erodes as the estate grows. 04 Monitor Successful Sign-ins, Not Only Failures Consent abuse, device code phishing, and token theft all produce clean successes. Failure-based monitoring is blind to the techniques that dominate real Azure intrusions. 05 Alert on Consent and Service Principal Credentials Both create access that no password reset revokes. They are low volume and high fidelity, making them ideal candidates for real-time alerting. 06 Watch Conditional Access Changes Closely An exclusion added for one account removes MFA for that account while the policy still shows as enabled. Treat every policy modification as a security event requiring review. 07 Enable Mailbox Auditing Including Owner Actions MailItemsAccessed is the only evidence proving an attacker actually read mail. Without it you can show access was possible but not what was taken. 08 Eliminate Legacy Authentication Legacy protocols bypass conditional access and cannot enforce MFA. Block them outright, then treat any remaining attempts as attack traffic rather than misconfiguration.

An Entra ID account takeover, from spraying through consent abuse to mailbox exfiltration. Password Spraying Against Legacy Authentication TimeGenerated: 2025-07-14T09:12:04Z UserPrincipalName: a.alqahtani@corp.com ResultType: 50126 IPAddress: 203.0.113.44 ClientAppUsed: Other clients AppDisplayName: Exchange ActiveSync ConditionalAccessStatus: notApplied AuthenticationRequirement: singleFactorAuthentication TimeGenerated: 2025-07-14T09:12:09Z UserPrincipalName: m.alharbi@corp.com ResultType: 50126 IPAddress: 203.0.113.44 ClientAppUsed: Other clients TimeGenerated: 2025-07-14T09:12:14Z UserPrincipalName: r.almutairi@corp.com ResultType: 50126 IPAddress: 203.0.113.44 ClientAppUsed: Other clients Legacy authentication was targeted deliberately: ConditionalAccessStatus is notApplied, meaning no policy evaluated these attempts and MFA could never have been enforced. Successful Sign-in from an Unmanaged Device TimeGenerated: 2025-07-14T09:40:53Z UserPrincipalName: r.almutairi@corp.com ResultType: 0 IPAddress: 203.0.113.44 LocationDetails: {"city":"Amsterdam","countryOrRegion":"NL"} AppDisplayName: Microsoft Office 365 Portal ClientAppUsed: Browser DeviceDetail: {"deviceId":"","operatingSystem":"Linux","browser":"Chrome 126.0"} RiskLevelDuringSignIn: high RiskEventTypesV2: ["unfamiliarFeatures","anonymizedIPAddress"] ConditionalAccessStatus: success AuthenticationRequirement: multiFactorAuthentication ResultType 0 means this succeeded, and MFA was satisfied. The empty deviceId shows an unmanaged Linux machine, and Identity Protection scored it high risk. A success can still be an intrusion. Device Code Phishing TimeGenerated: 2025-07-14T09:38:02Z UserPrincipalName: r.almutairi@corp.com ResultType: 0 AuthenticationProtocol: deviceCode AppDisplayName: Microsoft Office ResourceDisplayName: Microsoft Graph IPAddress: 203.0.113.44 LocationDetails: {"city":"Amsterdam","countryOrRegion":"NL"} DeviceDetail: {"deviceId":"","operatingSystem":"","browser":""} IncomingTokenType: none AuthenticationRequirement: multiFactorAuthentication Device code flow exists for devices without a keyboard, such as smart TVs. On a finance user's account it means they entered a code an attacker generated, handing over a fully MFA-satisfied token. Illicit Consent Grant OperationName: Consent to application InitiatedBy: {"user":{"userPrincipalName":"r.almutairi@corp.com","ipAddress":"203.0.113.44"}} TargetResources: [{"displayName":"Office365 Document Sync","type":"ServicePrincipal", "modifiedProperties":[{"displayName":"ConsentAction.Permissions", "newValue":"Scope: Mail.Read Mail.ReadWrite Files.ReadWrite.All User.Read offline_access"}]}] Result: success A plausibly named application granted persistent mailbox and file access. The offline_access scope gives it a refresh token, so it retains access indefinitely and a password reset changes nothing. Privilege Escalation via Role Assignment OperationName: Add member to role InitiatedBy: {"user":{"userPrincipalName":"r.almutairi@corp.com","ipAddress":"203.0.113.44"}} TargetResources: [{"userPrincipalName":"svc-sync@corp.com","type":"User", "modifiedProperties":[{"displayName":"Role.DisplayName","newValue":"Global Administrator"}]}] Result: success Category: RoleManagement The compromised user adding a service account to Global Administrator. That account now controls the entire tenant, including Microsoft 365 and every Azure subscription beneath it. Persistence via Service Principal Credential OperationName: Update application - Certificates and secrets management InitiatedBy: {"user":{"userPrincipalName":"svc-sync@corp.com","ipAddress":"203.0.113.44"}} TargetResources: [{"displayName":"Corp HR Integration","type":"Application", "modifiedProperties":[{"displayName":"KeyDescription", "newValue":"[KeyIdentifier=8f2a1c04,KeyType=Password,KeyUsage=Verify]"}]}] Result: success A new client secret added to an existing privileged application. The application continues functioning normally, no user is involved, and the attacker now holds a credential unaffected by any password reset. Conditional Access Policy Weakened OperationName: Update conditional access policy InitiatedBy: {"user":{"userPrincipalName":"svc-sync@corp.com","ipAddress":"203.0.113.44"}} TargetResources: [{"displayName":"CA001-Require MFA for All Users","type":"Policy", "modifiedProperties":[{"displayName":"ConditionalAccessPolicy", "oldValue":"{state:enabled, users:{excludeUsers:[]}}", "newValue":"{state:enabled, users:{excludeUsers:[r.almutairi@corp.com]}}"}]}] The policy remains enabled and looks healthy in the portal, but the compromised account is now excluded from MFA entirely. Only the audit log reveals this. Mailbox Exfiltration and Concealment Operation: New-InboxRule UserId: r.almutairi@corp.com ClientIP: 203.0.113.44 Parameters: [{"Name":"Name","Value":"."},{"Name":"ForwardTo","Value":"archive@badinfra.top"}, {"Name":"DeleteMessage","Value":"True"},{"Name":"From","Value":"finance@corp.com"}] Operation: MailItemsAccessed UserId: r.almutairi@corp.com ClientIP: 203.0.113.44 OperationProperties: [{"Name":"MailAccessType","Value":"Bind"},{"Name":"IsThrottled","Value":"True"}] Folders: [{"Path":"\Inbox","FolderItems":[{"InternetMessageId":"..."}]}] An inbox rule named with a single dot, forwarding finance mail externally and deleting the local copy. The MailItemsAccessed record with IsThrottled true means so much mail was read that Microsoft rate limited the auditing. Back

Google Cloud records administrative activity through Cloud Audit Logs , which are organised into four distinct streams with very different default behaviour. Admin Activity logs capture every operation that modifies configuration or metadata, are always enabled, cannot be disabled, and are retained for 400 days at no charge. System Event logs record Google-initiated actions such as automatic instance migration and are equally unavoidable. Those two guarantees are genuinely useful: unlike AWS CloudTrail, which can be stopped, the core Google Cloud audit trail cannot be turned off by an attacker. The other two streams are where the gaps appear. Data Access logs record reads of user data and non-modifying API calls, and they are disabled by default for every service except BigQuery. Enabling them is a deliberate decision with real cost implications, and the consequence of skipping it is the same as skipping CloudTrail data events in AWS: you can prove a bucket permission changed but not which objects were subsequently downloaded. Policy Denied logs capture requests blocked by VPC Service Controls or organisation policy, and they are generated automatically but charged, which leads some organisations to filter them out. What distinguishes Google Cloud operationally is the centrality of service accounts and impersonation. Rather than long-lived keys, the recommended pattern is short-lived token generation through generateAccessToken , granted by the Service Account Token Creator role. This is better security practice, but it creates impersonation chains that are genuinely difficult to follow: principal A impersonates service account B which impersonates C, and only the authenticationInfo.serviceAccountDelegationInfo field records the full path. Attackers exploit exactly this, and detections that only look at the immediate caller will attribute their actions to a legitimate service account.

Four audit log streams plus several supporting sources, each with its own default state and cost model: Log Type Description Admin Activity Audit Logs Every API call that modifies configuration or metadata: IAM policy changes, resource creation and deletion, service account key creation. Always enabled, cannot be disabled, free, and retained 400 days. The backbone of Google Cloud investigation. Data Access Audit Logs Reads of user data and non-modifying API calls such as storage.objects.get and bigquery data reads. Disabled by default for all services except BigQuery. Without these you cannot determine what data an attacker actually accessed. System Event Audit Logs Google-initiated actions taken without user involvement, such as automatic live migration of an instance or automatic instance termination. Always enabled and free. Policy Denied Audit Logs Requests rejected by VPC Service Controls, organisation policy, or context-aware access. Generated automatically but billed. Extremely useful because a denied request often reveals an attacker probing a boundary. VPC Flow Logs Network metadata sampled from virtual machine interfaces, including source, destination, ports, bytes, and geographic annotation. Enabled per subnet with a configurable sampling rate. Firewall Rules Logging Records connections allowed or denied by individual firewall rules. Enabled per rule rather than globally, so coverage is easy to leave incomplete. Security Command Center Findings Managed detection across misconfiguration, vulnerabilities, and threats, including Event Threat Detection which analyses audit logs directly. The Premium tier adds behavioural detections such as anomalous IAM grants. Access Transparency Logs Records actions taken by Google personnel on your content, available on eligible support tiers. Rarely relevant to attack detection but frequently required for regulatory assurance. Pro Tip: The guarantee that Admin Activity logs cannot be disabled applies to the log generation, not to your copy of it. An attacker with sufficient permissions can still delete a log sink , stopping delivery to your SIEM while the logs continue accumulating in the platform bucket where nobody is watching.

Cloud Logging routes entries through the Log Router into buckets and sinks. Understanding the default buckets prevents both surprise costs and surprise gaps. Destination Characteristics _Required Bucket Holds Admin Activity, System Event, and Access Transparency logs. Retention fixed at 400 days, cannot be changed or deleted, and incurs no charge _Default Bucket Holds everything else including Data Access logs. Default retention 30 days, configurable up to 3650 days, and billed on ingestion Custom Log Buckets User-created buckets with independent retention and optional Log Analytics for SQL querying BigQuery Sink Streams logs into datasets for SQL analysis and long term retention. The standard approach for security analytics at scale Cloud Storage Sink Archives logs as JSON files to a bucket. Cheapest long term retention, supports Bucket Lock for immutability Pub/Sub Sink Streams to an external SIEM in near real time. The standard integration path for Splunk, Chronicle, and similar platforms Aggregated Sink Configured at organisation or folder level to capture logs from every project beneath, including projects created later Pro Tip: The _Default bucket keeps Data Access logs for only 30 days. If you enable Data Access logging without also extending retention or configuring a sink, you gain visibility that expires before most breaches are even discovered.

These commands enable the streams that are off by default and route everything to a location an attacker in a member project cannot reach. Step 1: Enable Data Access Audit Logs # Fetch the current organisation IAM policy gcloud organizations get-iam-policy 123456789012 --format=json > policy.json # Add an auditConfigs block covering all services cat <<'JSON' > audit.json { "auditConfigs": [ { "service": "allServices", "auditLogConfigs": [ { "logType": "ADMIN_READ" }, { "logType": "DATA_READ", "exemptedMembers": ["serviceAccount:noisy-etl@proj.iam.gserviceaccount.com"] }, { "logType": "DATA_WRITE" } ] } ] } JSON gcloud organizations set-iam-policy 123456789012 policy-with-audit.json ADMIN_READ, DATA_READ, and DATA_WRITE must each be listed. Setting this at organisation level covers every current and future project, which is the only way to keep coverage complete as the estate grows. Step 2: Create an Aggregated Sink to BigQuery gcloud logging sinks create htl-org-security-sink \ bigquery.googleapis.com/projects/htl-security/datasets/cloud_audit \ --organization=123456789012 \ --include-children \ --use-partitioned-tables \ --log-filter='logName:"cloudaudit.googleapis.com" OR logName:"compute.googleapis.com%2Fvpc_flows"' # Grant the sink writer identity permission on the destination gcloud projects add-iam-policy-binding htl-security \ --member="$(gcloud logging sinks describe htl-org-security-sink \ --organization=123456789012 --format='value(writerIdentity)')" \ --role=roles/bigquery.dataEditor The include-children flag captures every project under the organisation, including ones created tomorrow. Without an aggregated sink, each new project starts unmonitored. Step 3: Extend Default Bucket Retention gcloud logging buckets update _Default \ --location=global \ --retention-days=365 \ --project=htl-production # Confirm both buckets gcloud logging buckets list --project=htl-production \ --format="table(name, retentionDays, lifecycleState, locked)" The _Default bucket keeps Data Access logs for only 30 days. Enabling data access logging without extending retention produces visibility that expires before most breaches are discovered. Step 4: Lock the Archive Against Tampering # Cloud Storage sink with Bucket Lock for immutable retention gsutil retention set 400d gs://htl-audit-archive gsutil retention lock gs://htl-audit-archive # Restrict who can modify the Log Router itself gcloud organizations add-iam-policy-binding 123456789012 \ --member="group:cloud-security@corp.com" \ --role=roles/logging.configWriter Bucket Lock is irreversible once applied, which is exactly the property that makes it valuable. Nobody, including an organisation administrator, can shorten the retention afterwards. Step 5: Enable VPC Flow Logs and Firewall Logging gcloud compute networks subnets update prod-subnet-me1 \ --region=me-central1 \ --enable-flow-logs \ --logging-aggregation-interval=interval-30-sec \ --logging-flow-sampling=1.0 \ --logging-metadata=include-all # Firewall logging is enabled per rule, not globally gcloud compute firewall-rules update allow-internal \ --enable-logging --logging-metadata=include-all Flow sampling defaults to 0.5, meaning half of all flows are discarded. Set it to 1.0 on sensitive subnets, because a sampled log cannot prove a connection did not happen. Step 6: Alert on Sink and Audit Config Changes gcloud logging metrics create sink_tampering \ --description="Log Router or audit config modified" \ --log-filter='protoPayload.methodName=( "google.logging.v2.ConfigServiceV2.DeleteSink" OR "google.logging.v2.ConfigServiceV2.UpdateSink" OR "google.logging.v2.ConfigServiceV2.UpdateBucket" OR "SetIamPolicy") AND protoPayload.serviceData.policyDelta.auditConfigDeltas:*' gcloud alpha monitoring policies create --policy-from-file=sink-alert.yaml The auditConfigDeltas filter is the important part: it fires when someone disables audit logging for a service, which is otherwise a quiet change buried inside a routine IAM policy update. Security Note: Admin Activity logs cannot be disabled, but the delivery of your copy can be. Deleting a sink stops the flow to your SIEM while logs continue accumulating in the platform bucket that nobody monitors. Alert on sink deletion with the same urgency as AWS StopLogging.

Google Cloud attacks centre on service accounts and IAM. These are the patterns that account for most real incidents. Service Account Key Creation Creating a long-lived JSON key for a privileged service account. The key never expires, works from anywhere, and is unaffected by any password or session policy. The most common Google Cloud persistence technique. Detect Critical Impersonation Chains Using Service Account Token Creator to generate tokens for progressively more privileged accounts. Only serviceAccountDelegationInfo reveals the true origin, so naive detections blame the final service account. Detect Critical Public IAM Binding Granting a role to allUsers or allAuthenticatedUsers on a bucket, dataset, or function. Exposes the resource to the entire internet in a single API call. Detect Critical IAM Privilege Escalation Self-granting roles/owner or roles/iam.securityAdmin through setIamPolicy. Also achievable indirectly through actAs on a privileged service account attached to a compute instance. Detect Critical Data Exfiltration Bulk object reads, BigQuery extract jobs to external buckets, or Cloud SQL exports. Visible only if Data Access logging is enabled for the relevant service. Detect High Risk Logging Evasion Deleting a log sink, disabling audit configs for a service, or operating in a project outside the aggregated sink scope. Stops your visibility without stopping log generation. Detect Critical Security Note: The roles/iam.serviceAccountUser and roles/iam.serviceAccountTokenCreator roles are frequently granted casually because they sound benign. Either one lets a principal act as a service account, inheriting all of its permissions, which makes them among the most dangerous grants in Google Cloud.

Every Cloud Audit Log entry shares the AuditLog protobuf structure. These are the fields that carry detection value. Field Description Category Example Value timestamp UTC time the request was received Timestamp 2025-07-14T09:41:22.481Z protoPayload.methodName The API method invoked Action google.iam.admin.v1.CreateServiceAccountKey protoPayload.serviceName Service that handled the request Target iam.googleapis.com authenticationInfo.principalEmail Identity that made the call Identity svc-deploy@proj.iam.gserviceaccount.com serviceAccountDelegationInfo Full impersonation chain when present Identity firstPartyPrincipal: r.almutairi@corp.com requestMetadata.callerIp Source address of the caller Source 203.0.113.44 callerSuppliedUserAgent Client library or tool used Source google-cloud-sdk gcloud/470.0.0 resourceName Full path of the resource acted upon Target projects/htl-prod/buckets/customer-data authorizationInfo.permission IAM permission checked Authorization storage.buckets.setIamPolicy authorizationInfo.granted Whether the permission was allowed Result true status.code gRPC status, absent or 0 on success Result 7 (PERMISSION_DENIED) serviceData.policyDelta Exact IAM bindings added or removed Action ADD roles/owner to user:... logName Which audit stream produced the entry Metadata cloudaudit.googleapis.com%2Factivity Pro Tip: Always read serviceAccountDelegationInfo alongside principalEmail . When impersonation is used, principalEmail shows the service account being impersonated, not the human or key that initiated the chain. Detections built on principalEmail alone attribute attacker actions to legitimate automation.

A short list of API methods accounts for most Google Cloud compromise. These belong on a real-time watchlist. Method Stage Why It Matters CreateServiceAccountKey Persistence Produces a non-expiring credential usable from anywhere. Should be rare in a mature environment that uses workload identity federation SetIamPolicy Escalation The universal permission change method. Inspect serviceData.policyDelta to see exactly which binding was added and to whom GenerateAccessToken / SignJwt Lateral Movement Service account impersonation. Legitimate in many pipelines, so baseline the normal chains and alert on new combinations DeleteSink / UpdateSink Evasion Stops log delivery to your SIEM. The Google Cloud equivalent of StopLogging and equally urgent storage.setIamPolicy Exfiltration Granting allUsers on a bucket exposes it publicly. The mechanism behind most Google Cloud data exposure incidents CreateServiceAccount Persistence New service accounts created outside the provisioning pipeline are attacker infrastructure compute.instances.setMetadata Execution Adding an SSH key or startup script to a running instance gives code execution as root without touching the guest OS bigquery.jobs.insert (extract) Exfiltration Exporting a dataset to a bucket the attacker controls copies an entire warehouse in one job SetOrgPolicy Evasion Removing constraints such as the one forbidding service account key creation weakens guardrails across the whole organisation cloudfunctions.functions.create Persistence A function with a privileged service account and an unauthenticated trigger is a durable backdoor reachable from the internet

These Logging query language and BigQuery statements cover the dominant Google Cloud attack paths. Service Account Key Created gcloud> gcloud logging read 'protoPayload.methodName="google.iam.admin.v1.CreateServiceAccountKey"' --organization=123456789012 --format="table(timestamp, protoPayload.authenticationInfo.principalEmail, protoPayload.resourceName, protoPayload.requestMetadata.callerIp)" --freshness=7d Long-lived keys should be rare. Every one is a credential that never expires and works from any address on the internet. Privileged Role Granted SQL> SELECT timestamp, protopayload_auditlog.authenticationInfo.principalEmail AS actor, binding.role, member FROM cloud_audit.cloudaudit_googleapis_com_activity, UNNEST(protopayload_auditlog.servicedata_v1_iam.policyDelta.bindingDeltas) AS binding, UNNEST([binding.member]) AS member WHERE binding.action = 'ADD' AND binding.role IN ('roles/owner','roles/editor','roles/iam.securityAdmin','roles/iam.serviceAccountTokenCreator') Unpacking bindingDeltas is what reveals the exact role and recipient. The role name alone in methodName is not enough. Resource Made Public gcloud> gcloud logging read 'protoPayload.methodName:"setIamPolicy" AND (protoPayload.serviceData.policyDelta.bindingDeltas.member="allUsers" OR protoPayload.serviceData.policyDelta.bindingDeltas.member="allAuthenticatedUsers")' --organization=123456789012 --freshness=30d allUsers means the entire internet. This single query catches the mechanism behind most Google Cloud data exposure incidents. Impersonation Chains SQL> SELECT timestamp, protopayload_auditlog.authenticationInfo.principalEmail AS impersonated, delegate.principalEmail AS origin, protopayload_auditlog.methodName FROM cloud_audit.cloudaudit_googleapis_com_activity, UNNEST(protopayload_auditlog.authenticationInfo.serviceAccountDelegationInfo) AS d, UNNEST([d.firstPartyPrincipal]) AS delegate WHERE delegate.principalEmail IS NOT NULL Reveals the human or key behind an impersonated service account. Without this join, attacker activity is attributed to legitimate automation. Logging Tampering gcloud> gcloud logging read 'protoPayload.methodName=("google.logging.v2.ConfigServiceV2.DeleteSink" OR "google.logging.v2.ConfigServiceV2.UpdateSink" OR "google.logging.v2.ConfigServiceV2.UpdateBucket")' --organization=123456789012 --freshness=30d Sink deletion stops delivery to your SIEM while logs keep accumulating unwatched in the platform bucket. Page on this. Permission Enumeration SQL> SELECT protopayload_auditlog.authenticationInfo.principalEmail AS actor, protopayload_auditlog.requestMetadata.callerIp AS ip, COUNT(*) AS denials, COUNT(DISTINCT protopayload_auditlog.serviceName) AS services FROM cloud_audit.cloudaudit_googleapis_com_activity WHERE protopayload_auditlog.status.code = 7 GROUP BY 1,2 HAVING denials > 25 Status code 7 is PERMISSION_DENIED. Many denials across many services is an attacker mapping what a stolen identity can reach. Instance Metadata Modified gcloud> gcloud logging read 'protoPayload.methodName="v1.compute.instances.setMetadata" OR protoPayload.methodName="v1.compute.projects.setCommonInstanceMetadata"' --organization=123456789012 --freshness=7d Adding an SSH key or startup script through metadata grants root on the instance without ever touching the guest operating system. BigQuery Data Extraction SQL> SELECT timestamp, protopayload_auditlog.authenticationInfo.principalEmail, protopayload_auditlog.servicedata_v1_bigquery.jobCompletedEvent.job.jobConfiguration.extract FROM cloud_audit.cloudaudit_googleapis_com_data_access WHERE protopayload_auditlog.servicedata_v1_bigquery.jobCompletedEvent.job.jobConfiguration.extract IS NOT NULL Extract jobs write dataset contents to Cloud Storage. Check whether the destination bucket belongs to your organisation at all. Verify Audit Config Coverage gcloud> gcloud organizations get-iam-policy 123456789012 --format="json(auditConfigs)" Run this as a scheduled control check. An empty result means Data Access logging is off everywhere and you cannot prove what was read. Outbound Volume from Flow Logs SQL> SELECT jsonPayload.connection.src_ip, jsonPayload.connection.dest_ip, SUM(CAST(jsonPayload.bytes_sent AS INT64))/1073741824 AS gb FROM vpc_flows.compute_googleapis_com_vpc_flows WHERE jsonPayload.reporter = 'SRC' GROUP BY 1,2 HAVING gb > 10 ORDER BY gb DESC Finds instances shipping large volumes outbound, catching exfiltration that never involves a storage API call.

s.h: Best Practices for Google Cloud Logging
s.t: Apply these practices so Google Cloud logs stay complete, durable, and attributable: 01 Enable Data Access Logs at Organisation Level They are off by default everywhere except BigQuery. Setting them once on the organisation policy covers every current and future project rather than leaving each one to be configured individually. 02 Use an Aggregated Sink with include-children Project-level sinks leave every newly created project unmonitored. An organisation-level aggregated sink captures projects that do not exist yet. 03 Extend _Default Bucket Retention Thirty days is shorter than typical time to detection. Raise it or route to BigQuery, otherwise Data Access logs expire before anyone thinks to look at them. 04 Always Resolve Impersonation Chains Read serviceAccountDelegationInfo alongside principalEmail. Without it every impersonated action is attributed to the service account rather than the identity that initiated it. 05 Alert on Sink Deletion Admin Activity logs cannot be disabled, but their delivery to you can be. Sink tampering is the Google Cloud equivalent of stopping CloudTrail and deserves the same response. 06 Ban Service Account Keys by Policy Apply the constraints/iam.disableServiceAccountKeyCreation organisation policy and use workload identity federation instead. This removes the most common persistence mechanism outright. 07 Raise Flow Log Sampling on Sensitive Subnets The default samples half of all flows. A sampled log can never prove a connection did not occur, which matters when the question is whether data left. 08 Lock the Archive Bucket Cloud Storage Bucket Lock makes retention irreversible. Once applied, no principal at any level can shorten it, which is what makes the archive genuinely tamper-proof.

A Google Cloud intrusion from compromised pipeline credential to exported dataset. Compromised Service Account Enumerating Permissions timestamp: 2025-07-14T09:41:22.481Z protoPayload.methodName: google.iam.admin.v1.ListServiceAccounts protoPayload.authenticationInfo.principalEmail: svc-deploy@htl-prod.iam.gserviceaccount.com protoPayload.requestMetadata.callerIp: 203.0.113.44 protoPayload.requestMetadata.callerSuppliedUserAgent: google-cloud-sdk gcloud/470.0.0 linux/6.1.0 protoPayload.status.code: 7 protoPayload.status.message: PERMISSION_DENIED logName: projects/htl-prod/logs/cloudaudit.googleapis.com%2Factivity A deployment service account calling from an external address with the gcloud CLI rather than its usual CI user agent. Status 7 shows the call was denied, but the attempt itself reveals the enumeration. Impersonation Chain in Action timestamp: 2025-07-14T09:47:33.221Z protoPayload.methodName: google.iam.credentials.v1.GenerateAccessToken protoPayload.authenticationInfo.principalEmail: svc-admin@htl-prod.iam.gserviceaccount.com protoPayload.authenticationInfo.serviceAccountDelegationInfo: [ { firstPartyPrincipal: { principalEmail: "svc-deploy@htl-prod.iam.gserviceaccount.com" } } ] protoPayload.resourceName: projects/-/serviceAccounts/svc-admin@htl-prod.iam.gserviceaccount.com protoPayload.requestMetadata.callerIp: 203.0.113.44 principalEmail shows svc-admin, but the delegation info reveals svc-deploy initiated it. Every subsequent action will appear to come from svc-admin unless you follow this chain. Privilege Escalation via SetIamPolicy timestamp: 2025-07-14T09:52:10.774Z protoPayload.methodName: SetIamPolicy protoPayload.authenticationInfo.principalEmail: svc-admin@htl-prod.iam.gserviceaccount.com protoPayload.resourceName: projects/htl-prod protoPayload.serviceData.policyDelta.bindingDeltas: [ { action: "ADD", role: "roles/owner", member: "serviceAccount:svc-deploy@htl-prod.iam.gserviceaccount.com" } ] protoPayload.authorizationInfo: [ { permission: "resourcemanager.projects.setIamPolicy", granted: true } ] The impersonated admin account grants roles/owner back to the originally compromised account. The bindingDeltas array is what makes the exact change visible. Persistence: Long-Lived Service Account Key timestamp: 2025-07-14T09:55:41.118Z protoPayload.methodName: google.iam.admin.v1.CreateServiceAccountKey protoPayload.authenticationInfo.principalEmail: svc-deploy@htl-prod.iam.gserviceaccount.com protoPayload.resourceName: projects/htl-prod/serviceAccounts/svc-admin@htl-prod.iam.gserviceaccount.com protoPayload.response.name: projects/htl-prod/serviceAccounts/svc-admin@.../keys/8f2a1c04e91b7d2 protoPayload.response.validAfterTime: 2025-07-14T09:55:41Z protoPayload.response.validBeforeTime: 9999-12-31T23:59:59Z The validBeforeTime of year 9999 is the point: this credential never expires, works from any address, and is unaffected by session or password policy. Bucket Exposed to the Internet timestamp: 2025-07-14T10:02:44.229Z protoPayload.methodName: storage.setIamPermissions protoPayload.authenticationInfo.principalEmail: svc-deploy@htl-prod.iam.gserviceaccount.com protoPayload.resourceName: projects/_/buckets/htl-customer-data protoPayload.serviceData.policyDelta.bindingDeltas: [ { action: "ADD", role: "roles/storage.objectViewer", member: "allUsers" } ] allUsers grants read access to every anonymous caller on the internet. One API call, and the bucket is public. Data Exfiltration via BigQuery Extract timestamp: 2025-07-14T10:11:03.441Z protoPayload.methodName: jobservice.jobcompleted protoPayload.authenticationInfo.principalEmail: svc-admin@htl-prod.iam.gserviceaccount.com protoPayload.serviceData.jobCompletedEvent.job.jobConfiguration.extract: { sourceTable: { datasetId: "customers", tableId: "pii_master" }, destinationUris: [ "gs://exfil-staging-9f2a/customers-*.csv" ], destinationFormat: "CSV" } protoPayload.serviceData.jobCompletedEvent.job.jobStatistics.totalProcessedBytes: 41882219043 A 41 GB extract of a table named pii_master written to a bucket outside the organisation. This appears only in Data Access logs, so an environment without them sees nothing at all. Code Execution via Instance Metadata timestamp: 2025-07-14T10:14:22.008Z protoPayload.methodName: v1.compute.instances.setMetadata protoPayload.authenticationInfo.principalEmail: svc-deploy@htl-prod.iam.gserviceaccount.com protoPayload.resourceName: projects/htl-prod/zones/me-central1-a/instances/prod-app-04 protoPayload.request.metadata.items: [ { key: "ssh-keys", value: "attacker:ssh-rsa AAAAB3NzaC1yc2EAAA... attacker@kali" } ] An SSH key injected through the metadata service. The guest operating system logs will show a successful key-based login with no preceding failed attempts, because the key was placed by the control plane. Logging Evasion: Sink Deleted timestamp: 2025-07-14T10:18:12.774Z protoPayload.methodName: google.logging.v2.ConfigServiceV2.DeleteSink protoPayload.authenticationInfo.principalEmail: svc-deploy@htl-prod.iam.gserviceaccount.com protoPayload.resourceName: projects/htl-prod/sinks/htl-org-security-sink protoPayload.requestMetadata.callerIp: 203.0.113.44 protoPayload.authorizationInfo: [ { permission: "logging.sinks.delete", granted: true } ] The sink is gone, so nothing further reaches the SIEM. Admin Activity logs keep accumulating in the _Required bucket, which is why this record still exists and why that bucket matters. Policy Denied: Attacker Blocked by VPC Service Controls timestamp: 2025-07-14T10:22:04.118Z protoPayload.methodName: storage.objects.get protoPayload.authenticationInfo.principalEmail: svc-admin@htl-prod.iam.gserviceaccount.com protoPayload.requestMetadata.callerIp: 203.0.113.44 protoPayload.status.code: 7 protoPayload.status.details: [ { violations: [ { type: "VPC_SERVICE_CONTROLS", description: "Request is prohibited by organization's policy" } ] } ] logName: projects/htl-prod/logs/cloudaudit.googleapis.com%2Fpolicy The perimeter held. Policy Denied logs are billed and therefore sometimes filtered out, yet they are among the clearest evidence of an attacker probing a boundary and being stopped. Back

Everything in Kubernetes passes through the API server, which makes the audit log the equivalent of CloudTrail for a cluster. Creating a pod, reading a secret, opening a shell inside a running container, and modifying a role binding are all API requests, and all of them can be recorded with the requesting identity, the source address, the object affected, and the authorisation decision. Without the audit log, a cluster is genuinely opaque: container logs show what applications printed, but nothing shows who instructed the cluster to do what. The critical fact is that audit logging is off by default in a self-managed cluster. It requires an audit policy file and API server flags, and if either is missing the cluster runs perfectly while recording nothing. Managed platforms differ: EKS control plane logging must be explicitly enabled per log type, AKS requires a diagnostic setting, and GKE enables Admin Activity audit logs automatically while leaving Data Access logging off. In every case the default state leaves at least one significant gap. The audit policy itself is where most of the value is decided. Each rule assigns a level of None , Metadata , Request , or RequestResponse , controlling how much of the request and response body is captured. Recording RequestResponse for everything produces unusable volume and writes secret contents into the log. Recording only Metadata for everything means you know a secret was read but not which one. A workable policy captures Metadata broadly, escalates to Request for security-relevant resources, and drops the high-volume noise from system components entirely.

Cluster visibility spans the control plane, the nodes, and the workloads themselves: Log Type Description API Server Audit Log The authoritative record of every request to the cluster, including the identity, verb, resource, namespace, source address, user agent, and authorisation decision. Disabled by default in self-managed clusters. The single most important cluster log. Container and Pod Logs Standard output and error from every container, collected by the kubelet. Application-level visibility rather than cluster-level, but essential for understanding what a compromised workload actually did. Kubelet Log The node agent, recording pod lifecycle, volume mounts, image pulls, and requests received on the kubelet API. Where node-level compromise and unauthorised kubelet access appear. Admission Controller Decisions Output from validating and mutating webhooks such as OPA Gatekeeper or Kyverno. Records policy violations that were blocked, which is a direct feed of attempted misconfiguration and attack. etcd Log The cluster datastore. Direct etcd access bypasses the API server and all of its auditing entirely, so authentication events here are high value and low volume. Controller Manager and Scheduler Control plane components recording reconciliation and pod placement decisions. Mostly operational, but useful when investigating why a workload landed on a particular node. Container Runtime Log containerd or CRI-O output covering image pulls, container creation, and runtime errors. Shows images pulled from unexpected registries. Runtime Security Events Syscall-level detections from Falco, Tetragon, or a commercial sensor. The only source that sees what happens inside a container after it starts, which the audit log never does. Pro Tip: The audit log records that a shell was opened into a pod through pods/exec , but never what was typed. Commands executed inside the container are visible only to a runtime sensor. Pairing audit logging with a runtime tool closes the largest single gap in container visibility.

Self-managed clusters write to the filesystem, while managed platforms deliver to the cloud provider's logging service. Source Location Audit Log (self-managed) Path set by --audit-log-path, commonly /var/log/kubernetes/audit/audit.log Audit Policy File /etc/kubernetes/audit-policy.yaml, referenced by --audit-policy-file API Server Manifest /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml on control plane nodes Container Logs /var/log/containers/ (symlinks) and /var/log/pods/<namespace>_<pod>_<uid>/ Kubelet Log journalctl -u kubelet on the node Amazon EKS CloudWatch log group /aws/eks/<cluster>/cluster, one stream per component Google GKE Cloud Logging, resource type k8s_cluster with logName cloudaudit.googleapis.com%2Factivity Azure AKS Log Analytics table AzureDiagnostics with Category kube-audit or kube-audit-admin etcd Data and Logs /var/lib/etcd/ with logs in the etcd pod or journal Pro Tip: On AKS, the kube-audit-admin category excludes read-only get and list requests and is typically a fraction of the volume of full kube-audit . It is the pragmatic default when full audit volume is unaffordable, though it loses visibility into reconnaissance.

A self-managed cluster needs both a policy file and API server flags. Managed platforms need their log types enabling explicitly. Step 1: Write a Practical Audit Policy apiVersion: audit.k8s.io/v1 kind: Policy omitStages: ["RequestReceived"] rules: # Never log the high volume, low value noise - level: None users: ["system:kube-proxy","system:apiserver"] verbs: ["watch","list"] - level: None nonResourceURLs: ["/healthz*","/readyz*","/livez*","/version","/metrics"] # Full request body for the resources that matter - level: Request resources: - group: "" # core resources: ["pods/exec","pods/attach","pods/portforward","pods/ephemeralcontainers"] - group: "rbac.authorization.k8s.io" resources: ["roles","rolebindings","clusterroles","clusterrolebindings"] # Metadata only for secrets: never write their contents to the log - level: Metadata resources: - group: "" resources: ["secrets","configmaps","serviceaccounts"] # Everything else at metadata level - level: Metadata omitStages: ["RequestReceived"] Order matters: the first matching rule wins. Secrets are deliberately kept at Metadata level, because Request or RequestResponse would write the secret values themselves into the audit log in cleartext. Step 2: Enable Auditing on the API Server # /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml spec: containers: - command: - kube-apiserver - --audit-policy-file=/etc/kubernetes/audit-policy.yaml - --audit-log-path=/var/log/kubernetes/audit/audit.log - --audit-log-maxage=30 - --audit-log-maxbackup=10 - --audit-log-maxsize=500 - --audit-log-format=json volumeMounts: - name: audit-policy mountPath: /etc/kubernetes/audit-policy.yaml readOnly: true - name: audit-log mountPath: /var/log/kubernetes/audit/ Both the policy file and the log directory must be mounted into the static pod. Forgetting the volume mounts is the most common reason auditing appears configured but produces nothing. Step 3: Enable Managed Platform Audit Logs # Amazon EKS aws eks update-cluster-config --name htl-prod \ --logging '{"clusterLogging":[{"types":["api","audit","authenticator","controllerManager","scheduler"],"enabled":true}]}' # Azure AKS az monitor diagnostic-settings create --name aks-audit \ --resource $(az aks show -g rg-prod -n htl-prod --query id -o tsv) \ --workspace <workspace-id> \ --logs '[{"category":"kube-audit","enabled":true}, {"category":"kube-audit-admin","enabled":true}, {"category":"kube-apiserver","enabled":true}, {"category":"guard","enabled":true}]' # Google GKE: Admin Activity is automatic, Data Access must be enabled gcloud container clusters update htl-prod --region me-central1 \ --logging=SYSTEM,WORKLOAD,API_SERVER,CONTROLLER_MANAGER,SCHEDULER EKS logging is off entirely by default, and the authenticator stream is the one that records IAM identity mapping. Enabling only api and audit leaves that gap open. Step 4: Deploy a Runtime Security Sensor helm repo add falcosecurity https://falcosecurity.github.io/charts helm install falco falcosecurity/falco --namespace falco --create-namespace \ --set driver.kind=modern_ebpf \ --set falcosidekick.enabled=true \ --set "falco.json_output=true" # Example rule: shell spawned inside a container # - rule: Terminal shell in container # condition: spawned_process and container and shell_procs and proc.tty != 0 # output: Shell in container (user=%user.name container=%container.name) # priority: WARNING The audit log records that pods/exec occurred but never the commands typed. A runtime sensor is the only source that observes activity inside a running container. Step 5: Enforce Policy at Admission # Pod Security Admission, the built-in baseline kubectl label namespace production \ pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted \ pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce-version=latest \ pod-security.kubernetes.io/audit=restricted \ pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn=restricted # Verify what would be blocked before enforcing kubectl label namespace legacy pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn=restricted --overwrite The audit and warn labels report violations without blocking, which lets you measure impact before enforcement. Admission denials are themselves a valuable detection feed. Step 6: Ship Audit Logs Off the Cluster # Fluent Bit input for the audit log on control plane nodes [INPUT] Name tail Path /var/log/kubernetes/audit/audit.log Parser json Tag k8s.audit Refresh_Interval 5 Mem_Buf_Limit 50MB Skip_Long_Lines On [OUTPUT] Name forward Match k8s.audit Host siem-collector.corp.local Port 24224 tls On Audit logs live on the control plane nodes, which an attacker with cluster-admin can reach. Shipping them off cluster is what preserves the evidence of the compromise. Security Note: Never set audit level to Request or RequestResponse for the secrets resource. Doing so writes every secret value into the audit log in cleartext, turning your security log into the highest value credential store in the environment.

Container attacks follow a consistent path: get into a pod, escape to the node, then escalate across the cluster. Exec into Pod Opening an interactive shell in a running container via pods/exec. Legitimate for debugging but the primary hands-on-keyboard technique. Commands typed are not recorded by the audit log. Detect Critical Privileged Pod Escape Creating a pod with privileged true, hostPID, hostNetwork, or a hostPath mount of the root filesystem. Grants root on the node itself, escaping the container boundary entirely. Detect Critical RBAC Escalation Binding a service account to cluster-admin, or exploiting the escalate and bind verbs. One ClusterRoleBinding is full control of every namespace and workload. Detect Critical Secret Harvesting Listing or reading secrets across namespaces. Kubernetes secrets are base64 encoded, not encrypted, unless encryption at rest is configured, so a list request returns usable credentials. Detect Critical Service Account Token Abuse Using a token mounted into a compromised pod to call the API. Signature: requests from a service account identity originating from a pod address rather than an administrator workstation. Detect High Risk Cryptomining Workloads Deploying pods pulling images from public registries with high resource requests. The most common outcome of an exposed dashboard or unauthenticated API server. Detect High Risk Security Note: The system:anonymous user and the system:unauthenticated group appearing in audit logs with successful authorisation decisions means the cluster accepts unauthenticated API requests. This is how exposed clusters are mass-compromised, and it should be treated as an active incident.

Every Kubernetes audit event is a JSON object with a stable schema. These are the fields detections are built on. Field Description Category Example Value requestReceivedTimestamp Time the API server received the request Timestamp 2025-07-14T09:41:22.481Z verb Action requested Action create user.username Authenticated identity Identity system:serviceaccount:default:build-sa user.groups Groups the identity belongs to Identity ["system:serviceaccounts","system:authenticated"] impersonatedUser Identity impersonated, when the impersonate verb is used Identity system:admin sourceIPs Client addresses including proxies Source ["10.244.3.17"] userAgent Client tool and version Source kubectl/v1.29.3 (linux/amd64) objectRef.resource Resource type targeted Target secrets objectRef.subresource Subresource such as exec or portforward Target exec objectRef.namespace Namespace of the target object Target kube-system objectRef.name Name of the specific object Target db-credentials responseStatus.code HTTP status returned Result 201 annotations.authorization.k8s.io/decision allow or forbid, with the reason alongside Authorization allow stage Point in request handling Metadata ResponseComplete Pro Tip: The authorization.k8s.io/reason annotation names the exact RBAC binding that permitted a request. When investigating how an identity was able to act, this field answers the question immediately rather than requiring you to reconstruct the role graph.

A short list of verb and resource combinations covers most Kubernetes attack activity. Verb and Resource Stage Why It Matters create pods/exec Execution Interactive shell in a running container. The commands typed are not audited, only the fact that a session opened create pods (privileged) Escape A pod with privileged, hostPID, or a hostPath root mount gives root on the node and escapes the container boundary create clusterrolebindings Escalation Binding any identity to cluster-admin grants total control of the cluster in a single object get / list secrets Credential Access Secrets are base64 encoded, not encrypted by default. A list across namespaces returns immediately usable credentials create pods/portforward Lateral Movement Tunnels traffic from a workstation directly to a pod, bypassing network policy and ingress controls entirely impersonate users or groups Escalation Acting as another identity. Legitimate for some controllers, but impersonating system:admin is escalation create serviceaccounts/token Persistence Minting a token for a privileged service account produces a credential that survives pod deletion patch daemonsets Persistence A DaemonSet runs on every node, including nodes added later. Ideal placement for a persistent implant delete events Evasion Removing Kubernetes events destroys the cluster's own activity record, though not the audit log create validatingwebhookconfigurations Evasion A malicious webhook can intercept every API request, and a failurePolicy of Ignore lets an attacker silently drop admission controls any verb as system:anonymous Initial Access Unauthenticated API access. If this appears with an allow decision, the cluster is open to the world

These jq and SIEM queries cover the container attack chain from access through escalation to persistence. Exec into Pods bash> jq -r 'select(.objectRef.subresource=="exec") | [.requestReceivedTimestamp, .user.username, .objectRef.namespace, .objectRef.name, .sourceIPs[0]] | @tsv' audit.log Every interactive session opened into a container. In a mature GitOps environment this should be rare enough to review individually. Privileged Pod Creation bash> jq -r 'select(.verb=="create" and .objectRef.resource=="pods") | select(.requestObject.spec.containers[]?.securityContext.privileged==true or .requestObject.spec.hostPID==true or .requestObject.spec.hostNetwork==true) | [.requestReceivedTimestamp, .user.username, .objectRef.namespace] | @tsv' audit.log Requires Request level auditing on pods. A privileged pod is root on the node, so this is container escape by design. Cluster Admin Binding bash> jq -r 'select(.objectRef.resource=="clusterrolebindings" and (.verb=="create" or .verb=="update")) | [.requestReceivedTimestamp, .user.username, .objectRef.name, (.requestObject.roleRef.name // "")] | @tsv' audit.log | grep -i "cluster-admin" One ClusterRoleBinding to cluster-admin is complete cluster takeover. Every occurrence needs a matching change record. Secret Enumeration SIEM> source="k8s:audit" objectRef.resource="secrets" verb IN ("get","list") | stats count, dc(objectRef.namespace) as namespaces by user.username, sourceIPs{} | where count > 20 OR namespaces > 3 An identity reading secrets across multiple namespaces is harvesting credentials. Application service accounts should touch only their own namespace. Anonymous API Access bash> jq -r 'select(.user.username=="system:anonymous" or (.user.groups[]? == "system:unauthenticated")) | [.requestReceivedTimestamp, .verb, .requestURI, .responseStatus.code, .sourceIPs[0]] | @tsv' audit.log Any result with a 2xx status means the cluster served an unauthenticated request. This is how exposed clusters are mass-compromised. Service Account Token Abuse SIEM> source="k8s:audit" user.username="system:serviceaccount:*" | stats dc(objectRef.resource) as resources, values(verb), count by user.username, sourceIPs{} | where resources > 5 A service account touching many resource types is behaving like an administrator, not an application. Usually means its token was stolen from a pod. Authorisation Failures bash> jq -r 'select(.annotations["authorization.k8s.io/decision"]=="forbid") | [.user.username, .verb, .objectRef.resource] | @tsv' audit.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -25 Repeated forbidden requests from one identity is permission enumeration, an attacker mapping what a compromised token can reach. Port Forwarding bash> jq -r 'select(.objectRef.subresource=="portforward") | [.requestReceivedTimestamp, .user.username, .objectRef.namespace, .objectRef.name] | @tsv' audit.log Port forwarding tunnels directly to a pod, bypassing network policy, ingress rules, and service mesh controls entirely. Images from Untrusted Registries bash> kubectl get pods -A -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.namespace}{"\t"}{.spec.containers[*].image}{"\n"}{end}' | grep -vE "registry.corp.local|gcr.io/htl-prod" Workloads pulling from Docker Hub or unknown registries. Cryptomining deployments are almost always public images. Verify Auditing Is Active bash> kubectl -n kube-system get pod -l component=kube-apiserver -o yaml | grep -E "audit-policy-file|audit-log-path|audit-log-maxage" If these flags are absent, the cluster is recording nothing at all while running perfectly. Check this first on any cluster you inherit.

Apply these practices so a cluster is not opaque at the moment you most need to see into it: 01 Turn Auditing On Before You Need It Self-managed clusters record nothing by default and give no warning. A cluster without an audit policy file cannot answer a single question about who did what. 02 Never Log Secret Contents Keep the secrets resource at Metadata level. Request or RequestResponse writes secret values into the audit log, turning it into the richest credential store you own. 03 Drop the Noise in the Policy, Not the SIEM Health probes, metrics scrapes, and system component watches dominate volume and carry no signal. Filtering them at the policy avoids paying to ingest them at all. 04 Pair Audit Logs with a Runtime Sensor The audit log stops at the container boundary. It records that a shell was opened but never what was typed, and only a runtime tool closes that gap. 05 Ship Logs Off the Control Plane Audit logs live on control plane nodes that a cluster-admin can reach. Forwarding them elsewhere is what preserves evidence of the compromise that granted that access. 06 Enable Every Managed Log Type EKS logging is entirely off by default, and enabling only api and audit misses the authenticator stream that maps IAM identities to cluster users. 07 Treat Admission Denials as Detections Pod Security Admission and policy engines log every blocked request. That is a direct feed of attempted misconfiguration and attack, already filtered for you. 08 Baseline Service Account Behaviour Application service accounts should touch a small, predictable set of resources in one namespace. Deviation from that is the clearest sign a pod token has been stolen.

A cluster compromise from stolen service account token to node-level persistence. Kubernetes secrets are base64 encoded, so the response contained usable credentials. One object, and it now controls every namespace and workload in the cluster. The nsenter command enters the host's namespaces directly, giving a root shell on the node itself.
